QUESTIONS.q: In the 'Types of Fragmentation Hemolysis' table at the bottom of p102, what are the Pathogenesis and Platelet count for Row 1 ('MAHA/march hemolysis')?
QUESTIONS.exp: Row 1 of Fragmentation Hemolysis table on p102: Type: MAHA/march hemolysis → Pathogenesis: HUS → Platelet: Low. (Book p102)

QUESTIONS.sec: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura & Fragmentation Types
QUESTIONS.q: In the 'Types of Fragmentation Hemolysis' table on p102, what are the Pathogenesis and Platelet count for Row 2 ('Cardiac')?
opts: Pathogenesis: HUS microangiopathic hemolysis; Platelet: Low
Pathogenesis: Cavernous hemangioma + 2° DIC; Platelet: High
Pathogenesis: Prosthetic valves related macroangiopathic hemolysis; Platelet: Normal
Pathogenesis: Infective endocarditis autoimmune lysis; Platelet: Low
QUESTIONS.exp: Row 2 of Fragmentation Hemolysis table on p102: Type: Cardiac → Pathogenesis: Prosthetic valves related macroangiopathic hemolysis → Platelet: Normal. (Book p102)

QUESTIONS.sec: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura & Fragmentation Types
QUESTIONS.q: In the 'Types of Fragmentation Hemolysis' table on p102, what are the Pathogenesis and Platelet count for Row 3 ('Consumption')?
opts: Pathogenesis: Prosthetic valves related macroangiopathic hemolysis; Platelet: Normal
Pathogenesis: Kasabach–Merritt syndrome (cavernous hemangioma + 2° DIC); Platelet: Low
Pathogenesis: Evans syndrome (warm AIHA + CVID); Platelet: Normal
Pathogenesis: Heyde syndrome (aortic stenosis + acquired vWD); Platelet: High
QUESTIONS.exp: Row 3 of Fragmentation Hemolysis table on p102: Type: Consumption → Pathogenesis: Kasabach Merritt syndrome : Cavernous hemangioma + 2° DIC → Platelet: Low. (Book p102)

QUESTIONS.sec: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura & Fragmentation Types
QUESTIONS.q: Match each Type of Fragmentation Hemolysis in the bottom table on p102 to its Pathogenesis and Platelet count — 1) MAHA / march hemolysis 2) Cardiac 3) Consumption … A) Prosthetic valves related macroangiopathic hemolysis; Platelet: Normal B) Kasabach–Merritt syndrome (cavernous hemangioma + 2° DIC); Platelet: Low C) HUS; Platelet: Low
QUESTIONS.exp: Table at bottom of p102: MAHA/march hemolysis → Pathogenesis: HUS, Platelet: Low; Cardiac → Pathogenesis: Prosthetic valves related macroangiopathic hemolysis, Platelet: Normal; Consumption → Pathogenesis: Kasabach Merritt syndrome (Cavernous hemangioma + 2° DIC), Platelet: Low. (Book p102)

QUESTIONS.sec: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura & Fragmentation Types
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE — in the 'Types of Fragmentation Hemolysis' table on p102, Cardiac (prosthetic valve-related macroangiopathic) hemolysis has a NORMAL platelet count, whereas MAHA/march hemolysis (HUS) and Consumption (Kasabach–Merritt syndrome) have a LOW platelet count.
opts: False — Kasabach–Merritt syndrome is characterized by extreme thrombocytosis
True — platelet count is Normal in all three types of fragmentation hemolysis
True — platelet count is Normal in cardiac prosthetic-valve hemolysis and Low in HUS and Kasabach–Merritt syndrome
False — cardiac prosthetic-valve hemolysis causes severe thrombocytopenia while HUS has normal platelets
QUESTIONS.exp: The p102 table explicitly contrasts Platelet: Low in MAHA/march hemolysis (HUS) and Consumption (Kasabach–Merritt syndrome: cavernous hemangioma + 2° DIC) with Platelet: Normal in Cardiac (prosthetic valves related macroangiopathic hemolysis). (Book p102)

QUESTIONS.sec: Inherited Hemolytic Anemias & Hereditary Spherocytosis: Genetics and RBC Membrane Structure
QUESTIONS.q: Match the category of inherited hemolytic anemia with its prototype disorder(s) — 1) Hemoglobinopathies 2) Membrane cytoskeleton disorders 3) Other RBC enzymopathies 4) Most common RBC enzymopathy … A) Hereditary spherocytosis B) G6PD deficiency C) Sickle cell anemia & thalassemia D) Pyruvate kinase & 5'-nucleotidase deficiency
QUESTIONS.exp: Inherited hemolytic anemias are classified into hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell anemia, thalassemia), membrane cytoskeleton disorders (hereditary spherocytosis), and enzymopathies (G6PD deficiency [most common], pyruvate kinase deficiency, and 5'-nucleotidase deficiency). (Book p103)

QUESTIONS.sec: Inherited Hemolytic Anemias & Hereditary Spherocytosis: Genetics and RBC Membrane Structure
QUESTIONS.q: Which is the most common inherited red blood cell enzymopathy causing hemolytic anemia?
QUESTIONS.exp: Under inherited hemolytic anemias, enzymopathies include G6PD deficiency (most common, m/c), pyruvate kinase deficiency, and 5'-nucleotidase deficiency. (Book p103)

QUESTIONS.sec: Inherited Hemolytic Anemias & Hereditary Spherocytosis: Genetics and RBC Membrane Structure
QUESTIONS.q: Which inherited red blood cell enzymopathy is specifically noted for producing prominent basophilic stippling on the peripheral blood smear?
QUESTIONS.exp: Basophilic stippling is characteristically seen in 5'-nucleotidase deficiency. (Book p103)

QUESTIONS.sec: Inherited Hemolytic Anemias & Hereditary Spherocytosis: Genetics and RBC Membrane Structure
QUESTIONS.q: All of the following are listed as biochemical markers of cholestasis on page 103 EXCEPT:
QUESTIONS.exp: The three listed markers of cholestasis are 5'-nucleotidase (printed as 5' nucleotidase deficiency), alkaline phosphatase, and gamma-glutamyl transferase. (Book p103)

QUESTIONS.sec: Inherited Hemolytic Anemias & Hereditary Spherocytosis: Genetics and RBC Membrane Structure
QUESTIONS.q: Hereditary spherocytosis is characterized by chronic compensated ______ hemolysis.
QUESTIONS.exp: Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) causes chronic compensated extravascular hemolysis. (Book p103)

QUESTIONS.sec: Inherited Hemolytic Anemias & Hereditary Spherocytosis: Genetics and RBC Membrane Structure
QUESTIONS.q: What is the most common mode of inheritance and underlying membrane protein defect in hereditary spherocytosis?
opts: Autosomal dominant inheritance; Ankyrin defect (more common than Band 3)
X-linked recessive inheritance; Glycophorin A defect
Autosomal recessive inheritance; β-spectrin defect (more common than Ankyrin)
Autosomal dominant inheritance; Band 4.1 defect (more common than Ankyrin)
QUESTIONS.exp: Hereditary spherocytosis is most commonly autosomal dominant, with ankyrin (ANK-1 gene) defects being more common than Band 3 defects (Ankyrin > Band 3). (Book p103)

QUESTIONS.sec: Inherited Hemolytic Anemias & Hereditary Spherocytosis: Genetics and RBC Membrane Structure
QUESTIONS.q: Autosomal recessive hereditary spherocytosis is classically caused by a defect in which RBC cytoskeleton protein?
QUESTIONS.exp: Autosomal recessive hereditary spherocytosis is associated with β-spectrin deficiency. (Book p103)

QUESTIONS.sec: Inherited Hemolytic Anemias & Hereditary Spherocytosis: Genetics and RBC Membrane Structure
QUESTIONS.q: What is the fundamental structural defect in the RBC membrane in hereditary spherocytosis?
opts: Inability to generate NADPH via the hexose monophosphate shunt
Defective pattern of the lipid bilayer between vertical and tangential associations
Polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin S chains into rigid tactoids
Failure of GPI-anchor synthesis due to somatic PIGA mutation
QUESTIONS.exp: The primary defect in hereditary spherocytosis is a defective pattern of the lipid bilayer between vertical and tangential associations. (Book p103)

QUESTIONS.sec: Inherited Hemolytic Anemias & Hereditary Spherocytosis: Genetics and RBC Membrane Structure
QUESTIONS.q: In the RBC membrane structure diagram, defects in Band 3 (an abundant integral membrane protein associated with HS) also cause which two red cell membrane disorders and confer protection against which parasite?
opts: Hereditary elliptocytosis and pyropoikilocytosis; protective against Babesia microti
Southeast Asian xerocytosis and echinocytosis; protective against Leishmania donovani
Hereditary ovalocytosis and stomatocytosis; protective against Plasmodium falciparum
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and acanthocytosis; protective against Plasmodium vivax
QUESTIONS.exp: Band 3 is abundant in the RBC membrane, associated with hereditary spherocytosis, hereditary ovalocytosis, and stomatocytosis, and is protective against Plasmodium falciparum. (Book p103)

QUESTIONS.sec: Inherited Hemolytic Anemias & Hereditary Spherocytosis: Genetics and RBC Membrane Structure
QUESTIONS.q: According to the RBC membrane structure diagram, what is the primary physiological role of the spectrin dimer and which two clinical disorders result from its defect?
opts: Catalyzes glutathione reduction in the cytosol; causes favism and neonatal kernicterus
Responsible for biconcavity of RBC (abundant in cytoskeleton); causes severe autosomal recessive HS in children/neonates and hereditary elliptocytosis
Serves as the extracellular sialoglycoprotein receptor; causes paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria
Acts as the primary anion channel in the lipid bilayer; causes hereditary ovalocytosis and stomatocytosis
QUESTIONS.exp: Spectrin dimer is abundant in the cytoskeleton and responsible for the biconcavity of the RBC; its defects cause severe autosomal recessive HS in children and neonates as well as hereditary elliptocytosis. (Book p103)

QUESTIONS.sec: Inherited Hemolytic Anemias & Hereditary Spherocytosis: Genetics and RBC Membrane Structure
QUESTIONS.q: Which gene is mutated in the most common autosomal dominant form of hereditary spherocytosis?
opts: PIGA gene (encoding phosphatidylinositol glycan class A)
QUESTIONS.exp: Mutation in the ANK-1 gene (autosomal dominant), which encodes ankyrin, is the most common cause of hereditary spherocytosis (m/c HS). (Book p103)

QUESTIONS.sec: Inherited Hemolytic Anemias & Hereditary Spherocytosis: Genetics and RBC Membrane Structure
QUESTIONS.q: In the RBC membrane cytoskeleton diagram on page 103, which accessory proteins are depicted at the junctional complexes on the cytoplasmic face of the lipid bilayer?
opts: Tropomyosin and Actin on one complex, and Band 4.1, Adducin, and Band 4.9 on the other
CD55 (DAF) and CD59 (MIRL) anchored via glycolipid tails
QUESTIONS.exp: The RBC cytoskeleton diagram illustrates Ankyrin linking Band 3 to the spectrin dimer, with Tropomyosin and Actin at one junctional complex and Band 4.1, Adducin, and Band 4.9 at the other. (Book p103)

QUESTIONS.sec: Inherited Hemolytic Anemias & Hereditary Spherocytosis: Genetics and RBC Membrane Structure
QUESTIONS.q: Plasmodium falciparum binds with ______ on the red blood cell surface, which is noted as the most abundant protein on the RBC membrane.
QUESTIONS.exp: Plasmodium falciparum binds with glycophorin, noted at the bottom of page 103 as the most abundant protein on the RBC membrane. (Book p103)

QUESTIONS.sec: Inherited Hemolytic Anemias & Hereditary Spherocytosis: Genetics and RBC Membrane Structure
QUESTIONS.q: Match the RBC membrane protein with its key attribute from the Structure of RBC diagram — 1) Band 3 2) Ankyrin 3) Spectrin dimer 4) Glycophorin … A) Cytoskeletal protein responsible for RBC biconcavity & elliptocytosis B) Integral protein associated with ovalocytosis & stomatocytosis C) Surface receptor bound by Plasmodium falciparum D) ANK-1 gene (AD) — most common cause of HS
QUESTIONS.exp: Band 3 is associated with HS, ovalocytosis, and stomatocytosis; Ankyrin (ANK-1 gene, AD) is the most common defect in HS; Spectrin dimer maintains biconcavity and is defective in severe AR HS and hereditary elliptocytosis; Glycophorin is bound by P. falciparum. (Book p103)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis: Pathogenesis, Clinical Features & Investigations
QUESTIONS.q: In the pathogenesis of hereditary spherocytosis, what immediate membrane event converts a biconcave red blood cell with a lipid bilayer defect into a sphere?
opts: Formation and detachment of microvesicles from the RBC membrane
Cross-linking of membrane sulfhydryl groups by precipitated Heinz bodies
Osmotic influx of sodium and water through leaky cation channels
Fc-receptor-mediated partial phagocytosis by hepatic Kupffer cells
QUESTIONS.exp: A defect in the lipid bilayer leads to microvesicle formation on the RBC membrane followed by detachment of the microvesicle from the membrane, causing the RBC to become spherical. (Book p104)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis: Pathogenesis, Clinical Features & Investigations
QUESTIONS.q: When a red blood cell loses membrane microvesicles and becomes spherical, a sphere has the ______ surface area to volume ratio.
QUESTIONS.exp: A sphere has the least surface area : volume ratio, which prevents degradation in the general circulation but prevents elongation in narrow splenic capillaries. (Book p104)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis: Pathogenesis, Clinical Features & Investigations
QUESTIONS.q: Why do spherocytes fail to traverse the splenic cords and undergo extravascular destruction by splenic macrophages?
opts: Normal RBC diameter is 3–4 μm whereas splenic capillaries measure 7–8 μm
Normal RBC diameter is 12–15 μm whereas splenic capillaries measure 8–10 μm
Spherocytes polymerize at splenic pH < 6.8 and occlude 15–20 μm venules
Normal RBC diameter is 7–8 μm whereas splenic capillaries measure only 3–4 μm, and spherical RBCs fail to elongate
QUESTIONS.exp: Because RBC diameter is 7–8 μm while splenic capillaries measure 3–4 μm, spherical RBCs fail to elongate and are destroyed by splenic macrophages (extravascular hemolysis). (Book p104)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis: Pathogenesis, Clinical Features & Investigations
QUESTIONS.q: All of the following are classic clinical features of hereditary spherocytosis listed on page 104 EXCEPT:
opts: Recurrent hemoglobinuria and pancytopenia with hepatic vein thrombosis
Aplastic crisis due to parvovirus B19
QUESTIONS.exp: Clinical features of hereditary spherocytosis are anemia, moderate splenomegaly, aplastic crisis due to parvovirus B19, gallstones, and intermittent jaundice. (Book p104)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis: Pathogenesis, Clinical Features & Investigations
QUESTIONS.q: Which viral infection classically precipitates an acute aplastic crisis in patients with hereditary spherocytosis?
QUESTIONS.exp: Aplastic crisis in hereditary spherocytosis is caused by Parvovirus B19. (Book p104)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis: Pathogenesis, Clinical Features & Investigations
QUESTIONS.q: A 19-year-old patient presents with intermittent jaundice, moderate splenomegaly, and pigment gallstones on ultrasound. Peripheral blood smear demonstrates round red blood cells lacking central pallor (microspherocytes). What red blood cell index pattern is expected?
opts: Decreased MCV (↓) and markedly decreased MCHC (↓↓)
Decreased MCV (↓) and markedly increased MCHC (↑↑)
QUESTIONS.exp: In hereditary spherocytosis, peripheral smear shows microspherocytes (round with no pallor) and red cell indices characteristically show ↓ MCV and ↑↑ MCHC. (Book p104)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis: Pathogenesis, Clinical Features & Investigations
QUESTIONS.q: In the diagnostic workup of hereditary spherocytosis, which investigation is listed as the MOST PREFERRED test and which is the GOLD STANDARD?
opts: Osmotic fragility test is most preferred; glycerol lysis (pink) test is the gold standard
Eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) test is most preferred; osmotic fragility is the gold standard
Direct Coombs test is most preferred; FLAER flow cytometry is the gold standard
Ektacytometry is most preferred; SDS-PAGE electrophoresis is the gold standard
QUESTIONS.exp: Under HS investigations on page 104: Ektacytometry is most preferred, and SDS-PAGE electrophoresis is the gold standard. (Book p104)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis: Pathogenesis, Clinical Features & Investigations
QUESTIONS.q: Match the diagnostic investigation in hereditary spherocytosis with its status or characteristic — 1) Ektacytometry 2) SDS-PAGE electrophoresis 3) Eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding test 4) Glycerol lysis / Pink test … A) Obsolete test B) Gold standard test C) Flow fluorescence test (less specific for ankyrin) D) Most preferred test
QUESTIONS.exp: In HS investigations: Ektacytometry is most preferred, SDS-PAGE electrophoresis is the gold standard, Eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) test measures RBC fluorescence (less specific for ankyrin), osmotic fragility has low sensitivity/specificity and is not used, and the glycerol lysis/pink test is obsolete. (Book p104)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis: Pathogenesis, Clinical Features & Investigations
QUESTIONS.q: In the Eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) test for hereditary spherocytosis, what is the principle and noted limitation?
opts: EMA binds with RBC membrane proteins to produce fluorescence; it is less specific for ankyrin defects
EMA precipitates unstable hemoglobin H inclusions; it is falsely negative in splenectomized patients
EMA measures glucose-6-phosphate oxidation under UV light; it is falsely normal during acute reticulocytosis
EMA chelates intracellular non-heme iron; it is only positive in hereditary elliptocytosis
QUESTIONS.exp: In the Eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) test, EMA binds with the RBC to produce fluorescence and is noted as less specific for ankyrin. (Book p104)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis: Pathogenesis, Clinical Features & Investigations
QUESTIONS.q: What saline concentrations and clinical utility are listed for the osmotic fragility test in hereditary spherocytosis on page 104?
opts: Printed principle lists (N) 3.0% hypertonic saline and HS rupture at 1.8% saline; it is the most preferred first-line screening investigation
Printed principle lists acidified serum lysis at pH 6.5 in 5% sucrose; it is more specific than SDS-PAGE electrophoresis for ankyrin defects
Printed principle lists (N) ≥ 0.7% saline and HS rupture at 0.3% (fragile RBCs); it has low sensitivity and specificity and is not used
Printed principle lists (N) 0.1% saline and HS rupture at 0.9% saline; it is the gold standard test with > 99% sensitivity and specificity
QUESTIONS.exp: The osmotic fragility test tests RBC rupture in hypotonic saline (printed on page 104 as '(N): Rupture of RBC in ≥ 0.7% saline; HS: Rupture at 0.3% → Fragile RBCs'); because it has low sensitivity and specificity, it is not used. (Book p104)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis: Pathogenesis, Clinical Features & Investigations
QUESTIONS.q: Which of the following statements regarding diagnostic tests for hereditary spherocytosis is TRUE?
opts: True — The osmotic fragility test has the highest sensitivity and specificity for hereditary spherocytosis
False — The glycerol lysis (pink) test is the current first-line screening test for hereditary spherocytosis
False — Red blood cell indices in hereditary spherocytosis characteristically show elevated MCV and decreased MCHC
True — Ektacytometry is the most preferred investigation, whereas SDS-PAGE electrophoresis is the gold standard
QUESTIONS.exp: Ektacytometry is the most preferred test and SDS-PAGE electrophoresis is the gold standard; MCV is decreased with markedly increased MCHC (↑↑), osmotic fragility has low sensitivity/specificity and is not used, and the glycerol lysis (pink) test is obsolete. (Book p104)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis Treatment & G6PD Deficiency: Genetics, HMP Shunt and Triggers
QUESTIONS.q: Match the severity grade of hereditary spherocytosis with its typical clinical presentation and definitive management — 1) Mild disease 2) Moderate disease 3) Severe disease 4) Concomitant gallbladder rule … A) Cholecystectomy is done only if gallstones are positive B) Seen in adults; supportive care C) Anemia & gallstones; splenectomy at puberty D) Seen in children with jaundice & complications; splenectomy at 3–4 years
QUESTIONS.exp: In HS treatment: mild disease (seen in adults) is managed with supportive care; moderate disease (anemia, gallstones) with splenectomy at puberty; severe disease (seen in children with jaundice and complications) with splenectomy at 3–4 years; and cholecystectomy is done only if gallstones are positive (+ve). (Book p105)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis Treatment & G6PD Deficiency: Genetics, HMP Shunt and Triggers
QUESTIONS.q: How is moderate hereditary spherocytosis (presenting with anemia and gallstones/cholelithiasis) managed surgically?
opts: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in early childhood
Supportive care alone with lifelong avoidance of splenectomy
Emergency splenectomy in the neonatal period (< 6 months of age)
Splenectomy at puberty (with cholecystectomy performed if gallstones are positive)
QUESTIONS.exp: Moderate HS presents with anemia and gallstones (cholelithiasis) and is treated with splenectomy at puberty; mild HS (seen in adults) receives supportive care. (Book p105)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis Treatment & G6PD Deficiency: Genetics, HMP Shunt and Triggers
QUESTIONS.q: A child with severe hereditary spherocytosis has persistent jaundice and transfusion-dependent complications. At what age is splenectomy recommended, and what pre-operative and post-operative considerations apply?
opts: Defer splenectomy until age 25 years; main post-operative risk is autoimmune warm hemolysis
Perform prophylactic cholecystectomy without splenectomy at 1 year of age
Splenectomy at 3–4 years of age; pre-operative vaccination is required, and post-operative risks include sepsis and thrombosis
Immediate splenectomy in the neonatal period (< 6 months); no vaccination needed until puberty
QUESTIONS.exp: Severe HS in children (jaundice, complications) is treated with splenectomy at 3–4 years of age. Pre-operative vaccination is mandatory, and post-operative complications include the risk of sepsis and thrombosis. (Book p105)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis Treatment & G6PD Deficiency: Genetics, HMP Shunt and Triggers
QUESTIONS.q: When performing splenectomy in a patient with hereditary spherocytosis, when is cholecystectomy indicated?
opts: Routinely in all patients undergoing splenectomy as prophylaxis
Never at the same sitting as splenectomy due to portal vein thrombosis risk
Only if serum alkaline phosphatase exceeds 1,000 IU/L
QUESTIONS.exp: As highlighted in the boxed note on page 105: Cholecystectomy is done only if gallstones are positive (+ve). (Book p105)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis Treatment & G6PD Deficiency: Genetics, HMP Shunt and Triggers
QUESTIONS.q: What are the two major post-operative risks following splenectomy highlighted on page 105?
QUESTIONS.exp: Under Splenectomy on page 105: Pre-operative requires vaccination, and post-operative carries the risk of sepsis and thrombosis. (Book p105)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis Treatment & G6PD Deficiency: Genetics, HMP Shunt and Triggers
QUESTIONS.q: What is the mode of inheritance, specific variant class highlighted, and pattern of hemolysis in Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency?
opts: Mitochondrial maternal inheritance; Class 3 Mediterranean type has ↑ NADPH; causes pure microangiopathic mechanical fragmentation hemolysis
Autosomal dominant inheritance; Class 1 African type has ↑ G6PD activity; causes isolated chronic extravascular hemolysis in the hepatic sinusoids
Autosomal recessive inheritance; Class 4 Asian type has absent Band 3 protein; causes isolated chronic extravascular hemolysis in the splenic cords
X-linked intermediate inheritance; Class 2 Mediterranean type has ↓ G6PD; causes combined hemolysis with acute intravascular > chronic extravascular hemolysis
QUESTIONS.exp: G6PD deficiency shows X-linked intermediate inheritance, Class 2 Mediterranean type has decreased (↓) G6PD activity, and hemolysis is combined (acute intravascular hemolysis > chronic extravascular hemolysis). (Book p105)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis Treatment & G6PD Deficiency: Genetics, HMP Shunt and Triggers
QUESTIONS.q: In the hexose monophosphate (HMP) shunt, G6PD converts glucose-6-phosphate into 6-phosphogluconolactone while generating ______, which maintains reduced glutathione to protect RBCs from oxidative injury.
QUESTIONS.exp: In the HMP shunt: G6PD → 6-phosphogluconolactone → NADPH → Reduced glutathione → Protects RBCs from oxidative injury. (Book p105)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis Treatment & G6PD Deficiency: Genetics, HMP Shunt and Triggers
QUESTIONS.q: Trace the exact sequence of the HMP shunt protective pathway depicted under G6PD Deficiency pathophysiology on page 105:
opts: G6PD → 2,3-BPG → Oxidized glutathione → Catalase → Prevents sickle polymerization
G6PD → Pyruvate → NADH → Methemoglobin reductase → Protects RBCs from osmotic lysis
G6PD → 6-Phosphogluconolactone → NADPH → Reduced glutathione → Protects RBCs from oxidative injury
G6PD → Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate → ATP → Na+/K+-ATPase → Maintains biconcavity
QUESTIONS.exp: The HMP shunt flowchart on page 105 shows: G6PD → 6 Phosphogluconolactone → NADPH → Reduced glutathione → Protects RBCs from oxidative injury. (Book p105)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis Treatment & G6PD Deficiency: Genetics, HMP Shunt and Triggers
QUESTIONS.q: Above what dose thresholds do aspirin and vitamin C precipitate oxidative hemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency?
opts: Aspirin > 325 mg and vitamin C > 250 mg
High-dose aspirin > 3 g/dL (3 g/day) and high-dose vitamin C > 1 g
Aspirin > 10 g and vitamin C > 10 g
Low-dose aspirin > 75 mg and vitamin C > 60 mg
QUESTIONS.exp: The precipitating drugs list specifies high-dose aspirin (> 3 g/dL as printed) and high-dose vitamin C (> 1 g) alongside primaquine, dapsone, sulfamethoxazole (cotrimoxazole), nitrofurantoin, rasburicase, methylene blue, and chloroquine. (Book p105)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis Treatment & G6PD Deficiency: Genetics, HMP Shunt and Triggers
QUESTIONS.q: All of the following drugs and exposures are listed as precipitants of acute oxidative hemolysis in G6PD deficiency EXCEPT:
opts: Methylene blue, fava beans, and acute infection
QUESTIONS.exp: Listed precipitants of G6PD hemolysis include primaquine, dapsone, sulfamethoxazole (cotrimoxazole), nitrofurantoin, rasburicase, high-dose aspirin (>3 g/dL), high-dose vitamin C (>1 g), methylene blue, chloroquine, infection, and fava beans. (Book p105)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis Treatment & G6PD Deficiency: Genetics, HMP Shunt and Triggers
QUESTIONS.q: Why is methylene blue contraindicated in a patient with G6PD deficiency (for example, during treatment of dapsone- or rasburicase-induced methemoglobinemia)?
opts: Methylene blue requires NADPH from the HMP shunt and is itself a precipitating oxidant drug that worsens hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
Methylene blue induces warm IgG autoantibodies against Rh antigens that trigger fulminant Fc-receptor-mediated splenic sequestration
Methylene blue irreversibly chelates mitochondrial iron in normoblasts and precipitates acute ringed sideroblastic arrest in the bone marrow
Methylene blue inhibits hepatic ferrochelatase and delta-ALA dehydratase, precipitating acute neurovisceral porphyria and vasospasm
QUESTIONS.exp: Methylene blue and rasburicase are both explicitly listed among the drugs that precipitate acute oxidative hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. (Book p105)

QUESTIONS.sec: Hereditary Spherocytosis Treatment & G6PD Deficiency: Genetics, HMP Shunt and Triggers
QUESTIONS.q: In G6PD deficiency, the ______ state is protective against malaria.
QUESTIONS.exp: As stated in the boxed note on page 105: Heterozygote is protective against malaria. (Book p105)

QUESTIONS.sec: G6PD Deficiency: Peripheral Smear, Diagnosis, Treatment & Anemia of Blood Loss
QUESTIONS.q: In G6PD deficiency, what are Heinz bodies composed of, and what red cell morphologies result when splenic macrophages pit them out?
opts: Heinz bodies are precipitates of denatured globin inside the RBC; their removal produces blister cells (hemighosts), bite cells, and triangle cells
Heinz bodies are nuclear DNA remnants; hepatic Kupffer cells convert them into target cells
Heinz bodies are precipitated ribosomal RNA aggregates; complement MAC converts them into spherocytes
Heinz bodies are iron-laden mitochondria; bone marrow macrophages convert them into acanthocytes
QUESTIONS.exp: On the peripheral smear in G6PD deficiency, Heinz bodies represent precipitation of denatured globin inside the RBC; also illustrated on page 106 are blister cells (hemighosts), bite cells, triangle cells, and Howell-Jolly bodies. (Book p106)

QUESTIONS.sec: G6PD Deficiency: Peripheral Smear, Diagnosis, Treatment & Anemia of Blood Loss
QUESTIONS.q: On the peripheral blood smear in oxidative hemolysis, blister cells are also known as ______.
QUESTIONS.exp: Page 106 labels blister cells on the peripheral smear as Hemighosts ('Blister cells (Hemighosts)'). (Book p106)

QUESTIONS.sec: G6PD Deficiency: Peripheral Smear, Diagnosis, Treatment & Anemia of Blood Loss
QUESTIONS.q: Match the peripheral blood smear red cell morphology depicted on page 106 with its description or disease association — 1) Heinz bodies 2) Blister cells 3) Helmet cells 4) Echinocytes … A) Also called hemighosts B) Classical of fragmented hemolysis C) Seen in CKD and pyruvate kinase deficiency D) Precipitation of denatured globin inside RBC
QUESTIONS.exp: Page 106 illustrates: Howell-Jolly bodies, Heinz bodies (precipitation of denatured globin inside RBC), blister cells (hemighosts), bite cells, triangle cells, helmet cells (classical of fragmented hemolysis), echinocytes (in CKD and pyruvate kinase deficiency), and basophilic stippling (also seen in 5'-pyrimidine nucleotidase). (Book p106)

QUESTIONS.sec: G6PD Deficiency: Peripheral Smear, Diagnosis, Treatment & Anemia of Blood Loss
QUESTIONS.q: Helmet cells on the peripheral blood smear panel on page 106 are highlighted as classical of which type of hemolysis?
QUESTIONS.exp: Helmet cells are labeled on page 106 as 'Classical of fragmented hemolysis'. (Book p106)

QUESTIONS.sec: G6PD Deficiency: Peripheral Smear, Diagnosis, Treatment & Anemia of Blood Loss
QUESTIONS.q: Echinocytes (burr cells with uniform short projections) shown on the peripheral smear panel on page 106 are characteristically associated with which two conditions?
opts: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) and pyruvate kinase deficiency
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and cold agglutinin disease
Hereditary spherocytosis and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia
QUESTIONS.exp: The peripheral smear gallery on page 106 highlights echinocytes in chronic kidney disease (CKD) and pyruvate kinase deficiency. (Book p106)

QUESTIONS.sec: G6PD Deficiency: Peripheral Smear, Diagnosis, Treatment & Anemia of Blood Loss
QUESTIONS.q: Which specific laboratory test is used as the screening test for G6PD deficiency, and how is the diagnosis confirmed?
opts: Fluorescent spot test for screening, followed by quantitative enzyme assay
Sucrose lysis test for screening, followed by FLAER flow cytometry

opts: Pleuritic chest pain > dyspnea, the latter in small and more peripheral emboli
Haemoptysis > dyspnea, the latter in large central emboli
Syncope > dyspnea, the latter in small and more peripheral emboli
Dyspnea (within seconds) > pleuritic chest pain, the latter in small and more peripheral emboli
QUESTIONS.exp: Page 209 prints 'Dyspnea (within seconds) > Pleuritic chest pain (in small & more peripheral emboli)' and separately 'Cough + hemoptysis (10–20% cases)'. Dyspnea outranks pain, and pain is tied to peripheral emboli. (Book p209)

QUESTIONS.sec: Dead-Space vs Shunt Physiology in PE, Symptoms/Signs, Vagal Bradycardia, Acute Cor Pulmonale Complications & Type I Respiratory Failure with A-a Gradient
QUESTIONS.q: Two separate findings on page 209 are each given the same 10–20% frequency. Which two are they?
opts: Cough with haemoptysis, and rales/↓ breath sounds
Pleuritic chest pain, and rales/↓ breath sounds
Cough with haemoptysis, and unexplained dyspnea
QUESTIONS.exp: The page prints 'Cough + hemoptysis (10–20% cases)' under symptoms and 'Tachypnea > Tachycardia > Rales/ ↓ breath sounds (10–20% cases)' under signs. Dyspnea, in contrast, carries no percentage because it is the most common symptom. (Book p209)

QUESTIONS.sec: Dead-Space vs Shunt Physiology in PE, Symptoms/Signs, Vagal Bradycardia, Acute Cor Pulmonale Complications & Type I Respiratory Failure with A-a Gradient
QUESTIONS.q: Page 209 explains one paradoxical sign of PE. Which mechanism is printed?
opts: Hypoxia induced intrapulmonary vagal stimulation → bradycardia
Hypoxia induced carotid body stimulation → bradycardia
QUESTIONS.exp: The sign line ends 'Hypoxia induced intrapulmonary vagal stimulation → Bradycardia'. Tachycardia is listed separately in the tachypnea > tachycardia > rales hierarchy, so the two coexist as different mechanisms. (Book p209)

QUESTIONS.sec: Dead-Space vs Shunt Physiology in PE, Symptoms/Signs, Vagal Bradycardia, Acute Cor Pulmonale Complications & Type I Respiratory Failure with A-a Gradient
QUESTIONS.q: Match each complication branch of acute cor pulmonale with its printed label — 1) Shock 2) S3 + hypotension 3) ↑ JVP … A) Acute RV failure B) Massive VTE C) Listed as a third consequence
QUESTIONS.exp: The cor pulmonale brace reads 'Shock (massive VTE)', 'S3 + hypotension (Acute RV failure)' and '↑ JVP'. Shock is attached to the massive group, S3 with hypotension to acute RV failure. (Book p209)

QUESTIONS.sec: Dead-Space vs Shunt Physiology in PE, Symptoms/Signs, Vagal Bradycardia, Acute Cor Pulmonale Complications & Type I Respiratory Failure with A-a Gradient
QUESTIONS.q: Which set of statements is printed under 'Type I respiratory failure' for PE on page 209?
opts: Hypoxia d/t shunt; PaCO2 raised d/t dead space → respiratory acidosis; normal alveolar-arterial O2 gradient
Hypoxia d/t ventilation-perfusion mismatch; PaCO2 normal (no parenchymal involvement) → respiratory alkalosis; ↓perfusion → ↓diffusion → widening of the alveolar-arterial O2 gradient
Hypoxia with hypercarbia d/t parenchymal involvement → respiratory acidosis; narrowing of the alveolar-arterial O2 gradient
Hypoxia d/t diffusion block; PaCO2 low d/t hyperventilation of unperfused alveoli → metabolic acidosis; normal gradient
QUESTIONS.exp: The three lines under type I failure are exactly the mismatch hypoxia, the normal PaCO2 with consequent respiratory alkalosis, and the widened (Alveolar O2 − Arterial O2) gradient via reduced perfusion and diffusion. The type 2 note on the same page requires parenchymal involvement. (Book p209)

QUESTIONS.sec: Dead-Space vs Shunt Physiology in PE, Symptoms/Signs, Vagal Bradycardia, Acute Cor Pulmonale Complications & Type I Respiratory Failure with A-a Gradient
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the two respiratory-failure notes on page 209.
opts: False — type 2 failure is defined there as hypoxia with a normal PaCO2
False — type 2 failure is said there to occur only in PE
True — type 2 failure is defined there as hypoxia plus hypercarbia and is seen in lung disease with parenchyma involved
True — type 1 failure is said there to require a raised PaCO2
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Type 2 respiratory failure : Hypoxia + hypercarbia' and 'Seen in lung diseases with parenchyma involved', which is precisely why uncomplicated PE produces type 1 failure. Type 1 by definition has a normal or low PaCO2. (Book p209)

QUESTIONS.sec: CXR Signs (Atelectatic Bands, Hampton's Hump, Pallas, Westermark, Fleischner), PAH Films & ECG Significance and Patterns (S1Q3T3)
QUESTIONS.q: Match each chest-radiograph sign on page 210 with its printed description — 1) Hampton's hump 2) Pallas sign 3) Westermark's sign 4) Fleischner sign … A) Enlarged central pulmonary artery B) Pleural based wedge shaped opacities C) Enlarged Rt descending artery D) Oligemia of Rt upper lung
QUESTIONS.exp: The figure captions read 'Pleural based wedge shaped opacities (Hamptons hump)', 'Enlarged Rt descending artery (Pallas sign)', 'Oligemia of Rt upper lung (Westermark's sign)' and 'Enlarged central pulmonary artery (Fleischner sign)'. (Book p210)

QUESTIONS.sec: CXR Signs (Atelectatic Bands, Hampton's Hump, Pallas, Westermark, Fleischner), PAH Films & ECG Significance and Patterns (S1Q3T3)
QUESTIONS.q: Which CXR finding on page 210 is marked as the most common?
opts: Oligemia of the right upper lung
QUESTIONS.exp: The first film is captioned 'Long linear bands of atelectasis (m/c)'. Hampton's hump, Westermark's and Pallas signs are all printed without a frequency label. (Book p210)

QUESTIONS.sec: CXR Signs (Atelectatic Bands, Hampton's Hump, Pallas, Westermark, Fleischner), PAH Films & ECG Significance and Patterns (S1Q3T3)
QUESTIONS.q: Westermark's sign on page 210 is the ______ of the right upper lung.
QUESTIONS.exp: The caption reads 'Oligemia of Rt upper lung (Westermark's sign)' — a zone of reduced vascular markings beyond the obstructed vessel, not increased flow or consolidation. (Book p210)

QUESTIONS.sec: CXR Signs (Atelectatic Bands, Hampton's Hump, Pallas, Westermark, Fleischner), PAH Films & ECG Significance and Patterns (S1Q3T3)
QUESTIONS.q: The page 210 PAH film is captioned with four findings. Which set is printed?
opts: Large central pulmonary arteries, left ventricular hypertrophy, delayed attenuation of pulmonary vessels, clear lung fields
Large central pulmonary veins, right atrial enlargement, rapid attenuation of pulmonary vessels, clear lung fields
Large central pulmonary arteries, right ventricular hypertrophy, rapid attenuation of pulmonary vessels, clear lung fields
Small central pulmonary arteries, right ventricular hypertrophy, rapid attenuation of pulmonary vessels, bilateral infiltrates
QUESTIONS.exp: The labelled film lists 'Large central pulmonary arteries', 'Right ventricular hypertrophy', 'Rapid attenuation of pulmonary vessels' and 'Clear lung fields'. The rapid tapering plus clear fields is what distinguishes vascular from parenchymal disease. (Book p210)

QUESTIONS.sec: CXR Signs (Atelectatic Bands, Hampton's Hump, Pallas, Westermark, Fleischner), PAH Films & ECG Significance and Patterns (S1Q3T3)
QUESTIONS.q: Two clinical purposes of the ECG in suspected PE are printed on page 210. Which pair?
opts: To rule out MI, and to identify RV strain/hypertrophy
To confirm the embolus, and to grade its size
To rule out pericarditis, and to identify LV strain/hypertrophy
To rule out MI, and to measure the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
QUESTIONS.exp: The block reads 'Clinical significance : To rule out MI. To identify RV strain/ hypertrophy.' The ECG is adjunctive, not diagnostic — a point reinforced by the S1Q3T3 line being labelled non-specific. (Book p210)

QUESTIONS.sec: CXR Signs (Atelectatic Bands, Hampton's Hump, Pallas, Westermark, Fleischner), PAH Films & ECG Significance and Patterns (S1Q3T3)
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the ECG patterns printed on page 210.
opts: False — the most common pattern is sinus tachycardia, the most common abnormality S1Q3T3
True — the most common pattern is a normal ECG, while the most common abnormality is sinus tachycardia
False — the most common abnormality is T inversion in V1–V4
True — S1Q3T3 is printed as a specific sign of RV infarction
QUESTIONS.exp: The patterns block reads 'Normal ECG : m/c pattern', 'Sinus tachycardia : m/c abnormality', 'Deep S waves in lead I > T inversion in V1–V4' and 'S1Q3T3 pattern : Non specific'. S1Q3T3 is explicitly non-specific. (Book p210)

QUESTIONS.sec: CXR Signs (Atelectatic Bands, Hampton's Hump, Pallas, Westermark, Fleischner), PAH Films & ECG Significance and Patterns (S1Q3T3)
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three are CXR captions from page 210, one is not printed there:
QUESTIONS.exp: Page 210 carries Hampton's hump, Pallas sign, Westermark's sign, Fleischner sign and long linear bands of atelectasis. 'Candle dripping' is the asbestos pleural-plaque sign printed much later, on page 227. (Book p210)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pulmonary Angiography Gold Standard, V/Q Scan Indications, D-Dimer, ECHO, the Wells Score Table and CTPA Signs (Saddle Embolus, Polo Mint Sign)
QUESTIONS.q: Which investigation does page 211 name as the gold standard, and what is its stated drawback?
opts: D-dimer — it is invasive and requires cannulation of the pulmonary artery
V/Q scan — it is only valid in patients with a normal chest radiograph
CTPA — it requires contrast and cannot be used in pregnancy
Pulmonary angiography — it is invasive, cannulating a vein to reach the pulmonary artery
QUESTIONS.exp: The block reads 'Pulmonary angiography : gold standard' and 'Invasive : Cannulates vein to reach pulmonary artery'. CTPA is described on page 207 as the IOC, a different label. (Book p211)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pulmonary Angiography Gold Standard, V/Q Scan Indications, D-Dimer, ECHO, the Wells Score Table and CTPA Signs (Saddle Embolus, Polo Mint Sign)
QUESTIONS.q: Match the investigation with its printed indication or purpose — 1) V/Q scan 2) D Dimer 3) ECHO … A) In low risk cases B) Pregnancy and contrast allergy C) To r/o alternate diagnosis (pericardial effusion)
QUESTIONS.exp: Page 211 lists 'V/Q scan — Indications : Pregnancy. contrast allergy', 'D Dimer — In low risk cases' and 'ECHO — To r/o alternate diagnosis (Pericardial effusion)'. The D-dimer is a rule-out tool in low-risk patients, not a confirmatory test. (Book p211)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pulmonary Angiography Gold Standard, V/Q Scan Indications, D-Dimer, ECHO, the Wells Score Table and CTPA Signs (Saddle Embolus, Polo Mint Sign)
QUESTIONS.q: Page 211's note states that any unexplained dyspnea with normal CXR/ECG/clinical examination is ______ unless proven otherwise.
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Any unexplained dyspnea with normal CXR/ECG/clinical examination is VTE unless proven otherwise.' This is the page's answer to the 'clear lung fields' presentation described on page 207. (Book p211)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pulmonary Angiography Gold Standard, V/Q Scan Indications, D-Dimer, ECHO, the Wells Score Table and CTPA Signs (Saddle Embolus, Polo Mint Sign)
QUESTIONS.q: In the Wells score table on page 211, two features score 3 points. Which two are printed?
opts: Clinical signs of DVT, and heart rate > 100/min
Recent surgery, and previous history of DVT/PE
Clinical signs of DVT, and alternative diagnosis less likely
QUESTIONS.exp: The two 3-point rows are 'Clinical signs of DVT' and 'Alternative diagnosis less likely'; HR >100/min, recent surgery and previous DVT/PE each score 1.5, and haemoptysis and malignancy each score 1. (Book p211)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pulmonary Angiography Gold Standard, V/Q Scan Indications, D-Dimer, ECHO, the Wells Score Table and CTPA Signs (Saddle Embolus, Polo Mint Sign)
QUESTIONS.q: Match each Wells-score total with the printed features that produce it — 1) 3 points 2) 1.5 points 3) 1 point … A) Haemoptysis and malignancy B) Clinical signs of DVT and alternative diagnosis less likely C) Heart rate > 100/min, recent surgery and previous DVT/PE
QUESTIONS.exp: The table scores clinical signs of DVT 3, alternative diagnosis less likely 3, HR >100/min 1.5, recent surgery 1.5, previous DVT/PE 1.5, haemoptysis 1 and malignancy 1. The three score bands therefore group the seven rows exactly as listed. (Book p211)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pulmonary Angiography Gold Standard, V/Q Scan Indications, D-Dimer, ECHO, the Wells Score Table and CTPA Signs (Saddle Embolus, Polo Mint Sign)
QUESTIONS.q: How is the Wells score used on page 211 to choose imaging?
opts: Low risk → V/Q scan; moderate and high risk → pulmonary angiography
All risk groups → D-dimer first, then CTPA only if the D-dimer is negative
Low risk → helical CTPA; moderate and high risk → D-dimer followed by CTPA
Low risk → D-dimer, and only if positive → CTPA; moderate and high risk → helical CTPA
QUESTIONS.exp: The flowchart reads 'Risk → Low → D Dimer + → CTPA' with a brace joining 'moderate' and 'High' to 'Helical CTPA'. The D-dimer is used to avoid imaging in low-risk patients, not to trigger it when negative. (Book p211)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pulmonary Angiography Gold Standard, V/Q Scan Indications, D-Dimer, ECHO, the Wells Score Table and CTPA Signs (Saddle Embolus, Polo Mint Sign)
QUESTIONS.q: The two CT captions on page 211 describe a saddle embolus and the 'polo mint sign'. What does the printed line above the polo-mint image say?
opts: Contrast fills the vessel completely with no filling defect
A thin rim of contrast persists around a central filling defect
A thin rim of thrombus persists around a central contrast column
A thick rim of thrombus surrounds a central contrast column
QUESTIONS.exp: The caption reads 'Thin rim of contrast persists around a central filling defect' — the ring of contrast around the clot is what produces the polo-mint appearance. (Book p211)

QUESTIONS.sec: Management: Heparin/LMWH Dosing, Severity Determination, Thrombolysis vs Catheter Therapy, Heparin Target Ranges, 3-Month Switch and IVC Filter
QUESTIONS.q: The first dose of anticoagulant on page 212 is weight-based. Which two doses are printed?
opts: 80 units/kg heparin IV, or 1 mg/kg s/c LMWH
80 units/kg heparin s/c, or 1 mg/kg IV LMWH
18 units/kg heparin IV, or 1 mg/kg s/c LMWH
100 units/kg heparin IV, or 1.5 mg/kg s/c LMWH
QUESTIONS.exp: The block reads 'First dose of anticoagulant : 80 units/kg heparin IV or 1 mg/kg s/c LMWH (Low molecular weight heparin)'. The 18 units/kg/hr figure belongs to the later infusion step, not the first dose. (Book p212)

QUESTIONS.sec: Management: Heparin/LMWH Dosing, Severity Determination, Thrombolysis vs Catheter Therapy, Heparin Target Ranges, 3-Month Switch and IVC Filter
QUESTIONS.q: After the first dose, page 212 asks the clinician to 'determine severity'. Which three findings are listed?
opts: Massive VTE (troponin +), submassive VTE (BNP +), extensive clot burden
Massive VTE (RV dilatation +), submassive VTE (hypotension +), minimal clot burden
Massive VTE (hypotension +), submassive VTE (RV dilatation +), extensive clot burden
Massive VTE (hypotension +), submassive VTE (RV dilatation +), isolated calf DVT
QUESTIONS.exp: The severity list is 'massive VTE (Hypotension +)', 'Submassive VTE (RV dilatation +)' and 'Extensive clot burden'. The bracket that decides 'Present' versus 'Absent' hangs off this severity assessment. (Book p212)

QUESTIONS.sec: Management: Heparin/LMWH Dosing, Severity Determination, Thrombolysis vs Catheter Therapy, Heparin Target Ranges, 3-Month Switch and IVC Filter
QUESTIONS.q: A hypotensive patient with PE is judged fit for thrombolysis. Which regimen and time window are printed on page 212?
opts: Streptokinase 1.5 million units IV, over 2 hrs, within 14 days
Alteplase 50 mg IV, over 1 hr, within 14 days
Alteplase 100 mg IV, over 2 hrs, within 14 days
Alteplase 100 mg IV, over 2 hrs, within 7 days
QUESTIONS.exp: The thrombolysis branch reads 'Thrombolysis with Alteplase — 100 mg IV. — Over 2 hrs. — within 14 days.' followed by 'Restart heparin & replace with warfarin'. (Book p212)

QUESTIONS.sec: Management: Heparin/LMWH Dosing, Severity Determination, Thrombolysis vs Catheter Therapy, Heparin Target Ranges, 3-Month Switch and IVC Filter
QUESTIONS.q: For a patient who is unfit for thrombolysis, what does page 212 recommend, and how is it labelled?
opts: Inferior vena cava filter, marked as '(Preferred)'
Catheter-based thrombolysis/embolectomy, marked as a last resort
QUESTIONS.exp: The unfit branch reads 'Catheter-based thrombolysis/ embolectomy (Preferred)'. The IVC filter is reserved for the end-of-3-months branch when oral anticoagulation is contraindicated. (Book p212)

QUESTIONS.sec: Management: Heparin/LMWH Dosing, Severity Determination, Thrombolysis vs Catheter Therapy, Heparin Target Ranges, 3-Month Switch and IVC Filter
QUESTIONS.q: For the 'Absent' severity branch, page 212 prints an infusion rate and two target ranges. Which set is printed?
opts: 18 units/kg/hr heparin; aPTT 2–3 times the upper limit; INR 1.5–2
18 units/kg/hr heparin; aPTT 1.5–2 times the upper limit; INR 2–3
80 units/kg/hr heparin; aPTT 1.5–2 times the upper limit; INR 2–3
18 units/kg/hr heparin; aPTT 1.5–2 times the upper limit; INR 1.5–2
QUESTIONS.exp: The branch reads 'Continue anticoagulation at 18 units/kg/hr Heparin' with 'Target — aPTT : 1.5 – 2 times the upper limit' and 'INR : 2 – 3'. The aPTT target is applied to heparin and the INR to warfarin. (Book p212)

QUESTIONS.sec: Management: Heparin/LMWH Dosing, Severity Determination, Thrombolysis vs Catheter Therapy, Heparin Target Ranges, 3-Month Switch and IVC Filter
QUESTIONS.q: At the end of 3 months, page 212 gives one switch rule and one exception pathway. Which statement matches the page?
opts: Switch to oral anticoagulants, lifelong only if a genetic mutation is negative; if contraindicated, perform catheter embolectomy
Stop anticoagulation at 3 months in all patients; if a genetic mutation is positive, extend heparin for 6 months
Switch to warfarin in preference to new oral anticoagulants, lifelong in all patients; if contraindicated, insert an inferior vena cava filter
Switch to oral anticoagulants (new oral anticoagulants > warfarin/vit K), lifelong if a genetic mutation is positive; if contraindicated, insert an inferior vena cava filter
QUESTIONS.exp: The block reads 'B. At the end of 3 months : Oral anticoagulants (New oral anticoagulants > warfarin/vit K) : Lifelong if genetic mutation (+). If C/I → Inferior vena cava filter.' The preference arrow points to the new oral agents, and lifelong therapy follows a positive genetic result. (Book p212)

QUESTIONS.sec: Management: Heparin/LMWH Dosing, Severity Determination, Thrombolysis vs Catheter Therapy, Heparin Target Ranges, 3-Month Switch and IVC Filter
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the post-thrombolysis sequence printed on page 212.
opts: False — after thrombolysis the page says to stop all anticoagulation
False — after thrombolysis the page says to give an IVC filter first
True — after thrombolysis the page says to restart heparin and then replace it with warfarin
True — after thrombolysis the page says to continue alteplase for 14 days
QUESTIONS.exp: The line beneath the alteplase block reads 'Restart heparin & replace with warfarin.' Alteplase is a finite 2-hour infusion, not a 14-day one; 14 days is the outer limit for starting it. (Book p212)

QUESTIONS.sec: Ohm's Law Applied to the Pulmonary Circulation (PAP − LAP = CO × PVR), the Five WHO Classes, Class 1 PAH Features and the Class-to-Affected-Vessel Figure
QUESTIONS.q: Page 213 maps Ohm's law onto the pulmonary circulation. Match each electrical term with its printed pulmonary equivalent — 1) Voltage 2) Current 3) Resistance … A) Cardiac output B) Pulmonary vascular resistance C) Pressure difference between pulmonary artery and left atrium
QUESTIONS.exp: The page reads 'V : Voltage → Pressure difference between pulmonary artery (PAP) & left atrium (LAP)', 'I : Current → Cardiac Output (CO)' and 'R : Resistance → Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR)'. (Book p213)

QUESTIONS.sec: Ohm's Law Applied to the Pulmonary Circulation (PAP − LAP = CO × PVR), the Five WHO Classes, Class 1 PAH Features and the Class-to-Affected-Vessel Figure
QUESTIONS.q: Which pair of equations is printed on page 213?
opts: PAP − LAP = CO ÷ PVR, therefore PAP = (CO ÷ PVR) + LAP
LAP − PAP = CO × PVR, therefore PAP = (CO × PVR) − LAP
PAP + LAP = CO × PVR, therefore PAP = (CO × PVR) − LAP
PAP − LAP = CO × PVR, therefore PAP = (CO × PVR) + LAP
QUESTIONS.exp: Page 213 prints 'Therefore, PAP-LAP = CO x PVR' and beneath it 'PAP = (CO x PVR) + LAP'. The pulmonary artery pressure is the flow times resistance plus the downstream left atrial pressure. (Book p213)

QUESTIONS.sec: Ohm's Law Applied to the Pulmonary Circulation (PAP − LAP = CO × PVR), the Five WHO Classes, Class 1 PAH Features and the Class-to-Affected-Vessel Figure
QUESTIONS.q: Page 213 splits the causes of a raised PAP along the equation. Which split is printed?
opts: ↑PVR causes class 1/2/3 pulmonary HTN; ↑LAP causes class 4 pulmonary HTN, the commonest cardiac cause being mitral regurgitation
↑CO causes class 1/3/4 pulmonary HTN; ↑LAP causes class 2 pulmonary HTN, the commonest cardiac cause being left ventricular hypertrophy
↑PVR causes class 1/3/4 pulmonary HTN; ↑LAP causes class 2 pulmonary HTN, the commonest cardiac cause being mitral stenosis
↑PVR causes class 2 pulmonary HTN; ↑LAP causes class 1/3/4 pulmonary HTN, the commonest cardiac cause being aortic stenosis
QUESTIONS.exp: The brace from 'For ↑PAP' reads '↑ PVR : Class 1/3/4 pulmonary HTN' and '↑ LAP : Cardiac cause (m/c : mitral stenosis) → Class 2 pulmonary HTN'. Resistance disease and downstream pressure disease occupy different classes. (Book p213)

QUESTIONS.sec: Ohm's Law Applied to the Pulmonary Circulation (PAP − LAP = CO × PVR), the Five WHO Classes, Class 1 PAH Features and the Class-to-Affected-Vessel Figure
QUESTIONS.q: Under Class 1 pulmonary artery hypertension, which three features are printed?
opts: Most common cause is hereditary, very poor prognosis with median survival < 19 months, elderly males
Most common cause is idiopathic (hence idiopathic pulmonary HTN), very poor prognosis with median survival < 9 months, young females
Most common cause is drug-induced, very poor prognosis with median survival < 9 months, elderly females
Most common cause is idiopathic, good prognosis with median survival > 9 years, young females
QUESTIONS.exp: Class 1 reads 'm/c cause : Idiopathic (Hence k/a Idiopathic pulmonary HTN)', 'very poor prognosis (median survival : <9 months)' and 'Young females'. The chronic thrombo-embolic class, not class 1, is the surgically responsive one. (Book p213)

QUESTIONS.sec: Ohm's Law Applied to the Pulmonary Circulation (PAP − LAP = CO × PVR), the Five WHO Classes, Class 1 PAH Features and the Class-to-Affected-Vessel Figure
QUESTIONS.q: The figure at the foot of page 213 labels each class by the vessel affected. Match the class with the affected structure — 1) Class 1 PAH 2) Class 2 PVH 3) Class 3 PH 4) Class 4 CTEPH … A) Capillary affected B) Arterioles affected C) Pulmonary artery affected D) Pulmonary vein affected
QUESTIONS.exp: The figure labels read 'Class 1: PAH — Arterioles affected', 'Class 2: PVH (Pulmonary vein affected)', 'Class 3: PH (Capillary affected)' and 'Class 4: CTEPH (Pulmonary artery affected)'. Class 5 is labelled multifactorial. (Book p213)

QUESTIONS.sec: Ohm's Law Applied to the Pulmonary Circulation (PAP − LAP = CO × PVR), the Five WHO Classes, Class 1 PAH Features and the Class-to-Affected-Vessel Figure
QUESTIONS.q: Which description of Class 3 pulmonary hypertension is printed on page 213?
opts: Pulmonary HTN secondary to left heart disease, with hypoxia related vasodilatation, good prognosis and mitral stenosis as the example
Pulmonary HTN due to chronic thromboembolic disease, responsive to surgery, with chronic bronchitis as the example
Pulmonary HTN secondary to chronic lung disease, with hypoxia related pulmonary vasoconstriction, very poor prognosis and chronic bronchitis as the example
Pulmonary HTN secondary to chronic lung disease, with hypercarbia related vasoconstriction, very poor prognosis and emphysema as the example
QUESTIONS.exp: Class 3 reads 'Pulmonary HTN secondary to chronic lung disease', 'Hypoxia related pulmonary vasoconstriction', 'very poor prognosis' and 'eg : In chronic bronchitis'. Class 4 carries the 'responsive to surgery' label. (Book p213)

QUESTIONS.sec: Ohm's Law Applied to the Pulmonary Circulation (PAP − LAP = CO × PVR), the Five WHO Classes, Class 1 PAH Features and the Class-to-Affected-Vessel Figure
QUESTIONS.q: The boxed note on page 213 states: hypoxia causes vasodilatation ______ in pulmonary vessels.
QUESTIONS.exp: The box reads 'Hypoxia : vasodilatation except in pulmonary vessels.' Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is the exception that drives class 3 disease, and it explains why the page links chronic lung disease to a raised PVR. (Book p213)

QUESTIONS.sec: Ohm's Law Applied to the Pulmonary Circulation (PAP − LAP = CO × PVR), the Five WHO Classes, Class 1 PAH Features and the Class-to-Affected-Vessel Figure
QUESTIONS.q: Which two remaining classes complete the page 213 classification, with their printed descriptors?
opts: Class 4: miscellaneous (multifactorial); Class 5: chronic thrombo-embolic pulmonary HTN (responsive to surgery)
Class 4: chronic thrombo-embolic pulmonary HTN (not responsive to surgery); Class 5: miscellaneous (unifactorial)
Class 4: pulmonary HTN of unclear cause (responsive to surgery); Class 5: mixed connective tissue disease
Class 4: chronic thrombo-embolic pulmonary HTN (responsive to surgery); Class 5: miscellaneous (multifactorial)
QUESTIONS.exp: The last two lines read 'Class 4 : Chronic thrombo-embolic pulmonary HTN (Responsive to surgery)' and 'Class 5 : miscellaneous (Multifactorial)'. The figure adds that class 4 affects the pulmonary artery and class 5 is multifactorial. (Book p213)

QUESTIONS.sec: PAH vs Systemic HTN Mortality Logic, Definition (Mean PAP > 20 mmHg), Cor Pulmonale, Wood-Unit PVR Split, Plexiform Arteriolopathy & Secondary Causes (BMPR2 to Appetite Suppressants)
QUESTIONS.q: What definition of pulmonary hypertension is printed on page 214?
opts: Systolic PAP > 20 mmHg at rest with right heart catheterisation
Mean PAP > 20 mmHg at rest with right heart catheterisation
Mean PAP > 20 mmHg on echocardiography at rest
Mean PAP > 25 mmHg at rest with right heart catheterisation
QUESTIONS.exp: The definition line reads 'mean PAP > 20 mmHg at rest with right heart catheterisation'. The measurement is a mean pressure, the threshold is 20, and the technique is right heart catheterisation, not echocardiography. (Book p214)

QUESTIONS.sec: PAH vs Systemic HTN Mortality Logic, Definition (Mean PAP > 20 mmHg), Cor Pulmonale, Wood-Unit PVR Split, Plexiform Arteriolopathy & Secondary Causes (BMPR2 to Appetite Suppressants)
QUESTIONS.q: How does page 214 define cor pulmonale, and which three causes are printed?
opts: RA dilatation ± RA failure; causes are COPD, mitral stenosis and thromboembolism
RV hypertrophy/dilatation ± RV failure; causes are COPD, pulmonary HTN and pulmonary stenosis
RV hypertrophy/dilatation ± RV failure; causes are COPD, pulmonary HTN and thromboembolism (the last giving acute cor pulmonale)
LV hypertrophy/dilatation ± LV failure; causes are systemic HTN, aortic stenosis and myocardial infarction
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Cor pulmonale : RV hypertrophy/dilatation ± RV failure', with causes 'COPD', 'Pulmonary HTN' and 'Thromboembolism → Acute cor pulmonale'. Cor pulmonale is right-heart disease from a pulmonary cause. (Book p214)

QUESTIONS.sec: PAH vs Systemic HTN Mortality Logic, Definition (Mean PAP > 20 mmHg), Cor Pulmonale, Wood-Unit PVR Split, Plexiform Arteriolopathy & Secondary Causes (BMPR2 to Appetite Suppressants)
QUESTIONS.q: Page 214 splits the classes by pulmonary vascular resistance in wood units. Which split is printed?
opts: PVR > 3 wood units → class I, III, IV; PVR < 3 wood units → class II, where PCWP (LAP) > 15 mmHg
PVR > 3 wood units → class II; PVR < 3 wood units → class I, III, IV, where PCWP (LAP) > 15 mmHg
PVR > 5 wood units → class I, III, IV; PVR < 5 wood units → class II, where PCWP (LAP) > 15 mmHg
PVR > 3 wood units → class I, III, IV; PVR < 3 wood units → class II, where PCWP (LAP) > 20 mmHg
QUESTIONS.exp: The brace reads '> 3 wood units → Class I, III, IV' and '< 3 wood units → Class II : PCWP (LAP) >15 mmHg'. The class II threshold is a wedge pressure of 15 mmHg, matching the upstream left-heart mechanism. (Book p214)

QUESTIONS.sec: PAH vs Systemic HTN Mortality Logic, Definition (Mean PAP > 20 mmHg), Cor Pulmonale, Wood-Unit PVR Split, Plexiform Arteriolopathy & Secondary Causes (BMPR2 to Appetite Suppressants)
QUESTIONS.q: The pathology of PAH is summarised on page 214 by a single term for the arterial lesion. Which term is printed, and which vessels are affected?
opts: Plexiform arteriopathy, with the pulmonary veins affected
Medial hypertrophy, with the pulmonary artery affected
Intimal fibroelastosis, with the arterioles affected
Plexiform arteriolopathy, with the arterioles affected
QUESTIONS.exp: Page 214 prints 'Plexiform arteriolopathy (Arterioles affected)' under the PAH heading, consistent with class 1 being an arteriolar disease in the page 213 figure. (Book p214)

QUESTIONS.sec: PAH vs Systemic HTN Mortality Logic, Definition (Mean PAP > 20 mmHg), Cor Pulmonale, Wood-Unit PVR Split, Plexiform Arteriolopathy & Secondary Causes (BMPR2 to Appetite Suppressants)
QUESTIONS.q: Match each secondary cause of PAH with its printed detail — 1) Hereditary 2) Acquired 3) Infection 4) Drugs … A) HIV B) Bone morphogenic protein receptor-2 (BMPR2) mutation C) Serotonin (appetite suppressants) D) Limited systemic sclerosis
QUESTIONS.exp: The list reads 'Hereditary : Bone morphogenic protein receptor-2 (BMPR2) mutation', 'Acquired : Limited systemic sclerosis', 'HIV' and 'Drugs : Serotonin (Appetite suppressants)'. HIV is listed as its own infective cause rather than under acquired autoimmune disease. (Book p214)

QUESTIONS.sec: PAH vs Systemic HTN Mortality Logic, Definition (Mean PAP > 20 mmHg), Cor Pulmonale, Wood-Unit PVR Split, Plexiform Arteriolopathy & Secondary Causes (BMPR2 to Appetite Suppressants)
QUESTIONS.q: A patient with cirrhosis develops pulmonary hypertension. Which mechanism does page 214 print for portal HTN?
opts: Splanchnic vasoconstriction → low-output circulation → ↓CO → pulmonary HTN
Splanchnic vasodilatation → hyperdynamic circulation → ↑CO → pulmonary HTN
QUESTIONS.exp: The page prints 'Portal HTN : Splanchnic vasodilatation → Hyperdynamic circulation → ↑CO → Pulmonary HTN'. This is a high-flow mechanism acting through the CO term of the equation on page 213, not a resistance or wedge mechanism. (Book p214)

QUESTIONS.sec: PAH vs Systemic HTN Mortality Logic, Definition (Mean PAP > 20 mmHg), Cor Pulmonale, Wood-Unit PVR Split, Plexiform Arteriolopathy & Secondary Causes (BMPR2 to Appetite Suppressants)
QUESTIONS.q: Which drug list is printed under the drug cause of PAH?
opts: Fenfluramine, dexfenfluramine, benfluorex, amiodarone and toxic rapeseed oil
Fenfluramine, dexfenfluramine, bosentan, aminorex and toxic rapeseed oil
Fenfluramine, dexfenfluramine, benfluorex, aminorex and ergotamine
Fenfluramine, dexfenfluramine, benfluorex, aminorex and toxic rapeseed oil
QUESTIONS.exp: The drug block prints 'Serotonin (Appetite suppressants)' — Fenfluramine, Dexfenfluramine, Benfluorex, Aminorex — and 'Toxic rapeseed oil'. Amiodarone, bosentan and ergotamine are not on this list. (Book p214)

QUESTIONS.sec: PAH vs Systemic HTN Mortality Logic, Definition (Mean PAP > 20 mmHg), Cor Pulmonale, Wood-Unit PVR Split, Plexiform Arteriolopathy & Secondary Causes (BMPR2 to Appetite Suppressants)
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the haemodynamic comparisons on page 214.
opts: True — PAP is far below systemic arterial pressure and PVR far below systemic vascular resistance, because the lungs are a low-resistance, high-compliance system
True — systemic hypertension causes RV hypertrophy while pulmonary hypertension causes LV dilatation
False — PVR exceeds systemic vascular resistance because the pulmonary circuit is in series
False — PAP exceeds systemic arterial pressure because the lungs receive the whole cardiac output
QUESTIONS.exp: The block reads 'PAP <<< SAP', 'PVR <<< SAR' and 'Lungs : Low resistance high compliance system', then 'Systemic HTN → LV hypertrophy' and 'Pulmonary HTN → RV dilatation → RV failure → ↑mortality'. The ventricular responses are the reverse of the option offered. (Book p214)

QUESTIONS.sec: PAH vs Systemic HTN Mortality Logic, Definition (Mean PAP > 20 mmHg), Cor Pulmonale, Wood-Unit PVR Split, Plexiform Arteriolopathy & Secondary Causes (BMPR2 to Appetite Suppressants)
QUESTIONS.q: A boxed equation on page 214 restates how systemic arterial pressure is generated. Which form is printed there?
opts: Systemic arterial pressure = CO × systemic vascular resistance + right atrial pressure
Systemic arterial pressure = CO × systemic vascular resistance + left atrial pressure
Systemic arterial pressure = CO × systemic vascular resistance − right atrial pressure
Systemic arterial pressure = CO × pulmonary vascular resistance + right atrial pressure
QUESTIONS.exp: The box reads 'Systemic arterial pressure = CO x systemic vascular resistance + Right atrial pressure'. Note the addend printed is the RIGHT atrial pressure, not the left — the same structural form as the pulmonary equation PAP = (CO × PVR) + LAP on page 213. (Book p214)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pathology Triad, Endothelin/NO/Prostacyclin Pathway Treatment Table, Clinical Presentation and the RV Dilatation and RV Failure Sign Chains
QUESTIONS.q: The three processes grouped under 'PATHOLOGY' on page 215 are:
QUESTIONS.exp: The bracket over the three arrows reads 'vasoconstriction', 'Remodeling' and 'Thrombosis'. All three converge on the raised PVR that defines the disease. (Book p215)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pathology Triad, Endothelin/NO/Prostacyclin Pathway Treatment Table, Clinical Presentation and the RV Dilatation and RV Failure Sign Chains
QUESTIONS.q: Match each pathway with its printed effect in PAH — 1) Endothelin pathway 2) Nitric oxide pathway 3) Prostacyclin pathway … A) Inhibited, with NO → ↑cGMP B) Promoted C) Inhibited, with prostacyclin → ↑cAMP
QUESTIONS.exp: The table rows read 'Endothelin pathway — Promoted', 'Nitric oxide pathway : NO → ↑cGMP — Inhibited' and 'Prostacyclin pathway : Prostacyclin → ↑cAMP — Inhibited'. Only the endothelin pathway is upregulated. (Book p215)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pathology Triad, Endothelin/NO/Prostacyclin Pathway Treatment Table, Clinical Presentation and the RV Dilatation and RV Failure Sign Chains
QUESTIONS.q: Match each pathway with the treatment class printed against it — 1) Endothelin pathway 2) Nitric oxide pathway 3) Prostacyclin pathway … A) Phosphodiesterase inhibitors B) Antagonists of endothelin receptors C) Prostacyclin analogues
QUESTIONS.exp: The treatment column reads 'Antagonists of endothelin receptors', 'Phosphodiesterase inhibitors' and 'Prostacyclin analogues' in that order. The logic is to block the promoted pathway and to replace the inhibited ones. (Book p215)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pathology Triad, Endothelin/NO/Prostacyclin Pathway Treatment Table, Clinical Presentation and the RV Dilatation and RV Failure Sign Chains
QUESTIONS.q: Which two symptoms are bracketed on page 215 as occurring 'without overt signs of heart & lung disease'?
QUESTIONS.exp: The presentation bracket joins 'Breathlessness' and 'Fatigue' to 'without overt signs of heart & lung disease'. Chest pain and syncope appear only later, once the right ventricle is under strain. (Book p215)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pathology Triad, Endothelin/NO/Prostacyclin Pathway Treatment Table, Clinical Presentation and the RV Dilatation and RV Failure Sign Chains
QUESTIONS.q: Which chain is printed on page 215 for RV dilatation in pulmonary hypertension?
opts: LV dilatation → septal push → ↓RV volume → ↓CO → breathlessness, fatigue, syncope
RV dilatation → septal push → ↓LV volume → ↓CO → breathlessness, fatigue, syncope
RV dilatation → septal push → ↑LV volume → ↓CO → breathlessness, fatigue, syncope
RV dilatation → tricuspid stenosis → ↓RV filling → ↓CO → breathlessness, fatigue, syncope
QUESTIONS.exp: The arrow chain reads 'RV dilatation → septal push → ↑ LV volume → ↓ CO' and then brackets the three consequences 'Breathlessness, Fatigue, Syncope'. Note the printed direction: LV volume rises here, the reverse of the massive-VTE chain on page 206. (Book p215)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pathology Triad, Endothelin/NO/Prostacyclin Pathway Treatment Table, Clinical Presentation and the RV Dilatation and RV Failure Sign Chains
QUESTIONS.q: How does page 215 explain chest pain in pulmonary hypertension?
opts: ↓RV filling + ↑RV afterload → RV ischemia → chest pain
RV dilatation → pericardial stretch → pericarditis → chest pain
↓LV filling + ↑LV afterload → LV ischemia → chest pain
↑RV filling + ↓RV afterload → RV ischemia → chest pain
QUESTIONS.exp: The line reads '↓ RV filling + ↑ RV afterload → RV ischemia → Chest pain'. Reduced filling reduces coronary perfusion while the raised afterload increases oxygen demand — a supply-demand mismatch in the right ventricle. (Book p215)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pathology Triad, Endothelin/NO/Prostacyclin Pathway Treatment Table, Clinical Presentation and the RV Dilatation and RV Failure Sign Chains
QUESTIONS.q: Which four findings are grouped under RV failure on page 215, and what happens to the apex?
opts: Pleural effusion, pulmonary edema, splenomegaly, and the apex shifts outwards
Ascites, edema, hepatomegaly, and the apex shifts inwards
Ascites, peripheral cyanosis, hepatomegaly, and the apex remains normal
Ascites, edema, hepatomegaly, and the apex shifts outwards
QUESTIONS.exp: The last bullet reads 'RV failure : Ascites, edema, hepatomegaly, apex shifts outwards.' The outward (leftward) apex shift accompanies the right ventricular enlargement. (Book p215)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pathology Triad, Endothelin/NO/Prostacyclin Pathway Treatment Table, Clinical Presentation and the RV Dilatation and RV Failure Sign Chains
QUESTIONS.q: Match each bedside sign with its printed explanation — 1) Loud P2 2) Wide splitting of P2 3) S3 4) JVP … A) 'a' waves B) Listed as an auscultatory sign in RV failure C) Pulmonary HTN → RA-RV dilatation → ↑diastolic filling pressure D) Listed as an auscultatory finding without a bracketed mechanism
QUESTIONS.exp: Under auscultation the page prints 'Loud P2' then, 'In RV failure', 'wide splitting of P2' and 'S3 (Pulmonary HTN → RA-RV dilatation → ↑Diastolic filling pressure)'; the JVP line reads 'a waves'. Only the S3 carries an explicit mechanism on the page. (Book p215)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pathology Triad, Endothelin/NO/Prostacyclin Pathway Treatment Table, Clinical Presentation and the RV Dilatation and RV Failure Sign Chains
QUESTIONS.q: A patient with long-standing pulmonary hypertension now has ascites, pedal oedema, a pulsatile liver and an apex beat displaced outwards. Which printed signs belong to this stage, and which finding is described as rare?
opts: RV failure with ascites, edema, hepatomegaly and an outward apex shift; clubbing is described as rare in the figure
LV failure with ascites, edema, hepatomegaly and an inward apex shift; clubbing is described as common
RV failure with clear lungs, a fixed split S2 and an inward apex shift; clubbing is described as rare
RV failure with ascites, edema, hepatomegaly and an outward apex shift; clubbing is described as universal
QUESTIONS.exp: The RV failure bullet reads 'Ascites, edema, hepatomegaly, apex shifts outwards', and the figure labels 'Clubbing rare' alongside 'Cold extremities', 'Peripheral edema' and a 'Large pulsatile liver'. The lungs are separately labelled clear. (Book p215)

QUESTIONS.sec: PA Catheterisation Gold Standard, the Three PAH Murmurs (Carvallo, Ejection Systolic, Graham Steell), CXR Findings, PA Aneurysm Causes and ECG RVH Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: Which investigation is named the gold standard for diagnosis on page 216?
QUESTIONS.exp: Page 216 opens with 'PA catheterisation : Gold standard for diagnosis.' This matches the page 214 definition, which required a mean PAP measured at right heart catheterisation. (Book p216)

QUESTIONS.sec: PA Catheterisation Gold Standard, the Three PAH Murmurs (Carvallo, Ejection Systolic, Graham Steell), CXR Findings, PA Aneurysm Causes and ECG RVH Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: Carvallo's sign on page 216 is attached to which murmur, and what does it describe?
opts: The pan systolic murmur, which increases on expiration; it is at the apex, low pitched and rumbling
The pan systolic murmur, which increases on inspiration; it is lower left sternal border, high pitched and blowing
The ejection systolic murmur, which decreases on inspiration; it is upper right sternal border, high pitched and blowing
The early diastolic murmur, which increases on inspiration; it is lower left sternal border, low pitched and rumbling
QUESTIONS.exp: Under '1. Pan systolic murmur' the page prints '↑ on inspiration : Carvallo's sign', 'Lower left sternal border' and 'High pitched, blowing'. The inspiratory increase is the right-sided (tricuspid regurgitation) manoeuvre. (Book p216)

QUESTIONS.sec: PA Catheterisation Gold Standard, the Three PAH Murmurs (Carvallo, Ejection Systolic, Graham Steell), CXR Findings, PA Aneurysm Causes and ECG RVH Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: Which description of Graham Steell's murmur is printed on page 216?
opts: Early diastolic murmur from LV dilatation in severe systemic HTN, heard sitting up, leaning forward and in fixed inspiration, indicating aortic regurgitation
Mid diastolic murmur from PA dilatation in mild PAH, heard in expiration, indicating pulmonary stenosis
Early systolic murmur from PA dilatation in severe PAH, heard leaning forward, indicating tricuspid regurgitation
Early diastolic murmur from PA dilatation in severe PAH, heard sitting up, leaning forward and in fixed expiration, indicating pulmonary regurgitation
QUESTIONS.exp: The third murmur reads 'Early diastolic murmur : Graham Steells murmur. D/t PA dilatation (Severe PAH). Sitting up, leaning forward and fixed expiration. Indicates pulmonary regurgitation +.' The murmur is diastolic because it is regurgitant flow back into the right ventricle. (Book p216)

QUESTIONS.sec: PA Catheterisation Gold Standard, the Three PAH Murmurs (Carvallo, Ejection Systolic, Graham Steell), CXR Findings, PA Aneurysm Causes and ECG RVH Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three murmurs are printed on page 216, one is not:
opts: Ejection systolic murmur d/t pulmonary stenosis
QUESTIONS.exp: Page 216 lists exactly three murmurs in PAH: pan systolic, ejection systolic from pulmonary stenosis, and the early diastolic Graham Steell's murmur. Mitral stenosis is mentioned on page 213 only as a cause of class 2 disease, not as a PAH murmur. (Book p216)

QUESTIONS.sec: PA Catheterisation Gold Standard, the Three PAH Murmurs (Carvallo, Ejection Systolic, Graham Steell), CXR Findings, PA Aneurysm Causes and ECG RVH Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: Which four findings are labelled on the PAH chest radiograph on page 216?
opts: Large central pulmonary arteries, right ventricular hypertrophy, rapid attenuation of pulmonary vessels and clear lung fields
Large central pulmonary veins, right atrial enlargement, delayed attenuation of pulmonary vessels and clear lung fields
Small central pulmonary arteries, right ventricular hypertrophy, rapid attenuation of pulmonary vessels and bilateral infiltrates
Large central pulmonary arteries, left ventricular hypertrophy, rapid attenuation of pulmonary vessels and clear lung fields
QUESTIONS.exp: The labelled film reads from top to bottom 'Large central pulmonary arteries', 'Right ventricular hypertrophy', 'Rapid attenuation of pulmonary vessels' and 'Clear lung fields'. Rapid tapering with clear fields separates vascular from parenchymal disease. (Book p216)

QUESTIONS.sec: PA Catheterisation Gold Standard, the Three PAH Murmurs (Carvallo, Ejection Systolic, Graham Steell), CXR Findings, PA Aneurysm Causes and ECG RVH Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: The page 216 figure caption names two diseases causing a pulmonary artery aneurysm: Behçet's and ______.
QUESTIONS.exp: The caption reads 'Pulmonary artery aneurysm : Behçet's, Takayasu'. Both are large-vessel arteritides, which is why the aneurysm appears in the PA rather than in the left-sided circulation alone. (Book p216)

QUESTIONS.sec: PA Catheterisation Gold Standard, the Three PAH Murmurs (Carvallo, Ejection Systolic, Graham Steell), CXR Findings, PA Aneurysm Causes and ECG RVH Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: Which ECG criterion for right ventricular hypertrophy is printed with the strip on page 216?
QUESTIONS.exp: The line beside the ECG reads 'r/s ratio > 1 in V1 (Indicates RVH)'. The accompanying note flips the normal pattern: 'Large S wave in V1' and 'Large r wave in V6' are the normal findings. (Book p216)

QUESTIONS.sec: PA Catheterisation Gold Standard, the Three PAH Murmurs (Carvallo, Ejection Systolic, Graham Steell), CXR Findings, PA Aneurysm Causes and ECG RVH Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the ECG note on page 216.
opts: True — the note says PAH abolishes the r wave in V6 while preserving the S wave in V1
False — the note says a normal ECG always shows an r/s ratio > 1 in V1
False — in a normal ECG there is a large r wave in V1 and a large S wave in V6
True — in a normal ECG there is a large S wave in V1 and a large r wave in V6
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Normal ECG : Large S wave in V1. Large r wave in V6.' RV hypertrophy reverses this dominance, which is exactly why 'r/s ratio > 1 in V1' is used as the criterion on the same page. (Book p216)

QUESTIONS.sec: Investigations to Exclude Other Causes (PFT, ECHO, V/Q, Sleep Study, HRCT, 6MWT), the Vaso-Reactivity Test, General Treatment and the NYHA-Stratified Drug and Surgical Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which pulmonary function pattern is printed for pulmonary hypertension on page 217?
opts: FEV1/FVC low, FVC normal, DLCO normal
QUESTIONS.exp: The PFT block reads 'FEV/FVC : Normal', 'FVC : Normal' and 'DLCO ↓'. A purely vascular disease leaves spirometry intact but reduces gas transfer, mirroring the vascular pattern of chapter 33. (Book p217)

QUESTIONS.sec: Investigations to Exclude Other Causes (PFT, ECHO, V/Q, Sleep Study, HRCT, 6MWT), the Vaso-Reactivity Test, General Treatment and the NYHA-Stratified Drug and Surgical Table
QUESTIONS.q: Match each investigation with the reason printed beside it on page 217 — 1) ECHO 2) V/Q scan 3) Sleep study 4) HRCT … A) To r/o interstitial lung disease B) To r/o chronic thromboembolic PAH C) To assess RV function and TR D) To r/o obstructive sleep apnea
QUESTIONS.exp: The lines read 'ECHO : To assess RV function, TR', 'V/Q scan : To r/o chronic thromboembolic PAH', 'Sleep study : To r/o obstructive sleep apnea' and 'HRCT : To r/o interstitial lung disease'. Each test is screening out a competing class of pulmonary hypertension. (Book p217)

QUESTIONS.sec: Investigations to Exclude Other Causes (PFT, ECHO, V/Q, Sleep Study, HRCT, 6MWT), the Vaso-Reactivity Test, General Treatment and the NYHA-Stratified Drug and Surgical Table
QUESTIONS.q: The 6-minute walk test on page 217 is done for which stated purpose?
QUESTIONS.exp: The line reads '6-minute walk test : To determine prognosis.' It is a functional and prognostic measure, not a diagnostic test — diagnosis rests on PA catheterisation per page 216. (Book p217)

QUESTIONS.sec: Investigations to Exclude Other Causes (PFT, ECHO, V/Q, Sleep Study, HRCT, 6MWT), the Vaso-Reactivity Test, General Treatment and the NYHA-Stratified Drug and Surgical Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which response defines a positive vaso-reactivity test on page 217?
opts: PAP decreases by 20 mmHg or PAP < 40 mmHg, with BP and CO unchanged; seen in 10% of cases
PAP decreases by 10 mmHg or PAP < 40 mmHg, with BP falling and CO rising; seen in 30% of cases
PAP decreases by 10 mmHg or PAP < 25 mmHg, with BP and CO unchanged; seen in 10% of cases
PAP decreases by 10 mmHg or PAP < 40 mmHg, with BP and CO unchanged; seen in 10% of cases
QUESTIONS.exp: The block reads 'Patient given nitric oxide (Potent PA vasodilator) → PAP measured', 'Positive test (10% cases) → PAP decreases by 10 mmHg/PAP < 40 mmHg' and a brace stating that BP and CO 'Remains the same'. The fall must be selective for the pulmonary circulation. (Book p217)

QUESTIONS.sec: Investigations to Exclude Other Causes (PFT, ECHO, V/Q, Sleep Study, HRCT, 6MWT), the Vaso-Reactivity Test, General Treatment and the NYHA-Stratified Drug and Surgical Table
QUESTIONS.q: What inference follows a positive vaso-reactivity test, and which drug and dose are printed?
opts: Pulmonary HTN responds to high dose CCBs — nifedipine 240 mg
