Pulmonary HTN responds to high dose CCBs — diltiazem 240 mg
Pulmonary HTN responds to phosphodiesterase inhibitors — sildenafil 240 mg
Pulmonary HTN responds to low dose CCBs — nifedipine 60 mg
QUESTIONS.exp: The inference line reads 'Positive test → Pulmonary HTN responds to high dose CCBs (Nifedipine 240 mg)'. The same 240 mg nifedipine figure is repeated in the specific-treatment table's first row. (Book p217)

QUESTIONS.sec: Investigations to Exclude Other Causes (PFT, ECHO, V/Q, Sleep Study, HRCT, 6MWT), the Vaso-Reactivity Test, General Treatment and the NYHA-Stratified Drug and Surgical Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which four general treatment measures are listed at the start of page 217, including one contraindication?
opts: Oral anticoagulants, long term O2 therapy, diuretics for right heart failure, and pregnancy permitted
Oral anticoagulants, long term O2 therapy, diuretics for right heart failure, and pregnancy contraindicated
Oral anticoagulants, long term O2 therapy, beta blockers for right heart failure, and pregnancy permitted
Oral anticoagulants, inhaled nitric oxide, diuretics for left heart failure, and pregnancy contraindicated
QUESTIONS.exp: The measures read 'Oral anticoagulants (To prevent thrombosis & thromboembolism)', 'Long term O2 therapy', 'Diuretics for right heart failure' and 'Pregnancy contraindicated'. Anticoagulation here is prophylaxis against in-situ thrombosis, not treatment of embolism. (Book p217)

QUESTIONS.sec: Investigations to Exclude Other Causes (PFT, ECHO, V/Q, Sleep Study, HRCT, 6MWT), the Vaso-Reactivity Test, General Treatment and the NYHA-Stratified Drug and Surgical Table
QUESTIONS.q: For NYHA I–3 disease, which drug pair is printed in the specific-treatment table?
QUESTIONS.exp: The NYHA I–3 row reads 'Tadalafil (Phosphodiesterase -5 inhibitor) + Ambrisentan (Endothelin receptor antagonist)'. Epoprostenol and treprostinil belong to the NYHA class-4 row, and nifedipine to the positive vaso-reactivity row above. (Book p217)

QUESTIONS.sec: Investigations to Exclude Other Causes (PFT, ECHO, V/Q, Sleep Study, HRCT, 6MWT), the Vaso-Reactivity Test, General Treatment and the NYHA-Stratified Drug and Surgical Table
QUESTIONS.q: A patient with PAH has symptoms at rest. Using the page 217 table, which prostanoid details are printed?
opts: Iloprost (most common) via a permanent tunnel catheter in the IJV, treprostinil via a microinfusion pump, and selexipag as a chemically stable oral prostacyclin derivative
Epoprostenol (most common) via a permanent tunnel catheter in the IJV, treprostinil orally, and selexipag as an inhaled prostacyclin analogue already available
Epoprostenol (most common) via a microinfusion pump, treprostinil via a permanent tunnel catheter in the IJV, and selexipag as an oral endothelin antagonist
Epoprostenol (most common) via a permanent tunnel catheter in the IJV, treprostinil via a microinfusion pump, and selexipag as a chemically stable oral prostacyclin derivative not yet available
QUESTIONS.exp: The class-4 row reads 'Prostanoids : Epoprostenol (m/c) via permanent tunnel catheter in IJV; Trepostinil (via microinfusion pump); Selexipag : Chemically stable, Orally active prostacyclin derivative, Not available yet.' The drug name is printed 'Trepostinil'. (Book p217)

QUESTIONS.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
QUESTIONS.q: Page 218 defines bronchiectasis as abnormal and irreversible dilatation of bronchi (initially medium sized, later the entire bronchial tree) plus ______ fibrosis of bronchioles.
QUESTIONS.exp: The definition joins 'Abnormal and irreversible dilatation of bronchi (Initially medium sized → entire bronchial tree)' with 'Obliterative fibrosis of bronchioles → Obstructive lung disease (can have restrictive component)'. The bronchiolar fibrosis explains the mixed obstructive-restrictive physiology. (Book p218)

QUESTIONS.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
QUESTIONS.q: How does the page 218 note define pseudobronchiectasis, and which two infections are named?
opts: Reversible dilatation of bronchi following infection — influenza and COVID
Reversible dilatation of bronchioles following obstruction — tuberculosis and measles
Irreversible dilatation of bronchioles following infection — influenza and COVID
Reversible dilatation of bronchi following fibrosis — influenza and tuberculosis
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Pseudobronchiectasis : Reversible dilatation of bronchi following infection (Influenza, COVID).' Reversibility is what separates it from the irreversible disease defined in the opening line. (Book p218)

QUESTIONS.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about how bronchiectasis is classified on page 218.
opts: False — it is listed among the restrictive lung diseases with no obstructive component
True — it is listed among the obstructive lung diseases and the definition adds that it can have a restrictive component
False — it is listed as a purely vascular lung disease
True — it is listed among the obstructive diseases but can never have a restrictive component
QUESTIONS.exp: The definition ends '→ Obstructive lung disease (can have restrictive component)', and the list of obstructive diseases places bronchiectasis at item d, after COPD, bronchial asthma and bronchiolitis. Both the obstructive label and the possible restrictive component are printed. (Book p218)

QUESTIONS.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
QUESTIONS.q: Which sequence does the page 218 pathogenesis flowchart print after the initial infective insult?
opts: Infection (mostly TB)/idiopathic → inflammation → cartilage hypertrophy → abnormal and reversible dilatation of bronchi
Infection (mostly TB)/idiopathic → inflammation → goblet cell hyperplasia → loss of smooth muscle → abnormal dilatation
Infection (mostly TB)/idiopathic → inflammation → loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue in bronchi → abnormal and irreversible dilatation of bronchi
Infection (mostly TB)/idiopathic → fibrosis → loss of cilia → abnormal and irreversible dilatation of bronchioles
QUESTIONS.exp: The flowchart runs 'Initial insult : Infection (mostly TB)/idiopathic' → 'Inflammation' → 'Loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue in bronchi (Bronchi & bronchiole both have smooth muscle)' → 'Abnormal & irreversible dilatation of bronchi'. Goblet cell hyperplasia sits on the separate mucus limb of the chart. (Book p218)

QUESTIONS.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
QUESTIONS.q: The flowchart parenthesises a fact about smooth muscle in the airways. Which statement is printed?
opts: Only bronchi have smooth muscle, bronchioles do not
Only bronchioles have smooth muscle, bronchi do not
Neither bronchi nor bronchioles have smooth muscle; only the trachea does
Bronchi and bronchioles both have smooth muscle
QUESTIONS.exp: The bracket after 'Loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue in bronchi' reads '(Bronchi & bronchiole both have smooth muscle)'. This contrasts with cartilage, which is lost at bronchiolar level and is discussed later in the chapter's treatment rationale. (Book p218)

QUESTIONS.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
QUESTIONS.q: The mucus limb of the page 218 flowchart runs through three steps. Which sequence is printed?
opts: Mucous gland hyperplasia → serous secretion → bronchospasm
Goblet cell atrophy → mucus inspissation → dilatation of airway
Goblet cell hyperplasia → mucus hypersecretion → obstruction of airway
Goblet cell hyperplasia → mucus hypersecretion → loss of cilia
QUESTIONS.exp: One arrow of the chart reads '3. Goblet cell hyperplasia → mucus hypersecretion → Obstruction of airway.' Loss of cilia is a separate numbered step (1) with its own downstream consequence, pooling of secretion. (Book p218)

QUESTIONS.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
QUESTIONS.q: Which chain is printed as step 1 on the left of the page 218 flowchart?
opts: Loss of goblet cells → loss of mucociliary escalator → pooling of secretion
Loss of cilia → loss of mucociliary escalator mechanism → pooling of secretion in airway
Loss of cilia → mucus hypersecretion → obstruction of airway
Loss of cartilage → airway collapse → pooling of secretion in airway
QUESTIONS.exp: Step 1 reads 'Loss of cilia → loss of micro ciliary escalator mechanism → pooling of secretion in airway', and the pooled secretion loops back into 'microbial colonisation leading to infusion' and inflammation. Cartilage loss is not part of this first step. (Book p218)

QUESTIONS.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
QUESTIONS.q: Match each numbered or arrowed step of the page 218 flowchart with its printed text — 1) Step 1 2) Step 2 3) Step 3 4) Arrow back into inflammation … A) Weakening & inflammation of bronchial wall B) Loss of cilia → loss of mucociliary escalator → pooling of secretion C) Microbial colonisation leading to infusion D) Goblet cell hyperplasia → mucus hypersecretion → obstruction of airway
QUESTIONS.exp: The flowchart numbers '1. Loss of cilia → loss of micro ciliary escalator mechanism → pooling of secretion in airway', '2. weakening & inflammation of bronchial wall' and '3. Goblet cell hyperplasia → mucus hypersecretion → Obstruction of airway', and the closed arrow returning to inflammation reads 'microbial colonisation leading to infusion'. (Book p218)

QUESTIONS.sec: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
QUESTIONS.q: Match each morphological type with the letter used in the page 219 grades figure — 1) Cylindrical/tubular 2) Varicose 3) Saccular/cystic … A) S B) C C) V
QUESTIONS.exp: The caption reads 'A normal bronchus (N) compared with the three grades of severity of bronchiectasis: cylindrical (C), varicose (V), and saccular (cystic) (S)'. The letters C, V and S follow the severity order shown. (Book p219)

QUESTIONS.sec: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
QUESTIONS.q: The page 219 note on traction bronchiectasis links it to fibrosis and to a classification. Which statement is printed?
opts: Traction bronchiectasis → elastolysis (restrictive type: classified under ILD)
Traction bronchiectasis → fibrosis (restrictive type: classified under ILD)
Traction bronchiectasis → fibrosis (obstructive type: classified under COPD)
Traction bronchiectasis → atelectasis (mixed type: classified under bronchiectasis)
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Traction bronchiectasis → Fibrosis (Restrictive type : Classified under ILD).' The dilatation is pulled open by surrounding fibrotic contraction, so the physiology is restrictive rather than obstructive. (Book p219)

QUESTIONS.sec: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
QUESTIONS.q: Which epidemiological details are printed in the page 219 note?
opts: Usually unilateral, most common lobe the left lower lobe, F > M, 20–40 yrs
Usually unilateral, most common lobe the left upper lobe, M > F, 50–70 yrs
Usually bilateral, most common lobe the right middle lobe, M > F, 20–40 yrs
Usually unilateral, most common lobe the left lower lobe, F > M, 50–70 yrs
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Bronchiectasis : usually unilateral (can become bilateral)', 'm/c lobe involved : Left lower lobe', 'F > m' and '50 – 70 yrs'. The right middle lobe is the site of Brock's syndrome on page 220, not the overall commonest lobe. (Book p219)

QUESTIONS.sec: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the laterality of bronchiectasis printed on page 219.
opts: True — it is usually unilateral but can become bilateral
True — the left lower lobe is spared because of its longer bronchus
False — it is always bilateral by definition
False — it is always unilateral and never becomes bilateral
QUESTIONS.exp: The note says 'usually unilateral (can become bilateral)'. It also names the left lower lobe as the commonest lobe involved, so the left lower lobe is the most, not the least, affected site. (Book p219)

QUESTIONS.sec: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
QUESTIONS.q: Match each histological panel caption with its letter on page 219 — 1) Fibrosis and cartilage destruction 2) Mucosal and mucous gland hyperplasia 3) Excessive mucus and exudate 4) Inflammatory cell infiltrate … A) b B) d C) a D) c
QUESTIONS.exp: The four panels are captioned 'a. Fibrosis and cartilage destruction', 'b. mucosal and mucous gland hyperplasia', 'c. Excessive mucus and exudate' and 'd. Inflammatory cell infiltrate'. Cartilage destruction is what allows the airway to dilate irreversibly. (Book p219)

QUESTIONS.sec: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
QUESTIONS.q: A patient with pulmonary fibrosis has dilated bronchi within the fibrotic zone on CT. How does page 219 classify this?
opts: Traction bronchiectasis, an obstructive type classified under COPD
Traction bronchiectasis, a restrictive type classified under ILD
Saccular bronchiectasis, a cystic type requiring resection
QUESTIONS.exp: Page 219 prints 'Traction bronchiectasis → Fibrosis (Restrictive type : Classified under ILD)'. The dilatation is part of the fibrotic process rather than a primary infective airway disease, which is why it is filed under ILD. (Book p219)

QUESTIONS.sec: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
QUESTIONS.q: Three morphological types of dilatation are shown on page 219. Which list is printed?
QUESTIONS.exp: The three labelled drawings read 'Cylindrical / tubular', 'Varicose' and 'Cystic', with the figure caption adding 'saccular (cystic) (S)'. Fusiform, beaded and moniliform are not printed here. (Book p219)

QUESTIONS.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
QUESTIONS.q: Match each named paediatric syndrome with its printed abnormality — 1) Mounier-Kuhn 2) William Campbell 3) Kartagener's syndrome 4) Young's syndrome … A) Azoospermia causing infertility B) Tracheobronchomegaly C) Primary ciliary dyskinesia D) Absence of cartilage
QUESTIONS.exp: The list reads 'Mounier Kuhn : Tracheobronchomegaly', 'William Campbell : Absence of cartilage', 'Kartagener's syndrome : Primary ciliary dyskinesia' and 'Young's syndrome : Azoospermia → Infertility'. Mounier-Kuhn enlarges the airway while William Campbell weakens it through missing cartilage. (Book p220)

QUESTIONS.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
QUESTIONS.q: Which triad does page 220 print for Kartagener's syndrome?
opts: Sinusitis, situs inversus and yellow nails
QUESTIONS.exp: The page reads 'Kartagener's syndrome : Primary ciliary dyskinesia (bronchiectasis, sinusitis & situs inversus)'. Azoospermia belongs to Young's syndrome, which sits immediately below it on the same list. (Book p220)

QUESTIONS.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
QUESTIONS.q: Three conditions are bracketed on page 220 as causing impaired mucociliary clearance. Which three are printed?
opts: Kartagener's syndrome, cystic fibrosis and yellow nail syndrome
Kartagener's syndrome, Young's syndrome and α1-antitrypsin deficiency
Kartagener's syndrome, cystic fibrosis and Young's syndrome
Cystic fibrosis, Young's syndrome and isolated IgA deficiency
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Impaired mucociliary clearance : Kartageners syndrome. Cystic fibrosis. Young's syndrome.' Yellow nail syndrome and α1-antitrypsin deficiency appear in the paediatric list above but not in the clearance bracket. (Book p220)

QUESTIONS.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
QUESTIONS.q: What does page 220 say about isolated IgA deficiency?
opts: It is the least common primary immunodeficiency
It is the most common secondary immunodeficiency
It is the commonest cause of bronchiectasis in adults
It is the most common primary immunodeficiency
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Isolated IgA deficiency : m/c primary immunodeficiency', and the adult list repeats 'Immunodeficiency (Also seen in childhood) : IgA deficiency (m/c)'. It is a predisposing cause, not the commonest overall cause of adult bronchiectasis. (Book p220)

QUESTIONS.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
QUESTIONS.q: Obliterative bronchiectasis due to infection in childhood is called ______ syndrome on page 220.
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Obliterative bronchiectasis d/t infection in childhood : mcleod's syndrome.' Brock's syndrome, printed lower on the same page, is a different entity — secondary lymphadenopathy causing right middle lobe bronchiectasis. (Book p220)

QUESTIONS.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
QUESTIONS.q: The adult aetiology list gives two percentages. Which pair is printed?
QUESTIONS.exp: The adult list reads 'Idiopathic : 30%' and 'Post-infection : mostly TB (40%)', with mechanical obstruction, immunodeficiency and autoimmune causes below them. TB dominates the adult post-infective group even though pertussis and measles dominate the paediatric one. (Book p220)

QUESTIONS.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
QUESTIONS.q: A patient with right middle lobe bronchiectasis is found to have enlarged hilar nodes compressing the lobar bronchus. Which eponym does page 220 print?
opts: McLeod's syndrome — obliterative bronchiectasis after childhood infection
Brock's syndrome — secondary lymphadenopathy causing right middle lobe bronchiectasis
William Campbell syndrome — absence of cartilage
QUESTIONS.exp: The adult mechanical-obstruction line reads 'Brock's syndrome : Secondary lymphadenopathy → Right middle lobe bronchiectasis'. The obstruction is extrinsic compression, not a primary airway wall defect. (Book p220)

QUESTIONS.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these appear in the paediatric aetiology list of page 220, one does not:
QUESTIONS.exp: The paediatric list contains pertussis/measles, the syndromes, cystic fibrosis, yellow nail syndrome and α1-antitrypsin deficiency. Sjögren syndrome is the autoimmune entry in the ADULT list at the foot of the page. (Book p220)

QUESTIONS.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: Which description of sputum is printed under the symptoms on page 221?
opts: Copious, foul smelling, three layered (mucus, mucopurulent, pus) with early morning exacerbation
Copious, odourless, four layered (mucus, mucopurulent, pus, blood) with early morning exacerbation
Copious, foul smelling, three layered (mucus, mucopurulent, pus) with evening exacerbation
Scanty, odourless, two layered (mucus, pus) with evening exacerbation
QUESTIONS.exp: The sputum sub-list reads 'Copius', 'Foul smelling', '3 layered : mucus, mucopurulent, pus' and 'early morning exacerbation'. The layering reflects the settling of different densities of secretions overnight. (Book p221)

QUESTIONS.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: How does page 221 explain haemoptysis in bronchiectasis?
opts: Due to erosion of granulation tissue into the pulmonary artery
Due to rupture of a thin walled vein on the bronchial wall
Due to bronchial artery hypertrophy from chronic inflammation
Due to rupture of a thin walled artery on the bronchial wall
QUESTIONS.exp: The line reads 'Hemoptysis : d/t rupture of thin walled vein on bronchial wall.' The vessel named is a vein, not an artery or granulation tissue. (Book p221)

QUESTIONS.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: Which auscultatory findings are printed, and in which type is clubbing described?
opts: Early and mid inspiratory coarse crackles with diffuse rhonchi; clubbing in adults, seen in the cylindrical type
Late inspiratory fine crackles with a pleural rub; clubbing in adults, seen in the varicose type
Early and mid inspiratory coarse crackles with diffuse rhonchi; clubbing in children, seen in the cystic type
Expiratory wheeze with diffuse rhonchi; clubbing in children, seen in the varicose type
QUESTIONS.exp: The findings read 'Clubbing in children (seen in cystic type)', then 'Early and mid inspiratory coarse crackles' and 'Diffuse rhonchi'. Coarse early-mid inspiratory crackles differ from the fine bibasal inspiratory crackles of fibrosis. (Book p221)

QUESTIONS.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: The page 221 note ties allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis to a specific bronchiectasis pattern. Which description is printed?
opts: Central, proximal, upper lobe bronchiectasis (usually b/l), which can go with interstitial lung disease
Central, distal, upper lobe bronchiectasis (usually unilateral), which can go with asthma only
Central, proximal, lower lobe bronchiectasis (usually b/l), which can go with emphysema
Peripheral, distal, lower lobe bronchiectasis (usually unilateral), which can go with COPD
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillius : Central, proximal, upperlobe bronchiectasis (usually b/l); Can go with interstitial lung disease (ILD).' The central-proximal distribution follows the larger airways colonised by Aspergillus. (Book p221)

QUESTIONS.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: The clinical-features section advises: 'always rule out bronchiectasis in recurrent ______.'
QUESTIONS.exp: The line reads 'Acute exacerbation d/t infection : Always rule out bronchiectasis in recurrent pneumonia.' Recurrent infection in the same segment is the clinical clue to an underlying dilated, poorly cleared airway. (Book p221)

QUESTIONS.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: Match each plain-film sign with its printed description — 1) Tram track sign 2) Bunch of grape appearance 3) Finger in glove appearance … A) Due to mucus inside B) Dilated airways with lack of tapering C) Clustered cystic spaces
QUESTIONS.exp: The film is captioned 'Tram track sign (Dilated airways with lack of tapering)', 'Bunch of grape appearance' and 'Finger in glove appearance (d/t mucus inside)'. Loss of tapering is the radiographic signature of the dilated airway. (Book p221)

QUESTIONS.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: Which three criteria for the CT diagnosis are printed under 'Volumetric multidetector helical CT scan : IOC'?
opts: Airway dilatation (1–1.5 times the adjacent vessels), lack of bronchial tapering, and tree-in-bud opacity (non-specific) from endobronchial obstruction giving nodules plus signet ring
Airway dilatation (1–1.5 times the adjacent vessels), lack of bronchial tapering, and honeycombing with traction Bronchiectasis
Airway narrowing (less than the adjacent vessels), lack of bronchial tapering, and tree-in-bud opacity
Airway dilatation (2–3 times the adjacent vessels), preserved bronchial tapering, and tree-in-bud opacity
QUESTIONS.exp: The three CT criteria read '1. Airway dilatation (1–1.5 times than adjacent vessels). 2. Lack of bronchial tapering. 3. Tree in bud opacity (Non-specific) : endobronchial obstruction → nodules + signet ring.' The ratio compares the airway with its adjacent vessel, not with a fixed diameter. (Book p221)

QUESTIONS.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: A young asthmatic with poorly controlled disease has central, proximal, upper lobe bronchiectasis on CT, and a background of interstitial lung disease is suspected. Which page 221 note applies?
opts: Sicca bronchiectasis — central, proximal, upper lobe bronchiectasis seen with haemoptysis and cough
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis — central, proximal, upper lobe bronchiectasis (usually b/l), which can go with ILD
Brock's syndrome — central, proximal, upper lobe bronchiectasis from secondary lymphadenopathy
Traction bronchiectasis — central, proximal, upper lobe bronchiectasis classified under ILD
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillius : Central, proximal, upperlobe bronchiectasis (usually b/l)' and 'Can go with interstitial lung disease (ILD)'. Sicca bronchiectasis, printed just above, is the TB-associated pattern with haemoptysis and cough. (Book p221)

QUESTIONS.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
QUESTIONS.q: The chest X-ray in bronchiectasis is introduced on page 221 with a single qualifier: 'X-Ray : ______ sensitivity'.
QUESTIONS.exp: The line reads 'X-Ray : Low sensitivity', which is why the volumetric multidetector helical CT scan is designated the IOC on the same page despite the classic tram track, bunch of grape and finger-in-glove signs. (Book p221)

QUESTIONS.sec: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
QUESTIONS.q: Match each complication with its printed qualifier — 1) Massive haemoptysis 2) Empyema 3) Secondary amyloidosis 4) Lung abscess … A) With bronchopleural fistula B) AA type C) Especially in dry bronchiectasis D) Listed without a qualifier
QUESTIONS.exp: The complication list reads '1. Cor pulmonale. 2. massive hemoptysis : especially in dry bronchiectasis. 3. Empyema with bronchopleural fistula. 4. Secondary Amyloidosis (AA). 5. Lung Abscess.' Dry bronchiectasis is the variant that bleeds rather than expectorates. (Book p222)

QUESTIONS.sec: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
QUESTIONS.q: Cor pulmonale is split on page 222 into acute and chronic types. Which two causes are printed?
opts: Acute: most common cause lung parenchymal disease; chronic: due to thromboembolism
Acute: most common cause thromboembolism; chronic: due to left heart disease
Acute: most common cause thromboembolism; chronic: due to lung parenchymal disease such as ILD, chronic bronchitis and bronchiectasis
Acute: most common cause pneumonia; chronic: due to ILD, chronic bronchitis and bronchiectasis
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Cor pulmonale : RV dilatation/hypertrophy +/− RV Failure' and then 'Types → Acute (m/c cause : thromboembolism)' and '→ Chronic (d/t lung parenchymal disease : ILD, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis)'. Acute cor pulmonale is embolic; chronic is parenchymal. (Book p222)

QUESTIONS.sec: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
QUESTIONS.q: Which concentration of nebulised hypertonic saline is printed under airway clearance on page 222?
QUESTIONS.exp: The airway-clearance line reads 'Nebulized 7% hypertonic saline, Steam inhalation, flutter valves', together with postural drainage. Hypertonic saline is used to osmotically draw water into secretions and make them easier to clear. (Book p222)

QUESTIONS.sec: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
QUESTIONS.q: Match each therapy with the role printed against it on page 222 — 1) Recombinant human DNase 2) Nebulized gentamycin 3) Nebulized 7% hypertonic saline … A) As prophylaxis B) Airway clearance agent C) Listed first among CF-associated therapies
QUESTIONS.exp: Under 'CF associated bronchiectasis' the page prints 'Recombinant human DNase' then 'Nebulized gentamycin as prophylaxis'. The 7% hypertonic saline belongs to the mainstay airway-clearance list above. The DNase thins DNA-rich secretions while the aminoglycoside suppresses chronic Pseudomonas. (Book p222)

QUESTIONS.sec: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
QUESTIONS.q: Macrolides have two roles in the page 222 treatment block. Which statement is printed?
opts: They do not reach effective lung concentrations, but have an immunomodulatory action recommended for 6–9 months
They reach effective concentration within lung and bronchial mucosa, and have an immunomodulatory action recommended for 3–6 months
They reach effective concentration within lung and bronchial mucosa, and have an immunomodulatory action recommended for 6–9 months
They reach effective concentration only in serum, and have an immunomodulatory action recommended for 6–9 months
QUESTIONS.exp: The antibiotic block reads 'macrolides & penicillin (Beta-lactams) : Reach effective concentration within lung and bronchial mucosa' and 'macrolides : immunomodulatory action - recommended for 6–9 months'. Both the penetration and the 6–9 month duration are printed. (Book p222)

QUESTIONS.sec: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
QUESTIONS.q: Which organism hierarchy is printed in the closing note on page 222?
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Organism infecting & weakening bronchial wall → Pseudomonas >> H. influenzae > S. pneumoniae.' The double arrow marks Pseudomonas as the dominant organism in damaged airways. (Book p222)

QUESTIONS.sec: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
QUESTIONS.q: A patient with long-standing bronchiectasis develops nephrotic-range proteinuria and a tissue biopsy shows AA deposits. Which page 222 complication does this represent?
opts: Secondary amyloidosis (AA), the fourth listed complication
Secondary amyloidosis (AL), the fourth listed complication
Empyema with bronchopleural fistula, the third listed complication
Cor pulmonale, the first listed complication
QUESTIONS.exp: The complication list includes '4. Secondary Amyloidosis (AA)'. Chronic infection drives serum amyloid A production, which is why the type is AA rather than AL. (Book p222)

QUESTIONS.sec: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
QUESTIONS.q: Which surgical and antibiotic strategy is printed for bronchiectasis on page 222?
opts: Bilateral lung transplant for localized disease, and oral antibiotics avoided because they do not reach the airway
Localized resection for localized bronchiectasis, and antibiotics chosen because macrolides and beta-lactams reach effective concentrations in lung and bronchial mucosa
Bilateral resection for bilateral bronchiectasis, and antibiotics chosen because aminoglycosides reach effective concentrations in lung and bronchial mucosa
Localized resection for diffuse bronchiectasis, and inhaled antibiotics as the only route
QUESTIONS.exp: The block reads 'Surgery : localized resection for localized bronchiectasis' and, under antibiotics, 'macrolides & penicillin (Beta-lactams) : Reach effective concentration within lung and bronchial mucosa'. Surgery is offered only when the disease is localised enough to remove completely. (Book p222)

QUESTIONS.sec: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
QUESTIONS.q: Which three disease groups are listed under 'Types' at the start of page 223?
opts: Pneumoconiosis, occupational asthma and hypersensitivity pneumonitis
Occupational asthma, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and Caplan syndrome
QUESTIONS.exp: The opening list reads 'Types : Pneumoconiosis. occupational asthma. Hypersensitive pneumonitis.' Silicosis and asbestosis are subtypes of pneumoconiosis listed further down the page, not parallel categories. (Book p223)

QUESTIONS.sec: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
QUESTIONS.q: How is pneumoconiosis defined on page 223?
opts: Accumulation of silica in the pleura with plaque formation
Accumulation of dust in lung and tissue reactions to its presence
Accumulation of dust in lung without any tissue reaction
Accumulation of organic dust in the alveoli with granuloma formation
QUESTIONS.exp: The definition reads 'accumulation of dust in lung & tissue reactions to its presence'. The tissue reaction is part of the definition, which is why the chapter separates the dusts by the pattern of reaction they provoke. (Book p223)

QUESTIONS.sec: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
QUESTIONS.q: Match each dust-particle size with its printed deposition site — 1) >3 µm 2) 0.5–3 µm 3) <0.5 µm … A) Alveoli B) Bronchiole C) Secondary bronchi
QUESTIONS.exp: The table reads '>3 µm — Secondary bronchi', '0.5–3 µm — Bronchiole' and '<0.5 µm — Alveoli'. The finest particles penetrate furthest, which is why alveolar dusts cause the pneumoconioses. (Book p223)

QUESTIONS.sec: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
QUESTIONS.q: Which pneumoconiosis is marked as the most common on page 223?
QUESTIONS.exp: The list reads '1. Silicosis : most common. 2. Asbestosis. 3. Coal worker pneumoconiosis (CWP). 4. Berylliosis.' The following page devotes a full risk-factor and table section to silicosis accordingly. (Book p223)

QUESTIONS.sec: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
QUESTIONS.q: What does the page 223 note say about byssinosis?
opts: It is hypersensitivity to organic dust exposure, with egg-shell calcification as its clinical feature
It is hypersensitivity to organic dust exposure, with recurrent Monday fever as its clinical feature
It is hypersensitivity to inorganic dust exposure, with recurrent Monday fever as its clinical feature
It is a pneumoconiosis from cotton dust, with progressive massive fibrosis as its clinical feature
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Byssinosis : Hypersensitivity to organic dust exposure' and 'Clinical features : Recurrent monday fever.' Monday fever describes the symptoms recurring on the first day back at work after the weekend. (Book p223)

QUESTIONS.sec: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three are printed as types of pneumoconiosis on page 223, one is listed separately as organic-dust hypersensitivity:
QUESTIONS.exp: The numbered pneumoconiosis list is silicosis, asbestosis, coal worker pneumoconiosis and berylliosis. Byssinosis appears only in the Note as hypersensitivity to organic dust — a different mechanism from dust accumulation with fibrosis. (Book p223)

QUESTIONS.sec: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
QUESTIONS.q: Particles larger than 3 µm are deposited in the ______, according to the page 223 table.
QUESTIONS.exp: The table pairs '>3 µm' with 'Secondary bronchi'. Particles of 0.5–3 µm reach the bronchiole and those below 0.5 µm reach the alveoli, which is where the interstitial reactions begin. (Book p223)

QUESTIONS.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
QUESTIONS.q: Which industries are listed as silicosis risk factors on page 224?
opts: Mining industry, quarries, blast furnaces, slate industry, sand stone industry, ceramics and rock cutting
Mining industry, battery manufacturing and textile industry
Textile industry, cement industry, ship building work and automobile industry
Ceramic industry, battery manufacturing and alloy industry
QUESTIONS.exp: The risk-factor list reads 'mining industry, Quarries, Blast furnaces, Slate industry, Sand stone industry, Ceramics, Rock cutting'. The textile/cement/shipbuilding list belongs to asbestosis on page 227 and the ceramic/battery/alloy list to berylliosis on page 229. (Book p224)

QUESTIONS.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
QUESTIONS.q: Which type of silica is most common, what is its composition, and which carries the higher occupational hazard?
opts: Crystalline silica (cristobalite); SiO2 (combined silica); higher risk of occupational hazard
Crystalline silica (quartz); SiO2 (free silica); higher risk of occupational hazard
Amorphous silica; SiO2 bound in silicates; higher risk of occupational hazard
Crystalline silica (quartz); SiO2 (free silica); lower risk of occupational hazard
QUESTIONS.exp: The block reads '1. Crystalline silica (Quartz) : m/c', 'Composition : SiO2 (Free silica)' and 'Higher risk of occupational hazard', with '2. Amorphous silica' as the second, lesser type. (Book p224)

QUESTIONS.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
QUESTIONS.q: Two features are printed for silicosis under 'FEATURES': lung parenchymal involvement with ______ pleural involvement, and a risk of malignancy and COPD.
QUESTIONS.exp: The line reads 'Lung parenchymal involvement (No pleural involvement)' and the next 'Risk of malignancy and COPD.' The absence of pleural disease is a printed point of contrast with asbestosis, which is dominated by pleural plaques. (Book p224)

QUESTIONS.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
QUESTIONS.q: The acute-versus-chronic silicosis table gives two exposure durations. Which pair is printed?
opts: Large quantity for 2 years (acute) versus 10–30 years (chronic)
Large quantity for 5 years (acute) versus 20–40 years (chronic)
Large quantity for 2 years (acute) versus 5–10 years (chronic)
Small quantity for 2 years (acute) versus 10–30 years (chronic)
QUESTIONS.exp: The exposure row reads 'Large quantity for 2 years' for acute silicosis and 'For 10–30 years' for chronic silicosis. The acute form needs an intense exposure over a short period, not a small one. (Book p224)

QUESTIONS.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
QUESTIONS.q: Which pathogenesis chain is printed for chronic silicosis in the table?
opts: Injury to capillary endothelium → alveolar haemorrhage and autoimmune illness (SLE, RA)
Injury to type II pneumocytes → progressive massive fibrosis and bronchogenic carcinoma
Injury to pulmonary alveolar macrophages → silicotuberculosis (primary TB) and immune deficiency (HIV)
Injury to pulmonary alveolar macrophages → silicotuberculosis (reactivation of latent TB) and autoimmune illness (SLE, RA)
QUESTIONS.exp: The chronic pathogenesis cell reads 'Injury to pulmonary alveolar macrophages', with a double-headed arrow to 'Silicotuberculosis (Reactivation of latent TB)' on one side and 'Autoimmune illness (SLE, RA)' on the other. The acute cell in the same row is printed as a dash. (Book p224)

QUESTIONS.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
QUESTIONS.q: In chronic silicosis, what frequency of chest signs is printed?
QUESTIONS.exp: The chronic clinical cell reads 'Chornic dry cough', 'Dyspnea on exertion' and 'Chest signs in 25% cases'. Most patients therefore have no chest signs despite established radiological disease. (Book p224)

QUESTIONS.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
QUESTIONS.q: Match each table row with its acute-silicosis entry — 1) Clinical features 2) Investigations 3) Prognosis … A) PAS positive milky white BAL B) Very poor C) Acute onset with severe dyspnea, hypoxia and weight loss
QUESTIONS.exp: Acute silicosis gives 'Acute onset : severe dyspnea, hypoxia, weight loss', 'PAS positive milky white BAL (Bronchoalveolar lavage)' and 'very poor' prognosis. The chronic column instead reads PFT with a mixed pattern and a dash for prognosis. (Book p224)

QUESTIONS.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
QUESTIONS.q: A sandblaster develops breathlessness, hypoxia and weight loss within two years, and lavage returns milky white PAS-positive fluid. Which diagnosis and prognostic statement match the page 224 table?
opts: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, with a very poor prognosis
Acute silicosis, with a very poor prognosis
Chronic silicosis, with a mixed pattern on spirometry
QUESTIONS.exp: The acute column combines 'Large quantity for 2 years', the dyspnea-hypoxia-weight loss triangle, 'PAS positive milky white BAL' and 'very poor' prognosis. Milky white PAS-positive lavage also appears under PAP on page 226, but the two-year heavy exposure and clinical triangle here are the printed acute-silicosis set. (Book p224)

QUESTIONS.sec: Radiology of Silicosis: Acute Crazy-Pavement CT Pattern and the Chronic Nodule-to-PMF Sequence with Egg-Shell Calcification and Upper Lobe ILD
QUESTIONS.q: Which three components make up the 'crazy pavement appearance' printed for acute silicosis on CT?
opts: Ground glass opacifications with destroyed lung structure, thin septa and multiple large nodules in pleura
Ground glass opacifications with intact structure of lung, thickened septa and multiple subpleural bullae
Consolidation with air bronchograms, thickened pleura and multiple centrilobular nodules
Ground glass opacifications with intact structure of lung, thickened septa and multiple centrilobular small nodules in parenchyma
QUESTIONS.exp: The CT panel is labelled 'Crazy pavement appearance : Ground glass opacifications (Intact structure of lung); Thickened septa; multiple centrilobular small nodules in parenchyma.' The preserved lung architecture distinguishes it from destructive fibrosis. (Book p225)

QUESTIONS.sec: Radiology of Silicosis: Acute Crazy-Pavement CT Pattern and the Chronic Nodule-to-PMF Sequence with Egg-Shell Calcification and Upper Lobe ILD
QUESTIONS.q: Which radiological progression is printed for chronic silicosis on page 225?
opts: Small unilateral asymmetric nodules → large conglomerate nodules (holly leaf appearance) + hilar lymphadenopathy with popcorn calcification → PMF, plus upper lobe interstitial lung disease
Large bilateral asymmetric nodules → small centrilobular nodules with angel wing appearance + hilar lymphadenopathy with egg shell calcification → PMF, plus lower lobe interstitial lung disease

Small bilateral symmetric centrilobular parenchymal nodules → large conglomerate nodules (angel wing appearance) ± cavitations + hilar lymphadenopathy with egg shell calcification → progressive massive fibrosis (PMF), plus upper lobe interstitial lung disease

Small bilateral symmetric centrilobular nodules → large conglomerate nodules (angel wing appearance) ± cavitations + hilar lymphadenopathy with egg shell calcification → PMF, plus lower lobe interstitial lung disease
QUESTIONS.exp: The film sequence on page 225 reads exactly from 'Small bilateral symmetric centrilobular parenchymal nodule' to 'Large conglomerate nodules (Angel wing appearance)' to '± Cavitations + Hilar lymphadenopathy with egg shell calcification' to 'Progressive massive fibrosis (PMF)', ending with 'upper lobe interstitial lung disease'. (Book p225)

QUESTIONS.sec: Radiology of Silicosis: Acute Crazy-Pavement CT Pattern and the Chronic Nodule-to-PMF Sequence with Egg-Shell Calcification and Upper Lobe ILD
QUESTIONS.q: The hilar node calcification of chronic silicosis on page 225 is described as ______ calcification.
QUESTIONS.exp: The label reads 'Hilar lymphadenopathy with egg shell calcification'. The hilar nodes calcify peripherally, giving a thin shell rather than a solid or popcorn density. (Book p225)

QUESTIONS.sec: Radiology of Silicosis: Acute Crazy-Pavement CT Pattern and the Chronic Nodule-to-PMF Sequence with Egg-Shell Calcification and Upper Lobe ILD
QUESTIONS.q: The large conglomerate nodules of chronic silicosis are described by which appearance on page 225?
QUESTIONS.exp: The caption reads 'Large conglomerate nodules (Angel wing appearance)'. Holly leaf and shaggy heart are the asbestos signs printed on page 227, and crazy pavement is the acute silicosis CT pattern. (Book p225)

QUESTIONS.sec: Radiology of Silicosis: Acute Crazy-Pavement CT Pattern and the Chronic Nodule-to-PMF Sequence with Egg-Shell Calcification and Upper Lobe ILD
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the two silicosis patterns on page 225.
opts: True — the chronic pattern is confined to the lower lobes
False — both patterns are described as crazy pavement on CT
False — the acute pattern is nodular progression to PMF, whereas the chronic pattern is crazy pavement
True — the acute pattern is a CT crazy-pavement appearance, whereas the chronic pattern progresses through nodules to PMF
QUESTIONS.exp: The acute column holds the single CT image captioned 'Crazy pavement appearance', while the chronic column holds the full film sequence of nodules → conglomerate nodules → PMF. The same chronic column ends with 'upper lobe interstitial lung disease'. (Book p225)

QUESTIONS.sec: Radiology of Silicosis: Acute Crazy-Pavement CT Pattern and the Chronic Nodule-to-PMF Sequence with Egg-Shell Calcification and Upper Lobe ILD
QUESTIONS.q: A quarry worker with 20 years of exposure has a chest film showing small symmetric nodules and egg-shell hilar calcification, and a CT showing upper lobe fibrosis. Which staging does page 225 support?
opts: Chronic silicosis with progressive massive fibrosis and upper lobe interstitial lung disease
Acute silicosis with crazy pavement pattern and milky white lavage
Chronic asbestosis with pleural plaques and lower lobe fibrosis
Coal worker pneumoconiosis with Caplan syndrome
QUESTIONS.exp: The chronic column of page 225 runs from the symmetric centrilobular nodules to conglomerate nodules with egg-shell hilar calcification to PMF, ending with upper lobe interstitial lung disease. Pleural plaques, by contrast, are the asbestos hallmark on page 227. (Book p225)

QUESTIONS.sec: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
QUESTIONS.q: Which conditions are listed on page 226 as showing a crazy pavement pattern of lung?
opts: Diffuse alveolar damage (DAD), allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP)
Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH), acute eosinophilic pneumonia (AEP) and pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis
Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH), hypersensitivity pneumonitis and sarcoidosis
Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH), acute eosinophilic pneumonia (AEP) and pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP)
QUESTIONS.exp: The note lists 'Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH)', 'Acute eosinophilic pneumonia (AEP)' and 'Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP)'. DAD and ABPA are not printed in this differential. (Book p226)

QUESTIONS.sec: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
QUESTIONS.q: What mechanism and lavage finding are printed for pulmonary alveolar proteinosis on page 226?
opts: Deficiency of GM-CSF receptors causing abnormal clearance of surfactant, with PAS positive milky white BAL
Antibodies against GM-CSF causing abnormal clearance of surfactant, with PAS positive milky white BAL
Antibodies against GM-CSF causing excessive surfactant production, with PAS negative thin BAL
Antibodies against surfactant protein-A causing abnormal clearance of surfactant, with PAS positive milky white BAL
QUESTIONS.exp: The PAP entry reads 'Antibodies against GM-CSF (Abnormal clearance of surfactant)' and 'PAS positive milky white BAL'. The defect is impaired macrophage clearance of surfactant driven by neutralising anti-GM-CSF antibodies. (Book p226)

QUESTIONS.sec: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
QUESTIONS.q: Which four features are printed as similarities between CWP and silicosis?
opts: Upper lobe involvement, injury to type II pneumocytes causing TB or autoimmune disease, ↑COPD, and pleural plaques ± calcification progressing to PMF
Upper lobe involvement, injury to PAMs causing TB or autoimmune disease, ↑COPD, and parenchymal nodules (<0.5 cm) with no cavitation
Upper lobe involvement, injury to PAMs causing TB or autoimmune disease, ↑COPD, and parenchymal nodules (>1 cm) ± cavitations progressing to PMF
Lower lobe involvement, injury to PAMs causing TB or autoimmune disease, ↓COPD, and parenchymal nodules (>3 cm) ± cavitations progressing to PMF
QUESTIONS.exp: The block reads 'Upper lobe involvement', 'Injury to PAMs → TB or autoimmune disease', '↑ COPD' and 'Parenchymal nodules (>1 cm) ± cavitations → PMF'. CWP is AKA black lung from coal dust exposure, with black pigmentation and fibrosis due to carbon pigment. (Book p226)

QUESTIONS.sec: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
QUESTIONS.q: The CWP-versus-silicosis table on page 226 has exactly three rows. Which set of entries is printed?
opts: Malignancy association present in silicosis and absent in CWP; hilar lymphadenopathy absent in silicosis and present in CWP; Caplan syndrome absent in silicosis and present in CWP
Malignancy association absent in silicosis and present in CWP; hilar lymphadenopathy present in silicosis and absent in CWP; Caplan syndrome present in silicosis and absent in CWP
Malignancy association present in silicosis and absent in CWP; hilar lymphadenopathy present in both; Caplan syndrome present in both
Malignancy association present in both; hilar lymphadenopathy absent in silicosis and present in CWP; Caplan syndrome absent in silicosis and present in CWP
QUESTIONS.exp: The table reads: 'Association with malignancy — Present (silicosis), Absent (CWP)'; 'Hilar lymphadenopathy — Absent (silicosis), Present (CWP)'; 'Caplan syndrome — Absent (silicosis), Present (CWP)'. This hilar row contradicts the chronic silicosis film label on page 225, a source inconsistency recorded in the caveat file. (Book p226)

QUESTIONS.sec: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
QUESTIONS.q: Which three components make up Caplan syndrome on page 226?
opts: Silicosis (necrobiotic nodule) + rheumatoid arthritis with IgM rheumatoid factor positive + active synovitis
Coal worker pneumoconiosis (necrobiotic nodule) + rheumatoid arthritis with IgA rheumatoid factor positive + inactive synovitis
Coal worker pneumoconiosis (necrobiotic nodule) + systemic lupus erythematosus with IgA rheumatoid factor positive + active synovitis
Coal worker pneumoconiosis (necrobiotic nodule) + rheumatoid arthritis with IgA rheumatoid factor positive + active synovitis
QUESTIONS.exp: The syndrome is spelled out as 'Coal worker pneumoconiosis (Necrobiotic nodule)' plus 'Rheumatoid arthritis : IgA rheumatoid factor positive' plus 'Active synovitis'. The serotype is IgA, and the arthritis must be active. (Book p226)

QUESTIONS.sec: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
QUESTIONS.q: A coal miner with rheumatoid arthritis has multiple peripheral lung nodules with cavitation. Which eponym applies, and what is the printed nodule size threshold for CWP?
opts: Silicosis with rheumatoid arthritis; CWP nodules are >1 cm
Caplan syndrome; CWP nodules are >3 cm
Caplan syndrome; CWP nodules are >1 cm
Caplan syndrome; CWP nodules are >1 mm
QUESTIONS.exp: Caplan syndrome is defined on page 226 as CWP with a necrobiotic nodule, rheumatoid arthritis (IgA rheumatoid factor positive) and active synovitis. The same page prints parenchymal nodules '(>1 cm) ± cavitations → PMF' for CWP. (Book p226)

QUESTIONS.sec: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these are printed under the page 226 crazy-pavement differential, one is not:
QUESTIONS.exp: The differential lists DAH, AEP and PAP only. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis appears on page 228 as a cause of non-caseating granuloma, a different list. (Book p226)

QUESTIONS.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
QUESTIONS.q: Match each fibre with its printed description on page 227 — 1) Serpentile/chrysotile 2) Crocidolite 3) Amosite … A) 90% of fibres, curly strands, less toxic B) Amphibole named first on the 10% limb C) Amphibole marked more dangerous
QUESTIONS.exp: The diagram reads 'Asbestos fibres' with a 90% limb to 'Serpentile/chrysotile (Curly strands) — Less toxic' and a 10% limb to 'Amphibole (Brittle long straight rods)', splitting into 'Crocidolite' and 'Amosite (more dangerous)'. Chrysotile is the only serpentine form listed. (Book p227)

QUESTIONS.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
QUESTIONS.q: Which amphibole is marked as more dangerous on page 227, and which two amphiboles are named?
opts: Crocidolite is marked more dangerous; the two amphiboles are crocidolite and amosite
Amosite is marked more dangerous; the two amphiboles are crocidolite and amosite
Amosite is marked more dangerous; the two amphiboles are amosite and tremolite
Chrysotile is marked more dangerous; the two amphiboles are chrysotile and amosite
QUESTIONS.exp: The amphibole limb names 'Crocidolite' and 'Amosite (more dangerous)'. Chrysotile sits on the serpentine limb and is labelled less toxic. (Book p227)

QUESTIONS.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
QUESTIONS.q: Match each pleural finding with its printed description — 1) Pleural plaques 2) Visceral pleural calcification 3) BAPE … A) Candle dripping and holly leaf sign B) Earliest, unilateral, hemorrhagic, exudative C) Crow feet sign
QUESTIONS.exp: The pleura table reads 'Pleural plaques (X-ray : Candle dripping, Holly leaf sign)', 'BAPE ... Earliest, unilateral, hemorrhagic, exudative' and 'Visceral pleural calcification (X-ray : Crow feet sign)'. Subpleural linear densities parallel to the plaque are also listed under the plaques. (Book p227)

QUESTIONS.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
QUESTIONS.q: Which set of features is printed for BAPE (benign asbestos related pleural effusion)?
opts: The earliest finding; unilateral, hemorrhagic and exudative, with eosin >25% and mesothelial cells <50%
The latest finding; bilateral, serous and transudative, with eosin <50% and mesothelial cells <25%
The earliest finding; unilateral, hemorrhagic and exudative, with eosin <25% and mesothelial cells <50%
The earliest finding; bilateral, hemorrhagic and exudative, with eosin <25% and mesothelial cells <50%
QUESTIONS.exp: The BAPE rows read 'Earliest, unilateral, hemorrhagic, exudative' and 'Eosin <25%, mesothelial cells <50%'. Both cell cut-offs are upper limits, and the fluid is exudative rather than transudative. (Book p227)

QUESTIONS.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
QUESTIONS.q: Bilateral lower lobe infiltrates with pleural plaques in asbestosis produce the ______ heart sign on page 227.
QUESTIONS.exp: The parenchymal row reads 'Bilateral lower lobe infiltrates with pleural plaques : Shaggy heart sign' and 'Diffuse massive fibrosis (DMF) of lower lobe'. The shaggy heart border is produced by the adjacent pleural and parenchymal disease, not by cardiomegaly. (Book p227)

QUESTIONS.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
QUESTIONS.q: Which parenchymal clinical features of asbestosis are printed in the right-hand column?
opts: No clinical signs, with fibrosis detectable only on imaging and a normal PFT pattern
Chest pain, dyspnea, and fibrosis with bibasal coarse inspiratory crackle, no clubbing and an obstructive PFT pattern
Chest pain, haemoptysis, and fibrosis with apical fine crackles, clubbing and a restrictive PFT pattern
Chest pain, dyspnea, and fibrosis with bibasal fine inspiratory crackle, clubbing and a restrictive PFT pattern
QUESTIONS.exp: The parenchyma column reads 'Chest pain', 'Dyspnea', and under 'Fibrosis': 'Bibasal fine inspiratory crackle', 'Clubbing' and 'PFT : Restrictive pattern'. The pleural column, in contrast, is the one printed with 'No clinical signs'. (Book p227)

QUESTIONS.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about pleural versus parenchymal asbestosis on page 227.
opts: False — both columns are printed as producing no clinical signs
True — the pleural column ends with 'no clinical signs', while the parenchymal column lists chest pain, dyspnoea and fibrosis signs
True — clubbing is printed under the pleural column only
False — the pleural column lists clubbing while the parenchymal column lists no signs
QUESTIONS.exp: The pleura column's clinical cell reads 'Progressive dyspnoea, Chest pain, No clinical signs', whereas the parenchyma column lists chest pain, dyspnoea, bibasal fine crackles, clubbing and a restrictive PFT. Clubbing belongs to the parenchymal disease. (Book p227)

QUESTIONS.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
QUESTIONS.q: A shipyard worker has unilateral haemorrhagic pleural fluid with 20% eosinophils and 40% mesothelial cells. Which page 227 entity is this, and what is its temporal relationship to other asbestos findings?
opts: BAPE — the earliest asbestos-related pleural finding
BAPE — the latest asbestos-related pleural finding
Malignant mesothelioma — with a latency of 10–30 years
Pleural plaque with visceral calcification — the crow feet sign
QUESTIONS.exp: BAPE is 'Earliest, unilateral, hemorrhagic, exudative' with 'Eosin <25%, mesothelial cells <50%'. The case values sit under both cut-offs, and BAPE is explicitly the earliest pleural manifestation, preceding plaques and calcification. (Book p227)

QUESTIONS.sec: Asbestos Malignancy: Lung Cancer vs Mesothelioma Table, Ferruginous Body, Berylliosis as Delayed Hypersensitivity with Non-Caseating Granulomas and the Granuloma Differential
QUESTIONS.q: Match each attribute with the asbestos-related tumour printed on page 228 — 1) Most common histology of lung cancer 2) Most common histology of mesothelioma 3) Latency of lung cancer 4) Latency of mesothelioma … A) > 30 years B) Adenocarcinoma > squamous cell carcinoma > small cell carcinoma C) 10–30 years D) Epitheloid > sarcomatoid
QUESTIONS.exp: The table reads 'Adenocarcinoma > Squamous cell carcinoma > small cell carcinoma' for lung cancer and 'Epitheloid > Sarcomatoid' for mesothelioma, with latency '10–30 years' and '> 30 years' respectively. Mesothelioma has the longer latency. (Book p228)

QUESTIONS.sec: Asbestos Malignancy: Lung Cancer vs Mesothelioma Table, Ferruginous Body, Berylliosis as Delayed Hypersensitivity with Non-Caseating Granulomas and the Granuloma Differential
QUESTIONS.q: Which pair of smoking associations and clinical features is printed for lung cancer versus mesothelioma?
opts: Lung cancer: smoking association present, chest pain + mass; mesothelioma: smoking association absent, cough + haemoptysis
Lung cancer: smoking association absent, cough + haemoptysis; mesothelioma: smoking association present, chest pain + mass
Lung cancer: smoking association present, cough + haemoptysis; mesothelioma: smoking association absent, chest pain + mass
Lung cancer: smoking association present, cough + haemoptysis; mesothelioma: smoking association present, chest pain + mass
QUESTIONS.exp: The row reads 'Smoking association — Present (lung cancer), Absent (mesothelioma)' and 'Clinical features — Cough + Hemoptysis versus Chest pain + mass'. Mesothelioma is the asbestos tumour not driven by smoking. (Book p228)

QUESTIONS.sec: Asbestos Malignancy: Lung Cancer vs Mesothelioma Table, Ferruginous Body, Berylliosis as Delayed Hypersensitivity with Non-Caseating Granulomas and the Granuloma Differential
QUESTIONS.q: Which mesothelioma markers and electron-microscopy features are printed on page 228?
opts: Markers cytokeratin 5/6 and WT-1; electron microscopy microvilli, desmosomes and tonofilaments
Markers pancytokeratin/calretinin; electron microscopy cilia, desmosomes and tonofilaments
Markers pancytokeratin/calretinin; electron microscopy microvilli, hemidesmosomes and tonofibrils
Markers pancytokeratin/calretinin; electron microscopy microvilli, desmosomes and tonofilaments
QUESTIONS.exp: The pathology cell lists 'markers : Pancytokeratin/calretinin', then 'electron microscopy : microvilli, Desmosomes, Tonofilaments'. The lung cancer pathology cell in the same row is printed as a dash. (Book p228)

QUESTIONS.sec: Asbestos Malignancy: Lung Cancer vs Mesothelioma Table, Ferruginous Body, Berylliosis as Delayed Hypersensitivity with Non-Caseating Granulomas and the Granuloma Differential
QUESTIONS.q: A ferruginous body is an asbestos body with a transparent core surrounded by ______ and protein, as printed on page 228.
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Ferruginous body : Asbestos body with transparent core surrounded by iron and protein.' The iron coating is what makes the body ferruginous and visible on stained sections. (Book p228)

QUESTIONS.sec: Asbestos Malignancy: Lung Cancer vs Mesothelioma Table, Ferruginous Body, Berylliosis as Delayed Hypersensitivity with Non-Caseating Granulomas and the Granuloma Differential
QUESTIONS.q: How is berylliosis characterised immunologically and histologically on page 228?
opts: Delayed hypersensitivity with caseating granulomas, clinically similar to tuberculosis
Immune complex deposition with non-caseating granulomas, clinically similar to rheumatoid arthritis
Delayed hypersensitivity with non-caseating granulomas, clinically similar to sarcoidosis
Immediate hypersensitivity with caseating granulomas, clinically similar to tuberculosis
QUESTIONS.exp: The entry reads 'Berylliosis : Delayed hypersensitivity with non caseating granulomas. Clinically similar to sarcoidosis.' Caseation is absent, which is why the differential on the same page lists other non-caseating granulomatous diseases. (Book p228)

QUESTIONS.sec: Asbestos Malignancy: Lung Cancer vs Mesothelioma Table, Ferruginous Body, Berylliosis as Delayed Hypersensitivity with Non-Caseating Granulomas and the Granuloma Differential
QUESTIONS.q: Match each condition listed under non-caseating granuloma on page 228 with its category — 1) Sarcoidosis 2) Cat scratch disease 3) Crohn's disease … A) Infection B) Idiopathic granulomatous disease C) Inflammatory bowel disease
QUESTIONS.exp: The list is 'Sarcoidosis, Tuberculosis, Lymphoma, Hypersensitive pneumonitis, Cat scratch disease, Berylliosis, Crohns disease.' Within it, cat scratch disease is infective and Crohn's is inflammatory bowel disease; sarcoidosis is the idiopathic comparator for berylliosis. (Book p228)

QUESTIONS.sec: Asbestos Malignancy: Lung Cancer vs Mesothelioma Table, Ferruginous Body, Berylliosis as Delayed Hypersensitivity with Non-Caseating Granulomas and the Granuloma Differential
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three appear in the page 228 list of conditions with non-caseating granuloma, one does not:
QUESTIONS.exp: The list of conditions with non-caseating granuloma includes sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, lymphoma, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, cat scratch disease, berylliosis and Crohn's disease. The option deliberately converts tuberculosis into its caseating form, which is not the printed entity. (Book p228)

QUESTIONS.sec: Berylliosis: Sarcoidosis Features That Are Absent, Industries, Upper Lobe ILD to PMF, Lymphocyte Proliferation Test, X-ray in 50% and the HRCT Triad
QUESTIONS.q: Which sarcoidosis findings are printed as ABSENT in berylliosis on page 229?
opts: Hilar adenopathy, ocular symptoms, parotid findings and erythema lesions
CNS symptoms, ocular symptoms, parotid findings and erythema (printed as erythemoid) lesions
CNS symptoms, cutaneous anergy, parotid findings and erythema lesions
CNS symptoms, ocular symptoms, parotid findings and erythema nodosum lesions
QUESTIONS.exp: The list reads 'Findings of sarcoidosis absent in berylliosis : CNS symptoms. Ocular symptoms. Parotid findings. erythemoid lesions.' Hilar adenopathy is NOT in this absent list — it appears under the berylliosis X-ray findings on the same page. (Book p229)

QUESTIONS.sec: Berylliosis: Sarcoidosis Features That Are Absent, Industries, Upper Lobe ILD to PMF, Lymphocyte Proliferation Test, X-ray in 50% and the HRCT Triad
QUESTIONS.q: Which three industries are printed as berylliosis risk factors?
opts: Ceramic industry, textile industry and alloy industry
Mining industry, battery manufacturing and alloy industry
Ceramic industry, battery manufacturing and alloy industry
Ceramic industry, battery manufacturing and ship building
QUESTIONS.exp: The risk factors read 'Ceramic industry', 'Battery manufacturing' and 'Alloy industry'. Textile, shipbuilding and mining belong to the asbestos and silica lists on pages 224 and 227. (Book p229)

QUESTIONS.sec: Berylliosis: Sarcoidosis Features That Are Absent, Industries, Upper Lobe ILD to PMF, Lymphocyte Proliferation Test, X-ray in 50% and the HRCT Triad
QUESTIONS.q: What proportion of berylliosis chest X-rays are normal, according to page 229?
QUESTIONS.exp: Under 'X-ray chest' the page prints 'Normal in 50% patients', then 'Hilar adenopathy' and '↑ interstitial markings'. A normal film therefore does not exclude the disease. (Book p229)

QUESTIONS.sec: Berylliosis: Sarcoidosis Features That Are Absent, Industries, Upper Lobe ILD to PMF, Lymphocyte Proliferation Test, X-ray in 50% and the HRCT Triad
QUESTIONS.q: Which investigation is printed as positive in berylliosis, and what does it test?
QUESTIONS.exp: The investigations block opens with 'Lymphocyte proliferation test : Positive.' This reflects the delayed hypersensitivity mechanism described on page 228. (Book p229)

QUESTIONS.sec: Berylliosis: Sarcoidosis Features That Are Absent, Industries, Upper Lobe ILD to PMF, Lymphocyte Proliferation Test, X-ray in 50% and the HRCT Triad
QUESTIONS.q: Which three HRCT findings are printed for berylliosis?
opts: Consolidation (classical), parenchymal nodules and septal lines
Ground glass appearance (classical), parenchymal nodules and septal lines
Ground glass appearance (classical), egg shell calcification and septal lines
Ground glass appearance (classical), honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis
QUESTIONS.exp: The HRCT list reads 'Ground glass appearance : Classical', 'Parenchymal nodules' and 'Septal lines'. Honeycombing and egg-shell calcification are printed elsewhere (asbestosis and silicosis respectively), not here. (Book p229)

QUESTIONS.sec: Berylliosis: Sarcoidosis Features That Are Absent, Industries, Upper Lobe ILD to PMF, Lymphocyte Proliferation Test, X-ray in 50% and the HRCT Triad
QUESTIONS.q: Which clinical features of berylliosis are printed on page 229?
opts: Cough with haemoptysis, with lower lobe ILD progressing to PMF
Dyspnea, with upper lobe ILD progressing to honeycombing only
Dyspnea, with upper lobe ILD progressing to PMF
Dyspnea, with lower lobe ILD progressing to PMF
QUESTIONS.exp: The features block reads 'Dyspnea' and 'upper lobe ILD → PMF'. Upper lobe predominance matches silicosis and CWP, in contrast with the lower lobe fibrosis of asbestosis. (Book p229)

QUESTIONS.sec: Berylliosis: Sarcoidosis Features That Are Absent, Industries, Upper Lobe ILD to PMF, Lymphocyte Proliferation Test, X-ray in 50% and the HRCT Triad
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about berylliosis as summarised across pages 228–229.
opts: True — it is a delayed hypersensitivity whose HRCT hallmark is honeycombing
False — it is a delayed hypersensitivity with caseating granulomas, mimics tuberculosis, and is confirmed by a positive lymphocyte proliferation test
False — it is an immediate hypersensitivity with caseating granulomas, mimics tuberculosis, and is confirmed by a negative lymphocyte proliferation test
True — it is a delayed hypersensitivity with non-caseating granulomas, mimics sarcoidosis, and is confirmed by a positive lymphocyte proliferation test
QUESTIONS.exp: Page 228 defines berylliosis as 'Delayed hypersensitivity with non caseating granulomas' and 'Clinically similar to sarcoidosis', and page 229 prints 'Lymphocyte proliferation test : Positive' with the classical HRCT finding of ground glass, not honeycombing. (Book p229)

QUESTIONS.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
QUESTIONS.q: Which thresholds define respiratory failure on page 230?
opts: Hypoxemic: PaO2 < 60 mmHg on room air with SpO2 < 90%; hypercapnic: PaCO2 > 50 mmHg on room air
Hypoxemic: PaO2 < 60 mmHg on oxygen; hypercapnic: PaCO2 > 50 mmHg on oxygen
Hypoxemic: PaO2 < 80 mmHg on room air with SpO2 < 90%; hypercapnic: PaCO2 > 45 mmHg on room air
Hypoxemic: PaO2 < 60 mmHg on room air with SpO2 < 80%; hypercapnic: PaCO2 > 50 mmHg on room air
QUESTIONS.exp: The definition box reads 'Hypoxemic : PaO2 <60 mmHg on room air, SpO2 <90%' and 'Hypercapnic : PaCO2 >50 mmHg on room air'. Both thresholds are specified on room air. (Book p230)

QUESTIONS.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
QUESTIONS.q: Match each abbreviation in the page 230 box with its printed meaning — 1) PAO2 2) PaO2 3) PaCO2 4) PAO2 − PaO2 … A) Partial pressure of carbon dioxide in artery (normal ~40 mmHg) B) Partial pressure of oxygen in alveoli C) Alveolocapillary oxygen gradient D) Partial pressure of oxygen in artery (normal ~97 mmHg)
QUESTIONS.exp: The box reads 'PAO2 : Partial pressure of oxygen in alveoli', 'PaO2 : Partial pressure of oxygen in artery (Normal ~97mmHg)', 'PaCO2 : Partial pressure of carbon dioxide in artery (Normal ~40mmHg)' and 'PAO2 − PaO2 : Alveolocapillary oxygen gradient'. The capital-A subscript is alveolar and the lower-case-a subscript arterial. (Book p230)

QUESTIONS.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
QUESTIONS.q: Which pathology chain is printed in the Type I column on page 230?
opts: Impaired diffusion → ventilatory failure, with the low (15 times) diffusion potential of CO and no hypercapnia
Impaired diffusion → oxygenation failure, with the high (150 times) diffusion potential of CO and no hypercapnia
Hypoventilation → oxygenation failure, with the high (150 times) diffusion potential of CO and hypercapnia
Impaired perfusion → oxygenation failure, with the high (150 times) diffusion potential of CO and no hypercapnia
QUESTIONS.exp: The Type I pathology cell reads 'Impaired diffusion → Oxygenation failure', then 'High (150 times) diffusion potential of CO' and 'No hypercapnia', with an alveolus-capillary diagram beneath. The 150-fold figure explains why CO transfer is used to measure diffusion. (Book p230)

QUESTIONS.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
QUESTIONS.q: Which set of partial pressures belongs to Type I respiratory failure on page 230?
QUESTIONS.exp: The partial-pressure column of Type I reads '↓PaO2', 'Normal PaCO2' and '↑PAO2 − PaO2'. A raised CO2 with a normal gradient is the Type II pattern, and a raised CO2 with a raised gradient the Type III pattern, both on the next page. (Book p230)

QUESTIONS.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
QUESTIONS.q: Which aetiological groups are listed in the Type I column besides ILD, pulmonary oedema/ARDS and pneumonia?
opts: Emphysema (↓surface area/volume), vascular causes such as thromboembolism and pulmonary HTN, pneumothorax, granulomatous lung disease, cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis
Emphysema (↑surface area/volume), vascular causes such as thromboembolism and pulmonary HTN, pneumothorax, granulomatous lung disease, cystic congenital heart disease and bronchiectasis
Emphysema (↓surface area/volume), vascular causes such as thromboembolism and pulmonary HTN, pneumothorax, granulomatous lung disease, cystic congenital heart disease and bronchiectasis
Pleural effusion, vascular causes such as thromboembolism and pulmonary HTN, pneumothorax, granulomatous lung disease, cystic congenital heart disease and bronchiectasis
QUESTIONS.exp: The Type I aetiology cell reads 'Fibrosis of interstitium : ILD', 'Fluid in interstitium, Pulmonary edema, ARDS', 'Exudate, Consolidation (Pneumonia)', 'Impaired alveolocapillary membrane unit ↓ surface area : Emphysema volume', then vascular causes, pneumothorax, granulomatous lung disease, cystic congenital heart disease and bronchiectasis. (Book p230)

QUESTIONS.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
QUESTIONS.q: Bronchial asthma appears as a special Type I entry with a bracketed explanation. Which statements are printed?
