opts: Airway disease with normal parenchyma → absent CO2 retention, and ↓PaO2 with (N)PaCO2 but ↑DLCO (normal diffusion)
Interstitial disease with normal airways → absent CO2 retention, and ↓PaO2 with (N)PaCO2 but ↑DLCO
Airway disease with normal parenchyma → absent CO2 retention, and ↓PaO2 with (N)PaCO2 but ↓DLCO (impaired diffusion)
Airway disease with abnormal parenchyma → present CO2 retention, and ↓PaO2 with ↑PaCO2 but ↓DLCO
QUESTIONS.exp: The asthma entry reads 'Airway disease (Normal parenchyma, → Absent CO2 retention)' and '↓PaO2, (N) PaCO2, ↑DLCO (normal diffusion)'. Because the alveolo-capillary membrane is spared, diffusion is preserved and CO2 is not retained. (Book p230)

QUESTIONS.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the Type I definition printed on page 230.
opts: False — Type I failure is a ventilatory failure with a raised PaCO2
False — the CO diffusion potential is quoted as 15 times on this page
True — Type I failure always requires a raised PAO2 − PaO2 with a raised PaCO2
True — Type I failure is an oxygenation failure with a normal PaCO2, and the CO diffusion potential is quoted as 150 times
QUESTIONS.exp: The Type I column reads 'Oxygenation failure', 'No hypercapnia' and 'High (150 times) diffusion potential of CO', with 'Normal PaCO2' in the pressure column. A raised CO2 would make it Type II or III. (Book p230)

QUESTIONS.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
QUESTIONS.q: A patient with severe asthma has PaO2 55 mmHg, a normal PaCO2 and normal diffusion. Using the page 230 asthma entry, why is CO2 not retained?
opts: Airway disease with abnormal parenchyma means present CO2 retention, so PaO2 falls with ↑PaCO2 and ↓DLCO
Airway disease with normal parenchyma means absent CO2 retention, so PaO2 falls with (N)PaCO2 and ↑DLCO
Interstitial disease with normal airways means absent CO2 retention, so PaO2 falls with (N)PaCO2 and ↓DLCO
Airway disease with normal parenchyma means present CO2 retention, so PaO2 falls with ↑PaCO2 and ↑DLCO
QUESTIONS.exp: The asthma rows read 'Airway disease (Normal parenchyma, → Absent CO2 retention)' and '↓PaO2, (N)PaCO2, ↑DLCO (normal diffusion)'. Because the alveolo-capillary membrane is intact, CO2 diffuses freely and the DLCO is preserved. (Book p230)

QUESTIONS.sec: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which Type III chain and aetiology pair are printed on page 231?
opts: Oxygenation failure → parenchymal damage → ventilatory failure, with ILD acting through ↓compliance and ARDS through ↓diffusion
Hypoventilation → parenchymal damage → oxygenation failure, with ILD acting through ↓compliance and ARDS through ↓diffusion
Ventilatory failure → parenchymal damage → oxygenation failure, with ILD acting through ↓diffusion and ARDS through ↑lung compliance
Oxygenation failure → parenchymal damage → ventilatory failure, with ILD acting through ↓diffusion and ARDS through ↓lung compliance
QUESTIONS.exp: The Type III row reads 'Oxygenation failure → Parenchymal damage → ventilatory failure', and the aetiology cell brackets 'ILD : ↓Diffusion' and 'ARDS : ↓Lung compliance' to 'Type 1 → Type 3 as disease progresses'. Type III therefore carries both a low PaO2 and a high PaCO2 with a raised gradient. (Book p231)

QUESTIONS.sec: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which Type IV mechanism and causes are printed on page 231?
opts: Hypotension → ↓diffusion across the membrane, with cardiogenic, hypovolemic and septic shock as causes
Hypotension → ↓perfusion of respiratory muscles, with cardiogenic, hypovolemic and septic shock as causes
Hypotension → ↓perfusion of respiratory muscles, with obstructive, neurogenic and anaphylactic shock as causes
Hypertension → ↑perfusion of respiratory muscles, with cardiogenic, hypovolemic and septic shock as causes
QUESTIONS.exp: The Type IV row reads 'Hypotension → ↓Perfusion of respiratory muscles' with the partial-pressure cell printed as a dash, and aetiology 'Cardiogenic shock, Hypovolemic shock, Septic shock'. The failure is of the respiratory pump, so pressures are not characteristic. (Book p231)

QUESTIONS.sec: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
QUESTIONS.q: The 'Type-3 respiratory failure' note on page 231 is set in anaesthesiology. Which mechanism is printed?
opts: ↓Functional residual capacity (tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume) → collapse (post-op atelectasis)
↓Vital capacity (residual volume + expiratory reserve volume) → collapse (post-op pneumonia)
↓Functional residual capacity (residual volume + expiratory reserve volume) → collapse (post-op atelectasis)
↑Functional residual capacity (residual volume + expiratory reserve volume) → collapse (post-op atelectasis)
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Type-3 Respiratory Failure : in Anesthesiology' with 'Pathology : ↓ Functional Residual Capacity (Residual Volume + Expiratory Reserve Volume)' leading to 'Collapse (Post op Atelectasis)'. Note the page uses 'Type-3' here for a perioperative mechanism distinct from the Type III parenchymal row above it (recorded in the caveat file). (Book p231)

QUESTIONS.sec: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which four causes of the anaesthesiology type-3 failure are printed?
opts: Supine position/obese/ascites, residual effects of anaesthesia, upper abdominal incision and airway secretions
Supine position/cachexia/ascites, muscle relaxants, upper abdominal incision and airway secretions
Supine position/obese/ascites, residual effects of anaesthesia, upper abdominal incision and pulmonary embolism
Prone position/obese/ascites, residual effects of anaesthesia, lower abdominal incision and airway secretions
QUESTIONS.exp: The aetiology list reads 'supine position, Obese, Ascites', 'Residual effects of Anesthesia', 'upper abdominal incision' and 'Airway secretions'. All four reduce FRC or impede its restoration after surgery. (Book p231)

QUESTIONS.sec: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which V/Q ratio values are printed under the hypoxemic-failure clinical approach?
opts: Normal 1.0; upper zone > 1 (non-dependent, ↓↓V and ↓↓Q); lower zone < 1 (dependent area)
Normal 0.8; upper zone > 1 (dependent area); lower zone < 1 (non-dependent area)
Normal 0.8; upper zone < 1 (non-dependent, ↓↓V and ↓↓Q); lower zone > 1 (dependent area)
Normal 0.8; upper zone > 1 (non-dependent, ↓↓V and ↓↓Q); lower zone < 1 (dependent area)
QUESTIONS.exp: The page prints 'Normal : 0.8', 'upper zone : >1 (Non-dependent area → ↓↓V, ↓↓Q)' and 'Lower zone : <1 (Dependent area)', adding that the ratio 'Indicates overall respiratory functional status of lung' and plays a role in type 1 failure. (Book p231)

QUESTIONS.sec: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
QUESTIONS.q: Match each physiology with its printed row in the ventilation table — 1) Dead space physiology 2) Shunt physiology 3) Normal matching … A) Ventilation absent, perfusion present, V/Q zero B) V/Q 0.8 C) Ventilation present, perfusion absent, V/Q infinite
QUESTIONS.exp: The table reads: dead space — ventilation present, perfusion absent, V/Q ∞, aetiology pulmonary embolism and pulmonary vascular disease; shunt — ventilation absent, perfusion present, V/Q zero, aetiology intracardiac/vascular shunts. Normal matching carries the V/Q of 0.8 printed above the table. (Book p231)

QUESTIONS.sec: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the Type III and Type IV rows on page 231.
opts: True — Type III has ↓PaO2 with ↑PaCO2 and ↑PAO2 − PaO2, while the Type IV partial-pressure cell is printed as a dash
True — Type IV is caused by parenchymal damage rather than by shock
False — Type IV is printed with a full set of partial pressures
False — Type III has ↓PaO2 with normal PaCO2 and a normal gradient
QUESTIONS.exp: The Type III pressure cell reads '↓PaO2, ↑PaCO2, ↑PAO2 − PaO2', whereas the Type IV cell contains only a dash, consistent with a perfusion failure of the respiratory muscles rather than a gas-exchange defect. (Book p231)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Two Flowcharts: Hypoxemic Failure Branches (V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, Dead Space, Type II vs Type III, Oxygen-Responsiveness, High Altitude) and Hypercapnic Failure Branches
QUESTIONS.q: The hypoxemic-failure flowchart begins with ↓PaO2 and three first-level branches. Which three are printed?
opts: Diffusion abnormality (Type III), V/Q = 0 shunt and V/Q = ∞ dead space
V/Q mismatch (Type I respiratory failure, diffusion abnormality), V/Q = 0 shunt and V/Q = ∞ dead space
V/Q mismatch (Type I respiratory failure, diffusion abnormality), V/Q = 0 dead space and V/Q = ∞ shunt
V/Q mismatch (Type II respiratory failure), V/Q = 1 shunt and V/Q = 0 dead space
QUESTIONS.exp: The three arrows from ↓PaO2 read 'V/Q mismatch : Type-I respiratory failure (Diffusion abnormality)', 'V/Q = 0 Shunt' and 'V/Q = ∞ Dead space'. The shunt and dead space branches reproduce page 209's definitions exactly. (Book p232)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Two Flowcharts: Hypoxemic Failure Branches (V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, Dead Space, Type II vs Type III, Oxygen-Responsiveness, High Altitude) and Hypercapnic Failure Branches
QUESTIONS.q: Match each flowchart terminal with its printed label — 1) Raised CO2 with a normal gradient 2) Raised CO2 with a raised gradient 3) Normal CO2 with a raised gradient not corrected by oxygen 4) Normal CO2 with a normal gradient … A) Shunt B) Hypoventilation (Type II) C) High altitude D) Hypoventilation plus another mechanism (Type III)
QUESTIONS.exp: The chart prints 'Hypoventilation (Type II)', 'Hypoventilation + Another mechanism (Type III)', then under Type I the oxygen-response test ends at 'v/Q : mismatch' (corrects) or 'Shunt' (does not correct), and 'High Altitude' sits on the branch with no gradient. (Book p232)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Two Flowcharts: Hypoxemic Failure Branches (V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, Dead Space, Type II vs Type III, Oxygen-Responsiveness, High Altitude) and Hypercapnic Failure Branches
QUESTIONS.q: According to the page 232 flowchart, how is a Type I hypoxaemia separated into V/Q mismatch versus shunt?
opts: Give oxygen: if the low PaO2 is corrected it is V/Q mismatch; if it is not corrected it is shunt
Measure the A-a gradient: if raised it is shunt; if normal it is V/Q mismatch
Give oxygen: if the low PaO2 is corrected it is shunt; if it is not corrected it is V/Q mismatch
Measure the PaCO2: if raised it is shunt; if normal it is V/Q mismatch
QUESTIONS.exp: The Type I branch runs 'Low PO2 Corrected with O2 → Yes → v/Q : mismatch' and '→ No → Shunt'. Shunted blood never contacts ventilated alveoli, so added oxygen cannot reach it. (Book p232)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Two Flowcharts: Hypoxemic Failure Branches (V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, Dead Space, Type II vs Type III, Oxygen-Responsiveness, High Altitude) and Hypercapnic Failure Branches
QUESTIONS.q: On the page 232 flowchart, a low PaO2 with a normal gradient and no CO2 retention leads to the terminal labelled ______.
QUESTIONS.exp: The far-right branch of the Type I limb ends at 'High Altitude'. There the inspired oxygen pressure itself is low, so the gradient stays normal — unlike shunt or V/Q mismatch. (Book p232)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Two Flowcharts: Hypoxemic Failure Branches (V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, Dead Space, Type II vs Type III, Oxygen-Responsiveness, High Altitude) and Hypercapnic Failure Branches
QUESTIONS.q: The hypercapnic-failure flowchart at the foot of page 232 begins with ↑PaCO2 and splits on the A-a gradient. Which two terminals are printed?
opts: Increased gradient → hypoventilation → generator, pumps, effector organ; normal gradient → V/Q mismatch, eg ARDS and ILD
Normal gradient → hypoventilation → generator and pumps only; increased gradient → diffusion defect, eg pulmonary embolism
Normal gradient → hypoventilation → generator, pumps, effector organ; increased gradient → V/Q mismatch, eg ARDS and ILD
Normal gradient → shunt; increased gradient → dead space, eg ARDS and ILD
QUESTIONS.exp: The chart reads '↑PaCO2 → PAO2 − PaO2', then 'Normal → Hypoventilation → Generator, Pumps, Effector organ' and 'Increased → v/Q mismatch eg : ARDS ILD'. The generator/pump/effector trio matches the Type II aetiology list on page 230. (Book p232)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Two Flowcharts: Hypoxemic Failure Branches (V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, Dead Space, Type II vs Type III, Oxygen-Responsiveness, High Altitude) and Hypercapnic Failure Branches
QUESTIONS.q: A patient has PaO2 50 mmHg, a normal PaCO2 and a raised A-a gradient; the PaO2 does not improve on 100% oxygen. Where does the page 232 algorithm place this?
opts: Type I respiratory failure with a shunt
Type II respiratory failure from hypoventilation
Type I respiratory failure with V/Q mismatch
Type III respiratory failure with a high altitude mechanism
QUESTIONS.exp: The Type I limb splits on oxygen responsiveness: corrected PaO2 means V/Q mismatch, uncorrected means 'Shunt'. A normal PaCO2 keeps the case out of the Type II and III Hypoventilation terminals. (Book p232)

QUESTIONS.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
QUESTIONS.q: Which synonyms for ARDS are printed at the top of page 233?
opts: Shock lung, acute lung injury, DAD, blast lung and acute interstitial pneumonia
Shock lung, acute lung injury, DAD, blast lung and acute alveolar injury
Shock lung, chronic lung injury, DAD, blast lung and acute alveolar injury
Stiff lung, acute lung injury, DAD, blast lung and acute alveolar injury
QUESTIONS.exp: The line reads 'AKA shock lung/acute lung injury/DAD/blast lung/acute alveolar injury.' Acute interstitial pneumonia is a separate idiopathic interstitial pneumonia listed on page 236, not a synonym for ARDS. (Book p233)

QUESTIONS.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
QUESTIONS.q: Which three 1992 AECC criteria carry numbers on page 233?
opts: PCWP > 18 mmHg, bilateral alveolar and interstitial infiltrates, and PaO2/FiO2 < 200
PCWP < 18 mmHg, unilateral alveolar infiltrates, and PaO2/FiO2 < 300
PCWP < 18 mmHg (measuring left atrial pressure), bilateral alveolar and interstitial infiltrates, and PaO2/FiO2 < 200
PCWP < 15 mmHg, bilateral alveolar and interstitial infiltrates, and PaO2/FiO2 < 200
QUESTIONS.exp: The AECC block reads 'Non cardiogenic pulmonary edema' with 'PCWP : <18 mm Hg (Suggestive of no cardiac abnormality)', then 'Bilateral alveolar and interstitial lung infiltrates on x-ray' and 'PaO2/FiO2 < 200'. The wedge pressure must be low, confirming a non-cardiogenic cause. (Book p233)

QUESTIONS.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
QUESTIONS.q: What limitation and mortality figures are printed for ARDS on page 233?
opts: Only 20% of patients meet the ARDS criteria; mortality 30–40% with post-ARDS residual disability
Only 20% of patients meet the ARDS criteria; mortality 70–75% with no residual disability
Only 50% of patients meet the ARDS criteria; mortality 70–75% with post-ARDS residual disability
Only 20% of patients meet the ARDS criteria; mortality 70–75% with post-ARDS residual disability
QUESTIONS.exp: The limitations line reads 'Only 20% patients meet ARDS criteria', and the note gives 'mortality : 70–75%' plus 'Post ARDS residual disability present'. Survivors are left with functional impairment, not a full recovery. (Book p233)

QUESTIONS.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
QUESTIONS.q: Which four Berlin 2012 criteria are numbered on page 233?
opts: Acute onset within 1 month of the insult, bilateral infiltrates not explained by effusion/collapse/nodules, non-cardiogenic with a normal ECHO, and oxygenation measured when PEEP ≥ 5 cm of H2O
Acute onset within 1 week of the insult, unilateral infiltrates not explained by effusion/collapse/nodules, cardiogenic with an abnormal ECHO, and oxygenation measured when PEEP ≥ 10 cm of H2O
Acute onset within 1 week of the insult, bilateral infiltrates not explained by effusion/collapse/nodules, non-cardiogenic with a normal ECHO, and oxygenation measured when PEEP ≥ 5 cm of H2O
Acute onset within 1 week of the insult, bilateral infiltrates, non-cardiogenic with a normal ECHO, and oxygenation measured on room air without PEEP
QUESTIONS.exp: The Berlin block reads '1. Acute onset : within 1 week of clinical insult/worsening respiratory symptoms', '2. Chest x-ray : Bilateral alveolar/Interstitial infiltrates not explained by effusion/collapse/nodules', '3. Non cardiogenic : Normal ECHO' and '4. Oxygenation :' with the brace 'when PEEP ≥ 5 cm of H2O'. The timing is one week, not one month. (Book p233)

QUESTIONS.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
QUESTIONS.q: Match each Berlin severity grade with its printed PaO2/FiO2 range — 1) Mild 2) Moderate 3) Severe … A) < 100 B) 100–200 C) 200–300
QUESTIONS.exp: The severity table reads 'mild — 200 – 300', 'moderate — 100 – 200' and 'severe — < 100'. Lower ratios indicate more severe disease, so the grades run from the highest range to the lowest. (Book p233)

QUESTIONS.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
QUESTIONS.q: Which three factors preventing pulmonary edema are printed at the foot of page 233?
opts: Retained intravascular protein, interstitial lymphatics draining fluid, and tight junctions between epithelial cells
Lost intravascular protein, interstitial lymphatics draining fluid, and tight junctions between epithelial cells
Retained intravascular protein, interstitial lymphatics draining fluid, and loose junctions between epithelial cells
Retained intravascular protein, blocked interstitial lymphatics, and tight junctions between endothelial cells
QUESTIONS.exp: The three bullets read 'Retained intravascular protein', 'Interstitial lymphatics drains fluid' and 'Tight junctions between epithelial cells'. ARDS breaks all three, which is why protein-rich fluid floods the alveolus. (Book p233)

QUESTIONS.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
QUESTIONS.q: A ventilated patient has ARDS onset three days after a urinary tract infection, bilateral infiltrates, a normal ECHO and PaO2/FiO2 of 150 on PEEP 8 cm H2O. Using the Berlin table, how is this graded and which AECC threshold has changed?
opts: Mild ARDS (200–300); the Berlin definition raises the AECC cut-off from 200 to 300 without grading
Moderate ARDS (100–200); the Berlin definition replaces the single AECC PaO2/FiO2 < 200 cut-off with three graded ranges measured on PEEP ≥ 5 cm H2O
Moderate ARDS (100–200); the Berlin definition removes the PEEP requirement entirely
Severe ARDS (< 100); the Berlin definition is identical to the AECC cut-off of 200
QUESTIONS.exp: The Berlin severity table reads 'mild 200 – 300', 'moderate 100 – 200' and 'severe < 100', with the brace 'when PEEP ≥ 5 cm of H2O'. The AECC instead used a single 'PaO2/FiO2 < 200' threshold, which is why it captured only about 20% of patients. (Book p233)

QUESTIONS.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these are printed as factors preventing pulmonary edema on page 233, one is not:
QUESTIONS.exp: The three protective factors are retained intravascular protein, interstitial lymphatics draining fluid, and tight junctions between epithelial cells. Leaky junctions are the pathological change of ARDS, not a protective mechanism. (Book p233)

QUESTIONS.sec: ARDS Etiology (Primary and Secondary), the Toxin-to-Hyaline-Membrane Pathogenesis Chain, Alveolar Consequences and the Three Pathological Phases
QUESTIONS.q: Which primary ARDS causes are printed on page 234?
opts: Pulmonary sepsis, massive blood transfusion, acute pancreatitis, TRALI, smoke inhalation, drowning and major burns
Non-pulmonary sepsis, massive blood transfusion, acute pancreatitis, TRALI, smoke inhalation, drowning and post surgery
Pulmonary sepsis, massive blood transfusion, acute pancreatitis, TRALI, smoke inhalation, drowning and post surgery
Pulmonary sepsis, minor blood transfusion, chronic pancreatitis, TRALI, smoke inhalation, drowning and post surgery
QUESTIONS.exp: The primary list reads 'Pulmonary sepsis', 'massive blood transfusion', 'Acute pancreatitis', 'Transfusion associated lung injury (TRALI)', 'Smoke inhalation', 'Drowning' and 'Post surgery'. QUESTIONS.exp: The 'Known (4)' arm branches parasite-related disease into hypersensitivity causing Loeffler syndrome and lung invasion by lung fluke, and completes the four heads with drug & toxin, tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE) and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) as the bulleted known causes. (Book p249)

QUESTIONS.sec: Eosinophilic Lung Disease Defined, Its Three Defining Features, Known versus Unknown Causes and Diseases Not Classified under ELD
QUESTIONS.q: Which four diseases form the 'Unknown (4)' arm of the etiology tree?
opts: Acute eosinophilic pneumonia (AEP), Loeffler syndrome, allergic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (AGPA) / eosinophilic GPA (EGPA) / Churg-Strauss syndrome, and idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome

Acute eosinophilic pneumonia (AEP), chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (CEP), allergic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (AGPA) / eosinophilic GPA (EGPA) / Churg-Strauss syndrome, and tropical pulmonary eosinophilia

Acute eosinophilic pneumonia (AEP), chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (CEP), allergic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (AGPA) / eosinophilic GPA (EGPA) / Churg-Strauss syndrome, and idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome
Acute eosinophilic pneumonia (AEP), chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (CEP), granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), and idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome
QUESTIONS.exp: The Unknown arm lists AEP, CEP, 'Allergic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (AGPA) / Eosinophilic GPA (EGPA)/Churg Strauss syndrome' under its three printed names, and idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome. Loeffler syndrome and TPE sit on the known side. (Book p249)

QUESTIONS.sec: Eosinophilic Lung Disease Defined, Its Three Defining Features, Known versus Unknown Causes and Diseases Not Classified under ELD
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these are printed on page 249 as diseases with eosinophilia but not classified under ELD, one is a true ELD cause:
QUESTIONS.exp: The Note lists bronchial Asthma, 'Cytogenic organising pneumonia' as printed, Langerhans cell histiocytosis and IgG4 related connective tissue disorder as eosinophilic diseases outside ELD. ABPA is one of the four known ELD heads in the tree above. (Book p249)

QUESTIONS.sec: Eosinophilic Lung Disease Defined, Its Three Defining Features, Known versus Unknown Causes and Diseases Not Classified under ELD
QUESTIONS.q: Which two not-classified diseases share an arrow on page 249, and where does it send them?
opts: 'Cytogenic organising pneumonia' as printed and bronchial Asthma are braced together and arrowed to ELD
'Cytogenic organising pneumonia' as printed and Langerhans cell histiocytosis are braced together and arrowed to ILD
Bronchial Asthma and IgG4 related connective tissue disorder are braced together and arrowed to ILD
Langerhans cell histiocytosis and IgG4 related connective tissue disorder are braced together and arrowed to ILD
QUESTIONS.exp: In the Note, 'Cytogenic organising pneumonia' (printed spelling, for cryptogenic organizing pneumonia) and Langerhans cell histiocytosis share one brace arrowed '→ ILD', returning both to the Chapter 39 grouping; the same Note adds that hypersensitivity pneumonitis is not grouped under ELD. (Book p249)

QUESTIONS.sec: Eosinophilic Lung Disease Defined, Its Three Defining Features, Known versus Unknown Causes and Diseases Not Classified under ELD
QUESTIONS.q: Which BAL threshold and which two diseases close page 249?
opts: BAL above 60%, in 'TEP' as printed (for TPE) and CEP
BAL at or above 40%, in ABPA and CEP
BAL at or above 25%, in TPE and AEP
BAL at or above 40%, in 'TEP' as printed (for TPE) and CEP
QUESTIONS.exp: The last bullet reads 'ELD with BAL ≥40%: TEP. CEP.' — TEP being the page's transposed printing of TPE, whose own BAL figure of at least 40% recurs on page 251. (Book p249)

QUESTIONS.sec: Eosinophilic Lung Disease Defined, Its Three Defining Features, Known versus Unknown Causes and Diseases Not Classified under ELD
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the page 249 classification boundaries.
opts: True — hypersensitivity pneumonitis is stated to be not grouped under ELD, even though it is an eosinophil-associated hypersensitivity disease in neighbouring chapters
False — hypersensitivity pneumonitis heads the list of unknown ELD causes
False — bronchial Asthma is classified under ELD because its inflammation is eosinophilic
True — hypersensitivity pneumonitis is grouped under ELD as a known cause

QUESTIONS.sec: Parasite-Related ELD (Loeffler Syndrome versus Lung Fluke Invasion), Drugs and Toxins, and Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia Pathogenesis
QUESTIONS.q: Match each parasite-related table row with its Loeffler versus lung-invasion pair on page 250 — 1) Organism 2) Mechanism 3) Symptoms 4) Treatment … A) Type 1 hypersensitivity to larvae versus metacercaria reaching lung and maturing to adult worm larvae as printed B) Ascaris lumbricoides most common, ahead of Ancylostoma, Necator and Strongyloides, versus the lung fluke Paragonimus westermani C) Self-limiting, resolving in 1–2 weeks, versus praziquantel as DOC D) Asthma mimic with cough, substernal discomfort and wheeze plus low grade fever, versus a dash
QUESTIONS.exp: The Loeffler column gives Ascaris (m/c) > Ancylostoma/Necator/Strongyloides, type 1 hypersensitivity to larvae, an Asthma-mimicking symptom set with low grade fever, and self-limited resolution in 1–2 weeks; the invasion column gives Paragonimus westermani maturing from metacercaria in lung, a dash for symptoms, and praziquantel as drug of choice. (Book p250)

QUESTIONS.sec: Parasite-Related ELD (Loeffler Syndrome versus Lung Fluke Invasion), Drugs and Toxins, and Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia Pathogenesis
QUESTIONS.q: Which findings fill the Loeffler syndrome column on page 250?
opts: Peripheral eosinophilia, raised IgE and migratory eosinophilic lung infiltrates
Peripheral eosinophilia, raised IgE and chocolate colored sputum
BAL eosinophilia only, raised IgE and cavitating nodules
Peripheral eosinophilia, normal IgE and fixed eosinophilic lung infiltrates
QUESTIONS.exp: The Findings cell reads 'Peripheral eosinophilia, ↑ IgE, migratory eosinophilic lung infiltrates'. Migratory infiltrates are the type 1 signature that hypersensitivity pneumonitis on page 257 is defined against. (Book p250)

QUESTIONS.sec: Parasite-Related ELD (Loeffler Syndrome versus Lung Fluke Invasion), Drugs and Toxins, and Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia Pathogenesis
QUESTIONS.q: Which pleural, lung and diagnostic findings fill the lung-invasion column?
opts: Pleura: eosinophilic pleural effusion; lung: cavitating nodules, ground glass opacification and brownish mucosal plugs; diagnosis by skin test
Pleura: eosinophilic pleural effusion; lung: cavitating nodules, ground glass opacification and chocolate colored sputum, with eosinophilia positive; diagnosis by eggs in sputum or ELISA
Pleura: chylous effusion; lung: cavitating nodules, ground glass opacification and chocolate colored sputum; diagnosis by eggs in sputum or ELISA
Pleura: eosinophilic pleural effusion; lung: migratory infiltrates and chocolate colored sputum; diagnosis by eggs in stool or ELISA
QUESTIONS.exp: The invasion cell reads 'Pleura: Eosinophilic pleural effusion. Lung: Cavitating nodules, ground glass opacification, chocolate colored sputum. Eosinophilia +ve. Diagnosis: Eggs in sputum or ELISA.' Lung fluke reappears as the first cause of eosinophils in pleural fluid on page 263. (Book p250)

QUESTIONS.sec: Parasite-Related ELD (Loeffler Syndrome versus Lung Fluke Invasion), Drugs and Toxins, and Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia Pathogenesis
QUESTIONS.q: A child with Ascaris develops cough, substernal discomfort, wheeze and low grade fever; blood shows eosinophilia with raised IgE and the film shows shifting infiltrates that clear within a fortnight untreated. Which table column and mechanism is this?
opts: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia — hypersensitivity to microfilariae, treated with DEC
Lung invasion by Paragonimus — metacercaria maturing in lung, treated with praziquantel
Loeffler syndrome — type 4 hypersensitivity to adults, treated with praziquantel
Loeffler syndrome — type 1 hypersensitivity to larvae, self limiting in 1–2 weeks
QUESTIONS.exp: Ascaris lumbricoides heads the Loeffler organisms, its mechanism is type 1 hypersensitivity to larvae, its symptoms mimic Asthma with low grade fever, its findings are migratory infiltrates, and it is 'Self limiting and resolve in 1–2 weeks'. (Book p250)

QUESTIONS.sec: Parasite-Related ELD (Loeffler Syndrome versus Lung Fluke Invasion), Drugs and Toxins, and Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia Pathogenesis
QUESTIONS.q: Which drug and toxin list is printed under known causes of ELD on page 250, and which entry leads it?
opts: NSAIDs, marked most common, then L-tryptophan, mustard oil, nitrofurantoin, minocycline and amoxicillin
NSAIDs, marked most common, then L-tryptophan, rapeseed oil, nitrofurantoin, minocycline and ampicillin
NSAIDs, marked most common, then L-tryptophan, rapeseed oil, nitrofurantoin, methotrexate and ampicillin
Nitrofurantoin, marked most common, then NSAIDs, L-tryptophan, rapeseed oil, minocycline and ampicillin
QUESTIONS.exp: Under 'Drug & Toxin' the bullets read 'NSAIDs (m/c)', L-Tryptophan, rapeseed oil, nitrofurantoin, minocycline and ampicillin. Rapeseed oil echoes the toxic rapeseed oil of pulmonary hypertension on page 214. (Book p250)

QUESTIONS.sec: Parasite-Related ELD (Loeffler Syndrome versus Lung Fluke Invasion), Drugs and Toxins, and Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia Pathogenesis
QUESTIONS.q: Which sex ratio, organisms and pathogenesis open tropical pulmonary eosinophilia on page 250?
opts: Females more than males; Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia malayi; direct invasion by adult filariae
Males more than females; Ascaris lumbricoides and Strongyloides; hypersensitivity to microfilarial larvae
Males more than females; Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia malayi; hypersensitivity to microfilarial larvae
Males equal to females; Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia malayi; hypersensitivity to microfilarial larvae
QUESTIONS.exp: The TPE block reads 'm > F', 'Organism: Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi' and 'Pathogenesis: Hypersensitivity to microfilarial larvae'. The hypersensitivity — not the worm burden — is the mechanism, as in Loeffler syndrome above it. (Book p250)

QUESTIONS.sec: Parasite-Related ELD (Loeffler Syndrome versus Lung Fluke Invasion), Drugs and Toxins, and Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia Pathogenesis
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these bullets are printed on page 250 as jointly suggesting the microfilarial association in TPE, one is not:
opts: High antifilarial antibody titres that diminish after cure
Microfilariae demonstrated in lung, liver and lymph node
QUESTIONS.exp: The brace collects microfilariae in lung/liver/LN, high antifilarial antibody titres falling after cure, and dramatic response to anti-filarial treatment as together suggesting 'association with microfilariae'. Eggs in sputum diagnose the lung fluke in the table above. (Book p250)

QUESTIONS.sec: Parasite-Related ELD (Loeffler Syndrome versus Lung Fluke Invasion), Drugs and Toxins, and Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia Pathogenesis
QUESTIONS.q: In TPE the three evidence bullets are braced to the conclusion: 'Suggest association with ______'.
QUESTIONS.exp: The brace reads 'Suggest association with microfilariae', matching the pathogenesis line 'Hypersensitivity to microfilarial larvae'. Metacercariae belong to Paragonimus in the same page's table. (Book p250)

QUESTIONS.sec: Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia: Acute-on-Chronic Symptoms, Laboratory and Radiological Findings, DEC Treatment, and the Unknown-Cause Table Histories and Presentations
QUESTIONS.q: Match each TPE symptom component on page 251 with its printed contents — 1) Chronic component 2) Acute component … A) Paroxysmal dry cough with dyspnoea and wheeze worse at night, stimulating status asthmaticus as printed B) Malaise, anorexia and weight loss with or without hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy
QUESTIONS.exp: As an 'Acute on chronic disease', TPE couples a chronic component of malaise, anorexia and weight loss ± hepatosplenomegaly/lymphadenopathy with an acute component of paroxysmal dry cough and nocturnal dyspnoea/wheeze that '(stimulate status asthmaticus)' as printed, for simulate. (Book p251)

QUESTIONS.sec: Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia: Acute-on-Chronic Symptoms, Laboratory and Radiological Findings, DEC Treatment, and the Unknown-Cause Table Histories and Presentations
QUESTIONS.q: Which three laboratory numbers are printed for TPE investigations?
opts: Marked peripheral eosinophilia above 3000 cells/mm³, BAL intense eosinophilic alveolitis at or above 40%, and serum IgE above 100 u/ml as printed
Marked peripheral eosinophilia above 1500 cells/mm³, BAL intense eosinophilic alveolitis at or above 40%, and serum IgE above 1000 u/ml as printed
Marked peripheral eosinophilia above 3000 cells/mm³, BAL eosinophils at or above 25%, and serum IgE above 500 u/ml as printed
Marked peripheral eosinophilia above 3000 cells/mm³, BAL intense eosinophilic alveolitis at or above 40%, and serum IgE above 1000 u/ml as printed
QUESTIONS.exp: Laboratory findings read 'marked peripheral eosinophilia (> 3000 cells/mm³)', 'BAL: Intense eosinophilic alveolitis (≥ 40 %)' and '↑ S. IgE (> 1000 u/ml)'. The 1500 figure belongs to idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome on page 252. (Book p251)

QUESTIONS.sec: Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia: Acute-on-Chronic Symptoms, Laboratory and Radiological Findings, DEC Treatment, and the Unknown-Cause Table Histories and Presentations
QUESTIONS.q: Which radiological findings and caption are printed for TPE?
opts: Bilateral indefinite mottling uniformly in both lung fields (middle and lower), increased bronchovascular markings, and cavitation with pleural effusion — the film captioned 'mottling pattern in x ray'

Bilateral indefinite mottling uniformly in both lung fields (upper and middle), increased bronchovascular markings, and cavitation with pleural effusion — the film captioned 'mottling pattern in x ray'
Bilateral indefinite mottling uniformly in both lung fields (middle and lower), increased bronchovascular markings, and pleural effusion without cavitation — the film captioned 'reverse bat wing'
Unilateral definite mottling, decreased bronchovascular markings, and honeycombing — the film captioned 'mottling pattern in x ray'
QUESTIONS.exp: Radiological findings read 'B/L indefinite mottling uniformly in both lung fields (middle & lower)', '↑ bronchovascular markings' and 'Cavitation and pleural effusion', and the chest film is captioned 'mottling pattern in x ray'. (Book p251)

QUESTIONS.sec: Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia: Acute-on-Chronic Symptoms, Laboratory and Radiological Findings, DEC Treatment, and the Unknown-Cause Table Histories and Presentations
QUESTIONS.q: Which TPE treatment statement, dose and course bullets are printed on page 251?
opts: DOC diethylcarbamazine (DEC) 6 mg/kg single dose, directly filaricidal to adult worms and microfilariae, with clinical improvement in 7 days and acute relapse in up to 20% requiring higher doses
DOC praziquantel for 14–21 days, directly filaricidal to adult worms and microfilariae, with clinical improvement in 7 days and acute relapse in up to 20% requiring higher doses

DOC diethylcarbamazine (DEC) 2 mg/kg orally three times daily for 14–21 days / 4 weeks as printed, directly filaricidal to adult worms and microfilariae, with clinical improvement in 7 days and acute relapse in up to 20% requiring higher doses
DOC diethylcarbamazine (DEC) 2 mg/kg orally three times daily for 14–21 days / 4 weeks as printed, active only against microfilariae, with clinical improvement in 7 days and no relapses
QUESTIONS.exp: Treatment reads 'DOC: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) 2 mg/kg orally TID for 14 – 21 days / 4 weeks', 'Directly filaricidal to both adult & microfilariae', 'Clinical improvement in 7 days' and 'Acute relapse in upto 20% require higher doses'. Praziquantel was the lung-fluke DOC on page 250. (Book p251)

QUESTIONS.sec: Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia: Acute-on-Chronic Symptoms, Laboratory and Radiological Findings, DEC Treatment, and the Unknown-Cause Table Histories and Presentations
QUESTIONS.q: Match each unknown-cause column with its printed History and Pathogenesis rows on page 251 — 1) AEP 2) CEP 3) Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome … A) History atopy in 33–50%, pathogenesis a dash B) History a dash, pathogenesis a myeloproliferative disorder with JAK2/PDGFRα mutation C) History restarted smoking, pathogenesis a dash
QUESTIONS.exp: History gives 'Restarted smoking' for AEP, 'Atopy (33 – 50 %)' for CEP and a dash for the hypereosinophilic syndrome, while Pathogenesis is dashed for both pneumonias and names a 'myeloproliferative disorder: JAK2/PDGFRα mutation' only for the syndrome. (Book p251)

QUESTIONS.sec: Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia: Acute-on-Chronic Symptoms, Laboratory and Radiological Findings, DEC Treatment, and the Unknown-Cause Table Histories and Presentations
QUESTIONS.q: Which presentation timeline is drawn for acute eosinophilic pneumonia on page 251?
opts: Viral fever-like symptoms of fever and cough progressing over 2–3 days to dyspnea, tachypnea and hypoxia in an ARDS-like presentation, lasting 3–4 weeks
Viral fever-like symptoms of fever and cough progressing over 2–3 weeks to dyspnea, tachypnea and hypoxia in an ARDS-like presentation, lasting 3–4 days
Viral fever-like symptoms progressing over 2–3 days to hemoptysis and cavitation, lasting 3–4 weeks
Subacute low grade fever, wheeze and night sweats over 2–3 days, lasting 3–4 weeks
QUESTIONS.exp: The AEP cell arrows 'viral fever like symptoms (fever, cough) — 2–3 days — Dyspnea, tachypnea, hypoxia (ARDS like presentation)' and adds 'Lasts 3–4 weeks'. ARDS and crazy-pavement AEP were already cross-referenced on page 225. (Book p251)

QUESTIONS.sec: Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia: Acute-on-Chronic Symptoms, Laboratory and Radiological Findings, DEC Treatment, and the Unknown-Cause Table Histories and Presentations
QUESTIONS.q: Which presentation fills the chronic eosinophilic pneumonia column?
opts: A 30–40 year old with females more than males, subacute presentation, low grade fever, wheeze, night sweats and weight loss, without any ARDS mention
A 30–40 year old with females more than males, subacute presentation, low grade fever, wheeze, night sweats and weight loss, plus cough, dyspnea and ARDS
A 50–70 year old with females more than males, subacute presentation, low grade fever, wheeze, night sweats and weight loss, plus cough, dyspnea and ARDS
A 30–40 year old with males more than females, acute presentation, high grade fever and weight gain, plus cough and dyspnea
QUESTIONS.exp: The CEP cell reads '30 – 40 yr (F > M)', 'Subacute presentation', 'Low grade fever, wheeze, night sweats, weight loss' and 'Cough, dyspnea, ARDS'. Both eosinophilic pneumonias can thus reach an ARDS picture by this table. (Book p251)

QUESTIONS.sec: Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia: Acute-on-Chronic Symptoms, Laboratory and Radiological Findings, DEC Treatment, and the Unknown-Cause Table Histories and Presentations
QUESTIONS.q: Which multisystem presentation is printed for idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome?
opts: Lung-limited disease: RS in 40% with TB-like disease, ARDS and pulmonary HTN, and no cardiac involvement printed

End-organ damage across respiratory system, CNS, CVS and peripheral nerves: RS in 40% with TB-like disease, ARDS and pulmonary HTN; CNS neuropsychiatric dysfunction in 60%; CVS valvular regurgitation only

End-organ damage across respiratory system, CNS, CVS and peripheral nerves: RS in 40% with TB-like disease, ARDS and pulmonary HTN; CNS neuropsychiatric dysfunction in 60%; CVS eosinophilic myocarditis and endomyocardial fibrosis

End-organ damage across respiratory system, CNS, CVS and peripheral nerves: RS in 60% with TB-like disease, ARDS and pulmonary HTN; CNS neuropsychiatric dysfunction in 40%; CVS eosinophilic myocarditis and endomyocardial fibrosis
QUESTIONS.exp: The cell lists 'multisystem involvement: End organ damage', 'RS + CNS + CVS + peripheral neuropathy', 'RS (40%): TB like, ARDS, pulm HTN', 'CNS: Neuropsychiatric dysfunction (60 %)' and 'CVS: Eosinophilic myocarditis, endomyocardial fibrosis'. The percentages belong to RS 40 and CNS 60 in that order. (Book p251)

QUESTIONS.sec: Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia: Acute-on-Chronic Symptoms, Laboratory and Radiological Findings, DEC Treatment, and the Unknown-Cause Table Histories and Presentations
QUESTIONS.q: A man who has just restarted smoking develops fever and cough, then within three days is tachypneic and hypoxic with an ARDS-like picture that settles over a month. Which unknown-cause column is he in?
QUESTIONS.exp: Restarted smoking is the AEP history cell, and its 2–3 day progression from viral-like symptoms to ARDS-like hypoxia lasting 3–4 weeks is drawn only in that column. CEP is the subacute disease of atopic women aged 30–40. (Book p251)

QUESTIONS.sec: Unknown Causes of ELD: Investigations in AEP, CEP and Idiopathic Hypereosinophilic Syndrome with Their Steroid Responses
QUESTIONS.q: Which investigations are printed for AEP on page 252, with their captions?
opts: Peripheral blood eosinophilia above 3000; BAL at or above 40% eosinophils; X-ray peripheral infiltrates captioned 'X ray in AEP'; and CT honeycombing

Peripheral blood leukocytosis; BAL lymphocytosis; X-ray diffuse bilateral infiltrates like ARDS captioned 'X ray in AEP'; and CT diffuse parenchymal ground glass opacity with consolidation captioned 'CT in AEP'
Peripheral blood leukocytosis; BAL with increased eosinophils and increased IgE; X-ray diffuse bilateral infiltrates like ARDS captioned 'X ray in AEP'; and CT reverse bat wing appearance

Peripheral blood leukocytosis; BAL with increased eosinophils and increased IgE; X-ray diffuse bilateral infiltrates like ARDS captioned 'X ray in AEP'; and CT diffuse parenchymal ground glass opacity with consolidation captioned 'CT in AEP'
QUESTIONS.exp: The AEP investigations cell reads 'Peripheral blood: leukocytosis. BAL: ↑ eosinophil, ↑ IgE. X-ray: diffuse b/l infiltrates (like ARDS)' over the films captioned 'X ray in AEP', and 'CT: Diffuse parenchymal ground glass opacity, consolidation' over the scans captioned 'CT in AEP'. (Book p252)

QUESTIONS.sec: Unknown Causes of ELD: Investigations in AEP, CEP and Idiopathic Hypereosinophilic Syndrome with Their Steroid Responses
QUESTIONS.q: Which imaging signature defines CEP investigations on page 252?
opts: Batwing appearance without perihilar sparing, with central opacities
Photographic negative of pulmonary edema with diffuse bilateral infiltrates like ARDS
Reverse bat wing appearance, also called the photographic negative of pulmonary edema, with perihilar sparing present and peripheral opacities
Reverse bat wing appearance, also called the photographic negative of pulmonary edema, with perihilar infiltrates and peripheral sparing

QUESTIONS.sec: Unknown Causes of ELD: Investigations in AEP, CEP and Idiopathic Hypereosinophilic Syndrome with Their Steroid Responses
QUESTIONS.q: Match each CEP image on page 252 with its printed caption — 1) The chest film labelled A 2) The CT beside it … A) CT: peripheral pulmonary opacities, predominantly right B) X ray: peripheral pulmonary infiltrate, predominantly right
QUESTIONS.exp: The film is captioned 'X ray: Peripheral pulmonary infiltrate (predominantly right)' and the scan 'CT: Peripheral pulmonary opacities (predominantly right)'. Both captions stress the same right-sided peripheral pattern. (Book p252)

QUESTIONS.sec: Unknown Causes of ELD: Investigations in AEP, CEP and Idiopathic Hypereosinophilic Syndrome with Their Steroid Responses
QUESTIONS.q: Which blood criterion and X-ray description are printed for idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome on page 252?
opts: BAL eosinophilia at or above 40% for more than 6 months, with X-ray showing transient focal or diffuse pulmonary infiltrates
Peripheral eosinophilia above 1500/µL for more than 6 months, with X-ray showing transient focal or diffuse pulmonary infiltrates
Peripheral eosinophilia above 1500/µL for more than 6 months, with X-ray showing fixed peripheral infiltrates
Peripheral eosinophilia above 3000/µL for more than 6 weeks, with X-ray showing transient focal or diffuse pulmonary infiltrates
QUESTIONS.exp: The syndrome cell reads 'Peripheral eosinophilia > 1500 /µl for > 6 months. X ray: Transient focal or diffuse pulmonary infiltrates.' The 3000 threshold and the 40% BAL figure belong to TPE on page 251. (Book p252)

QUESTIONS.sec: Unknown Causes of ELD: Investigations in AEP, CEP and Idiopathic Hypereosinophilic Syndrome with Their Steroid Responses
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the Treatment row that closes the unknown-causes table.
opts: True — 'Steroid' is printed across the AEP and CEP columns while idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome is 'unresponsive to steroid'
False — AEP is unresponsive to steroid while the hypereosinophilic syndrome responds
True — 'Steroid' is printed only under CEP, with AEP left untreated in the row
False — all three unknown causes are printed as steroid responsive
QUESTIONS.exp: The merged treatment cell reads 'Steroid' spanning the AEP and CEP columns, against 'unresponsive to steroid' for idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome — the myeloproliferative biology of page 251 made visible as drug resistance. (Book p252)

QUESTIONS.sec: Unknown Causes of ELD: Investigations in AEP, CEP and Idiopathic Hypereosinophilic Syndrome with Their Steroid Responses
QUESTIONS.q: A 35-year-old atopic woman with weeks of low grade fever, night sweats and weight loss has BAL eosinophils of 45% and a film showing peripheral opacities sparing the perihilar lung, predominantly on the right. Which diagnosis and printed sign-name fit?
opts: Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia — batwing appearance of pulmonary edema itself
Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome — transient focal infiltrates, steroid unresponsive
Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia — reverse bat wing, the photographic negative of pulmonary edema
Acute eosinophilic pneumonia — diffuse infiltrates like ARDS
QUESTIONS.exp: Age 30–40 with female predominance, atopy in 33–50%, the subacute constitutional presentation, BAL at or above 40% and perihilar-sparing peripheral opacities are the CEP column from pages 251–252, whose sign is the reverse bat wing or photographic negative of pulmonary edema. (Book p252)

QUESTIONS.sec: Unknown Causes of ELD: Investigations in AEP, CEP and Idiopathic Hypereosinophilic Syndrome with Their Steroid Responses
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these are printed investigation findings of the unknown ELD causes on page 252, one belongs to a known cause on an earlier page:
opts: BAL at or above 40% eosinophils in CEP
Peripheral eosinophilia above 1500/µL for over 6 months in the hypereosinophilic syndrome
Diffuse parenchymal ground glass opacity with consolidation on CT in AEP
Eggs in sputum as the diagnostic test
QUESTIONS.exp: Eggs in sputum diagnose Paragonimus lung invasion, a known parasite cause on page 250. The other three findings sit in the AEP, CEP and hypereosinophilic-syndrome investigation cells of page 252. (Book p252)

QUESTIONS.sec: Unknown Causes of ELD: Investigations in AEP, CEP and Idiopathic Hypereosinophilic Syndrome with Their Steroid Responses
QUESTIONS.q: In the CEP investigations cell, perihilar ______ is marked present alongside the peripheral opacities.
QUESTIONS.exp: The bullet reads 'Perihilar sparing +', the negative space at the lung centres that makes the image the photographic negative of cardiogenic pulmonary edema, whose batwing is perihilar instead. (Book p252)

QUESTIONS.sec: Aspergillus Microbiology and Its Four Lung Manifestations, with the ABPA Colonisation-to-Bronchiectasis Pathogenesis Flowchart
QUESTIONS.q: Which causative-organism hierarchy and identifying features open the microbiology on page 253?
opts: Aspergillus fumigatus, a saprophyte, ahead of niger, flavus and terreus; identified by conidiophore, septate hyphae and its saprophyte nature
Aspergillus niger ahead of fumigatus, flavus and terreus; identified by conidiophore, septate hyphae and its saprophyte nature
Aspergillus fumigatus, a saprophyte, ahead of niger, flavus and terreus; identified by conidiophore, aseptate hyphae and its parasitic nature
Aspergillus fumigatus ahead of clavatus, niger and flavus; identified by conidial heads only

QUESTIONS.sec: Aspergillus Microbiology and Its Four Lung Manifestations, with the ABPA Colonisation-to-Bronchiectasis Pathogenesis Flowchart
QUESTIONS.q: Match each microbiology image on page 253 with its printed caption — 1) Green GMS-stained lung tissue image 2) Blue image on the right … A) Conidial head B) Fungal balls and hyphae of A. fumigatus in GMS stained lung tissue
QUESTIONS.exp: The left micrograph is captioned 'Fungal balls & hyphae of A. fumigatus in GMS stained lung tissue' and the right one simply 'Conidial head', matching two of the three identifying features listed beside them. (Book p253)

QUESTIONS.sec: Aspergillus Microbiology and Its Four Lung Manifestations, with the ABPA Colonisation-to-Bronchiectasis Pathogenesis Flowchart
QUESTIONS.q: Which four manifestations of Aspergillus in lung are drawn on page 253?
opts: ABPA; aspergilloma; acute necrotising aspergillosis; and allergic aspergillus sinusitis
Aspergilloma; chronic necrotising aspergillosis, also called chronic cavitating pulmonary aspergillosis; angio invasive aspergillosis; and aspergillus tracheobronchitis with ABPA excluded
ABPA; aspergilloma; chronic necrotising aspergillosis, also called chronic cavitating pulmonary aspergillosis; and angio invasive aspergillosis
ABPA; aspergilloma; chronic necrotising aspergillosis, also called chronic fibrosing pulmonary aspergillosis; and angio invasive aspergillosis
QUESTIONS.exp: The 'manifestations in lung' tree has four arms: ABPA, aspergilloma, 'Chronic necrotising aspergillosis/ Chronic cavitating pulmonary aspergillosis' and 'Angio invasive aspergillosis'. (Book p253)

QUESTIONS.sec: Aspergillus Microbiology and Its Four Lung Manifestations, with the ABPA Colonisation-to-Bronchiectasis Pathogenesis Flowchart
QUESTIONS.q: Match each non-ABPA manifestation with its printed descriptors — 1) Aspergilloma 2) Chronic necrotising or cavitating aspergillosis 3) Angio invasive aspergillosis … A) Bronchial wall invasion, typically in COPD, with thick walled cavities B) Common in neutropenic people and long term steroids, with blood stream infection and bone marrow transplant infections C) Underlying cavity mostly due to TB
QUESTIONS.exp: Aspergilloma carries the single bullet 'underlying cavity mostly due to TB'; chronic necrotising disease carries bronchial wall invasion, typical COPD setting and thick walled cavities; angio invasive disease carries the neutropenic/long-term-steroid host with blood stream and bone marrow transplant infections. (Book p253)

QUESTIONS.sec: Aspergillus Microbiology and Its Four Lung Manifestations, with the ABPA Colonisation-to-Bronchiectasis Pathogenesis Flowchart
QUESTIONS.q: Which opening steps does the ABPA pathogenesis flowchart print?
opts: In long standing bronchial Asthma or cystic fibrosis the organism colonises the airway, provoking a complex hypersensitivity reaction of Type IV greater than Type III
In long standing COPD the organism invades the airway wall, provoking a complex hypersensitivity reaction of Type III greater than Type I
In neutropenic patients the organism colonises the airway, provoking a complex hypersensitivity reaction of Type I greater than Type III
In long standing bronchial Asthma or cystic fibrosis the organism colonises the airway, provoking a complex hypersensitivity reaction of Type I greater than Type III
QUESTIONS.exp: The flowchart descends 'In patients with long standing bronchial asthma (BA) or cystic fibrosis (CF) → Organism colonises the airway → Complex hypersensitivity reaction + (Type I > Type III)'. Type IV greater than III is hypersensitivity pneumonitis on page 257. (Book p253)

QUESTIONS.sec: Aspergillus Microbiology and Its Four Lung Manifestations, with the ABPA Colonisation-to-Bronchiectasis Pathogenesis Flowchart
QUESTIONS.q: Match each numbered consequence in the pathogenesis flowchart with its printed downstream path — 1) First numbered arm 2) Eosinophilic inflammation 3) Mucus plugs containing septate hyphae in the bronchial wall … A) Cough with sputum yielding bronchial mucosal plugs with hyphae and eosinophils, and atelectasis B) Eosinophilia with raised IgE, with no further arrow C) Migratory lung infiltrates, and weakening of the bronchial wall due to inflammation leading to bronchiectasis
QUESTIONS.exp: Arm 1 ends at 'Eosinophilia ↑ IgE'; arm 2, eosinophilic inflammation (also fed by an arrow back from arm 3), splits to migratory lung infiltrates and to weakening of bronchial wall ending in bronchiectasis; arm 3 splits to cough with sputum containing bronchial mucosal plugs (hyphae and eosinophils) and to atelectasis. (Book p253)

QUESTIONS.sec: Aspergillus Microbiology and Its Four Lung Manifestations, with the ABPA Colonisation-to-Bronchiectasis Pathogenesis Flowchart
QUESTIONS.q: A long-standing asthmatic coughs up plugs in which septate hyphae and eosinophils are found, has shifting infiltrates, and is developing bronchiectasis from a weakened bronchial wall. Which single printed mechanism drives all three?
opts: Airway colonisation by Aspergillus with a complex Type I greater than Type III hypersensitivity reaction
Type IV greater than Type III hypersensitivity to inhaled organic dust
Colonisation of a TB cavity forming an aspergilloma
Angioinvasion by Aspergillus in a neutropenic host
QUESTIONS.exp: Mucus plugs with hyphae and eosinophils, migratory infiltrates and wall-weakening bronchiectasis are arms 3 and 2 of the ABPA flowchart, all descending from colonisation plus Type I > Type III hypersensitivity in Asthma or CF. (Book p253)

QUESTIONS.sec: Aspergillus Microbiology and Its Four Lung Manifestations, with the ABPA Colonisation-to-Bronchiectasis Pathogenesis Flowchart
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the flowchart's bronchiectasis route on page 253.
opts: True — bronchiectasis is reached through atelectasis in the third arm
True — bronchiectasis is reached through eosinophilic inflammation weakening the bronchial wall, not through the mucus-plug arm, whose terminals are plugs in sputum and atelectasis
False — bronchiectasis is the direct terminal of the mucus-plug arm
False — migratory infiltrates, not wall weakening, arrow into bronchiectasis
QUESTIONS.exp: Only the 'weakening of bronchial wall due to inflammation' sub-arrow of eosinophilic inflammation descends to 'Bronchiectasis'; the mucus-plug arm ends at bronchial mucosal plugs in sputum and at atelectasis. (Book p253)

QUESTIONS.sec: Th2 Eosinophilic Inflammation, Central Proximal Bronchiectasis on Imaging, ABPA Clinical Features and the Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes (Rheumatology)
QUESTIONS.q: Which immune note and which four bronchiectasis features open page 254?
opts: Eosinophilic inflammation is Th2 mediated through IL 4, IL 5 and IL 13; ABPA bronchiectasis is bilateral, upper lobe, peripheral and distal
Eosinophilic inflammation is Th2 mediated through IL 1, IL 6 and TNF; ABPA bronchiectasis is bilateral, upper lobe, central and proximal
Eosinophilic inflammation is Th2 mediated through IL 4, IL 5 and IL 13; ABPA bronchiectasis, differentiating it from standard bronchiectasis, is bilateral, upper lobe, central and proximal
Eosinophilic inflammation is Th1 mediated through IL 4, IL 5 and IL 13; ABPA bronchiectasis is unilateral, lower lobe, central and proximal
QUESTIONS.exp: The Note reads 'Eosinophilic inflammation: Th2 mediated (IL 4, IL 5, IL 13)' — the TH2 trio of page 244 — and 'Features of bronchiectasis in ABPA (To differentiate from standard bronchiectasis): Bilateral, upper lobe, Central, Proximal'. Standard bronchiectasis on page 238 was unilateral. (Book p254)

QUESTIONS.sec: Th2 Eosinophilic Inflammation, Central Proximal Bronchiectasis on Imaging, ABPA Clinical Features and the Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes (Rheumatology)
QUESTIONS.q: Match each page 254 image with its printed labels and caption — 1) Top-left CT lung window 2) Top-right HRCT thorax 3) Bottom-left gross specimen 4) Bottom-right CT chest … A) Tree in bud appearance labelled, captioned central bronchiectasis B) Mucus plugs labelled, captioned hyperattenuated mucus C) Cystic bronchiectasis of central aspects labelled, soft tissue upper lobe nodules representing mucoid impaction with dilated bronchi D) Captioned bronchi distended with mucus in ABPA
QUESTIONS.exp: The four images are captioned 'CT (lung window): Soft tissue upper lobe nodules represent mucoid impaction with dilated bronchi' under the cystic central bronchiectasis label; 'HRCT thorax: Central bronchiectasis' under the tree in bud label; 'Bronchi distended with mucus (ABPA)'; and 'CT chest: Hyperattenuated mucus' under the mucus plugs label. (Book p254)

QUESTIONS.sec: Th2 Eosinophilic Inflammation, Central Proximal Bronchiectasis on Imaging, ABPA Clinical Features and the Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes (Rheumatology)
QUESTIONS.q: Which clinical presentation is printed for ABPA on page 254?
opts: Recurrent acute exacerbation in a patient with chronic, steroid dependent or refractory-to-treatment or acute bronchial Asthma, or with cystic fibrosis
Recurrent hemoptysis in a patient with a TB cavity
Recurrent acute exacerbation in a neutropenic patient on long term steroids
A first acute exacerbation in a patient with newly diagnosed Asthma or COPD
QUESTIONS.exp: Presentation reads 'Recurrent acute exacerbation in a patient with chronic/steroid dependent/refractory to treatment/acute BA or CF', returning to the Asthma-or-CF host of the pathogenesis chart. (Book p254)

QUESTIONS.sec: Th2 Eosinophilic Inflammation, Central Proximal Bronchiectasis on Imaging, ABPA Clinical Features and the Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes (Rheumatology)
QUESTIONS.q: Which symptoms, sign frequency and course are printed for ABPA?
opts: Fever with cough and expectoration of a brownish thick mucosal plug; signs — crackles and clubbing — in 80–85%; and a course that rarely causes upper lobe fibrosis
Fever with cough and expectoration of a brownish thick mucosal plug; signs — crackles and clubbing — in only 15–20%; and a course that rarely causes upper lobe fibrosis
Afebrile cough with gelatinous sputum; signs in only 15–20%; and a course that rarely causes upper lobe fibrosis
Fever with cough and expectoration of chocolate colored sputum; signs in only 15–20%; and a course that commonly causes upper lobe fibrosis
QUESTIONS.exp: Symptoms read 'Fever + cough with expectoration (Brownish thick mucosal plug)', Signs 'Only in 15 – 20 %: Crackles, Clubbing', and Course 'Rarely cause upper lobe fibrosis'. Chocolate sputum belongs to lung fluke on page 250 and gelatinous sputum to PAP on page 242. (Book p254)

QUESTIONS.sec: Th2 Eosinophilic Inflammation, Central Proximal Bronchiectasis on Imaging, ABPA Clinical Features and the Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes (Rheumatology)
QUESTIONS.q: A steroid-dependent asthmatic with recurrent exacerbations expectorates brownish thick plugs; most such patients, the page warns, will show neither of the two listed signs. What are those signs and their combined frequency?
opts: Crackles and fever, present in 80% of patients
Wheeze and clubbing, present in only 15–20% of patients
Crackles and clubbing, present in only 15–20% of patients
Clubbing and hemoptysis, present in only 5% of patients
QUESTIONS.exp: Under Signs the page gives only 'Crackles' and 'Clubbing' and heads them 'Only in 15 – 20 %', so their absence in a plug-producing refractory asthmatic argues nothing against ABPA. (Book p254)

QUESTIONS.sec: Th2 Eosinophilic Inflammation, Central Proximal Bronchiectasis on Imaging, ABPA Clinical Features and the Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes (Rheumatology)
QUESTIONS.q: ABPA rarely causes upper lobe fibrosis, and the first cause-group in the closing Note is Rheumatology, naming ankylosing spondylitis and ______.
QUESTIONS.exp: The Note 'upper lobe fibrosis causes: 1. Rheumatology:' lists ankylosing spondylitis on the left and sarcoidosis on the right of the same line, the pair already braced as CTDs in the upper-lobe ILD list on page 242. (Book p254)

QUESTIONS.sec: Th2 Eosinophilic Inflammation, Central Proximal Bronchiectasis on Imaging, ABPA Clinical Features and the Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes (Rheumatology)
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these descriptors are printed for ABPA bronchiectasis on page 254, one describes standard bronchiectasis instead:
QUESTIONS.exp: ABPA bronchiectasis is bilateral, upper lobe, central and proximal, expressly 'to differentiate from standard bronchiectasis', which on pages 218 and 238 is usually unilateral with a left lower lobe predominance. (Book p254)

QUESTIONS.sec: Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes Completed, ABPA Diagnostic Criteria with IgE, PFT Pattern and the Five Imaging Captions
QUESTIONS.q: Which groups complete the upper lobe fibrosis causes at the top of page 255?
opts: Occupational exposure with silicosis, coal worker's pneumoconiosis and berylliosis; and lung conditions ABPA, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and TB
Occupational exposure with silicosis, coal worker's pneumoconiosis and berylliosis; and lung conditions ABPA, LAM, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and TB
Occupational exposure with asbestosis, silicosis and berylliosis; and lung conditions ABPA, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and TB
Drug exposure with bleomycin and amiodarone; and lung conditions ABPA, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and TB
QUESTIONS.exp: Groups 2 and 3 read 'Occupational exposure: Silicosis, Coal worker's pneumoconiosis, Berylliosis' and 'Lung conditions: ABPA, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, Hypersensitivity pneumonitis, TB', continuing group 1 from page 254 and matching the upper-lobe ILD page 242. (Book p255)

QUESTIONS.sec: Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes Completed, ABPA Diagnostic Criteria with IgE, PFT Pattern and the Five Imaging Captions
QUESTIONS.q: Which obligatory criteria and thresholds does the ABPA evaluation print on page 255?
opts: After a predisposing Asthma or CF, either obligatory criterion suffices: IgE above 100 IU/ml, or a positive immediate skin test to Aspergillus
After a predisposing Asthma or CF, both obligatory criteria are required: IgE above 1000 IU/ml, and precipitins against Aspergillus
After a predisposing Asthma or CF, both obligatory criteria are required: IgE above 1000 IU/ml, and a positive immediate skin test or increased IgE antibody to Aspergillus
Obligatory criteria come first with IgE above 1000 IU/ml, and predisposing Asthma or CF is merely supportive
QUESTIONS.exp: Criteria run '1. Predisposing asthma or CF. 2. Obligatory criteria: a. IgE >1000 IU/ml. b. Positive immediate skin test or increased IgE antibody to Aspergillus.' Precipitins sit one tier down among the supportive criteria. (Book p255)

QUESTIONS.sec: Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes Completed, ABPA Diagnostic Criteria with IgE, PFT Pattern and the Five Imaging Captions
QUESTIONS.q: Which supportive criteria, and how many of them, does the diagnosis require?
opts: Any two of eosinophilia above 1500/µL, precipitins or raised IgE antibody to Aspergillus, and consistent radiographic opacities
Any two of eosinophilia above 500/µL, precipitins or raised IgG antibody to Aspergillus, and consistent radiographic opacities
All three of eosinophilia above 500/µL, precipitins or raised IgG antibody to Aspergillus, and consistent radiographic opacities
Any one of eosinophilia above 500/µL, precipitins or raised IgG antibody to Aspergillus, and consistent radiographic opacities
QUESTIONS.exp: Item 3 reads 'Supportive criteria: Any 2 — a. Eosinophilia >500 /µL. b. Precipitins/↑ IgG antibody to Aspergillus. c. Consistent radiographic opacities.' The antibody class here is IgG, where the obligatory tier used total and specific IgE. (Book p255)

QUESTIONS.sec: Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes Completed, ABPA Diagnostic Criteria with IgE, PFT Pattern and the Five Imaging Captions
QUESTIONS.q: Match each evaluation bullet on page 255 with its printed statement — 1) Most useful test 2) Predominant PFT pattern 3) Stage 5 PFT pattern … A) Fibrosis with a restrictive pattern B) Obstructive pattern predominantly, attributed to bronchiectasis C) IgE levels, for both diagnosis and follow up
QUESTIONS.exp: The bullets read 'most useful test for diagnosis and follow up: IgE levels' and 'PFT pattern: Obstructive pattern predominantly (Bronchiectasis). Stage 5: Fibrosis (Restrictive).' The restrictive pattern is reserved for the fibrotic final stage. (Book p255)

QUESTIONS.sec: Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes Completed, ABPA Diagnostic Criteria with IgE, PFT Pattern and the Five Imaging Captions
QUESTIONS.q: Match each imaging caption on page 255 with its printed expansion — 1) Fleeting infiltrates over the dated film series 2) Tram track shadows 3) Finger in glove 4) Trees in bud, as printed … A) Mucoid impaction in dilated bronchi B) Cylindrical and proximal bronchiectasis of the upper lobe with thickening of the bronchial wall, the nodules C) Parenchymal infiltrates which are irregular and transient D) Parallel linear shadows extending from the hilum in bronchial distribution
QUESTIONS.exp: Captions read 'Fleeting infiltrates: Parenchymal infiltrates which are irregular and transient' under the six dated films, 'Tram track shadows: Parallel linear shadows extending from hilum in bronchial distribution', 'Finger in glove: Mucoid impaction in dilated bronchi', and 'Trees in bud: Cylindrical and proximal bronchiectasis of upper lobe with thickening of bronchial wall (Nodules)', with a separate 'Saccular dilatation' label on the last scan. (Book p255)

QUESTIONS.sec: Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes Completed, ABPA Diagnostic Criteria with IgE, PFT Pattern and the Five Imaging Captions
QUESTIONS.q: An asthmatic has IgE of 1400 IU/ml, a positive immediate skin test to Aspergillus, eosinophilia of 700/µL and consistent opacities, but negative precipitins. Does the page 255 scheme diagnose ABPA, and what will follow-up track?
opts: Yes — but follow-up tracks the eosinophil count as the most useful test
No — all three supportive criteria are required, and only two are present
Yes — both obligatory criteria and two supportive criteria are met, and IgE levels are the most useful test for diagnosis and follow up
No — precipitins are obligatory, so the scheme fails despite the IgE and skin test
QUESTIONS.exp: Predisposing Asthma, IgE above 1000 IU/ml and a positive immediate skin test satisfy tiers 1 and 2, and eosinophilia above 500/µL plus consistent radiographic opacities give the 'Any 2' supportive criteria; precipitins are supportive, not obligatory. (Book p255)

QUESTIONS.sec: Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes Completed, ABPA Diagnostic Criteria with IgE, PFT Pattern and the Five Imaging Captions
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the ABPA PFT statements on page 255.
opts: True — the predominant pattern is restrictive, turning obstructive at Stage 5
True — the predominant pattern is obstructive because of bronchiectasis, while restriction appears only at Stage 5 with fibrosis
False — the predominant pattern is restrictive from the first stage
False — Stage 5 fibrosis is printed with an obstructive pattern
QUESTIONS.exp: The bullet reads 'PFT pattern: Obstructive pattern predominantly (Bronchiectasis). Stage 5: Fibrosis (Restrictive).' Airway disease obstructs until end-stage fibrosis restricts, echoing the pure-airway logic of page 243. (Book p255)

QUESTIONS.sec: X-Ray Findings Unlikely or Against ABPA, the Steroid–Itraconazole–Omalizumab Treatment Flowchart and IgE Monitoring
QUESTIONS.q: Which two findings are graded merely 'Unlikely' against an ABPA diagnosis on page 256?
opts: Bronchial wall thickening, and small nodules, with the bracket that they occur only in tree in bud
Bronchial wall thickening, and an air fluid level
Pleural involvement, and small nodules, with the bracket that they occur only in tree in bud
QUESTIONS.exp: Under 'X-Ray findings against diagnosis of ABPA' the 'Unlikely:' tier lists only bronchial wall thickening and 'Small nodules (Only in tree in bud)'. Wall thickening and nodules did appear inside the page 255 tree-in-bud caption, hence unlikely rather than against. (Book p256)

QUESTIONS.sec: X-Ray Findings Unlikely or Against ABPA, the Steroid–Itraconazole–Omalizumab Treatment Flowchart and IgE Monitoring
QUESTIONS.q: Which five findings are graded fully 'Against' the diagnosis?
opts: Pleural involvement, lymphadenopathy, consolidation, cavitation and perihilar involvement
Pleural effusion, lymphadenopathy, consolidation, air fluid level and basal involvement
Pleural involvement, lymphadenopathy, fleeting infiltrates, air fluid level and perihilar involvement
Pleural involvement, lymphadenopathy, consolidation, air fluid level and perihilar involvement
QUESTIONS.exp: The 'Against:' tier lists pleural involvement, lymphadenopathy and consolidation on the left and air fluid level with perihilar involvement on the right. Fleeting infiltrates argue for ABPA on page 255, not against it. (Book p256)

QUESTIONS.sec: X-Ray Findings Unlikely or Against ABPA, the Steroid–Itraconazole–Omalizumab Treatment Flowchart and IgE Monitoring
QUESTIONS.q: A presumed ABPA film instead shows lymphadenopathy, pleural involvement and a perihilar consolidation with an air fluid level. How does page 256 grade this collection?
opts: These findings sit in the 'Unlikely' tier, so ABPA remains probable
Every one of these findings sits in the 'Against' tier, so the film argues against ABPA
Only the air fluid level is against ABPA; the rest are consistent with it
These are the classic fleeting infiltrates of ABPA and support the diagnosis
QUESTIONS.exp: Pleural involvement, lymphadenopathy, consolidation, air fluid level and perihilar involvement make up the complete 'Against' list. The merely unlikely tier holds only bronchial wall thickening and small nodules. (Book p256)

QUESTIONS.sec: X-Ray Findings Unlikely or Against ABPA, the Steroid–Itraconazole–Omalizumab Treatment Flowchart and IgE Monitoring
QUESTIONS.q: Which first-line treatment and duration does the page 256 flowchart print, and with what adjunct?
opts: Four weeks of steroid, marked DOC, plus postural drainage alone
Twelve weeks of steroid, marked DOC, plus omalizumab from the start
Twelve weeks of steroid, marked DOC, plus an airway clearance device or hypertonic saline
Sixteen weeks of itraconazole, marked DOC, plus an airway clearance device or hypertonic saline
QUESTIONS.exp: Treatment opens '12 weeks steroid (DOC) + airway clearance device/hypertonic saline' — the hypertonic saline and clearance pairing carried over from bronchiectasis care on page 222. (Book p256)

QUESTIONS.sec: X-Ray Findings Unlikely or Against ABPA, the Steroid–Itraconazole–Omalizumab Treatment Flowchart and IgE Monitoring
QUESTIONS.q: A patient relapses whenever steroids are tapered, then fails the next step too. Which printed ladder has she climbed?
opts: Steroid dependence or relapse leads to 16 weeks of voriconazole, and no resolution leads to mepolizumab
Steroid dependence or relapse leads to 12 further weeks of steroid, and no resolution leads to itraconazole
Steroid dependence or relapse leads to omalizumab, and no resolution leads to 16 weeks of itraconazole
Steroid dependence or relapse leads to 16 weeks of itraconazole therapy, and no resolution on that leads to omalizumab
QUESTIONS.exp: The arrows read 'Steroid dependent/relapse → 16 week Itraconazole therapy → No resolution → Omalizumab' — the anti-IgE biologic of page 247 reserved for the last printed step. (Book p256)

QUESTIONS.sec: X-Ray Findings Unlikely or Against ABPA, the Steroid–Itraconazole–Omalizumab Treatment Flowchart and IgE Monitoring
QUESTIONS.q: The closing Note of the chapter instructs that ______ levels are to be monitored periodically.
QUESTIONS.exp: The Note reads 'IgE levels to be monitored periodically', completing the arc from page 255, where IgE was the most useful test for diagnosis and follow up. (Book p256)

QUESTIONS.sec: X-Ray Findings Unlikely or Against ABPA, the Steroid–Itraconazole–Omalizumab Treatment Flowchart and IgE Monitoring
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these are printed steps or agents in the ABPA treatment flow on page 256, one is borrowed from another chapter:
opts: Twelve weeks of steroid as DOC
Sixteen weeks of itraconazole for steroid dependence or relapse
QUESTIONS.exp: The ladder is steroid (DOC) with airway clearance or hypertonic saline, then itraconazole, then omalizumab. Whole lung lavage treats pulmonary alveolar proteinosis on page 242 and never enters ABPA care. (Book p256)

QUESTIONS.sec: Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis: Type IV over III Pathogenesis, Absent Type I Features, and the Twelve-Disease Etiology Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which synonym and host line open hypersensitivity pneumonitis on page 257?
opts: AKA extrinsic allergic alveolitis, occurring usually in smokers
AKA extrinsic allergic alveolitis, occurring usually in non smokers
AKA intrinsic allergic alveolitis, occurring usually in non smokers
AKA extrinsic allergic bronchiolitis, occurring usually in non smokers
QUESTIONS.exp: The head of the chapter reads 'AKA extrinsic allergic alveolitis' and 'usually in non smokers' — a useful counterweight to the smoking-associated cystic and interstitial diseases of pages 236–240. (Book p257)

QUESTIONS.sec: Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis: Type IV over III Pathogenesis, Absent Type I Features, and the Twelve-Disease Etiology Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which pathogenesis chain is printed for HP on page 257?
opts: Repeated organic dust inhalation causes hypersensitivity of Type III greater than IV, producing predominantly neutrophilic inflammation of terminal airways, alveoli and interstitium
Single organic dust inhalation causes hypersensitivity of Type IV greater than III, producing predominantly lymphocytic inflammation of large airways only
Repeated inorganic dust inhalation causes hypersensitivity of Type I greater than III, producing predominantly eosinophilic inflammation of terminal airways, alveoli and interstitium
Repeated organic dust inhalation causes hypersensitivity of Type IV greater than III, producing predominantly lymphocytic inflammation of terminal airways, alveoli and interstitium
QUESTIONS.exp: The chain reads 'Repeated organic dust inhalation → Hypersensitivity (Type IV > III) → Inflammation (Predominantly lymphocytic) of terminal airways, alveoli & interstitium'. Repetition, the IV-over-III order and the lymphocyte all matter. (Book p257)

QUESTIONS.sec: Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis: Type IV over III Pathogenesis, Absent Type I Features, and the Twelve-Disease Etiology Table
QUESTIONS.q: Because there is no type 1 hypersensitivity in HP, which three absences does the pathology block print?
opts: No lymphocytosis, no raised IgE and no diffuse infiltrates
No eosinophilia, no raised IgE and no granulomas
No eosinophilia, no raised IgE and no migratory lung infiltrates
No eosinophilia, no precipitins and no migratory lung infiltrates
QUESTIONS.exp: The block reads 'No type 1 hypersensitivity → No: Eosinophilia, ↑ IgE, migratory lung infiltrates' — precisely the type 1 triad that Loeffler syndrome displayed on page 250. (Book p257)

QUESTIONS.sec: Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis: Type IV over III Pathogenesis, Absent Type I Features, and the Twelve-Disease Etiology Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which infiltrate evolution and granuloma statement complete the pathology on page 257?
opts: Pulmonary infiltrates are diffuse initially and become a reticulo-nodular pattern, and non caseating granulomas are present
Pulmonary infiltrates are peripheral initially and become diffuse, and non caseating granulomas are present
Pulmonary infiltrates are migratory initially and become reticular, and caseating granulomas are present
Pulmonary infiltrates are diffuse initially and become a reticulo-nodular pattern, and granulomas are absent
QUESTIONS.exp: The bullets read 'Pulmonary infiltrates: Diffuse (Initially) → Reticulo-nodular pattern' and 'Non caseating granulomas present', the same evolution the CXR line repeats on page 259. (Book p257)

QUESTIONS.sec: Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis: Type IV over III Pathogenesis, Absent Type I Features, and the Twelve-Disease Etiology Table
QUESTIONS.q: Match each thermophilic-actinomycete Disease in the etiology table with its printed source — 1) Farmer's lung, marked most common 2) Bagassosis, marked second most common 3) Mushroom worker's lung … A) Moldy compost or mushroom B) Moldy hay C) Moldy sugarcane
QUESTIONS.exp: Farmer's lung (m/c) comes from moldy hay, bagassosis (2nd m/c) from moldy sugarcane and mushroom worker's lung from moldy compost/mushroom, all three sharing the merged antigen cell 'Thermophilic actinomycete: Thermoactinomyces vulgaris (m/c antigen)'. (Book p257)

QUESTIONS.sec: Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis: Type IV over III Pathogenesis, Absent Type I Features, and the Twelve-Disease Etiology Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which antigen cell is shared by the next four rows of the etiology table, and which sources accompany them?
