opts: Aspergillus clavatus covers compost lung (compost), tobacco worker's lung (barley), malt worker's lung (mold on tobacco) and cheese washer's lung, whose source cell is blank
Aspergillus fumigatus covers compost lung (compost), tobacco worker's lung (mold on tobacco), malt worker's lung (barley) and cheese washer's lung
Thermoactinomyces vulgaris covers compost lung, tobacco worker's lung, malt worker's lung and cheese washer's lung from cheese washings
Aspergillus clavatus covers compost lung (compost), tobacco worker's lung (mold on tobacco), malt worker's lung (barley) and cheese washer's lung, whose source cell is blank
QUESTIONS.exp: The second merged antigen cell, 'Aspergillus clavatus', spans compost lung, tobacco worker's lung, malt worker's lung and cheese washer's lung, with sources compost, mold on tobacco and barley printed for the first three and the cheese washer source left blank. (Book p257)

QUESTIONS.sec: Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis: Type IV over III Pathogenesis, Absent Type I Features, and the Twelve-Disease Etiology Table
QUESTIONS.q: Match each remaining etiology-table Disease with its printed source and antigen pairing — 1) Hot tub, humidifier or air conditioner lung 2) Bird fancier's lung 3) Wood trimmer's lung 4) Familial HP and chemical worker's lung … A) Source pigeon, parrot or chicken with avian droppings as antigen B) Familial HP from wood pulp with Bacillus subtilis, and chemical worker's lung from polyurethane foams (isocyanate) with its antigen cell blank C) Source cell blank with Cladosporium and MAC as antigens D) Source cell blank with Rhizopus as antigen
QUESTIONS.exp: Hot tub/humidifier/air conditioner lung pairs a blank source with Cladosporium and MAC; bird fancier's lung pairs pigeon/parrot/chicken with avian droppings; wood trimmer's lung pairs a blank source with Rhizopus; familial HP pairs wood pulp with Bacillus subtilis; and chemical worker's lung prints polyurethane foams (isocyanate) with a blank antigen cell. (Book p257)

QUESTIONS.sec: Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis: Type IV over III Pathogenesis, Absent Type I Features, and the Twelve-Disease Etiology Table
QUESTIONS.q: A non-smoking pigeon keeper develops lymphocytic alveolitis with non caseating granulomas, no eosinophilia and a normal IgE. Which Disease, source and antigen does the page 257 table assign him?
opts: Mushroom worker's lung — moldy compost source, Thermoactinomyces antigen
Bird fancier's lung — pigeon source, avian droppings antigen
Farmer's lung — moldy hay source, Thermoactinomyces vulgaris antigen
Bird fancier's lung — pigeon source, Aspergillus clavatus antigen
QUESTIONS.exp: Bird fancier's lung is the only row sourced to 'Pigeon/ parrot/ chicken' with antigen 'Avian droppings', and the absent eosinophilia and IgE rise are the no-type-1 signature printed above the table. (Book p257)

QUESTIONS.sec: Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis: Type IV over III Pathogenesis, Absent Type I Features, and the Twelve-Disease Etiology Table
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the superlatives printed inside the etiology table.
opts: False — bagassosis is marked most common and farmer's lung second most common
False — Aspergillus clavatus is marked the most common antigen
True — bird fancier's lung is marked most common because its row is printed in red
True — farmer's lung is marked the most common Disease and Thermoactinomyces vulgaris the most common antigen, while bagassosis is marked second most common
QUESTIONS.exp: The table tags 'Farmer's lung (m/c)', 'Bagassosis (2nd m/c)' and, in the merged cell, 'Thermoactinomyces vulgaris (m/c antigen)'. Bird fancier's lung is highlighted in red ink but carries no frequency tag. (Book p257)

QUESTIONS.sec: Acute, Subacute and Chronic Presentations, Complications, Non-Caseating Granuloma and Emphysema Notes, Precipitins and BAL CD8/CD4
QUESTIONS.q: Match each HP presentation tempo on page 258 with its printed fate — 1) Acute 2) Subacute 3) Chronic … A) Marked most common B) Can cause fibrosis, that is ILD C) Self resolving
QUESTIONS.exp: Presentation reads 'Acute: Self resolving', 'Subacute: m/c' and 'Chronic: Can cause fibrosis (ILD)', returning HP to the ILD classification of page 236 in its chronic form. (Book p258)

QUESTIONS.sec: Acute, Subacute and Chronic Presentations, Complications, Non-Caseating Granuloma and Emphysema Notes, Precipitins and BAL CD8/CD4
QUESTIONS.q: Which clinical features and timescale define the acute form of HP?
opts: Gradually progressive dyspnea and cough, resolving in 2–4 days
Fever, chills and cough with a raised IgE, resolving in 2–4 weeks
Fever, chills and cough with a raised ESR, resolving in 2–4 days
Fever, chills and cough with a raised ESR, resolving in 2–4 hours as printed
QUESTIONS.exp: The acute form reads 'Fever, chills, cough (↑ ESR)' with 'Resolves in 2–4 days' beneath it. The raised marker is ESR, not the IgE that type 1 disease would raise. (Book p258)

QUESTIONS.sec: Acute, Subacute and Chronic Presentations, Complications, Non-Caseating Granuloma and Emphysema Notes, Precipitins and BAL CD8/CD4
QUESTIONS.q: Which three statements define the subacute form of HP?
opts: Gradually progressive dyspnea and cough with fatiguability, no systemic features, and diffuse involvement without lobar preference as printed
Gradually progressive dyspnea and cough with fatiguability, no systemic features, and upper lobe involvement
Gradually progressive dyspnea and cough with fatiguability, prominent systemic features, and lower lobe involvement
Abrupt dyspnea and cough with fever and chills, and upper lobe involvement
QUESTIONS.exp: The subacute form reads 'Gradually progressive dyspnea & cough + fatiguability', 'No systemic features' and 'Upper lobe involvement' — the lobar preference that placed HP in the upper-lobe lists on pages 242 and 255. (Book p258)

QUESTIONS.sec: Acute, Subacute and Chronic Presentations, Complications, Non-Caseating Granuloma and Emphysema Notes, Precipitins and BAL CD8/CD4
QUESTIONS.q: Match each named HP Disease with its printed complication on page 258 — 1) Bird fancier's lung 2) Farmer's lung … A) Emphysematous changes B) Rarely causes fibrosis or ILD
QUESTIONS.exp: Complications read 'Bird fancier's lung: Rarely cause fibrosis/ ILD' and 'Farmer's lung: Emphysematous changes'. The commonest HP thus ends in emphysema rather than the fibrosis the chronic form threatens. (Book p258)

QUESTIONS.sec: Acute, Subacute and Chronic Presentations, Complications, Non-Caseating Granuloma and Emphysema Notes, Precipitins and BAL CD8/CD4
QUESTIONS.q: Which seven causes of non caseating granulomas are listed in the page 258 Note?
opts: HP, 30% of TB as printed, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, cat scratch disease, Crohn's disease and berylliosis
Sarcoidosis, 30% of TB as printed, lymphoma, cat scratch disease, Crohn's disease, berylliosis and ABPA
HP, 30% of TB as printed, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, cat scratch disease, Crohn's disease and silicosis
HP, TB without any percentage, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, cat scratch disease, ulcerative colitis and berylliosis
QUESTIONS.exp: The Note lists HP itself, '30 % TB', lymphoma, sarcoidosis, cat scratch disease, Crohn's disease and berylliosis — berylliosis having been introduced as the sarcoid mimic on pages 228–229. HP heads its own granuloma list. (Book p258)

QUESTIONS.sec: Acute, Subacute and Chronic Presentations, Complications, Non-Caseating Granuloma and Emphysema Notes, Precipitins and BAL CD8/CD4
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these are printed on page 258 as diseases causing emphysematous changes apart from COPD, one is not:
QUESTIONS.exp: The second Note lists farmer's lung, cryptogenic organising pneumonia and coal worker's pneumoconiosis (rare) as non-COPD emphysema causes. Bird fancier's lung, in the complications block above, rarely causes fibrosis instead. (Book p258)

QUESTIONS.sec: Acute, Subacute and Chronic Presentations, Complications, Non-Caseating Granuloma and Emphysema Notes, Precipitins and BAL CD8/CD4
QUESTIONS.q: What does the Management section print about serum precipitin in HP?
opts: It is always negative because HP has no type III component
It is specific and diagnostic, arising due to type I hypersensitivity
It can be positive but is non-specific, arising due to type IV hypersensitivity
It can be positive but is non-specific, arising due to type III hypersensitivity
QUESTIONS.exp: Investigations read 'S. precipitin: Can be positive (Non specific): D/t type III hypersensitivity' — the junior partner in the Type IV > III mechanism leaving a serological trace that cannot confirm the diagnosis. (Book p258)

QUESTIONS.sec: Acute, Subacute and Chronic Presentations, Complications, Non-Caseating Granuloma and Emphysema Notes, Precipitins and BAL CD8/CD4
QUESTIONS.q: BAL in HP shows lymphocytosis with the printed fraction CD8/CD4 greater than ______.
QUESTIONS.exp: The BAL line reads 'Lymphocytosis: CD 8 / CD 4 > 2', a CD8-dominant lavage. The inverted ratio for sarcoidosis is given as a mirror note on the next page. (Book p258)

QUESTIONS.sec: Acute, Subacute and Chronic Presentations, Complications, Non-Caseating Granuloma and Emphysema Notes, Precipitins and BAL CD8/CD4
QUESTIONS.q: Four days after shovelling moldy hay a farmer's fever, chills and cough with raised ESR settle on their own, but over the following seasons he develops emphysematous change rather than fibrosis. Which tempo and which complication has he shown, in the page's terms?
opts: The subacute form of bird fancier's lung, which rarely causes fibrosis
The acute self-resolving form of farmer's lung, whose printed complication is emphysematous change
The chronic form of farmer's lung, whose printed complication is fibrosis in every case
The acute form of bagassosis, whose printed complication is emphysematous change
QUESTIONS.exp: Fever, chills, cough and raised ESR resolving in 2–4 days is the acute form, moldy hay makes it farmer's lung, and farmer's lung alone carries 'Emphysematous changes' as its complication on this page. (Book p258)

QUESTIONS.sec: PFT, CXR and CT in HP with the Head Cheese Pattern, Steroid Response versus Irreversible Fibrosis, and the HP versus ABPA Difference Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which PFT and CXR statements open page 259, and what captions the chest film?
opts: The PFT is restrictive in acute HP; CXR moves from diffuse opacities to reticulonodular shadows; and the film is captioned 'mosaic tiles attenuation'
In chronic ILD/fibrosis the PFT is obstructive; CXR moves from diffuse opacities to reticulonodular shadows; and the film is captioned 'CXR infiltrates in acute HP'
In chronic ILD/fibrosis the PFT is restrictive; CXR moves from diffuse opacities to reticulonodular shadows; and the film, labelled A, is captioned 'CXR infiltrates in acute HP'
In chronic ILD/fibrosis the PFT is restrictive; CXR moves from reticulonodular shadows to diffuse opacities; and the film is captioned 'CXR infiltrates in chronic HP'
QUESTIONS.exp: The page opens 'PFT: In chronic form (ILD/ fibrosis): Restrictive pattern' and 'CXR: Diffuse opacities → Reticulonodular shadows', with film A captioned 'CXR infiltrates in acute HP' — the evolution already stated in the pathology on page 257. (Book p259)

QUESTIONS.sec: PFT, CXR and CT in HP with the Head Cheese Pattern, Steroid Response versus Irreversible Fibrosis, and the HP versus ABPA Difference Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which three CT findings are printed for HP on page 259?
opts: Centrilobular nodules, bilateral ground glass opacities, and mosaic attenuation or head cheese pattern of varying densities on the same CT
Centrilobular nodules, unilateral ground glass opacities, and honeycombing
Centrilobular nodules, bilateral consolidations, and mosaic attenuation or head cheese pattern of uniform density
Perilobular nodules, bilateral ground glass opacities, and crazy pavement pattern
QUESTIONS.exp: CT lists 'Centrilobular nodules', 'B/L ground glass opacities (GGO)' and 'mosaic attenuation/ Head cheese pattern (varying densities on same CT)'. Mosaic attenuation was the HP row of the HRCT table on page 241. (Book p259)

QUESTIONS.sec: PFT, CXR and CT in HP with the Head Cheese Pattern, Steroid Response versus Irreversible Fibrosis, and the HP versus ABPA Difference Table
QUESTIONS.q: Match each CT image on page 259 with its printed label and caption — 1) Left scan marked B with red arrows 2) Right scan … A) Captioned mosaic tiles attenuation B) Nodular opacity arrows, captioned bilateral GGO and nodular opacity, the pair jointly captioned CT in HP
QUESTIONS.exp: Scan B carries 'Nodular opacity' arrows over the caption 'B/L GGO & nodular opacity', the right scan is captioned 'mosaic tiles attenuation', and both together are labelled 'CT: HP'. (Book p259)

QUESTIONS.sec: PFT, CXR and CT in HP with the Head Cheese Pattern, Steroid Response versus Irreversible Fibrosis, and the HP versus ABPA Difference Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which mirror-image BAL Note is printed for sarcoidosis on page 259?
opts: BAL lymphocytosis with CD4/CD8 greater than 2 indicates sarcoidosis — the inverse of HP's CD8/CD4 dominance
BAL lymphocytosis with CD4/CD8 less than 1 indicates sarcoidosis
BAL lymphocytosis with CD8/CD4 greater than 2 indicates sarcoidosis, identical to HP
QUESTIONS.exp: The Note reads 'BAL lymphocytosis with CD 4 / CD 8 > 2: Sarcoidosis', deliberately inverting the CD8/CD4 > 2 of HP on page 258 so the two granulomatous diseases separate on lavage. (Book p259)

QUESTIONS.sec: PFT, CXR and CT in HP with the Head Cheese Pattern, Steroid Response versus Irreversible Fibrosis, and the HP versus ABPA Difference Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which two treatment statements are printed for HP on page 259?
opts: The subacute form responds to antifungals, but once fibrosis is present the Disease is irreversible
The acute form requires steroids, and fibrosis reverses with prolonged therapy
The subacute form responds to steroids, but once fibrosis is present the Disease is irreversible
All forms respond to steroids including established fibrosis
QUESTIONS.exp: Treatment reads 'Subacute form: Respond to steroids' and 'If fibrosis (+): Irreversible' — placing the therapeutic window in the most common, subacute, presentation before chronic fibrosis supervenes. (Book p259)

QUESTIONS.sec: PFT, CXR and CT in HP with the Head Cheese Pattern, Steroid Response versus Irreversible Fibrosis, and the HP versus ABPA Difference Table
QUESTIONS.q: Match each row of the HP versus ABPA table with its printed pair — 1) Pathology 2) Radiographic features 3) Skin test reaction 4) Blood markers … A) ABPA migratory infiltrates with bronchiectatic changes versus HP diffuse infiltrates becoming reticulonodular opacities B) ABPA positive to A. fumigatus versus HP positive to A. clavatus C) ABPA eosinophilia positive, IgG precipitins positive and serum IgE markedly raised versus HP eosinophilia negative, precipitins positive and serum IgE normal D) ABPA airway colonisation with eosinophilic inflammation and hypersensitivity I plus III versus HP non caseating granulomas with lymphocytic inflammation and hypersensitivity IV over III
QUESTIONS.exp: Pathology contrasts colonisation and eosinophilic (I + III) inflammation in ABPA with granulomas and lymphocytic (IV > III) inflammation in HP; radiology contrasts migratory bronchiectatic change with diffuse-to-reticulonodular infiltrates; skin tests are positive to fumigatus in ABPA and clavatus in HP; and blood work separates only on eosinophilia and IgE, since IgG Aspergillus precipitins of type III hypersensitivity are positive in both. (Book p259)

QUESTIONS.sec: PFT, CXR and CT in HP with the Head Cheese Pattern, Steroid Response versus Irreversible Fibrosis, and the HP versus ABPA Difference Table
QUESTIONS.q: Two patients are skin-test positive to an Aspergillus species with positive IgG precipitins. One has eosinophilia, a markedly raised IgE and migratory infiltrates with bronchiectasis; the other has no eosinophilia, a normal IgE and reticulonodular opacities. Using the page 259 table, name each.
opts: The first is HP reacting to A. clavatus; the second is ABPA reacting to A. fumigatus
The first is ABPA reacting to A. fumigatus; the second is HP reacting to A. clavatus
Both are ABPA, separated only by Disease stage
The first is ABPA reacting to A. clavatus; the second is HP reacting to A. fumigatus
QUESTIONS.exp: Shared precipitins cannot separate them, but eosinophilia with ↑↑ IgE and migratory bronchiectatic infiltrates fill the ABPA column (fumigatus), while absent eosinophilia, normal IgE and reticulonodular opacities fill the HP column (clavatus). (Book p259)

QUESTIONS.sec: PFT, CXR and CT in HP with the Head Cheese Pattern, Steroid Response versus Irreversible Fibrosis, and the HP versus ABPA Difference Table
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the shared row of the HP versus ABPA table.
opts: True — peripheral eosinophilia is also printed positive in both diseases
False — serum IgE, not precipitins, is the shared positive row
True — IgG Aspergillus precipitins, labelled type III hypersensitivity, are the one test printed positive in both diseases
False — precipitins are positive in ABPA but negative in HP
QUESTIONS.exp: The row 'IgG Aspergillus precipitins (Type III hypersensitivity)' reads '+ve' under both ABPA and HP, reflecting the type III component each mechanism carries; eosinophilia and IgE split the columns instead. (Book p259)

QUESTIONS.sec: PFT, CXR and CT in HP with the Head Cheese Pattern, Steroid Response versus Irreversible Fibrosis, and the HP versus ABPA Difference Table
QUESTIONS.q: The varying densities coexisting on one HP CT are given the alternative name of the ______ pattern.
QUESTIONS.exp: The CT bullet reads 'mosaic attenuation/ Head cheese pattern (varying densities on same CT)'. Crazy pavement belonged to silicosis and PAP on page 225, and reverse halo to COP on page 240. (Book p259)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Anatomy and Fluid Composition, Detection Thresholds, and Light's Criteria with the Diuretic Disadvantage
QUESTIONS.q: Which pleural cavity statements open the anatomy on page 260?
opts: The cavity is lined by endothelial cells; its pressure is negative due to pleural lymphatics and vacuum; and the pleura is the coupling organ between lungs and chest wall

The cavity is lined by mesothelial cells, which produce surfactant as printed; its pressure is negative due to pleural lymphatics and vacuum; and the pleura is the coupling organ between lungs and chest wall
The cavity is lined by mesothelial cells, which produce surfactant as printed; its pressure is positive due to pleural lymphatics; and the pleura separates the lungs from each other
The cavity is lined by mesothelial cells; its pressure is negative due to elastic recoil alone as printed; and the pleura is the coupling organ between lungs and chest wall
QUESTIONS.exp: The bullets read 'Lined by: mesothelial cells (produce surfactant)', 'Negative intrapleural pressure d/t → Pleural lymphatics, vacuum' and 'Coupling organ b/w lungs and chest wall' — the lymphatic-vacuum mechanism already drawn on page 193. (Book p260)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Anatomy and Fluid Composition, Detection Thresholds, and Light's Criteria with the Diuretic Disadvantage
QUESTIONS.q: Which normal volume and detection thresholds are printed for pleural fluid on page 260?
opts: Normal amount 10–20 ml; minimum to detect an effusion is 50 mL by USG and lateral X-ray, 200 mL by CXR PA view and 300 mL clinically
Normal amount 10–20 ml; minimum to detect an effusion is 50 mL clinically, 200 mL by USG and 300 mL by CXR PA view
Normal amount 10–20 ml; minimum to detect an effusion is 50 mL by USG and lateral X-ray, 300 mL by CXR PA view and 200 mL clinically
Normal amount 50 ml; minimum to detect an effusion is 100 mL by USG and lateral X-ray, 200 mL by CXR PA view and 300 mL clinically
QUESTIONS.exp: The page gives 'Normal amount of pleural fluid (PF): 10–20 ml' and 'minimum amount of pleural fluid needed to detect effusion by: USG and lateral X-Ray: 50mL. CXR PA view: 200 mL. Clinically: 300 mL.' Sensitivity falls from ultrasound to film to the bedside. (Book p260)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Anatomy and Fluid Composition, Detection Thresholds, and Light's Criteria with the Diuretic Disadvantage
QUESTIONS.q: Match each pleural layer with its printed origin and pain property — 1) Parietal pleura 2) Visceral pleura … A) Develops, printed 'Developes', from splanchnopleural mesoderm and is pain insensitive B) Develops, printed 'Developes', from somatopleuric mesoderm and is pain sensitive
QUESTIONS.exp: Types of pleura read 'Parietal: Developes from somatopleuric mesoderm (pain sensitive)' and 'Visceral: Developes from splanchnopleural mesoderm (Pain insensitive)', the verb spelled 'Developes' in both lines. (Book p260)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Anatomy and Fluid Composition, Detection Thresholds, and Light's Criteria with the Diuretic Disadvantage
QUESTIONS.q: Which cellular percentages compose normal pleural fluid on page 260?
QUESTIONS.exp: Composition reads 'macrophages: 70%. Lymphocytes: 25%. mesothelial cells: 1–5%.' The lining cell appears only as a small shed minority in its own fluid. (Book p260)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Anatomy and Fluid Composition, Detection Thresholds, and Light's Criteria with the Diuretic Disadvantage
QUESTIONS.q: Which chemical composition is printed for normal pleural fluid?
opts: Glucose approximately equal to blood glucose, protein 1–1.5 g/dL, and LDH equal to plasma LDH
Glucose approximately equal to blood glucose, protein 1–1.5 g/dL, and LDH below 50% of plasma LDH
Glucose half of blood glucose, protein 1–1.5 g/dL, and LDH below 50% of plasma LDH
Glucose approximately equal to blood glucose, protein 3–5 g/dL, and LDH above 50% of plasma LDH
QUESTIONS.exp: The right-hand composition bullets read 'Glucose ~ blood glucose', 'Protein: 1–1.5 g/dL' and 'LDH: < 50% of plasma LDH' — the low protein and LDH baseline that Light's criteria below are built to detect departures from. (Book p260)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Anatomy and Fluid Composition, Detection Thresholds, and Light's Criteria with the Diuretic Disadvantage
QUESTIONS.q: What purpose is printed for Light's criteria on page 260?
opts: To distinguish between exudative and transudative pleural effusion
To distinguish tuberculous from malignant pleural effusion
To decide which effusions need an intercostal drain
To distinguish pleural effusion from pleural thickening
QUESTIONS.exp: Under 'LIGHT'S CRITERIA' the single bullet reads 'Distinguish between exudative and transudative pleural effusion', the gateway decision for the cause lists on page 261. (Book p260)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Anatomy and Fluid Composition, Detection Thresholds, and Light's Criteria with the Diuretic Disadvantage
QUESTIONS.q: Which three numbered ratios form Light's criteria as printed?
opts: Pleural fluid to serum albumin at or above 0.5; pleural fluid to serum LDH at or above 0.6; and pleural fluid LDH above one-third of the upper limit of normal serum LDH
Pleural fluid to serum protein above 0.6; pleural fluid to serum LDH above 0.5; and pleural fluid LDH above two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH
Pleural fluid to serum protein at or above 0.5; pleural fluid to serum LDH at or above 0.6; and serum LDH above two-thirds of the upper limit of pleural fluid LDH
Pleural fluid to serum protein at or above 0.5; pleural fluid to serum LDH at or above 0.6; and pleural fluid LDH above two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH
QUESTIONS.exp: The three criteria are printed as fractions: pleural fluid protein over serum protein '≥ 0.5', pleural fluid LDH over serum LDH '≥ 0.6', and 'Pleural fluid LDH > 2/3rd of upper limit of normal S. LDH'. (Book p260)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Anatomy and Fluid Composition, Detection Thresholds, and Light's Criteria with the Diuretic Disadvantage
QUESTIONS.q: Match each Light's-criteria outcome with its printed classification — 1) Any one criterion present 2) All three negative … A) Transudative B) Exudative
QUESTIONS.exp: The brace beside the three criteria reads 'Any 1 present → exudative' and 'All 3 negative → transudative'. One positive ratio is enough to call the fluid an exudate. (Book p260)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Anatomy and Fluid Composition, Detection Thresholds, and Light's Criteria with the Diuretic Disadvantage
QUESTIONS.q: A CCF patient on diuretics has an effusion meeting one Light criterion. Which printed disadvantage and which substitute test apply?
opts: One-third of such patients are wrongly classified as exudate, so the criteria are simply repeated after stopping diuretics as printed
All such patients are wrongly classified, so the serum–pleural fluid albumin gradient is used, a lower gradient indicating transudative fluid
One-third are wrongly classified as transudate, so pleural fluid NT pro BNP replaces Light's criteria
One-third of such patients are wrongly classified as exudate, so the serum–pleural fluid albumin gradient is used instead, a higher gradient indicating transudative fluid
QUESTIONS.exp: Disadvantages read 'In patients with CCF on diuretics → 1/3rd wrongly classified as exudate' and 'Instead use: Serum pleural fluid albumin gradient (Higher → transudative)'. NT pro BNP enters only as a cause marker on pages 261 and 263. (Book p260)

QUESTIONS.sec: Transudative and Exudative Causes, Drugs Causing Effusion, TB Effusion Presentation and General Examination Signs
QUESTIONS.q: Which ten transudative causes are numbered on page 261?
opts: CCF (NT pro BNP in pleural fluid), cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypothyroidism, hypoalbuminemia, Budd-Chiari syndrome, chronic constrictive pericarditis, SVC obstruction as printed 'SVC obstructive', peritoneal dialysis and urinothorax

CCF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hyperthyroidism, hypoalbuminemia, Budd-Chiari syndrome, chronic constrictive pericarditis, SVC obstruction, peritoneal dialysis and urinothorax, with no NT pro BNP bracket printed
CCF (NT pro BNP in pleural fluid), cirrhosis, nephritic syndrome, hypothyroidism, hypoalbuminemia, Budd-Chiari syndrome, acute pericarditis, SVC obstruction, peritoneal dialysis and urinothorax

CCF (NT pro BNP in pleural fluid), cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypothyroidism, hypoalbuminemia, Budd-Chiari syndrome, chronic constrictive pericarditis, pulmonary embolism, peritoneal dialysis and urinothorax
QUESTIONS.exp: The transudative column numbers CCF with '(NT pro BNP in PF)', cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypothyroidism, hypoalbuminemia, Budd-Chiari syndrome, chronic constrictive pericarditis, 'SVC obstructive', peritoneal dialysis and urinothorax. Pulmonary embolism is kept for the both-types note below. (Book p261)

QUESTIONS.sec: Transudative and Exudative Causes, Drugs Causing Effusion, TB Effusion Presentation and General Examination Signs
QUESTIONS.q: Urinothorax, the tenth transudative cause, is bracketed as low pH with high creatinine and an ______ odor.
QUESTIONS.exp: The bracket reads '(low pH + high creatinine + ammoniacal odor)' — urine chemistry announcing itself in the pleural space. (Book p261)

QUESTIONS.sec: Transudative and Exudative Causes, Drugs Causing Effusion, TB Effusion Presentation and General Examination Signs
QUESTIONS.q: Which six exudative causes are numbered opposite, and which braces qualify them?
opts: TB, pneumonia, malignancy, connective tissue disorders branching to scleroderma and SLE, acute pancreatitis and esophageal rupture — the last two braced as predominant left side pleural effusion
TB, pneumonia, malignancy, connective tissue disorders branching to RA and SLE, acute pancreatitis and esophageal rupture — braced as predominant right side pleural effusion
TB, pneumonia, malignancy, connective tissue disorders branching to RA and SLE, acute pancreatitis and esophageal rupture — the last two braced together as predominant left side pleural effusion
TB, pneumonia, malignancy, vasculitis, acute pancreatitis and esophageal rupture — the last two braced as predominant left side pleural effusion
QUESTIONS.exp: The exudative column numbers TB, pneumonia, malignancy, connective tissue disorders with arrows to RA and SLE, acute pancreatitis and esophageal rupture, with a brace over the last two reading 'Predominant left side PE'. (Book p261)

QUESTIONS.sec: Transudative and Exudative Causes, Drugs Causing Effusion, TB Effusion Presentation and General Examination Signs
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these statements are printed under CAUSES on page 261, one reverses the page:
opts: Pulmonary embolism is numbered among the pure transudative causes
Acute pancreatitis and esophageal rupture give predominantly left-sided effusions
Pulmonary infarction and pulmonary embolism cause both exudative and transudative effusions
Nitrofurantoin, dantrolene, methysergide and bromocriptine are the listed drugs causing pleural effusion
QUESTIONS.exp: Pulmonary infarction and pulmonary embolism appear only under 'Diseases with both exudative & transudative PE', never in either numbered column. The drug list — nitrofurantoin, dantrolene, methysergide, bromocriptine — follows immediately below. (Book p261)

QUESTIONS.sec: Transudative and Exudative Causes, Drugs Causing Effusion, TB Effusion Presentation and General Examination Signs
QUESTIONS.q: Which patients and pain story are printed for pleural effusion with TB?
opts: Twenty to thirty years old, females more than males, on first exposure to TB, with pain absent throughout
Fifty to seventy years old, females more than males, on first exposure to TB, with pain decreasing due to the effusion itself
Twenty to thirty years old, males more than females, on reactivation TB, with pleuritic pain that increases as the effusion grows
Twenty to thirty years old, females more than males, on first exposure to TB, with pleuritic pain initially — for example pain on inspiration — that then decreases due to the effusion itself
QUESTIONS.exp: PE with TB reads '20–30 yrs old', 'F > m' and 'First exposure to TB', braced to 'Pleuritic pain initially (E.g., pain on inspiration) → pain decreases d/t PE' as fluid separates the inflamed pleural surfaces. (Book p261)

QUESTIONS.sec: Transudative and Exudative Causes, Drugs Causing Effusion, TB Effusion Presentation and General Examination Signs
QUESTIONS.q: Which delayed outcome is arrowed for primary TB effusion on page 261?
opts: Over 25–30 years, 5–10% develop miliary TB as printed
Over 5–10 years, 25–30% of patients with effusion due to primary TB develop pulmonary TB
QUESTIONS.exp: The arrow reads 'Patients with PE d/t primary TB — 5–10 yrs → 25–30% develop pulmonary TB', making the effusion a marker of future parenchymal disease. (Book p261)

QUESTIONS.sec: Transudative and Exudative Causes, Drugs Causing Effusion, TB Effusion Presentation and General Examination Signs
QUESTIONS.q: Match each examination step with its printed effusion findings — 1) Inspection 2) Palpation 3) Percussion 4) Auscultation … A) Reduced breath sound and reduced vocal resonance B) Stony dullness C) Tracheal deviation to the opposite side D) Tracheal deviation confirmed, with reduced vocal fremitus and reduced chest movement
QUESTIONS.exp: General examination runs inspection showing tracheal deviation to the opposite side, palpation confirming that deviation with '↓ vocal fremitus' and '↓ Chest movement', percussion giving 'Stony dullness', and auscultation giving '↓ Breath sound' and '↓ vocal resonance'. (Book p261)

QUESTIONS.sec: Transudative and Exudative Causes, Drugs Causing Effusion, TB Effusion Presentation and General Examination Signs
QUESTIONS.q: A film beside the examination list shows a white-out left hemithorax. Which caption does it carry, tying image to examination?
opts: 'Left sided PE showing tracheal deviation to left'
'Left sided PE showing tracheal deviation to right'
'Loculated PE on the right with a central trachea'
'Right sided PE showing tracheal deviation to right'
QUESTIONS.exp: The caption reads 'Left sided PE showing tracheal deviation to right', the radiographic counterpart of the inspection finding printed beside it. The loculated right effusion with a central trachea is the contrasting film on page 263. (Book p261)

QUESTIONS.sec: Parapneumonic Effusion and Empyema, Low-pH Causes, and Chylothorax versus Pseudochylothorax
QUESTIONS.q: Match each parapneumonic row with its uncomplicated versus complicated pair on page 262 — 1) Pathogenesis 2) Glucose and pH 3) LDH and protein 4) Gram stain … A) Normal glucose with pH 7.3–7.4 versus glucose below 60, printed g/L, with pH below 7.2 B) Negative versus positive C) Inflammation with exudative leak versus bacterial invasion with fibrin and septation D) High LDH and high protein versus very high LDH above 1000 and very high protein
QUESTIONS.exp: Uncomplicated or synpneumonic or simple parapneumonic effusion is an inflammatory exudative leak with normal glucose, pH 7.3–7.4, high LDH and protein and a negative Gram stain; the complicated effusion adds bacterial invasion with fibrin and septation, glucose '< 60 g/L' as printed, pH '< 7.2', 'very high' LDH above 1000 and protein, and a positive Gram stain. (Book p262)

QUESTIONS.sec: Parapneumonic Effusion and Empyema, Low-pH Causes, and Chylothorax versus Pseudochylothorax
QUESTIONS.q: Which five statements define empyema under the parapneumonic table?
opts: It is a complicated parapneumonic effusion with macroscopic pus, with pleural fluid protein above 5 g/dL, pleural fluid LDH below 1000 IU/L and a split pleura sign on CT
It is an uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion with microscopic pus, with pleural fluid protein above 8 g/dL, pleural fluid LDH above 1000 IU/L and a split pleura sign on CT

It is a complicated parapneumonic effusion with macroscopic pus, the common complication of parapneumonic effusion (grammar as printed), with pleural fluid protein above 8 g/dL, pleural fluid LDH above 1000 IU/L and a split pleura sign on CT
It is a complicated parapneumonic effusion with macroscopic pus, with pleural fluid protein above 8 g/dL, pleural fluid LDH above 1000 IU/L and an air bronchogram on CT
QUESTIONS.exp: Empyema bullets read 'Complicated parapneumonic effusion + macroscopic pus', 'Common complications of parapneumonic effusion', 'P.F. protein > 8 g/dL', 'P.F. LDH > 1000 IU/L' and 'CT: Split pleura sign'. (Book p262)

QUESTIONS.sec: Parapneumonic Effusion and Empyema, Low-pH Causes, and Chylothorax versus Pseudochylothorax
QUESTIONS.q: Match each CT image under the empyema bullets with its printed caption — 1) Left scan, labelled C 2) Right scan, labelled D … A) Pulmonary abscess B) Empyema with split pleura sign
QUESTIONS.exp: Scan C is captioned 'Empyema: Split pleura sign' and scan D 'Pulmonary abscess', setting the pleural collection against its parenchymal mimic. (Book p262)

QUESTIONS.sec: Parapneumonic Effusion and Empyema, Low-pH Causes, and Chylothorax versus Pseudochylothorax
QUESTIONS.q: Which three causes of low pleural fluid pH are numbered in the Note, and which carries a prognostic arrow?
opts: SLE, complicated parapneumonic effusion, and malignancy — with malignancy arrowed to poor prognosis
Rheumatoid arthritis, uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion, and malignancy — with rheumatoid arthritis arrowed to poor prognosis
Rheumatoid arthritis, complicated parapneumonic effusion, and malignancy — with malignancy arrowed to poor prognosis
Rheumatoid arthritis, complicated parapneumonic effusion, and TB — with TB arrowed to poor prognosis
QUESTIONS.exp: The Note 'Low pH of pleural fluid' numbers rheumatoid arthritis, complicated parapneumonic effusion and 'malignancy → poor prognosis'. The same rheumatoid fluid reappears with the lowest glucose on page 263. (Book p262)

QUESTIONS.sec: Parapneumonic Effusion and Empyema, Low-pH Causes, and Chylothorax versus Pseudochylothorax
QUESTIONS.q: Match each row of the chylothorax versus pseudochylothorax table with its printed pair — 1) Appearance 2) Causes 3) Pathogenesis 4) Pleural fluid … A) Pleural thickening producing an exudative effusion enriched with cholesterol crystals in pseudochylothorax versus lymphatic rupture in chylothorax B) Trauma and lymphoma in chylothorax versus TB and RA in pseudochylothorax C) Raised triglyceride and raised cholesterol in chylothorax versus raised cholesterol crystals with cholesterol above 250 mg/dL in pseudochylothorax D) Milky white, merged across both columns
QUESTIONS.exp: Appearance 'milky white' spans both diseases; causes split trauma/lymphoma against TB/RA; pathogenesis splits lymphatic rupture against pleural thickening enriching an exudate with cholesterol crystals; and fluid splits raised triglyceride with raised cholesterol against cholesterol crystals quantified as cholesterol above 250 mg/dL. (Book p262)

QUESTIONS.sec: Parapneumonic Effusion and Empyema, Low-pH Causes, and Chylothorax versus Pseudochylothorax
QUESTIONS.q: A pneumonia patient's effusion now yields macroscopic pus, a positive Gram stain, pH 7.0, LDH above 1000 and protein above 8 g/dL, and CT shows the pleura split around the collection. Which printed stage is this?
opts: Complicated parapneumonic effusion still short of empyema
QUESTIONS.exp: Macroscopic pus is the defining step beyond a complicated parapneumonic effusion, and the protein above 8 g/dL, LDH above 1000 IU/L and split pleura sign are empyema's three printed corroborations. (Book p262)

QUESTIONS.sec: Parapneumonic Effusion and Empyema, Low-pH Causes, and Chylothorax versus Pseudochylothorax
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the two milky effusions on page 262.
opts: False — only chylothorax is milky white; pseudochylothorax is straw coloured as printed
True — both look milky white, but chylothorax is a lymphatic rupture after trauma or lymphoma, while pseudochylothorax is a thickened-pleura exudate of TB or RA enriched with cholesterol crystals
True — both are transudates from lymphatic rupture
False — chylothorax is caused by TB and RA and pseudochylothorax by trauma
QUESTIONS.exp: The merged appearance cell is 'milky white' for both, after which causes and pathogenesis diverge exactly as the correct option states, and pseudochylothorax is expressly an exudative effusion in its pathogenesis cell. (Book p262)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Fluid Glucose, ICD Indications, Eosinophils in Pleural Fluid, and Tuberculous and Neoplastic Effusion Diagnosis
QUESTIONS.q: Which pleural fluid glucose tiers open page 263?
opts: Below 60 mg/dL in RA, empyema, malignancy and TB; and below 30 mg/dL specifically in RA
Below 60 mg/dL in RA, empyema, malignancy and SLE, with SLE bracketed below 20% as printed; and below 30 mg/dL specifically in RA
Below 60 mg/dL in RA, empyema and malignancy only; and below 30 mg/dL in empyema
Below 30 mg/dL in RA, empyema, malignancy and SLE; and below 60 mg/dL in RA
QUESTIONS.exp: Pleural fluid glucose lists '<60 mg/dL: RA, Empyema, malignancy, SLE (<20%)' across its two columns and then '<30 mg/dL: RA', leaving rheumatoid fluid the deepest glucose sink, matching its low pH on page 262. (Book p263)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Fluid Glucose, ICD Indications, Eosinophils in Pleural Fluid, and Tuberculous and Neoplastic Effusion Diagnosis
QUESTIONS.q: The line beneath the glucose tiers states that NT pro BNP in pleural fluid points to a ______ cause.
QUESTIONS.exp: The line reads 'NT pro BNP in PF: Cardiac cause', bookending the identical bracket after CCF at the head of the transudative column on page 261. (Book p263)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Fluid Glucose, ICD Indications, Eosinophils in Pleural Fluid, and Tuberculous and Neoplastic Effusion Diagnosis
QUESTIONS.q: Which four indications for an intercostal drain are numbered on page 263?
opts: 'Calculated effusion' as printed, pleural fluid pH below 7.2, pleural fluid glucose below 60 mg/dL, and pus in the pleural space
'Calculated effusion' as printed, pleural fluid pH below 7.4, pleural fluid glucose below 30 mg/dL, and organisms on culture alone
'Calculated effusion' as printed, pleural fluid pH below 7.2, pleural fluid glucose below 60 mg/dL, and a positive Light criterion
Free-flowing effusion, pleural fluid pH below 7.2, pleural fluid glucose below 60 mg/dL, and pus in the pleural space
QUESTIONS.exp: Indications for ICD number '1. Calculated effusion. 2. PF pH <7.2. 3. PF Glucose <60 mg/dL. 4. Pus in pleural space.' The first item is preserved verbatim as printed; the film beside the list captions a loculated effusion, the concept the item evidently intends. (Book p263)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Fluid Glucose, ICD Indications, Eosinophils in Pleural Fluid, and Tuberculous and Neoplastic Effusion Diagnosis
QUESTIONS.q: Which six causes of eosinophils in pleural fluid are numbered on page 263?
opts: Lung fluke, asbestosis, histoplasmosis, lung infarction, malignancy, and hemo- or pneumothorax
Ascaris, asbestosis, histoplasmosis, lung infarction, drugs causing pleural effusion, and hemo- or pneumothorax
Lung fluke, silicosis, histoplasmosis, lung infarction, drugs causing pleural effusion, and chylothorax
Lung fluke, asbestosis, histoplasmosis, lung infarction, drugs causing pleural effusion, and hemo- or pneumothorax
QUESTIONS.exp: The list runs lung fluke (the eosinophilic effusion of page 250), asbestosis (whose benign effusion carried a raised eosinophil count on page 228), histoplasmosis, lung infarction, 'Drugs causing PE' from page 261, and 'Hemo/pneumothorax'. (Book p263)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Fluid Glucose, ICD Indications, Eosinophils in Pleural Fluid, and Tuberculous and Neoplastic Effusion Diagnosis
QUESTIONS.q: Match each label on the page 263 chest film with its printed annotation — 1) The circled midline structure with a right-pointing arrow 2) The long arrow to the right basal opacity, the film lettered A … A) CXR showing loculated pleural effusion on the right B) Trachea central
QUESTIONS.exp: The circled trachea is annotated 'Trachea central' — pointedly not deviated — while the lower arrow reads 'CXR: Loculated P.E on R', the contained collection that does not shift the mediastinum as the free left effusion of page 261 did. (Book p263)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Fluid Glucose, ICD Indications, Eosinophils in Pleural Fluid, and Tuberculous and Neoplastic Effusion Diagnosis
QUESTIONS.q: Which sensitivity ladder is printed for diagnosing tuberculous pleural effusion?
opts: Pleural fluid AFB stain 10–20%, AFB culture 45–50% and CBNAAT 25–50%, with pleural biopsy plus biopsy culture at 90%
Pleural fluid AFB stain 10–20%, AFB culture 25–50% and CBNAAT 45–50%, with pleural biopsy plus biopsy culture at 90%
Pleural fluid AFB stain 10–20%, AFB culture 25–50% and CBNAAT 45–50%, with pleural biopsy alone at 50%
Pleural fluid AFB stain 45–50%, AFB culture 25–50% and CBNAAT 10–20%, with pleural biopsy plus biopsy culture at 90%
QUESTIONS.exp: The sensitivity table climbs through fluid tests — AFB stain 10–20%, AFB culture 25–50%, CBNAAT 45–50% — to 'Pleural biopsy + biopsy culture' at 90%, printed in red as the decisive row. (Book p263)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Fluid Glucose, ICD Indications, Eosinophils in Pleural Fluid, and Tuberculous and Neoplastic Effusion Diagnosis
QUESTIONS.q: Which causes head neoplastic exudative effusion at the foot of page 263?
opts: Most common cause metastasis from carcinoma of the lung as printed, and mesothelioma
Lymphoma as the most common cause, and metastasis from carcinoma of the breast
Most common cause mesothelioma as printed, and metastasis from carcinoma of the ovary
Most common cause mesothelioma as printed, and metastasis from carcinoma of the breast
QUESTIONS.exp: Cause arrows to 'm/c cause: mesothelioma' and 'metastasis from: CA breast', preserved as printed. Lymphoma enters only in the prognosis line as the exception. (Book p263)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Fluid Glucose, ICD Indications, Eosinophils in Pleural Fluid, and Tuberculous and Neoplastic Effusion Diagnosis
QUESTIONS.q: Cytology of a suspected malignant effusion is negative, as it will be in half of cases by this page. Which printed next investigation and overall prognosis apply?
opts: VAT, as printed, or CT-guided biopsy; prognosis good except in lymphoma
Repeat cytology until positive; prognosis poor except in mesothelioma as printed
VAT, as printed, or CT-guided biopsy; prognosis poor except in lymphoma
Pleural fluid CBNAAT; prognosis poor except in lymphoma
QUESTIONS.exp: Investigation arrows to 'Cytology: low sensitivity (50%)' and 'VAT or CT guided biopsy' — VAT preserved as printed for video-assisted thoracoscopy — and the chapter closes 'Prognosis: Poor (Except in Lymphoma)'. CBNAAT belongs to the tuberculous table above. (Book p263)

QUESTIONS.sec: Pleural Fluid Glucose, ICD Indications, Eosinophils in Pleural Fluid, and Tuberculous and Neoplastic Effusion Diagnosis
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these are printed indications or findings tied to draining or sampling fluid on page 263, one belongs to a different threshold on the same page:
opts: Pus in the pleural space as an indication for ICD
Pleural fluid pH below 7.2 as an indication for ICD
Pleural fluid glucose below 60 mg/dL as an indication for ICD
Pleural fluid glucose below 30 mg/dL as an indication for ICD
QUESTIONS.exp: The ICD list uses glucose below 60 mg/dL, not 30; the below-30 tier belongs to rheumatoid fluid in the glucose block at the top of the page. pH below 7.2 and pus in the pleural space are ICD items 2 and 4. (Book p263)

QUESTIONS.sec: Obstructive Breathing Events in REM, the >10-second Apnea and Hypopnea Thresholds, the Apnea Hypopnea Index Bands and the Eight Risk Factors
QUESTIONS.q: Which pair of features defines obstructive sleep apnea syndrome in the Introduction on page 264?
opts: Obstructive breathing events plus morning headache as the only complaint
Obstructive breathing events (manifesting as snoring) plus excessive day time sleepiness/fatigue
Obstructive breathing events (manifesting as snoring) plus cor pulmonale
Central apnoeic events plus excessive day time sleepiness/fatigue
QUESTIONS.exp: The Introduction sentence reads 'Obstructive breathing events (manifesting as snoring) + excessive day time sleepiness/fatigue' — snoring is the event and day-time sleepiness the consequence. (Book p264)

QUESTIONS.sec: Obstructive Breathing Events in REM, the >10-second Apnea and Hypopnea Thresholds, the Apnea Hypopnea Index Bands and the Eight Risk Factors
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the stage of sleep in which the obstructive breathing events occur, as printed on page 264.
opts: True — obstructive breathing events occur equally in every sleep stage
False — the events occur only in non-REM sleep
True — obstructive breathing events occur in the REM phase
False — the events occur only in slow-wave (deep) sleep
QUESTIONS.exp: The first bullet under 'Obstructive breathing events' is 'Occur in REM phase', before the apnea and hypopnea definitions. (Book p264)

QUESTIONS.sec: Obstructive Breathing Events in REM, the >10-second Apnea and Hypopnea Thresholds, the Apnea Hypopnea Index Bands and the Eight Risk Factors
QUESTIONS.q: How long must breathing cease for the printed definition of apnea to be satisfied?
QUESTIONS.exp: The page defines 'Apnea: Cessation of breathing > 10s', the same 10-second cut-off used for hypopnea on the next line. (Book p264)

QUESTIONS.sec: Obstructive Breathing Events in REM, the >10-second Apnea and Hypopnea Thresholds, the Apnea Hypopnea Index Bands and the Eight Risk Factors
QUESTIONS.q: Hypopnea is reduced breathing >10 s in which the amplitude of breathing falls by more than ______ or there is an O₂ desaturation ≥4%.
QUESTIONS.exp: The bracket reads '(Amplitude of breathing falls >50% or O2 desaturation ≥4%)', so the amplitude half and the 4% desaturation are the two alternatives. (Book p264)

QUESTIONS.sec: Obstructive Breathing Events in REM, the >10-second Apnea and Hypopnea Thresholds, the Apnea Hypopnea Index Bands and the Eight Risk Factors
QUESTIONS.q: Match the obstructive event to its printed threshold — 1) Apnea 2) Hypopnea … A) Reduced breathing >10 s (amplitude falls >50% or O₂ desaturation ≥4%) B) Cessation of breathing >10 s
QUESTIONS.exp: The two bullets read 'Apnea: Cessation of breathing >10s' and 'Hypopnea: Reduced breathing >10s (Amplitude of breathing falls >50% or O2 desaturation ≥4%)'. (Book p264)

QUESTIONS.sec: Obstructive Breathing Events in REM, the >10-second Apnea and Hypopnea Thresholds, the Apnea Hypopnea Index Bands and the Eight Risk Factors
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these are printed as signs of disturbed sleep on page 264, one is not:
QUESTIONS.exp: The line reads 'Signs of disturbed sleep: Snoring, grunting, choking.' Nocturnal dyspnea is not part of that list. (Book p264)

QUESTIONS.sec: Obstructive Breathing Events in REM, the >10-second Apnea and Hypopnea Thresholds, the Apnea Hypopnea Index Bands and the Eight Risk Factors
QUESTIONS.q: Which sequence describes obesity hypoventilation syndrome in the Note on page 264?
opts: Obesity → hyperventilation → ↓PaCO₂, and excessive day time sleepiness is not present usually
Obesity → airflow obstruction → ↓PaO₂, and excessive day time sleepiness is not present usually
Obesity → hypoventilation → ↑PaCO₂, and excessive day time sleepiness is always present
Obesity → hypoventilation → ↑PaCO₂, and excessive day time sleepiness is not present usually
QUESTIONS.exp: The note is 'Obesity hypoventilation syndrome: Obesity → hypoventilation → ↑PaCO2. Excessive day time sleepiness not present usually.' — the absent sleepiness is what separates it from OSAS. (Book p264)

QUESTIONS.sec: Obstructive Breathing Events in REM, the >10-second Apnea and Hypopnea Thresholds, the Apnea Hypopnea Index Bands and the Eight Risk Factors
QUESTIONS.q: The Apnea Hypopnea Index divides the total number of apnea and hypopnea by the ______.
QUESTIONS.exp: The fraction is printed as 'Total number of apnea and hypopnea / Total sleep time' — hence an index per hour of sleep, not per hour in bed. (Book p264)

QUESTIONS.sec: Obstructive Breathing Events in REM, the >10-second Apnea and Hypopnea Thresholds, the Apnea Hypopnea Index Bands and the Eight Risk Factors
QUESTIONS.q: Match each Apnea Hypopnea Index band to its printed label — 1) <5 2) 5–15 3) 15–30 4) >30 … A) Normal B) Mild OSAS C) Moderate OSAS D) Severe OSAS
QUESTIONS.exp: The ladder reads '<5: Normal. 5–15: mild OSAS. 15–30: moderate OSAS. >30: Severe OSAS', with the last line adding CPAP. (Book p264)

QUESTIONS.sec: Obstructive Breathing Events in REM, the >10-second Apnea and Hypopnea Thresholds, the Apnea Hypopnea Index Bands and the Eight Risk Factors
QUESTIONS.q: Which bands are bracketed together as needing only lifestyle modification?
opts: All bands below 30, including the normal band
QUESTIONS.exp: The brace joins '5–15: mild OSAS' and '15–30: moderate OSAS' to 'Needs only lifestyle modification'; only '>30: Severe OSAS' needs CPAP. (Book p264)

QUESTIONS.sec: Obstructive Breathing Events in REM, the >10-second Apnea and Hypopnea Thresholds, the Apnea Hypopnea Index Bands and the Eight Risk Factors
QUESTIONS.q: A 54-year-old obese man has an Apnea Hypopnea Index of 32 on polysomnography. Using the printed bands, he falls in which group and needs what treatment?
opts: Moderate OSAS (15–30) needing only lifestyle modification
Severe OSAS (>30) needing only lifestyle modification
QUESTIONS.exp: The severity ladder places >30 in 'Severe OSAS → Needs treatment using CPAP (Continuous positive airway pressure)'; 32 is therefore severe and CPAP-treated. (Book p264)

QUESTIONS.sec: Obstructive Breathing Events in REM, the >10-second Apnea and Hypopnea Thresholds, the Apnea Hypopnea Index Bands and the Eight Risk Factors
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three are printed risk factors for OSAS on page 264, one is not:
opts: Female sex with a M : F ratio of 1 : 3
QUESTIONS.exp: The risk list prints 'male sex (M : F = 3 : 1)' with obesity, central fat, age 50–60, postmenopausal state, alcohol, sedatives and smoking — the sex ratio is inverted in the odd option. (Book p264)

QUESTIONS.sec: Obstructive Breathing Events in REM, the >10-second Apnea and Hypopnea Thresholds, the Apnea Hypopnea Index Bands and the Eight Risk Factors
QUESTIONS.q: The risk factor line prints the sex distribution of OSAS as M : F = ______.
QUESTIONS.exp: The bullet is 'male sex (M : F = 3 : 1)', i.e. three men for every woman, before 'Age 50–60 yrs' and 'Postmenopausal state'. (Book p264)

QUESTIONS.sec: Snoring and the Day-time Symptom List, the Suspect-OSAS Note, the Vagal Sudden-Death Chain, Complications, the Obsolete Epworth Scale and the Two Polysomnography Traces
QUESTIONS.q: Which description of snoring is printed under Clinical features on page 265?
opts: Cardinal symptom, continuous and unvarying, and more in the lateral position
A late symptom, intermittent/waxing & waning, and more in the upright position
Cardinal symptom, intermittent/waxing & waning with long periods of silence, and more in the supine position
Cardinal symptom, intermittent/waxing & waning, and abolished in the supine position
QUESTIONS.exp: The snoring block reads 'Cardinal symptom', 'Intermittent/waxing & waning/long periods of silence' and 'more in supine position' — the silence is what distinguishes it from continuous snoring. (Book p265)

QUESTIONS.sec: Snoring and the Day-time Symptom List, the Suspect-OSAS Note, the Vagal Sudden-Death Chain, Complications, the Obsolete Epworth Scale and the Two Polysomnography Traces
QUESTIONS.q: Two night-time symptoms listed immediately after snoring are nocturia and ______.
QUESTIONS.exp: The list runs 'Snoring: ... • Nocturia. • sudden waking up at night.' before the day-time symptom block begins. (Book p265)

QUESTIONS.sec: Snoring and the Day-time Symptom List, the Suspect-OSAS Note, the Vagal Sudden-Death Chain, Complications, the Obsolete Epworth Scale and the Two Polysomnography Traces
QUESTIONS.q: Match each day-time symptom to its printed descriptor — 1) Morning headache/confusion 2) Cognitive defects 3) Sexual dysfunction … A) Poor concentration, personality & mood changes (depression & anxiety) B) Impotence & decreased libido C) Non-restorative sleep
QUESTIONS.exp: The brackets print 'morning headache/confusion (Non-restorative sleep)', 'cognitive defects: Poor concentration, personality mood changes (Depression & anxiety)' and 'sexual dysfunction: impotence, & decreased libido'. (Book p265)

QUESTIONS.sec: Snoring and the Day-time Symptom List, the Suspect-OSAS Note, the Vagal Sudden-Death Chain, Complications, the Obsolete Epworth Scale and the Two Polysomnography Traces
QUESTIONS.q: Which two situations does the Note box direct you to suspect OSAS in?
opts: Unexplained pulmonary hypertension and unexplained polycythemia
Unexplained pulmonary hypertension and unexplained eosinophilia
Unexplained systemic hypertension and unexplained thrombocytopenia
Unexplained cor pulmonale and unexplained anemia
QUESTIONS.exp: The boxed note reads 'Always suspect OSAS in: • unexplained pulmonary hypertension. • unexplained polycythemia.' — both qualified by 'unexplained'. (Book p265)

QUESTIONS.sec: Snoring and the Day-time Symptom List, the Suspect-OSAS Note, the Vagal Sudden-Death Chain, Complications, the Obsolete Epworth Scale and the Two Polysomnography Traces
QUESTIONS.q: A 46-year-old snorer is found to have a raised hemoglobin and hematocrit with no hematological disease, and echocardiography shows pulmonary hypertension without a cardiac cause. Which sleep diagnosis should be suspected from the printed note?
QUESTIONS.exp: Both 'unexplained pulmonary hypertension' and 'unexplained polycythemia' sit inside the suspect-OSAS box, so the combination points to OSAS rather than to obesity hypoventilation, whose day-time sleepiness is usually absent. (Book p265)

QUESTIONS.sec: Snoring and the Day-time Symptom List, the Suspect-OSAS Note, the Vagal Sudden-Death Chain, Complications, the Obsolete Epworth Scale and the Two Polysomnography Traces
QUESTIONS.q: Which chain is drawn under 'Risk of sudden cardiac death' in Complications on page 265?
opts: Sympathetic stimulation → tachycardia + hypertension → cardiac rhythm abnormality (premature beat, asystole, VT, cardiac arrest)
Vagal stimulation → tachycardia + hypoxia → cardiac rhythm abnormality (premature beat, asystole, VT, cardiac arrest)
Vagal stimulation → bradycardia + hypoxia → cardiac rhythm abnormality (premature beat, asystole, VT, cardiac arrest)
Vagal stimulation → bradycardia + hypoxia → left ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic failure
QUESTIONS.exp: The flow prints 'vagal stimulation → Bradycardia + Hypoxia' and then 'cardiac rhythm abnormality (Premature beat, asystole, VT, cardiac arrest)'. (Book p265)

QUESTIONS.sec: Snoring and the Day-time Symptom List, the Suspect-OSAS Note, the Vagal Sudden-Death Chain, Complications, the Obsolete Epworth Scale and the Two Polysomnography Traces
QUESTIONS.q: Match each complication group to its printed mechanism — 1) Stroke and congestive cardiac failure 2) Metabolic syndrome … A) No mechanism bracketed on the page B) Due to HTN
QUESTIONS.exp: The brace 'due to HTN' encloses stroke and congestive cardiac failure only, while metabolic syndrome stands alone with no bracket on the page. (Book p265)

QUESTIONS.sec: Snoring and the Day-time Symptom List, the Suspect-OSAS Note, the Vagal Sudden-Death Chain, Complications, the Obsolete Epworth Scale and the Two Polysomnography Traces
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these arrhythmias are printed inside the complication chain, one is not:
QUESTIONS.exp: The bracket prints 'Premature beat, asystole, VT, cardiac arrest'. Atrial flutter is not anywhere in that printed list of rhythm abnormalities. (Book p265)

QUESTIONS.sec: Snoring and the Day-time Symptom List, the Suspect-OSAS Note, the Vagal Sudden-Death Chain, Complications, the Obsolete Epworth Scale and the Two Polysomnography Traces
QUESTIONS.q: The Epworth sleepiness scale questionnaire is dismissed on page 265 as ______.
QUESTIONS.exp: Under Investigations the page writes 'eps-worth sleepiness scale questionnaire: obsolete', leaving polysomnography as the investigation that follows. (Book p265)

QUESTIONS.sec: Snoring and the Day-time Symptom List, the Suspect-OSAS Note, the Vagal Sudden-Death Chain, Complications, the Obsolete Epworth Scale and the Two Polysomnography Traces
QUESTIONS.q: What do the two polysomnography figures on page 265 demonstrate?
opts: Central apnea without respiratory effort and obstructive apnea with persistent respiratory effort
Central apnea with persistent respiratory effort and obstructive apnea without respiratory effort
Obstructive apnea in REM and obstructive apnea in non-REM sleep
QUESTIONS.exp: The two captions read 'Central apnea without respiratory effort' and 'Obstructive apnea with persistent respiratory effort' — effort is the discriminator between the two traces. (Book p265)

QUESTIONS.sec: Snoring and the Day-time Symptom List, the Suspect-OSAS Note, the Vagal Sudden-Death Chain, Complications, the Obsolete Epworth Scale and the Two Polysomnography Traces
QUESTIONS.q: A polysomnography trace shows repeated cessation of airflow with continued, increasing respiratory effort. Which caption from page 265 matches this trace?
opts: Obstructive apnea with absent respiratory effort
Obstructive apnea with persistent respiratory effort
Central apnea with persistent respiratory effort
QUESTIONS.exp: Airflow stops while effort persists in the second trace, captioned 'Obstructive apnea with persistent respiratory effort'; loss of effort would make it central. (Book p265)

QUESTIONS.sec: Snoring and the Day-time Symptom List, the Suspect-OSAS Note, the Vagal Sudden-Death Chain, Complications, the Obsolete Epworth Scale and the Two Polysomnography Traces
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three are day-time symptoms printed on page 265, one is a night-time symptom from the same page:
QUESTIONS.exp: Morning headache, dry throat, day-time sleepiness, cognitive defects, sexual dysfunction and GERD sit in the day-time list, whereas 'sudden waking up at night' is printed with nocturia above it. (Book p265)

QUESTIONS.sec: Severe OSAS Treated with CPAP and the Nasal and Full-face Mask Captions
QUESTIONS.q: What treatment is printed for severe OSAS on page 266?
QUESTIONS.exp: The page states 'Treatment: Severe OSAS : CPAP', followed only by two mask photographs. (Book p266)

QUESTIONS.sec: Severe OSAS Treated with CPAP and the Nasal and Full-face Mask Captions
QUESTIONS.q: CPAP, the treatment of severe OSAS, stands for ______ positive airway pressure.
QUESTIONS.exp: Page 264 had already expanded 'CPAP (Continuous positive airway pressure)' and page 266 repeats the acronym as the severe-OSAS treatment. (Book p266)

QUESTIONS.sec: Severe OSAS Treated with CPAP and the Nasal and Full-face Mask Captions
QUESTIONS.q: Match each CPAP mask caption on page 266 to its printed picture — 1) Left photograph 2) Right photograph … A) A man wearing a full face mask B) A sleeping man with a nasal mask
QUESTIONS.exp: The left photograph is captioned 'Nasal mask' and the right 'Full face mask'; the page prints no third mask type. (Book p266)

QUESTIONS.sec: Severe OSAS Treated with CPAP and the Nasal and Full-face Mask Captions
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about treatment on page 266.
opts: True — severe OSAS is treated with CPAP, shown in nasal and full face mask forms
True — severe OSAS is treated with CPAP, and only a nasal mask is illustrated
False — CPAP is restricted to mild OSAS
False — severe OSAS is treated with surgery
QUESTIONS.exp: The single treatment line reads 'Severe OSAS : CPAP', and the two captions show both a nasal mask and a full face mask. (Book p266)

QUESTIONS.sec: Severe OSAS Treated with CPAP and the Nasal and Full-face Mask Captions
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three statements about the page 266 treatment block are true, one contradicts it:
opts: The treatment named for severe OSAS is CPAP
CPAP is reserved for mild OSAS, while severe disease needs lifestyle modification alone
A nasal mask is illustrated as one way of delivering CPAP
A full face mask is illustrated as another way of delivering CPAP
QUESTIONS.exp: Page 266 prints only 'Severe OSAS : CPAP' with the nasal and full face masks; lifestyle modification alone was the page 264 brace for mild and moderate disease, the exact reverse. (Book p266)

QUESTIONS.sec: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features
QUESTIONS.q: Which GOLD 2023 definition opens the chapter on page 267?
opts: Chronic persistent respiratory symptoms due to abnormalities of airway/alveoli resulting in progressive airflow limitation
Acute respiratory symptoms due to infection of the airway/alveoli resulting in progressive airflow limitation
Chronic intermittent respiratory symptoms due to pulmonary vascular disease resulting in progressive airflow limitation
Chronic persistent respiratory symptoms due to abnormalities of airway/alveoli resulting in reversible airflow limitation
QUESTIONS.exp: The two bullets read 'global initiative for COPD' and 'chronic persistent respiratory symptoms d/t abnormalities of airway/alveoli resulting in progressive airflow limitation'. (Book p267)

QUESTIONS.sec: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features
QUESTIONS.q: The definition heading names GOLD 2023, in which GOLD stands for ______ initiative for COPD.
QUESTIONS.exp: The first bullet expands the acronym as 'global initiative for COPD', lower-case 'g' as printed, before the definition itself. (Book p267)

QUESTIONS.sec: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features
QUESTIONS.q: Match each COPD classification tree to its printed branches — 1) Based on clinical presentation 2) Based on pathology … A) Large airway, small airway (diameter <2 mm), alveoli, pulmonary vasculature B) Chronic bronchitis, emphysema
QUESTIONS.exp: The upper tree splits clinical presentation into chronic bronchitis and emphysema, while the lower tree splits pathology into large airway, small airway (diameter <2 mm), alveoli and pulmonary vasculature. (Book p267)

QUESTIONS.sec: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features
QUESTIONS.q: At which diameter does the printed pathology tree define a small airway?
QUESTIONS.exp: The small airway branch carries the bracket '(Diameter <2 mm)', sitting between large airway and alveoli in the pathology tree. (Book p267)

QUESTIONS.sec: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features
QUESTIONS.q: How is the diagnosis of COPD made on page 267?
opts: Symptoms (dyspnea) plus chest X-ray for confirmation
QUESTIONS.exp: The line reads 'Diagnosis: Symptoms (Dyspnea) + Spirometry (For confirmation)' — symptoms raise it and spirometry confirms it. (Book p267)

QUESTIONS.sec: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three are printed risk factors for COPD on page 267, one reverses a printed word:
QUESTIONS.exp: The risk list prints 'Low birth weight (Pre terms)' with tobacco smoking, cooking-fuel smoke, occupational dust, vapours, fumes and other chemicals; high birth weight is not on it. (Book p267)

QUESTIONS.sec: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features
QUESTIONS.q: Which four clinical features are listed for COPD on page 267?
opts: Dyspnea, chronic cough, clubbing and wheeze
Fever, chronic cough, recurrent lower respiratory tract infection and wheeze
Dyspnea, hemoptysis, recurrent lower respiratory tract infection and wheeze
Dyspnea, chronic cough, recurrent lower respiratory tract infection and wheeze

Concurrent influenza infection, and cavity with hemoptysis and pneumatocele
Recent hospitalization, and a simple parapneumonic effusion
Concurrent influenza infection, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy

QUESTIONS.sec: Community Acquired MRSA, the Outpatient to ICU Organism Shift, MRSA and MDR Risk within Three Months, and Pneumococcal Morphology, Culture and Haemolysis Chart
QUESTIONS.q: Match each care setting to its printed organisms — 1) Outpatient 2) Inpatient non-ICU 3) Inpatient ICU … A) Strep pneumoniae, MRSA and multidrug resistant gram-negative B) Strep pneumoniae, virus, mycoplasma, chlamydia and H. influenza C) Strep pneumoniae from ↓CMI, respiratory viruses and Legionella

Congestive heart failure, hemodialysis, antibiotic use and hospitalization within the last 3 months, and structural lung disease
Diabetes, hemodialysis, antibiotic use within the last 3 months, and pleural effusion

QUESTIONS.sec: Community Acquired MRSA, the Outpatient to ICU Organism Shift, MRSA and MDR Risk within Three Months, and Pneumococcal Morphology, Culture and Haemolysis Chart

Gram-positive diplococci in pairs only, without a capsule
Gram-negative diplococci in chains, flame shaped or lanceolate
Gram-positive cocci in clusters, spherical and non-capsulated

QUESTIONS.sec: Community Acquired MRSA, the Outpatient to ICU Organism Shift, MRSA and MDR Risk within Three Months, and Pneumococcal Morphology, Culture and Haemolysis Chart

Alpha hemolytic, partial hemolysis in 5% blood agar, with a golden pigment and a comet-tail appearance
Gamma hemolytic, no hemolysis on blood agar, with a grey colony and a mucoid appearance
Alpha hemolytic, partial hemolysis in 5% blood agar, with green colour and a draughtsman or carrom coin appearance

QUESTIONS.sec: Community Acquired MRSA, the Outpatient to ICU Organism Shift, MRSA and MDR Risk within Three Months, and Pneumococcal Morphology, Culture and Haemolysis Chart

QUESTIONS.sec: Community Acquired MRSA, the Outpatient to ICU Organism Shift, MRSA and MDR Risk within Three Months, and Pneumococcal Morphology, Culture and Haemolysis Chart

QUESTIONS.sec: Pneumococcus against Viridans, the Four Toxins, the Quellung Reaction, Type 3 Invasiveness and the CAP Risk and Poor-Prognosis Notes

Capsular polysaccharide, pneumolysin, streptolysin O and pneumococcal somatic C antigen

QUESTIONS.sec: Pneumococcus against Viridans, the Four Toxins, the Quellung Reaction, Type 3 Invasiveness and the CAP Risk and Poor-Prognosis Notes

Diabetes, nephrotic syndrome, hemodialysis, COPD with bronchiectasis, cardiac failure and age >65 years
Diabetes, chronic kidney disease, peritoneal dialysis, asthma, cardiac failure and age >65 years
Diabetes, chronic kidney disease, hemodialysis, COPD with bronchiectasis, cardiac failure and age >50 years

QUESTIONS.sec: Pneumococcus against Viridans, the Four Toxins, the Quellung Reaction, Type 3 Invasiveness and the CAP Risk and Poor-Prognosis Notes

Steroid consumption, transplant, neutropenia and HIV
Steroid or monoclonal antibody consumption, transplant and neutropenia
Monoclonal antibody consumption, transplant, neutropenia and chemotherapy

QUESTIONS.sec: Pneumococcus against Viridans, the Four Toxins, the Quellung Reaction, Type 3 Invasiveness and the CAP Risk and Poor-Prognosis Notes
QUESTIONS.q: Which two findings are printed as markers of a poor prognosis in CAP?

Hypothermia and leukocytosis, the latter usually with typical organisms
Hypothermia and leukopenia, the latter usually with atypical organisms
Hyperthermia and leukocytosis, the latter usually with typical organisms

High spiking fever, dull chest pain, cough with scanty sputum, hemoptysis and dyspnea
High spiking fever, pleuritic chest pain, cough, hemoptysis and abdominal pain

Abdominal pain is the only symptom, and classical signs are always present
Fever is always the only symptom, and classical signs are exaggerated
Confusion might be the only symptom, and classical signs may not be present

Classical signs are always present in older patients, so confusion can be ignored

QUESTIONS.sec: Extrapulmonary Mycoplasma, and the Air Bronchogram, Silhouette, Golden S and Mediastinal Shift Captions

QUESTIONS.sec: Mycoplasma against Legionella Films, the Fibrocalcific Scar, Necrotising Klebsiella and the Pneumatocele Cascade with Its 4 mm Rule

QUESTIONS.sec: Mycoplasma against Legionella Films, the Fibrocalcific Scar, Necrotising Klebsiella and the Pneumatocele Cascade with Its 4 mm Rule

Dense white opacity → focal suppurative lung abscess → fibrosis and scarring → air entry into abscess → gas within consolidation → air-fluid levels → cavity

Alcoholics and post viral infection, with progression to pneumothorax, an association with MRSA and a size under 4 mm
IV drug abusers and post tubercular scarring, with progression to cavity, an association with MRSA and a size under 4 mm

QUESTIONS.sec: Mycoplasma against Legionella Films, the Fibrocalcific Scar, Necrotising Klebsiella and the Pneumatocele Cascade with Its 4 mm Rule

QUESTIONS.sec: Mycoplasma against Legionella Films, the Fibrocalcific Scar, Necrotising Klebsiella and the Pneumatocele Cascade with Its 4 mm Rule
