opts: Annular contraction → leaflets come close (coaptation zone) → sudden tensing of the leaflet → S1
Annular contraction → leaflets come close (coaptation zone) → gradual relaxation of the leaflet → S1
Annular dilatation → leaflets separate (coaptation zone) → sudden tensing of the leaflet → S1
Papillary contraction → chordae shorten → leaflets evert → S1
QUESTIONS.exp: The physiology column reads 'Annular contraction → Leaflet come close (Coaptation zone) → Sudden tensing of leaflet → S1'. (Book p297)

QUESTIONS.sec: The 0.8-Second Cycle, the 0.3-Second Systolic and 0.5-Second Diastolic Phase Lists, the 70 to 30 Per Cent Filling Split, and the S1 Valve Apparatus with Annular Contraction and Coaptation
QUESTIONS.q: The two components of S1 are M1 from closure of the mitral valve and T1 from closure of the tricuspid valve, separated by less than ______ ms and therefore not appreciated.
QUESTIONS.exp: The bracket beside M1 and T1 reads '<30 ms difference (not appreciated)', which is why S1 is heard as a single sound. (Book p297)

QUESTIONS.sec: The 0.8-Second Cycle, the 0.3-Second Systolic and 0.5-Second Diastolic Phase Lists, the 70 to 30 Per Cent Filling Split, and the S1 Valve Apparatus with Annular Contraction and Coaptation
QUESTIONS.q: On an intracardiac recording M1 precedes T1 by 20 ms. How does that interval appear at the bedside?
opts: As a wide split S1, because any measurable difference is audible
As a soft S1, because the components cancel each other
As a fixed split S1 that widens with inspiration
As a single S1, because a difference under 30 ms is not appreciated
QUESTIONS.exp: The bracket beside M1 and T1 reads '<30 ms difference (not appreciated)', so the two components fuse into one heard sound. (Book p297)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
QUESTIONS.q: Which three leaflet abnormalities make S1 soft according to the first factor on page 298?
opts: An incompetent leaky leaflet as in MR, a perforated leaflet as in infective endocarditis, and a calcific immobile leaflet as in calcific MS
An incompetent leaky leaflet as in MR, a perforated leaflet as in rheumatic fever, and a calcific mobile leaflet as in calcific MS
A stenotic leaflet as in MS, a perforated leaflet as in infective endocarditis, and a calcific immobile leaflet as in calcific MS
An incompetent leaky leaflet as in AR, a perforated leaflet as in infective endocarditis, and a calcific immobile leaflet as in calcific AS
QUESTIONS.exp: The integrity branch ends in 'soft S1' through a. incompetent valve leaflet (leaky) → regurgitation (MR), b. perforation of leaflet (infective endocarditis) and c. calcific for immobile leaflet (calcific MS). (Book p298)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
QUESTIONS.q: How does the position of the leaflet at end diastole differ in a normal valve and in stenosis, and what does that do to S1?
opts: Normally the leaflet floats wide open in the filled LV, but stenosis reduces LV filling so the valve sits semiclosed and closes from a short distance, making S1 soft
Normally the leaflet floats semiclosed in the filled LV, but stenosis increases LV filling so the valve sits wide apart and closes from a distance, making S1 loud
Normally the leaflet floats semiclosed in the filled LV, but stenosis reduces LV filling so the valve sits wide apart and closes from a distance, making S1 loud
Normally the leaflet floats semiclosed in the empty LV, but stenosis reduces LV filling so the valve sits wide apart and closes from a distance, making S1 loud
QUESTIONS.exp: The block reads 'Normal: Semiclosed position floating in the filled LV', then stenosis → reduced LV filling → valve wide apart → close from a distance → loud S1, the example being MS. (Book p298)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
QUESTIONS.q: Match each heart rate state to its printed effect on S1 — 1) Bradycardia 2) Tachycardia … A) Loud S1 B) Soft S1
QUESTIONS.exp: Bradycardia lengthens the PR interval, increases filling and brings the valves closer, so S1 is soft; tachycardia shortens the PR interval, reduces filling and makes the valves close from a distance, so S1 is loud. (Book p298)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
QUESTIONS.q: Which two timing abnormalities are printed for closure, with their examples?
opts: Delayed closure gives a soft S1 as in MS, and premature closure gives a loud S1 as in AR
Delayed closure gives a loud S1 as in MR, and premature closure gives a soft S1 as in AS
Delayed closure gives a loud S1 as in AR, and premature closure gives a soft S1 as in MS
Delayed closure gives a loud S1 as in MS, and premature closure gives a soft S1 as in AR
QUESTIONS.exp: The timing block reads 'a. Delayed closure: Loud S1, e.g. MS → ↑LAP → more time for LVP > LAP' and 'b. Premature closure: soft S1, e.g. AR → LVP ↑ rapidly'. (Book p298)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
QUESTIONS.q: Which dP/dt states are printed, and which examples accompany them?
opts: A leaky valve gives an ineffective isovolumetric contraction with loss of dP/dt and a soft S1 (MR, myocarditis), while exercise or high output raises contractility and dP/dt and gives a loud S1
A leaky valve preserves dP/dt and gives a loud S1 (MR, myocarditis), while exercise lowers contractility and gives a soft S1
A leaky valve gives loss of dP/dt and a loud S1 (MR, myocarditis), while exercise raises dP/dt and gives a soft S1
A stenotic valve gives loss of dP/dt and a soft S1 (AS, MS), while exercise raises dP/dt and gives a loud S1
QUESTIONS.exp: The factor reads 'dP/dt of isovolumetric contraction' with a. leaky valve → ineffective IVC → loss of dP/dt → ↓velocity → soft S1 (MR, myocarditis) and b. exercise/high output → ↑contractility → ↑dP/dt → loud S1. (Book p298)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
QUESTIONS.q: How do thoracic transmission factors change S1 on page 298?
opts: Obesity, emphysema and pericardial effusion reduce the intensity of S1 alone, while a thin chest wall raises only the murmurs
Obesity, emphysema and pleural effusion reduce the intensity of all auscultatory events giving a soft S1, while a thin chest wall raises intensity
Obesity, emphysema and pericardial effusion reduce the intensity of all auscultatory events giving a soft S1, while a thin chest wall raises intensity giving a loud S1
Obesity, emphysema and pericardial effusion raise the intensity of all auscultatory events giving a loud S1, while a thin chest wall lowers intensity
QUESTIONS.exp: The sixth factor reads 'Obesity, emphysema, pericardial effusion → ↓intensity of all auscultatory events → soft S1' and 'Thin chest wall → ↑intensity → loud S1'. (Book p298)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
QUESTIONS.q: A young woman with a long PR interval on ECG has a strikingly soft first heart sound. Which printed mechanism explains it?
opts: Bradycardia shortens diastole, so filling is less, the valve leaflets sit wide apart and closure velocity rises
Bradycardia lengthens diastole, so filling is greater, the valve leaflets sit closer and closure velocity falls
The long PR interval delays closure, so the leaflets travel further and S1 becomes loud
The long PR interval perforates the leaflets, so S1 becomes soft
QUESTIONS.exp: The velocity-of-contraction block explicitly ties '↑ PR interval (diastole) → ↑ filling → valve are closer → ↓ velocity' to a soft S1 in bradycardia. (Book p298)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
QUESTIONS.q: A patient with calcific mitral stenosis has a soft first heart sound. Which of the six printed factors explains it?
opts: The valve sits wide apart at end diastole and closes from a distance
The chest wall is thin, dampening transmission
Loss of leaflet integrity, because the calcific leaflet is immobile
The PR interval is short, reducing filling before closure
QUESTIONS.exp: Under integrity of the valve leaflet, 'c. Calcific for immobile leaflet (Calcific MS)' leads to a soft S1; the wide-apart position of MS would instead make S1 loud. (Book p298)

QUESTIONS.sec: S1 in Aortic Stenosis, Regurgitation, Mitral Stenosis and Mitral Regurgitation, Loud T1 Causes, the Aortic Ejection Click, and Varying, Intermittent and Wide Split S1
QUESTIONS.q: Match each valve lesion to its printed S1 — 1) Aortic stenosis 2) Aortic regurgitation 3) Mitral stenosis 4) Mitral regurgitation … A) Soft S1 unrelated to severity B) Normal C) Soft S1 D) Loud S1 unrelated to severity
QUESTIONS.exp: The table reads AS normal, AR soft S1, MS loud S1 (unrelated to severity) and MR soft S1 (unrelated to severity), in that column order. (Book p299)

QUESTIONS.sec: S1 in Aortic Stenosis, Regurgitation, Mitral Stenosis and Mitral Regurgitation, Loud T1 Causes, the Aortic Ejection Click, and Varying, Intermittent and Wide Split S1
QUESTIONS.q: Match each lesion to the printed reason for its S1 — 1) Aortic regurgitation 2) Mitral stenosis 3) Mitral regurgitation … A) Loss of integrity and loss of dP/dt of isovolumetric contraction B) Position wide apart, increased velocity and delayed closure C) Premature closure (acute and chronic AR)
QUESTIONS.exp: The reason row gives AR premature closure in acute and chronic disease, MS position wide apart with ↑velocity and delayed closure, and MR loss of integrity with loss of dP/dt of isovolumetric contraction. (Book p299)

QUESTIONS.sec: S1 in Aortic Stenosis, Regurgitation, Mitral Stenosis and Mitral Regurgitation, Loud T1 Causes, the Aortic Ejection Click, and Varying, Intermittent and Wide Split S1
QUESTIONS.q: Which three conditions give a loud T1, and by what shared mechanism?
opts: MS, ASD and total anomalous pulmonary venous connection, all through increased mitral flow
TS, ASD and total anomalous pulmonary venous connection, all through increased tricuspid flow
TS, ASD and Ebstein anomaly, all through increased tricuspid flow
TS, VSD and total anomalous pulmonary venous connection, all through increased tricuspid flow

QUESTIONS.sec: S1 in Aortic Stenosis, Regurgitation, Mitral Stenosis and Mitral Regurgitation, Loud T1 Causes, the Aortic Ejection Click, and Varying, Intermittent and Wide Split S1
QUESTIONS.q: What produces the loud heart sound in aortic stenosis, and with what can it be confused?
opts: A bicuspid aortic valve producing an aortic ejection click, which can be confused for S1
A bicuspid pulmonary valve producing a pulmonary ejection click, which can be confused for S1
A calcified aortic valve producing an opening snap, which can be confused for S2
A bicuspid aortic valve producing an aortic ejection click, which can be confused for S2

QUESTIONS.sec: S1 in Aortic Stenosis, Regurgitation, Mitral Stenosis and Mitral Regurgitation, Loud T1 Causes, the Aortic Ejection Click, and Varying, Intermittent and Wide Split S1
QUESTIONS.q: How is S1 described in rheumatic mitral regurgitation with a preserved leaflet, and why?

Normal S1, because the leaflet is preserved
Soft S1, because of calcific immobile leaflets
Soft S1, because of associated myocarditis

QUESTIONS.sec: S1 in Aortic Stenosis, Regurgitation, Mitral Stenosis and Mitral Regurgitation, Loud T1 Causes, the Aortic Ejection Click, and Varying, Intermittent and Wide Split S1
QUESTIONS.q: What determines S1 when mitral stenosis and mitral regurgitation coexist, and what does moderate MS do through the right heart?

QUESTIONS.sec: S1 in Aortic Stenosis, Regurgitation, Mitral Stenosis and Mitral Regurgitation, Loud T1 Causes, the Aortic Ejection Click, and Varying, Intermittent and Wide Split S1
QUESTIONS.q: Match each variable-S1 pattern to its printed causes — 1) Varying S1 2) Intermittent S1 … A) Complete heart block with AV dissociation giving cannon S1, and VT with AV dissociation B) Atrial fibrillation from varying cycle length and atrial flutter

QUESTIONS.sec: S1 in Aortic Stenosis, Regurgitation, Mitral Stenosis and Mitral Regurgitation, Loud T1 Causes, the Aortic Ejection Click, and Varying, Intermittent and Wide Split S1
QUESTIONS.q: Match each wide split S1 cause to its printed side of the split — 1) Ectopic from LV and LV pacing 2) Ebstein anomaly 3) RBBB, TS and RA myxoma … A) Late T1 B) Early M1 (mechanical, with a sail sound from loud T1) C) Early M1 (electrical)
QUESTIONS.exp: The wide split S1 tree places ectopic from LV and LV pacing under early M1 electrical, Ebstein anomaly under early M1 mechanical with the sail sound from loud T1, and RBBB, TS and RA myxoma under late T1. (Book p299)

QUESTIONS.sec: S1 in Aortic Stenosis, Regurgitation, Mitral Stenosis and Mitral Regurgitation, Loud T1 Causes, the Aortic Ejection Click, and Varying, Intermittent and Wide Split S1
QUESTIONS.q: In Ebstein anomaly the wide split S1 carries a ______ sound because T1 is loud.

QUESTIONS.sec: S1 in Aortic Stenosis, Regurgitation, Mitral Stenosis and Mitral Regurgitation, Loud T1 Causes, the Aortic Ejection Click, and Varying, Intermittent and Wide Split S1
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about combined mitral stenosis and mitral regurgitation on page 299.

QUESTIONS.sec: Reverse Split S1, the S1 to S2 Sequence through Crossover Pressure, and the Hangout Interval with Its 30 and 80 Millisecond Aortic and Pulmonary Values
QUESTIONS.q: Match each reverse split S1 cause to its printed mechanism — 1) Right sided pacing or right sided ectopic 2) LBBB 3) MS or LA myxoma … A) Delayed M1 (mechanical) B) Early T1 (electrical) C) Delayed M1 (electrical)
QUESTIONS.exp: Reverse split runs T1 before M1, with early T1 from right sided pacing or ectopic, delayed M1 electrical in LBBB, and delayed M1 mechanical in MS or LA myxoma. (Book p300)

QUESTIONS.sec: Reverse Split S1, the S1 to S2 Sequence through Crossover Pressure, and the Hangout Interval with Its 30 and 80 Millisecond Aortic and Pulmonary Values
QUESTIONS.q: After S1, which structures open and which sound is associated with their opening?

The aortic and pulmonary valves open, and this is associated with ejection clicks
The aortic and pulmonary valves close, and this is associated with ejection clicks
The mitral and tricuspid valves open, and this is associated with opening snaps
QUESTIONS.exp: The S1–S2 flow reads S1 → isovolumetric contraction → 'Aortic and pulmonary valves open: associated with ejection clicks' → rapid ejection → reduced ejection. (Book p300)

QUESTIONS.sec: Reverse Split S1, the S1 to S2 Sequence through Crossover Pressure, and the Hangout Interval with Its 30 and 80 Millisecond Aortic and Pulmonary Values
QUESTIONS.q: Which point in the printed cycle follows the rise of aortic and pulmonary artery pressures?
opts: The point of dicrotic notch, where aortic pressure falls below CVP, followed by the hangout interval and valve closure with S2
The point of isovolumetric relaxation, where aortic pressure exceeds CVP, followed by the opening snap
The point of crossover pressure, where aortic pressure exceeds CVP and pulmonary pressure exceeds RVP, followed by the hangout interval and valve closure with S2
The point of crossover pressure, where aortic pressure falls below CVP and pulmonary pressure falls below RVP, followed by valve closure with S2
QUESTIONS.exp: The chart prints 'Point of crossover pressure (Aortic pressure > CVP, Pulmonary pressure > RVP)' → 'Hangout interval (protodiastole)' → 'valve closure – S2'. (Book p300)

QUESTIONS.sec: Reverse Split S1, the S1 to S2 Sequence through Crossover Pressure, and the Hangout Interval with Its 30 and 80 Millisecond Aortic and Pulmonary Values
QUESTIONS.q: The hangout interval is defined as the time between crossover pressure and ______.
QUESTIONS.exp: The definition reads 'Time between crossover pressure & valve closure', with protodiastole in brackets beside it. (Book p300)

QUESTIONS.sec: Reverse Split S1, the S1 to S2 Sequence through Crossover Pressure, and the Hangout Interval with Its 30 and 80 Millisecond Aortic and Pulmonary Values
QUESTIONS.q: On which two determinants does the printed hangout interval depend?
opts: The ventricular contractility and the valve area
The flow across the valve and the vessel length
The pressure beyond the valve and the distensibility of the vessel
The pressure beyond the valve and the valve area

QUESTIONS.sec: Reverse Split S1, the S1 to S2 Sequence through Crossover Pressure, and the Hangout Interval with Its 30 and 80 Millisecond Aortic and Pulmonary Values
QUESTIONS.q: Which hangout interval is printed for the aorta and which for the pulmonary artery?

50 ms for the aorta and 80 ms for the pulmonary artery
30 ms for the aorta and 50 ms for the pulmonary artery
30 ms for the aorta and 80 ms for the pulmonary artery

QUESTIONS.sec: Reverse Split S1, the S1 to S2 Sequence through Crossover Pressure, and the Hangout Interval with Its 30 and 80 Millisecond Aortic and Pulmonary Values
QUESTIONS.q: What is printed about the gap between A2 and P2, at rest and during inspiration?
opts: The gap is 50 ms and is appreciable, and during inspiration it exceeds 50 ms because venous return rises
The gap is 50 ms and is not appreciable, and during inspiration it falls below 50 ms because venous return rises
The gap is 30 ms and is appreciable, and during expiration it exceeds 50 ms because venous return rises
The gap is 80 ms and is appreciable, and during inspiration it exceeds 80 ms because venous return rises
QUESTIONS.exp: The two closing bullets read 'Gap between A2 & P2: 50ms (appreciable)' and 'During inspiration: >50ms (d/t ↑ venous return)'. (Book p300)

QUESTIONS.sec: Reverse Split S1, the S1 to S2 Sequence through Crossover Pressure, and the Hangout Interval with Its 30 and 80 Millisecond Aortic and Pulmonary Values
QUESTIONS.q: A patient has an audible split in the second sound during inspiration only, about 50 ms wide. What is the printed explanation?
opts: Inspiration reduces venous return, narrowing the A2–P2 gap below 50 ms
Inspiration increases venous return, widening the A2–P2 gap beyond the appreciable 50 ms
Expiration increases venous return, widening the A2–P2 gap beyond the appreciable 50 ms
Inspiration delays aortic valve closure, reversing the order to P2 then A2
QUESTIONS.exp: The page prints the resting gap as 50 ms and adds 'During inspiration: >50 ms (d/t ↑ venous return)', which is the physiological split of S2. (Book p300)

QUESTIONS.sec: Reverse Split S1, the S1 to S2 Sequence through Crossover Pressure, and the Hangout Interval with Its 30 and 80 Millisecond Aortic and Pulmonary Values
QUESTIONS.q: At rest the A2–P2 gap measures 50 ms and during inspiration it widens further. What does page 300 call this?
opts: A paradoxical split, because P2 precedes A2
An appreciable physiological gap that exceeds 50 ms in inspiration because venous return rises
A fixed split, because the gap does not change with respiration
A single S2, because a 50 ms gap cannot be heard
QUESTIONS.exp: The page prints the resting gap as 50 ms and 'appreciable', with 'During inspiration: >50 ms (d/t ↑ venous return)'; a fixed or paradoxical split behaves differently. (Book p300)

QUESTIONS.sec: S2 as Aortic and Pulmonary Closure at 120–150 Hz, the Four Determinants of A2 and P2, Their Behaviour in Valve Disease, the Four-Column Table and the Six Causes of a Single S2
QUESTIONS.q: With which event is the second heart sound associated, and at what frequency is it printed?

Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves, at a high frequency of 120–150 Hz
Opening of the aortic and pulmonary valves, at a high frequency of 120–150 Hz
Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves, at a low frequency of 20–40 Hz

QUESTIONS.sec: S2 as Aortic and Pulmonary Closure at 120–150 Hz, the Four Determinants of A2 and P2, Their Behaviour in Valve Disease, the Four-Column Table and the Six Causes of a Single S2
QUESTIONS.q: Match each determinant to its printed effect — 1) Systemic hypertension 2) Pulmonary hypertension 3) Hyperkinetic state 4) Pulmonary artery dilatation … A) Loud P2 from raised pressure beyond the valve B) Loud A2 C) Loud A2 and P2 together D) Loud P2 from the dilated vessel itself

QUESTIONS.sec: S2 as Aortic and Pulmonary Closure at 120–150 Hz, the Four Determinants of A2 and P2, Their Behaviour in Valve Disease, the Four-Column Table and the Six Causes of a Single S2
QUESTIONS.q: How is A2 affected in aortic stenosis from a bicuspid valve against a degenerative cause?
opts: A bicuspid aortic valve gives a soft A2, while a degenerative cause gives a soft A2 as well
A bicuspid aortic valve gives a loud A2, while a degenerative cause gives a loud A2 as well
A bicuspid aortic valve gives a soft A2, while a degenerative cause gives a loud A2
A bicuspid aortic valve gives a loud A2, while a degenerative cause gives a soft A2

QUESTIONS.sec: S2 as Aortic and Pulmonary Closure at 120–150 Hz, the Four Determinants of A2 and P2, Their Behaviour in Valve Disease, the Four-Column Table and the Six Causes of a Single S2
QUESTIONS.q: Which A2 does aortic regurgitation produce from valve pathology, and which from root pathology?
opts: Soft A2 from rheumatic valve pathology, and loud A2 (tambour S2) from root pathology as in ankylosing spondylitis
Soft A2 from rheumatic valve pathology, and loud A2 (tambour S2) from root pathology as in syphilis
Soft A2 from rheumatic valve pathology, and soft A2 (tambour S2) from root pathology as in Marfan syndrome
Loud A2 from rheumatic valve pathology, and soft A2 from root pathology as in syphilis
QUESTIONS.exp: The AR block reads 'd/t value pathology (Rheumatic) → Soft A2' and 'd/t root pathology → Loud A2 (tambour S2) (syphilis)'. (Book p301)

QUESTIONS.sec: S2 as Aortic and Pulmonary Closure at 120–150 Hz, the Four Determinants of A2 and P2, Their Behaviour in Valve Disease, the Four-Column Table and the Six Causes of a Single S2
QUESTIONS.q: What does moderate mitral stenosis do to P2, and what happens if pulmonary hypertension is joined by right ventricular failure?

QUESTIONS.sec: S2 as Aortic and Pulmonary Closure at 120–150 Hz, the Four Determinants of A2 and P2, Their Behaviour in Valve Disease, the Four-Column Table and the Six Causes of a Single S2
QUESTIONS.q: Match each four-column table entry to its printed group — 1) Loud A2 2) Loud P2 3) Soft A2 4) Soft P2 … A) Valvular PS B) Hyperkinetic state, HTN, aortic root dilatation and BAV C) Valvular AS (degenerative) and AR D) PHTN and ASD
QUESTIONS.exp: The table groups loud A2 as hyperkinetic state, HTN, aortic root dilatation and BAV; loud P2 as PHTN and ASD; soft A2 as valvular AS of degenerative type and AR; soft P2 as valvular PS. (Book p301)

QUESTIONS.sec: S2 as Aortic and Pulmonary Closure at 120–150 Hz, the Four Determinants of A2 and P2, Their Behaviour in Valve Disease, the Four-Column Table and the Six Causes of a Single S2

QUESTIONS.sec: S2 as Aortic and Pulmonary Closure at 120–150 Hz, the Four Determinants of A2 and P2, Their Behaviour in Valve Disease, the Four-Column Table and the Six Causes of a Single S2

QUESTIONS.sec: Wide Split S2 above 50 ms with Its Variable and Fixed Arms, and the Paradoxical Split with Early P2 and Delayed A2 Causes

Above 50 ms, and the split is then heard even in expiration
Above 30 ms, and the split is then heard only in inspiration
Above 50 ms, and the split is then heard only in inspiration
QUESTIONS.exp: The heading reads 'Wide split S2 (>50 ms)' with the line 'Split heard even in expiration', the expiration audibility being the clinical marker. (Book p302)

QUESTIONS.sec: Wide Split S2 above 50 ms with Its Variable and Fixed Arms, and the Paradoxical Split with Early P2 and Delayed A2 Causes
QUESTIONS.q: Match each wide variable split cause to its printed side — 1) LV pacing or LV ectopic 2) MR 3) RBBB or PS 4) PHTN with RVF as in MS … A) Late P2 from right ventricular pressure and failure B) Early A2, electrical C) Early A2, mechanical D) Late P2 from delayed right-sided activation or outflow obstruction
QUESTIONS.exp: The variable tree gives early A2 from LV pacing/ectopic electrically and MR mechanically, while late P2 covers RBBB, PS, VSD with a left-to-right shunt, cardiac tamponade and PHTN with RVF in MS. (Book p302)

QUESTIONS.sec: Wide Split S2 above 50 ms with Its Variable and Fixed Arms, and the Paradoxical Split with Early P2 and Delayed A2 Causes

Any cause of a wide variable split plus significant RV failure, and VSD where RV and LV filling change equally
Any cause of a narrow split plus significant RV failure, and ASD where RV filling alone changes with respiration
Any cause of a wide variable split plus significant RV failure, and ASD where RV and LV filling change equally in expiration and inspiration
QUESTIONS.exp: The fixed column reads 'Any cause of wide variable split + significant RV failure' and 'ASD (similar degree of alteration in RV & LV filling during expiration & inspiration)'. (Book p302)

QUESTIONS.sec: Wide Split S2 above 50 ms with Its Variable and Fixed Arms, and the Paradoxical Split with Early P2 and Delayed A2 Causes

opts: A split heard in expiration only, with A2 before P2
A split heard in inspiration and not in expiration, with A2 before P2
A split heard in expiration and not in inspiration, with P2 before A2
A split heard in both phases equally, with P2 before A2

QUESTIONS.sec: Wide Split S2 above 50 ms with Its Variable and Fixed Arms, and the Paradoxical Split with Early P2 and Delayed A2 Causes
QUESTIONS.q: Match each reverse split cause to its printed side — 1) Right side pacing or ectopic, and WPW type B 2) TR 3) LBBB 4) AS, AR and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy … A) Delayed A2 from left bundle branch block B) Early P2, electrical C) Early P2, mechanical D) Delayed A2 from aortic valve or myocardial disease
QUESTIONS.exp: The reverse split tree gives early P2 electrically from right side pacing/ectopic and WPW type B, early P2 mechanically from TR, and delayed A2 in LBBB as against AS, AR and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. (Book p302)

QUESTIONS.sec: Wide Split S2 above 50 ms with Its Variable and Fixed Arms, and the Paradoxical Split with Early P2 and Delayed A2 Causes
QUESTIONS.q: The early P2 of a paradoxical split is printed for right side pacing or ectopic and for WPW syndrome type ______.

QUESTIONS.sec: Wide Split S2 above 50 ms with Its Variable and Fixed Arms, and the Paradoxical Split with Early P2 and Delayed A2 Causes
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three are printed as causes of a delayed A2 in reverse split, one causes an early P2:
QUESTIONS.exp: The delayed A2 column reads LBBB, AS, AR and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), while TR sits in the early P2 mechanical column. (Book p302)

QUESTIONS.sec: Wide Split S2 above 50 ms with Its Variable and Fixed Arms, and the Paradoxical Split with Early P2 and Delayed A2 Causes
QUESTIONS.q: A patient's second sound is split in expiration and single in inspiration, with P2 preceding A2. What is the printed name and mechanism?
opts: A reverse or paradoxical split, from delayed A2 as in LBBB
A wide split, from early A2 as in LV pacing
A fixed split, as in ASD
A single S2, as in severe pulmonary hypertension

QUESTIONS.sec: The Diastolic Continuation from Protodiastole to Atrial Systole, the O-P-Time-S3-S4 Sequence, Early, Mid and Late Diastolic Position, and S3 with Its Three Mechanisms and Four Valve Lesions

Protodiastole → semilunar valves open → isovolumetric contraction → AV valves open → rapid filling → reduced filling → atrial systole
Protodiastole → AV valves closed → isovolumetric relaxation → semilunar valves open → rapid filling → reduced filling → atrial systole

QUESTIONS.sec: The Diastolic Continuation from Protodiastole to Atrial Systole, the O-P-Time-S3-S4 Sequence, Early, Mid and Late Diastolic Position, and S3 with Its Three Mechanisms and Four Valve Lesions

QUESTIONS.exp: The brackets read '70% filling (Passive)' under rapid and reduced filling and '30% filling (Active)' under atrial systole. (Book p303)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Diastolic Continuation from Protodiastole to Atrial Systole, the O-P-Time-S3-S4 Sequence, Early, Mid and Late Diastolic Position, and S3 with Its Three Mechanisms and Four Valve Lesions

Ventricular or protodiastolic gallop rhythm, seen in the rapid filling phase
Atrial or presystolic gallop rhythm, seen in atrial systole

QUESTIONS.sec: The Diastolic Continuation from Protodiastole to Atrial Systole, the O-P-Time-S3-S4 Sequence, Early, Mid and Late Diastolic Position, and S3 with Its Three Mechanisms and Four Valve Lesions

opts: A non-stenosed AV valve, excluding MS and TS
A stenosed AV valve, excluding MR and AR
A non-stenosed AV valve, excluding MR and AR
A non-stenosed semilunar valve, excluding AS and PS

QUESTIONS.sec: The Diastolic Continuation from Protodiastole to Atrial Systole, the O-P-Time-S3-S4 Sequence, Early, Mid and Late Diastolic Position, and S3 with Its Three Mechanisms and Four Valve Lesions
QUESTIONS.q: Match each S3 mechanism to its printed setting — 1) Physiological 2) Increased end systolic volume 3) Less than normal filling … A) LVH, RVH and RCMP B) Young people, athletes and hyperkinetic states C) LV or RV failure
QUESTIONS.exp: The three arms read physiological excessive rapid filling into a hypercompliant ventricle across a normal AV valve in the young, athletes and hyperkinetic states; increased end systolic volume seen in LV/RV failure, the commonest setting; and less than normal filling of a hypertrophic non-compliant ventricle in LVH, RVH and RCMP. (Book p303)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Diastolic Continuation from Protodiastole to Atrial Systole, the O-P-Time-S3-S4 Sequence, Early, Mid and Late Diastolic Position, and S3 with Its Three Mechanisms and Four Valve Lesions
QUESTIONS.q: How does the timing of a pathological S3 compare with a physiological S3, and which valve lesions produce S3?
opts: Pathological S3 occurs earlier than physiological S3; it is heard in MS and AR, but not in MR or AS
Pathological S3 occurs later than physiological S3; it is heard in MR with or without LVF and in severe AS from LVH, but not in MS or AR with LVF
Pathological S3 occurs earlier than physiological S3; it is heard only in MS and TS
Pathological S3 occurs earlier than physiological S3; it is heard in MR with or without LVF and in severe AS from LVH, but not in MS or AR with LVF
QUESTIONS.exp: The line reads 'Pathological S3 occurs earlier than physiological S3', and the valvular diagram prints MR heard with or without LVF, AS seen in severe AS, MS not seen and AR not seen except with LVF. (Book p303)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Diastolic Continuation from Protodiastole to Atrial Systole, the O-P-Time-S3-S4 Sequence, Early, Mid and Late Diastolic Position, and S3 with Its Three Mechanisms and Four Valve Lesions
QUESTIONS.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three statements about S3 on page 303 are printed, one contradicts the page:
opts: S3 is seen in the rapid filling phase
S3 is also called the ventricular or protodiastolic gallop
S3 is a high pitched early systolic sound heard with the diaphragm
S3 is not seen in mitral stenosis or tricuspid stenosis
QUESTIONS.exp: S3 is a low pitched sound (the page lists it with S4 and tumour plop), occurs in the rapid filling phase, is a protodiastolic gallop and is excluded by a stenosed AV valve; nothing on the page makes it high pitched or systolic. (Book p303)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Diastolic Continuation from Protodiastole to Atrial Systole, the O-P-Time-S3-S4 Sequence, Early, Mid and Late Diastolic Position, and S3 with Its Three Mechanisms and Four Valve Lesions
QUESTIONS.q: A lean 20-year-old athlete has a third heart sound at the apex, with excessive rapid filling of a hypercompliant ventricle and no cardiac disease. Which of the three printed mechanisms does he represent?
opts: Pathological — increased end systolic volume in a dilated ventricle
Physiological — excessive rapid filling into a hypercompliant ventricle
Pathological — less than normal filling of a hypertrophic non-compliant ventricle
Pathological — rapid filling across a stenosed AV valve
QUESTIONS.exp: The three mechanisms are physiological excessive rapid filling into a hypercompliant ventricle in the young or athletic, increased end systolic volume in a dilated ventricle (LVF, MR, AR) and less than normal filling of a hypertrophic non-compliant ventricle (LVH, RVH, RCMP); a stenosed AV valve precludes S3. (Book p303)

QUESTIONS.sec: The Diastolic Continuation from Protodiastole to Atrial Systole, the O-P-Time-S3-S4 Sequence, Early, Mid and Late Diastolic Position, and S3 with Its Three Mechanisms and Four Valve Lesions
QUESTIONS.q: TRUE or FALSE about the valve lesions in which S3 is seen, as printed on page 303.
opts: False — S3 requires a stenosed AV valve
False — S3 is always seen in aortic regurgitation with LVF
True — S3 is not seen in mitral stenosis or tricuspid stenosis
True — S3 is a constant finding in mitral stenosis

QUESTIONS.sec: S3 Features with Left Lateral Position, Leg Raising and the Heart-Failure Caveat, the Pericardial Knock of Constrictive Pericarditis, and S4 with Its Four Prerequisites and Its Valve-Disease Table

In the supine position at the apex; it varies with respiration, and a physiological S3 appears only in the upright position
In the left lateral position at the apex; it varies with inspiration, and a physiological S3 disappears in the upright position
QUESTIONS.exp: The features read 'Auscultated in: Left lateral position; At the apex', 'Does not vary with respiration' and 'Physiological S3 disappears in upright position'. (Book p304)

QUESTIONS.sec: S3 Features with Left Lateral Position, Leg Raising and the Heart-Failure Caveat, the Pericardial Knock of Constrictive Pericarditis, and S4 with Its Four Prerequisites and Its Valve-Disease Table

It reduces venous return so that S3 disappears even if it was heard in the left lateral position
It augments venous return so that a pericardial knock appears in constrictive pericarditis
It augments venous return so that S3 is heard even if it was not heard in the left lateral position
QUESTIONS.exp: The arrow reads 'Passive leg raising: Augments venous return → S3 heard even if not heard in left lateral', a bedside trick to unmask the sound. (Book p304)

QUESTIONS.sec: S3 Features with Left Lateral Position, Leg Raising and the Heart-Failure Caveat, the Pericardial Knock of Constrictive Pericarditis, and S4 with Its Four Prerequisites and Its Valve-Disease Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which three conditions are printed as heart failure without S3?
QUESTIONS.exp: The note reads 'Heart failure without S3 → MS, TS, pericardial tamponade', the same stenotic-pair logic that excludes S3 at the valve. (Book p304)

QUESTIONS.sec: S3 Features with Left Lateral Position, Leg Raising and the Heart-Failure Caveat, the Pericardial Knock of Constrictive Pericarditis, and S4 with Its Four Prerequisites and Its Valve-Disease Table

Chronic constrictive pericarditis, where the rock-like pericardium structurally restricts diastolic filling by the pericardial shell
Chronic constrictive pericarditis, where the pericardium is thin and offers no resistance to filling

QUESTIONS.sec: S3 Features with Left Lateral Position, Leg Raising and the Heart-Failure Caveat, the Pericardial Knock of Constrictive Pericarditis, and S4 with Its Four Prerequisites and Its Valve-Disease Table
QUESTIONS.q: Match each pericardial knock feature to what it is printed to do — 1) High pitched and louder with inspiration 2) Early diastolic timing 3) Disappears after pericardiectomy … A) Distinguishes it from S3 B) Confirms the pericardial origin C) Places it in early diastole
QUESTIONS.exp: The knock features are high pitched and louder with inspiration, bracketed 'To differentiate from S3'; early diastolic sound; and 'Disappears following pericardiectomy', which proves the pericardial source. (Book p304)

QUESTIONS.sec: S3 Features with Left Lateral Position, Leg Raising and the Heart-Failure Caveat, the Pericardial Knock of Constrictive Pericarditis, and S4 with Its Four Prerequisites and Its Valve-Disease Table
QUESTIONS.q: Which other name and phase are printed for S4, and with which venous wave does it correlate?

Atrial or protodiastolic gallop, seen in rapid filling and correlating with the A-wave in the JVP
Ventricular or presystolic gallop, seen in atrial systole and correlating with the V-wave in the JVP
Atrial or presystolic gallop, seen in atrial systole and correlating with the C-wave in the JVP

QUESTIONS.sec: S3 Features with Left Lateral Position, Leg Raising and the Heart-Failure Caveat, the Pericardial Knock of Constrictive Pericarditis, and S4 with Its Four Prerequisites and Its Valve-Disease Table

QUESTIONS.sec: S3 Features with Left Lateral Position, Leg Raising and the Heart-Failure Caveat, the Pericardial Knock of Constrictive Pericarditis, and S4 with Its Four Prerequisites and Its Valve-Disease Table

Ventricular contraction increases LV end-diastolic fibre length; it is not seen in MS, MR or AR, but is heard in AS
Atrial contraction decreases LV end-diastolic fibre length; it is not seen in MS, MR or AR, but is heard in AS
Atrial contraction increases LV end-diastolic fibre length; it is not seen in MS, MR or AR, but is heard in AS

QUESTIONS.sec: S3 Features with Left Lateral Position, Leg Raising and the Heart-Failure Caveat, the Pericardial Knock of Constrictive Pericarditis, and S4 with Its Four Prerequisites and Its Valve-Disease Table

QUESTIONS.q: A patient in atrial fibrillation has no fourth heart sound despite LVH. Which printed prerequisite explains the absence?

QUESTIONS.sec: The Three S4 Settings, the Opening Snap in Mitral Stenosis with Its S2-OS Interval Ladder and Auscultation Rules, and the Low Pitched Tumour Plop of Atrial Myxoma

It is produced by closure of the AV valve and represents isovolumetric contraction

QUESTIONS.sec: The Three S4 Settings, the Opening Snap in Mitral Stenosis with Its S2-OS Interval Ladder and Auscultation Rules, and the Low Pitched Tumour Plop of Atrial Myxoma

QUESTIONS.q: Which mechanism produces the opening snap in mitral stenosis?

A raised left ventricular pressure with thickened leaflets causes a sudden doming motion of the valves into the LA
A raised left atrial pressure with thinned leaflets causes a gradual doming motion of the valves into the LV
A raised left atrial pressure with thickened leaflets causes a sudden doming motion of the valves into the LV

QUESTIONS.sec: The Three S4 Settings, the Opening Snap in Mitral Stenosis with Its S2-OS Interval Ladder and Auscultation Rules, and the Low Pitched Tumour Plop of Atrial Myxoma
QUESTIONS.q: How does a rising left atrial pressure change the S2–OS interval in mitral stenosis?

It opens the AV valves later, so the opening snap comes later and the S2–OS interval lengthens; S2–OS is directly proportional to LAP
It opens the AV valves earlier, so the opening snap comes earlier and the S2–OS interval shortens; S2–OS is inversely proportional to LAP
It opens the AV valves earlier, so the opening snap comes earlier and the S2–OS interval lengthens; S2–OS is directly proportional to LAP

QUESTIONS.q: Match each severity of mitral stenosis to its printed intervals and pressures — 1) Mild MS 2) Severe MS … A) S2–OS 40–60 mmHg with LAP >15 mmHg B) S2–OS >120 mmHg with LAP <5 mmHg

QUESTIONS.sec: The Three S4 Settings, the Opening Snap in Mitral Stenosis with Its S2-OS Interval Ladder and Auscultation Rules, and the Low Pitched Tumour Plop of Atrial Myxoma

QUESTIONS.sec: The Three S4 Settings, the Opening Snap in Mitral Stenosis with Its S2-OS Interval Ladder and Auscultation Rules, and the Low Pitched Tumour Plop of Atrial Myxoma
QUESTIONS.q: Which three descriptors are printed inside the ovals for tumour plop?

UNITS.title: Definition & Bristol Chart
UNITS.sec: Definition & Bristol Chart
UNITS.guide:
Definition >200 mL/24 h and Bristol Types 1-7.
Link Type numbers to stool form and clinical label.
Severe constipation (1) through severe diarrhea (7) in strict order.

UNITS.title: Physiology & Macronutrients
UNITS.sec: Physiology & Macronutrients
UNITS.guide:
Luminal → Mucosal (small intestine, maximum) → Post mucosal.
Fat is most calorie-dense and most specific in malabsorption.
List carbs and proteins as the other macronutrients.

UNITS.title: Frequency Classification & Acute Etiology
UNITS.sec: Frequency Classification & Acute Etiology
UNITS.guide:
Acute <2w (nuisance), Persistent >2w, Chronic >4w.
Acute viral m/c overall: Norovirus adults, Rotavirus children, self-limiting.
Classify by duration first in the flowchart.

UNITS.title: Chronic Diarrhea & Malassimilation
UNITS.sec: Chronic Diarrhea & Malassimilation
UNITS.guide:
Chronic D/d: Osmotic→malabsorption, Secretory→tumor/toxin, Inflammatory→IBD.
Malassimilation = maldigestion + malabsorption.
Diminished digestion/absorption of one or more nutrients.

UNITS.title: Osmotic Diarrhea & Steatorrhea
UNITS.sec: Osmotic Diarrhea & Steatorrhea
UNITS.guide:
Osmotic = most consistent symptom of malabsorption.
Steatorrhea = hallmark: pale bulky fatty malodorous greasy stools.
Pathology: ↓ fat absorption → ↑ stool osmolality → draws water → osmotic diarrhea.

UNITS.title: Steatorrhea Investigations
UNITS.sec: Steatorrhea Investigations
UNITS.guide:
72-h fecal fat = gold standard with 100 g/day fat input.
Normal <7 g/day; steatorrhea >7 g/d for 3 d (D3-D5) or ≥7% excretion.
Qualitative: Sudan III, Sudan IV, Oil red O.

UNITS.title: Secretory Diarrhea & Stool Osmotic Gap
UNITS.sec: Secretory Diarrhea & Stool Osmotic Gap
UNITS.guide:
Secretory: ETEC/V. cholera heat-labile toxin + rotavirus; VIPoma→WDHA + hypoK + acidosis; no structural damage.
Gap table: Osmotic >100 + pH<5.5 vs Secretory <50 + ↑Na+K + pH>6.0 + no change on fasting.
Formula 290−2(Na⁺+K⁺), normal 50-100; factitious case adolescent female.

UNITS.title: Factitious & Anatomical Classification
UNITS.sec: Factitious & Anatomical Classification
UNITS.guide:
Factitious unsupervised ~16 vs supervised ~279.
Small vs Large etiology + full clinical table (volume, consistency, frequency, pus/blood/mucus, tenesmus, dyschezia, pain, fever, cramps, bloating, weight loss, vomiting, steatorrhoea) in order.
Weight loss/vomiting/steatorrhoea distinguish persistent small intestinal.

UNITS.title: Approach to Diarrhea
UNITS.sec: Approach to Diarrhea
UNITS.guide:
Duration first: <2w = infection, >4w = small vs large.
<2w Small (large volume, viral/ETEC/cholera, self-limiting) vs Large (fever/pain/blood, Shigella etc).
>4w Small osmotic (>100 gap, improves) vs secretory (VIPoma) vs Large inflammatory (UC).

UNITS.title: Basics of Absorption & Stages
UNITS.sec: Basics of Absorption & Stages
UNITS.guide:
Three stages in order: Luminal → Mucosal → Post mucosal.
Luminal is enzymes mediated; mucosal is the enterocyte brush border.
Post mucosal is movement from the mucosal epithelial cell into blood.

UNITS.title: Anatomy of the Small Intestine
UNITS.sec: Anatomy of the Small Intestine
UNITS.guide:
Proximal 2/3 = maximum absorption (jejunum > duodenum).
Distal 1/3 = bile acid, vitamin B12 and Mg2+ (ileum).
Fix the segment before learning each nutrient.

UNITS.title: Histology: Mucosa
UNITS.sec: Histology: Mucosa
UNITS.guide:
Villi are the specific feature and are surrounded by crypts of Lieberkühn.
Paneth cells sit at the crypt base and make alpha defensins, lysozymes, phospholipase A2.
Renewal every 48-72 hrs; interstitial cells of Cajal are pacemaker cells.

UNITS.title: Small Intestine Layers & Peyer's Patches
UNITS.sec: Small Intestine Layers & Peyer's Patches
UNITS.guide:
Layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria, serosa.
Peyer's patches are macroscopic lymphoid aggregates of the ileal submucosa.
In typhoid they hypertrophy.

UNITS.title: Fat Absorption: Luminal Phase
UNITS.sec: Fat Absorption: Luminal Phase
UNITS.guide:
Bile acids + pancreatic lipase act on triglyceride → lipolysis → fatty acids + glycerol.
Micelles then pass into enterocytes by passive diffusion.
Chronic pancreatitis removes the lipase step.

UNITS.title: Bile Acid Physiology
UNITS.sec: Bile Acid Physiology
UNITS.guide:
Body pool 4 g, maintained by enterohepatic circulation.
Synthesis (7α-hydroxylase, rate limiting) → cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid → conjugation with glycine/taurine → bile salts.
Colonic bacterial deconjugation gives deoxycholic and lithocholic acid.

UNITS.title: Defects in Luminal & Mucosal Phase
UNITS.sec: Defects in Luminal & Mucosal Phase
UNITS.guide:
Luminal: chronic pancreatitis (lipase) and bile acid defect (secretion/synthesis/reabsorption).
Bile duct destruction in cirrhosis, PBC, PSC; ileal dysfunction in TB/Crohn's; early deconjugation in SIBO.
Mucosal: coeliac disease, Whipple disease, tropical sprue.

UNITS.title: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
UNITS.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
UNITS.guide:
LCFA + glycerol → esterification → chylomicrons → intestinal lymphatics.
Disorders: abetalipoproteinaemia and intestinal lymphangiectasia.
Chain length >12 / 8-12 / <8; only long chain needs lipolysis and micelles; short chain is colonic and substantial in stool.

UNITS.title: Carbohydrate Absorption Mechanism
UNITS.sec: Carbohydrate Absorption Mechanism
UNITS.guide:
Disaccharidases on the brush border: lactase, maltase, sucrase, trehalase.
Gut: SGLT1 (active) for glucose/galactose, GLUT5 for fructose.
Liver: GLUT2 entry then galactokinase, fructokinase, glucokinase.

UNITS.title: Defects in Carbohydrate Absorption
UNITS.sec: Defects in Carbohydrate Absorption
UNITS.guide:
Congenital forms are autosomal recessive.
Selective = lactase deficiency; global = small intestinal mucosal defect (coeliac, Whipple's, tropical sprue).
Primary (m/c) lactase deficiency is allele persistence; secondary follows infections and IBS.

UNITS.title: Protein Absorption & Selective Defects
UNITS.sec: Protein Absorption & Selective Defects
UNITS.guide:
Trypsinogen → trypsin → activates chymotrypsin and elastase.
Selective defects: enterokinase deficiency, Hartnup's disease (pellagra), cystinuria (COLA).
COLA = cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine.

UNITS.title: Lactose Intolerance: Physiology to Pathogenesis
UNITS.sec: Lactose Intolerance: Physiology to Pathogenesis
UNITS.guide:
Lactose (milk, cheese) → lactase (brush border) → glucose + galactose.
Congenital autosomal recessive versus acquired ↓ activity (primary allele persistence, secondary infections/IBS).
Unabsorbed carbohydrate is fermented to acid and H2, methane, CO2.

UNITS.title: Lactose Intolerance: Presentation & Investigations
UNITS.sec: Lactose Intolerance: Presentation & Investigations
UNITS.guide:
90 min post prandial distension, bloating, cramps; acidic diaper dermatitis in children.
Stool pH acidic; lactose hydrogen breath test positive at H2 > 20 ppm.
Lactose-glucose blood test is obsolete; treat with diet and calcium.

UNITS.title: Abetalipoproteinemia
UNITS.sec: Abetalipoproteinemia
UNITS.guide:
AKA neuroacanthocytosis; autosomal recessive; apoB48 → defective esterification → no chylomicrons.
Triad: ataxia (vitamin E), retinitis pigmentosa, steatorrhea; smear shows acanthocytes.
Post prandial endoscopic biopsy is 100% diagnostic with enterocyte vacuolation.

UNITS.title: Intestinal Lymphangiectasia
UNITS.sec: Intestinal Lymphangiectasia
UNITS.guide:
Chylomicrons cross intestinal lymphatics into blood.
Primary = dilated channels; secondary = lymphoma or Crohn's with lymphatic obstruction.
Protein losing enteropathy with fecal α-1 antitrypsin elevated; treat with medium chain triglyceride diet.

UNITS.title: Steps for Evaluating Malabsorption
UNITS.sec: Steps for Evaluating Malabsorption
UNITS.guide:
Confirm the diagnosis (clinically and by investigations).
Then confirm global versus selective malabsorption.
Finally confirm the aetiology.

UNITS.title: Clinical Features: Gastrointestinal
UNITS.sec: Clinical Features: Gastrointestinal
UNITS.guide:
Small intestinal, >4 weeks, osmotic, improves on fasting — the most consistent symptom.
Fat → steatorrhea; carbohydrate → bloating and dyspepsia.
Protein → foul smelling stools, ascites, edema; plus unexplained weight loss.

UNITS.title: Clinical Features: Musculoskeletal & Cutaneous
UNITS.sec: Clinical Features: Musculoskeletal & Cutaneous
UNITS.guide:
Musculoskeletal: fat malabsorption with impaired vitamin D and Ca2+ → tetany, fracture, bone pain.
Niacin → hyperpigmentation; vitamin C → perifollicular hemorrhage and curly hair.
Vitamin K → bruisability; Zn/EFA → acrodermatitis; vitamin A → follicular hyperkeratosis.

UNITS.title: Clinical Features: Miscellaneous & Kidney Stones
UNITS.sec: Clinical Features: Miscellaneous & Kidney Stones
UNITS.guide:
Coeliac → growth retardation; proximal disease → folate/iron deficiency; distal → B12 deficiency.
B12/E → neuropathy and ataxia; B12 → glossitis, cheliosis, stomatitis; vitamin A → night blindness.
Free oxalate is absorbed in the colon → oxaluria → Ca2+ oxalate stones; pain, constipation and fever are NOT features.

UNITS.title: Fat Malabsorption Tests
UNITS.sec: Fat Malabsorption Tests
UNITS.guide:
Qualitative: Sudan III.
Quantitative (gold standard): fecal fat excretion >7 g/day.
The fecal fat excretion test is the gold standard investigation for malabsorption.

UNITS.title: D-Xylose Test
UNITS.sec: D-Xylose Test
UNITS.guide:
Best and most specific test; D-xylose is a pentose monosaccharide.
It assesses intact small intestinal mucosa.
25 g orally after fasting; urine collected over 4-6 hours; normal ≥4.5 g, <4.5 g positive.

UNITS.title: False Positives & Hydrogen Breath Tests
UNITS.sec: False Positives & Hydrogen Breath Tests
UNITS.guide:
False positives: renal failure (defective excretion), rapid transit (hyperthyroidism, vomiting), SIBO (organisms utilise D-xylose), ascites.
Lactose H2 breath test: for lactase deficiency, positive >20 ppm.
Lactulose H2 breath test: H2 within 90 minutes = SIBO; after 90 minutes = normal.

UNITS.title: Obsolete Tests & Biopsy Diagnoses
UNITS.sec: Obsolete Tests & Biopsy Diagnoses
UNITS.guide:
Obsolete: acid steatocrit and C-14 triolein breath test (fat); C-13 egg white breath test (protein).
Stool elastase/chymotrypsin → pancreatic insufficiency; fecal α-1 antitrypsin → lymphangiectasia; NIRA is newer.
Biopsy diagnoses: Whipple's disease, agammaglobulinaemia, abetalipoproteinaemia.

UNITS.title: Schilling Test
UNITS.sec: Schilling Test
UNITS.guide:
Phase I: 1000 μg unlabelled B12 IM to saturate stores, then 1 μg oral radiolabelled B12, then urine B12.
<7% positive, 7-10% normal.
Phase II: intrinsic factor → pernicious anaemia; pancreatic enzymes → chronic pancreatitis; antibiotics → SIBO; still <7% = ileal disease.

UNITS.title: Global Malabsorption: Overview
UNITS.sec: Global Malabsorption: Overview
UNITS.guide:
Defective absorption of carbohydrate, fat and protein from small intestinal mucosal dysfunction.
Fat is the most sensitive, most specific and most energy dense nutrient.
Three causes: celiac disease, Whipple's disease, tropical sprue.

UNITS.title: Celiac Disease: Features & Iceberg Phenomenon
UNITS.sec: Celiac Disease: Features & Iceberg Phenomenon
UNITS.guide:
AKA celiac sprue / gluten sensitive enteropathy / non-tropical sprue.
Iceberg phenomenon: only 50% present classically, missed through physician unawareness.
HLA DQ2/DQ8 is the most important predisposition; the disease is proximal small intestinal.

UNITS.title: Celiac Disease: Types
UNITS.sec: Celiac Disease: Types
UNITS.guide:
Classical: 50% present with symptoms of malabsorption.
Atypical: symptoms other than malabsorption; silent: asymptomatic, serology positive.
Latent: asymptomatic, antibodies negative, HLA susceptibility present.

UNITS.title: Celiac Pathophysiology & Disease Progression
UNITS.sec: Celiac Pathophysiology & Disease Progression
UNITS.guide:
HLA DQ2/DQ8 → gluten (wheat, barley, rye, oats) → prolamine (most toxic) → gliadin (chief antigen).
Tissue transglutaminase deamidates gliadin-bound glutamine → activates T cells.
Gluten-free diet: 90% revert (clinically 3 weeks, histologically 6 months); 10% refractory → steroids.

UNITS.title: Celiac Clinical Features
UNITS.sec: Celiac Clinical Features
UNITS.guide:
Classical: osmotic diarrhea, distension, foul smelling stool, weight loss; IBS symptoms in 30%.
Atypical: short stature, fracture/osteopenia, ataxia/neuropathy, iron deficiency anemia not due to blood loss.
Other: secondary hyperparathyroidism, cerebral calcification, hyposplenism with Howell-Jolly bodies, follicular hyperkeratosis, edema/ascites, cryptogenic cirrhosis.

UNITS.title: Celiac Associations
UNITS.sec: Celiac Associations
UNITS.guide:
Definite: dermatitis herpetiformis (most important), Down syndrome, type I DM, IgA nephropathy, IgA deficiency, bird-fancier lung, lymphocytic colitis, cerebral calcification with epilepsy.
Dermatitis herpetiformis: papulovesicular extensor lesions with linear IgA at the dermoepidermal junction.
Probable: cryptogenic transaminitis, idiopathic short stature, refractory iron deficiency anemia, cerebellar ataxia.

UNITS.title: Celiac Diagnosis: Serology & Biopsy
UNITS.sec: Celiac Diagnosis: Serology & Biopsy
UNITS.guide:
Anti-TTG IgA: most important for diagnosis and monitoring; specificity 98%.
Anti-endomysial IgA: indirect immunofluorescence, sensitivity 99%, specificity 73%, subjective and cumbersome.
Anti-deamidated gliadin peptide IgG for IgA deficiency; anti-gliadin obsolete. Biopsy: mucosal total villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, normal thickness, lamina propria lymphocytes, Marsh score.

UNITS.title: Celiac Interpretation, Complications & Treatment
UNITS.sec: Celiac Interpretation, Complications & Treatment
UNITS.guide:
Both positive = celiac; both negative = not celiac (test HLA DQ2/DQ8 if suggestive).
Serology positive/biopsy negative: repeat biopsy; serology negative/biopsy positive: non-specific (tropical sprue, cow's milk intolerance).
Refractory disease is premalignant: EATL, small intestinal adenocarcinoma, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma; diet is rice/corn/maize/potato/soybean with gluten restriction.

UNITS.title: Whipple's Disease: Presentation
UNITS.sec: Whipple's Disease: Presentation
UNITS.guide:
Chronic multisystem disease of joints, GIT, CNS and CVS; M > F, 50-60 years.
Pan-intestinal, proximal more than distal; Tropheryma whipplei is a gram positive actinobacterium that cannot be cultured because of slow doubling time.
Diagnosis is by biopsy.

UNITS.title: Whipple's Disease: Clinical Features
UNITS.sec: Whipple's Disease: Clinical Features
UNITS.guide:
Joints first in >80%: large joints, migratory arthralgia > arthritis.
GIT 2-3 years later: diarrhea (most consistent), weight loss, abdominal pain with mesenteric lymphadenopathy.
Neuro 40%: rapidly progressive dementia (m/c) and oculomasticatory myorhythmia (m/c specific); CVS: culture negative endocarditis, mitral valve > myocarditis > pericarditis, HACEK group.

UNITS.title: Whipple's Disease: Diagnosis & Treatment
UNITS.sec: Whipple's Disease: Diagnosis & Treatment
UNITS.guide:
Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy is 100% diagnostic; PCR identifies Tropheryma whipplei.
PAS positive foamy macrophages in epithelium, lamina propria and submucosa with enlarged villi.
Induction IV ceftriaxone 2 g for 14 days (best); maintenance co-trimoxazole prevents relapse and penetrates the CNS.

UNITS.title: Tropical Sprue: Pathogenesis
UNITS.sec: Tropical Sprue: Pathogenesis
UNITS.guide:
Most common cause of malabsorption in India, Bangladesh and Pakistan.
Infective diarrhea → toxigenic coliforms (E. coli, Klebsiella) → fermentation products, mainly ethanol.
Structural damage impairs folic acid absorption → 2-3 weeks → pan-intestinal involvement with defective B12, bile acid and Mg2+ absorption.

UNITS.title: Tropical Sprue: Features, Investigations & Treatment
UNITS.sec: Tropical Sprue: Features, Investigations & Treatment
UNITS.guide:
Chronic watery voluminous small bowel diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, prominent folic acid deficiency, hyperpigmentation from B12 deficiency.
Biopsy resembles celiac disease but serology is negative; stool examined for ova, cyst and trophozoite to rule out giardiasis.
Folic acid 5 mg daily plus tetracycline 250 mg QID for 3-6 months; relapse in 20%.

UNITS.title: Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea
UNITS.sec: Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea
UNITS.guide:
Bile acid diarrhea (cholorrhea) is seen in tropical sprue from defective FGF-19; limited ileal disease leaves compensatory excess hepatic bile acid removing Na+, Cl− and K+.
Fatty acid diarrhea needs severe ileal disease: no compensatory release → malabsorption → fatty acid in colon → steatorrhea >20 g.
Cholestyramine helps bile acid diarrhea; a low-fat diet helps fatty acid diarrhea.

UNITS.title: Short Bowel Syndrome: Definition & Etiology
UNITS.sec: Short Bowel Syndrome: Definition & Etiology
UNITS.guide:
Short bowel syndrome: < 200 cm; very severe: < 100 cm.
Adult: mesenteric vascular disease (ischemia with resection) more than Crohn's disease.
Child: necrotising enterocolitis.

UNITS.title: Short Bowel Syndrome: Clinical Presentation
UNITS.sec: Short Bowel Syndrome: Clinical Presentation
UNITS.guide:
Hyperoxaluria: unabsorbed LCFA bind calcium, free oxalate is absorbed and forms oxalate stones.
Absent ileum → cholesterol gallstones from supersaturation.
D-lactic acidosis from gram positive anaerobes (Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium) causing CNS features; hypergastrinemia; hypomagnesemia; defective ileal break with rapid gastric emptying.

UNITS.title: Short Bowel Syndrome: Deficiencies & Management
UNITS.sec: Short Bowel Syndrome: Deficiencies & Management
UNITS.guide:
Iron: absent duodenum > jejunum; Ca2+, folate, vitamins A, D, E: absent jejunum; vitamin K rarely because bacteria migrate when the ileocecal valve is lost.
SIBO from loss of the ileocecal valve.
Diet: medium chain fatty acids and complex carbohydrates; total parenteral nutrition when the colon is absent; teduglutide is an oral GLP-2 analogue.

UNITS.title: SIBO: Physiology, Pathology & Etiology
UNITS.sec: SIBO: Physiology, Pathology & Etiology
UNITS.guide:
AKA blind loop syndrome / stagnant bowel syndrome.
Proximal small intestine normally has no bacteria; ileum has Enterobacteriaceae; colon has anaerobes.
Overgrowth of non-toxigenic anaerobes proximally; causes are anatomical defects, motility disorders (IBS, scleroderma, diabetes, amyloidosis), immunodeficiency and HIV.

UNITS.title: SIBO: Presentation, Investigations & Management
UNITS.sec: SIBO: Presentation, Investigations & Management
UNITS.guide:
Bacteria compete for nutrients and consume B12: bloating and belching are most common; B12 deficiency, macrocytic anemia, steatorrhea, unexplained diarrhea.
Jejunal aspirate >10^3 CFU/mL is gold standard; lactulose H2 breath test is preferred; indican is obsolete; B12 low, folate and vitamin K high.
Rifaximin 550 mg BD for 7-10 days; avoid macrolides.

UNITS.title: Entities of IBD & Microscopic Colitis
UNITS.sec: Entities of IBD & Microscopic Colitis
UNITS.guide:
Four entities are listed, but IBD currently means UC and CD only.
Microscopic colitis follows long-term PPI and NSAID use: chronic non-bloody voluminous watery diarrhea with a normal examination and normal endoscopy.
Biopsy: collagenous colitis (collagen band, Sjogren's) versus lymphocytic colitis (intra-epithelial lymphocytes, celiac disease).

UNITS.title: Diversion Colitis & Normal Histology of Colon
UNITS.sec: Diversion Colitis & Normal Histology of Colon
UNITS.guide:
Diversion colitis occurs in patients using colostomy bags after surgery for bowel malignancies.
Normal colonic layers, innermost to outermost: mucosal epithelial cells, lamina propria, muscularis mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria, serosa.
Learn the order — it anchors every depth-of-invasion comparison that follows.

UNITS.title: Colonic Mucosa & Definition of Diarrhea
UNITS.sec: Colonic Mucosa & Definition of Diarrhea
UNITS.guide:
Colonic mucosa has no villi.
Crypts contain microvilli for water absorption; goblet cells secrete mucus.
Diarrhea is defined as a stool volume above 200 mL.

UNITS.title: Epidemiology of UC and Crohn's Disease
UNITS.sec: Epidemiology of UC and Crohn's Disease
UNITS.guide:
Overall CD > UC and males > females; peaks at 15-30 and 70-90 years.
Ethnicity: Jews > non-Jewish white > African American > Hispanic > Asian.
Smoking protects against UC but causes CD; appendicectomy protects against UC; OCP raises CD risk; concordance is significant and greater in CD; antibiotics in the first year triple the risk.

UNITS.title: Genetic Syndromes Associated with IBD
UNITS.sec: Genetic Syndromes Associated with IBD
UNITS.guide:
Childhood IBD is grouped as UC-like non-granulomatous versus CD-like granulomatous; Turner's syndrome is listed as most common.
Wiskott-Aldrich: WASP mutation, X-linked recessive, eczema plus sino-pulmonary infection plus microplatelet thrombocytopenia.
Hermansky-Pudlak: autosomal recessive with platelet dysfunction, pulmonary fibrosis and oculocutaneous albinism; von Gierke type I with glucose-1-phosphatase deficiency.

UNITS.title: IPEX Syndrome & Early Onset Childhood IBD
UNITS.sec: IPEX Syndrome & Early Onset Childhood IBD
UNITS.guide:
Loss of Foxp3 function reduces regulatory T-cell tolerance and causes IPEX.
Triad: dermatitis, endocrinopathy (type I DM / thyroiditis) and UC-like enteropathy.
Supportive care, gene therapy and genetic testing; T-reg marker is CD25; early onset IBD reflects IL-10 pathway defects.

UNITS.title: Pathogenesis of IBD
UNITS.sec: Pathogenesis of IBD
UNITS.guide:
Exogenous and endogenous factors drive a dysregulated mucosal immune response in a genetically susceptible host.
UC: unclear pathogenesis with Th2 overactivity.
Crohn's: NOD2/CARD15 on chromosome 16, defective innate immunity (intracellular organisms, Paneth cell defensins), defective autophagy, Th1 overactivity and loss of protective Faecalibacterium.

UNITS.title: Ulcerative Colitis: Site & Macroscopy
UNITS.sec: Ulcerative Colitis: Site & Macroscopy
UNITS.guide:
Rectum alone is involved in 50%.
Hemorrhagic, edematous, ulcerated granular mucosa with pseudopolyps from epithelial regeneration.
Chronic disease rarely gives a lead pipe atrophic featureless colon; fulminant colitis rarely gives toxic megacolon with a diameter above 6 cm.

UNITS.title: Ulcerative Colitis: Microscopy
UNITS.sec: Ulcerative Colitis: Microscopy
UNITS.guide:
Cryptitis with loss of crypt architecture.
Paneth cell metaplasia distal to the hepatic flexure.
Basal plasma cells and lymphoid aggregates are the earliest finding and flag relapse; transmural disease, skip lesions, fistulas, strictures and fissures all argue against UC.

UNITS.title: Crohn's Disease: Site & Macroscopy
UNITS.sec: Crohn's Disease: Site & Macroscopy
UNITS.guide:
Anywhere from mouth to anus; ileocolitis 40-50%, ileitis 30-40%, colitis 15-20%.
Deep transmural asymmetric skip lesions; aphthous ulcers are earliest, linear serpiginous ulcers most visible.
Cobblestoning, perianal fissures and fistulas, terminal ileal fibrosis and stenosis, and creeping fat.

UNITS.title: Crohn's Disease: Microscopy
UNITS.sec: Crohn's Disease: Microscopy
UNITS.guide:
Involvement up to the muscularis propria with non-caseating granulomas at any level, even extraintestinal.
Mesenteric lymphadenopathy; cryptitis and crypt abscesses with normal crypt architecture.
Pyloric metaplasia, lymphoid aggregates and fibrosis; granuloma differential includes sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, cat scratch disease, berylliosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

UNITS.title: Ulcerative Colitis: Clinical Features
UNITS.sec: Ulcerative Colitis: Clinical Features
UNITS.guide:
Features are described by the level of involvement: proctitis, proctosigmoiditis and proctocolitis.
Proctitis gives painless bleeding per rectum (differential: hemorrhoids and malignancies); proctosigmoiditis gives streaks of blood onto formed stool; proctocolitis gives large bowel diarrhea with small frequent stools containing blood, pus and mucus, plus tenesmus.
Physical examination is normal, slow proximal transit causes constipation, systemic symptoms are very rare because the lineage is Th2, and 90% have a relapsing course.

UNITS.title: Fecal Calprotectin & Endoscopy in UC
UNITS.sec: Fecal Calprotectin & Endoscopy in UC
UNITS.guide:
Fecal calprotectin is the most sensitive biomarker and is used to assess severity, treatment response and relapse.
Endoscopy shows symmetrical, superficial, continuous involvement.
Erythematous red velvety mucosa is earliest; vascularity is decreased; the mucosa shows ulcerations with fine granulations and friability; inflammatory pseudopolyps and, very rarely, a lead pipe colon.

UNITS.title: Radiology: Barium Enema in UC
UNITS.sec: Radiology: Barium Enema in UC
UNITS.guide:
Barium enema is the radiological heading for ulcerative colitis.
Fine mucosal granularities are the earliest change, followed by serrations giving a hazy margin, mild luminal narrowing and loss of rectal valves.
Deep ulcers reaching the submucosa give collar stud ulcers; backwash ileitis inflames the terminal ileum; chronic disease gives a lead pipe and fulminant disease toxic megacolon.

UNITS.title: Crohn's Disease: Clinical Features
UNITS.sec: Crohn's Disease: Clinical Features
UNITS.guide:
Ileocolitis is the commonest pattern: episodic right lower quadrant pain relieved by diarrhea.
Fever, weight loss and systemic symptoms reflect the Th1 profile with IL-2 and interferon gamma.
Jejunoileitis causes malabsorption; a palpable inflammatory mass comes from bowel wall thickening; obstruction, enterovesical more than perianal fistulas, and fissures progressing to fibrosed strictures complete the list.

UNITS.title: Endoscopy & Cross Sectional Imaging in Crohn's
UNITS.sec: Endoscopy & Cross Sectional Imaging in Crohn's
UNITS.guide:
The target sign, mucosal ulcers with a translucent mound of edema, is the earliest radiological and endoscopic finding.
Rose thorn ulcers, fissures and the string sign reflect transmural disease; the string sign itself is fibrosed bowel.
CT has a limited role because MR enterography is preferred: target appearance from wall thickening, comb sign from a hypervascular mesentery, and fat halo sign with soft tissue inner and outer layers around a fatty middle layer.

UNITS.title: Intestinal Tuberculosis versus Crohn's Disease
UNITS.sec: Intestinal Tuberculosis versus Crohn's Disease
UNITS.guide:
Crohn's: ileocaecal valve commonly involved, four or more segments especially terminal ileum and ileocaecal valve, longitudinal ulcers, and frequent cobblestoning, aphthous and perianal lesions.
Tuberculosis: ileocaecal valve usually strictured and patulous, fewer than four segments especially ileocaecal valve and ascending colon, transverse ulcers, and rare cobblestoning, aphthous and perianal lesions.
Transverse ulcers plus a patulous strictured valve with fewer than four segments is the tuberculosis pattern.

UNITS.title: Extraintestinal Manifestations of IBD
UNITS.sec: Extraintestinal Manifestations of IBD
UNITS.guide:
Most extraintestinal manifestations are most common in Crohn's disease; uveitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis and pyoderma gangrenosum are most common in ulcerative colitis.
Eye: episcleritis extends from conjunctivitis and parallels bowel activity; uveitis is more dangerous, can cause vision loss and is unrelated to bowel activity.
Skin: painful pretibial papules of erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, pyoderma vegetans, aphthous ulcers and Sweet syndrome. Joints: type I pauciarticular arthritis parallels the bowel; type II axial arthritis does not.

UNITS.title: Others, Other Investigations & Serology
UNITS.sec: Others, Other Investigations & Serology
UNITS.guide:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is most common in ulcerative colitis and fibroses intra and extrahepatic ducts; two thirds of PSC patients have UC and 5% of UC patients have PSC.
Others: gallstones and oxalate renal stones, osteopenia and osteoporosis in over 40% from long term drug use, hepatic steatosis and raised thromboembolic risk.
Fecal calprotectin and lactoferrin separate relapse from infectious diarrhea and rise during relapse. Serology: p-ANCA and anti-goblet cell antibody for UC; ASCA, Omp-C, anti-pancreatic antibody, anti-Ia and anti-flagellin for Crohn's.

UNITS.title: Truelove And Witt's Classification
UNITS.sec: Truelove And Witt's Classification
UNITS.guide:
Mild: fewer than four stools per day, no fever, no tachycardia, mild anemia, ESR below 30 mm per hour.
Moderate sits between mild and severe.
Severe: more than ten stools per day with blood, fever above 37.5 °C, heart rate above 90, hemoglobin below 75% of normal and ESR above 30 mm per hour.

UNITS.title: Medical Management of Ulcerative Colitis
UNITS.sec: Medical Management of Ulcerative Colitis
UNITS.guide:
5-ASA is the mainstay, but plain 5-ASA is absorbed in the small intestine and never reaches the rectum; delayed release mesalamine is the drug of choice for mild disease.
Induction: topical 5-ASA or oral mesalamine for mild, add oral steroids for moderate, intravenous steroid for severe.
Steroid refractory moderate disease moves to azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine; severe disease adds intravenous anti-TNF or cyclosporine, and maintenance uses azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine with low dose anti-TNF or oral cyclosporine.

UNITS.title: Sulfasalazine & Surgery in Ulcerative Colitis
UNITS.sec: Sulfasalazine & Surgery in Ulcerative Colitis
UNITS.guide:
Sulfasalazine is 5-ASA carried by sulfapyridine, absorbed at the rectum, and abandoned in G6PD deficiency.
Azathioprine side effects are hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression and pancreatitis.
Surgery is proctocolectomy with ileoanal anastomosis for toxic megacolon, perforation, uncontrollable hemorrhage, dysplasia or carcinoma, and medically refractory disease.

UNITS.title: Crohn's Disease: Grading & Medical Management
UNITS.sec: Crohn's Disease: Grading & Medical Management
UNITS.guide:
Grading: mild-moderate has no dehydration, obstruction, weight loss or systemic features; moderate-severe lies between; severe-fulminant means fever, cachexia, obstruction and peritoneal signs despite steroids.
Objectives are endoscopic mucosal healing and prevention of strictures and fistulae.
Drugs: antibiotics, corticosteroids with their dependency risk, 5-ASA, immunomodulators and biologics such as infliximab, adalimumab and certolizumab pegol.

UNITS.title: Crohn's Disease: Management by Severity
UNITS.sec: Crohn's Disease: Management by Severity
UNITS.guide:
Induction: oral budesonide 9 mg per day for mild-moderate, oral steroids for moderate-severe, intravenous steroids for severe-fulminant.
Maintenance: none for mild-moderate, azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine for moderate-severe, periodic anti-TNF for severe-fulminant.
Fistulizing disease needs anti-TNF with or without immunomodulators then surgery; avoid smoking and NSAIDs; never maintain with oral 5-ASA, corticosteroids or budesonide. Newer agents: natalizumab, ustekinumab and vedolizumab.

UNITS.title: Malignancy in IBD
UNITS.sec: Malignancy in IBD
UNITS.guide:
Risk exists in both ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease: lymphoma, leukemia, myelodysplasia and cholangiocarcinoma from primary sclerosing cholangitis.
IBD related carcinoma arises ten to fifteen years younger, in any segment of diseased colon, as a signet ring cell carcinoma.
Genetics invert the sporadic pattern: sporadic is APC early and p53 late, IBD related is p53 early and APC late. Five year survival is 50% for both.

UNITS.title: Definitions & Site Patterns
UNITS.sec: Infectious Diarrhoea: Definitions & Patterns
UNITS.guide:
Acute diarrhoea ≤2 weeks is infectious unless proved otherwise.
Duration branches: <1 week benign/viral or complicated/bacterial; >1 week protozoal.
Separate small-bowel large-volume watery stool from large-bowel small-volume bloody stool.

UNITS.title: Small- and Large-Bowel Organisms
UNITS.sec: Small- and Large-Bowel Organisms
UNITS.guide:
Small bowel: ETEC/V. cholerae toxins, preformed-toxin bacteria, Cryptosporidium, microsporidium, Giardia.
Large bowel: Shigella, Campylobacter, non-typhoid Salmonella, EIEC, V. parahaemolyticus, Entamoeba.
Typhoid is a small-bowel invasion with fever/pain and no diarrhoea in the note.

UNITS.title: Preformed-Toxin Food Poisoning
UNITS.sec: Preformed-Toxin Food Poisoning
UNITS.guide:
S. aureus: preformed heat-stable toxin, 1–6 h, custard/pork/canned meat, vomiting via 5-HT3.
B. cereus heat-stable: fried rice/vomiting; heat-labile: formed toxin, 6–12 h, diarrhoea/cAMP.
The source also lists Yersinia and E. coli among heat-stable-toxin producers.

UNITS.title: Vibrio, ETEC & Secretory Diarrhoea
UNITS.sec: Vibrio, ETEC & Secretory Diarrhoea
UNITS.guide:
V. cholerae is non-invasive; toxin activates adenyl cyclase; TCP attaches to mucosa.
Large-volume watery stool, dehydration and hypokalaemic normal-gap acidosis; the page names Ringer lactate.
V. parahaemolyticus: raw fish/Kanagawa; ETEC LT raises cAMP and is linked to travellers' diarrhoea.

UNITS.title: HUS and Shigella
UNITS.sec: HUS and Shigella
UNITS.guide:
Childhood HUS: 90% EHEC O157:H7/Shigella dysenteriae toxins; 10% pneumococcal neuraminidase.
Shigella invasion affects all four bowel-wall layers; enterotoxin causes diarrhoea and Shiga-like toxin is cytotoxic.
The note contrasts diarrhoea with arthritis against IBD markers and extraintestinal signs.

UNITS.title: Salmonella and Campylobacter
UNITS.sec: Salmonella and Campylobacter
UNITS.guide:
Typhoid: diarrhoea in week two, perforation, marrow suppression and intestinal bleeding.
C. jejuni is faeco-oral, incubates 2–4 days, and is linked to IBD, GBS and IPSID/lymphoma.
The page's culture and azithromycin notes are explicitly not routine for small-bowel diarrhoea.

UNITS.title: C. difficile Enterocolitis
UNITS.sec: Clostridioides difficile Enterocolitis
UNITS.guide:
GDH + toxin A/B EIA → confirm if both positive; discordant results go to PCR/NAAT.
The p51 flowchart separates non-severe, severe and fulminant disease by WBC/creatinine and ileus/shock/megacolon.
Treatment entries reproduce the book for study; they are not current clinical guidance.

UNITS.title: Regions, Glands & Cells
UNITS.sec: Stomach Regions, Glands & Cells
UNITS.guide:
Fundus above GES; body between GES and incisura; antrum below incisura.
Fundic, oxyntic and pyloric glands contain region-specific ECL, parietal, chief, mucous and G cells.
Review secretions and the diagram labels: rugae, curvatures, papillae and duodenum.

UNITS.title: Mucosal Defence and Wall
UNITS.sec: Gastric Mucosal Defence and Wall
UNITS.guide:
Defence layers: pre-epithelial, epithelial/restitution and subepithelial.
Separate damaging exposures from mucus, bicarbonate, blood-flow, barrier and repair protection.
Auerbach = motility; Meissner = secretion; ICC generate BER.

UNITS.title: Acid Regulation & Acute Gastritis
UNITS.sec: Acid Regulation and Acute Gastritis
UNITS.guide:
Histamine/cAMP, gastrin/CCK-B and acetylcholine/M3-Ca²⁺ cooperate to increase acid.
The BAO/MAO threshold is >0.6; the page gives MAO at 6 pm and least output at 6 am.
Gastritis is histologic; acute phlegmonous gastritis is severe and linked to neutrophils.

UNITS.title: Chronic & Hypertrophic Gastritis
UNITS.sec: Chronic and Hypertrophic Gastritis
UNITS.guide:
Type A: less common autoimmune, patchy corpus, parietal-cell antibodies; Type B: commoner, multifocal, H. pylori.
Follow each type's complications and malignancy arrow; retain the four gastritis associations.
Ménétrier disease: TGF-α/foveolar hyperplasia → mucus/protein loss; surgery is main treatment in the text.

UNITS.title: H. pylori Biology & Virulence
UNITS.sec: Helicobacter pylori: Biology and Virulence
UNITS.guide:
Gram-negative, urease/oxidase/catalase positive; antral, flagellated, non-invasive and deep in mucosal gel.
Transmission is faeco-oral; the source lists ulcer/cancer associations and enzyme actions.
Know the roles of VacA, LPS, outer proteins, type IV secretion and CagA effectors.

UNITS.title: H. pylori, Dyspepsia & Testing
UNITS.sec: H. pylori Gastritis, Dyspepsia and Testing
UNITS.guide:
Antral-predominant → duodenal ulcer; corpus atrophy → metaplasia/dysplasia/carcinoma; pan-gastritis → MALToma.
Dyspepsia symptom cluster, one-week PPI note and alarm indications precede H. pylori investigations.
Rapid urease uses antral biopsy; stool antigen and urea-breath testing confirm eradication after a one-month gap.

UNITS.title: Treatment & Test of Cure
UNITS.sec: H. pylori Treatment and Test of Cure
UNITS.guide:
The p58 first-line and OBTM second-line regimens are transcribed as printed.
The p59 algorithm tests, treats, waits at least one month and branches by stool antigen/urea breath result.
Persistent positivity proceeds to later-line sensitivity-guided specialist review; this is book study, not current guidance.

UNITS.title: Types and Comparisons
UNITS.sec: Gastrinoma Types and Comparisons
UNITS.guide:
Sporadic (80%) versus MEN1-associated (20%) differ in number/size, age, sex, location and risk.
Sporadic tumours are listed as more aggressive; MEN1 disease is usually smaller and less aggressive.
Keep the note separating insulinoma as the commonest functional pancreatic NET overall.

UNITS.title: Triangle and Gastrin Effects
UNITS.sec: Gastrinoma Triangle and Gastrin Effects
UNITS.guide:
Triangle points: cystic duct/CBD, D2–D3 and pancreatic body–neck junctions.
Gastrin → parietal cells → HCl; mucosal injury yields GU/DU.
Acid can inactivate pancreatic enzymes, linking to diarrhoea, steatorrhoea and malabsorption.

UNITS.title: Clinical Features
UNITS.sec: Clinical Features and Diarrhoea
UNITS.guide:
Abdominal pain is the most important symptom; PUD is the commonest manifestation.
Unusual D2+ ulcers, refractory GU/DU, recurrence and diarrhoea raise suspicion in the page.
Diarrhoea has secretory and enzyme-inactivation/steatorrhoea components.

UNITS.title: Tests and Imaging
UNITS.sec: Biochemical and Receptor Imaging
UNITS.guide:
Fasting gastrin: <200 normal, 200–1000 needs confirmation; preserve the source's >1000 wording.
Secretin gives a paradoxical gastrin rise ≥200 pg/mL in the printed test.
SRS/¹¹¹In, octreotide rationale, EUS caveat, BAO/MAO and DOTATATE note are inventoried.

UNITS.title: Treatment and Surgical Anatomy
UNITS.sec: Treatment and Surgical Anatomy
UNITS.guide:
MEN1: high-dose PPI 60–80 mg; surgery when >2.5 cm.
Sporadic: PPI + octreotide then surgery; procedure follows head/body-tail/duodenal location.
The page says gastrectomy is not required and names liver as the commonest metastasis site.

UNITS.title: Definition & Associations
UNITS.sec: Definition and Associations
UNITS.guide:
IBS is presented as a functional bowel disorder/reaction to stress.
Associations: lactose intolerance, celiac disease, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue and generalized anxiety.
The clinical list is more common in women and under age 45.

UNITS.title: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV & Red Flags
UNITS.sec: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV and Red Flags
UNITS.guide:
