Other organs: Spleen (splenomegaly + hyposplenism Howell-Jolly bodies); GI (malabsorption, diarrhea, gastroparesis); ANS (postural hypotension, anhidrosis); CNS (Alzheimer's Aβ, cerebral amyloid angiopathy lobar hemorrhage); Endocrine (MTC calcitonin, Type II DM amylin).
Mucocutaneous/hemorrhagic signs: Periorbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes'), Factor X deficiency, macroglossia, waxy eyelid papules, 'shoulder pad' sign, amyloid nails.
Diagnosis & Rx: Abdominal fat pad biopsy = IOC (or rectum/kidney) → Congo red apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Rx: AL → CyBorD + Daratumumab; AA → treat cause / Colchicine in FMF; ATTR → Tafamidis.

UNITS.title: Myeloid Progenitor Lineages, Thrombopoiesis (Early vs Late), Megakaryocyte Stages & Morphological Variants
UNITS.sec: Myeloid Progenitor Lineages, Thrombopoiesis (Early vs Late), Megakaryocyte Stages & Morphological Variants
UNITS.guide:
Lineages & thrombopoiesis (p169): common myeloid progenitor → RBC, granulocyte, monocyte, megakaryocyte → platelet; thrombopoietin boxed as 'From kidneys and liver' acting on the myeloid stem cell. Thrombopoiesis → Early requires thrombopoietin ('From liver'), IL-3 (platelet development) and IL-11 (recombinant = Oprelvekin, for chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia); Late requires SDF-1.
Megakaryocyte maturation: myeloid stem cell → megakaryoblast → megakaryocyte → platelet precursor extensions → platelets; Stage II basophilic, Stage III maximal granules with multilobed nuclei, Stage IV mature with lesser granules and pyknotic nuclei; endomitosis = multiplication of megakaryocytes.
Morphological variations (photos): giant megakaryocyte in ITP, dwarf in CML, cloud in primary myelofibrosis, staghorn in essential thrombocytosis.

UNITS.title: Platelet Counts, Lifespan, Sample Handling, Pseudothrombocytopenia & Platelet Transfusion (SDP vs RDP)
UNITS.sec: Platelet Counts, Lifespan, Sample Handling, Pseudothrombocytopenia & Platelet Transfusion (SDP vs RDP)
UNITS.guide:
Basics (p170): lifespan 10 days, normal 1.5–4 lakh/µL, life span in stored blood 72 hrs; thresholds — thrombocytopenia < 1,00,000/µL, bleeding < 20,000/µL, significant bleeding < 10,000/µL.
Investigations: coagulation studies need platelet poor plasma, platelet studies need platelet rich plasma, all at room temperature except lupus anticoagulant at 4°C. Pseudothrombocytopenia = satellitism, caused by EDTA, clumping of platelets, remedied by re-sampling in 3.2% trisodium citrate.
Transfusion: complete within 20 mins; SDP = apheresis/costly, RDP = pooling & centrifugation/cheap/commonly used; 1 unit SDP or 4–6 units RDP raise the count by 30,000–50,000/µL, whereas 1 unit RDP alone raises it by 6,000/µL.

UNITS.title: Platelet Cascade I: Endothelial Antiplatelet/Anticoagulant/Fibrinolytic Roles, vWF Adhesion Receptors & Granules
UNITS.sec: Platelet Cascade I: Endothelial Antiplatelet/Anticoagulant/Fibrinolytic Roles, vWF Adhesion Receptors & Granules
UNITS.guide:
Adhesion (p171): endothelial injury is mandatory; endothelium is antithrombotic, subendothelium prothrombotic. Antiplatelet = PGI₂, nitric oxide, ADPase. Anticoagulant = heparin-like molecules (with AT-III, inactivating II, IX, X, XI, XII), thrombomodulin (thrombin → protein C → inactivates V and VIII), TFPI (inactivates VII and X; tissue factor = III). Fibrinolysis = release of tPA.
Adhesion mechanism: endothelial injury → release of vWF; sources megakaryocyte and endothelium (coiled form in Weibel-Palade granule); receptors Gp VI on collagen and Gp Ib-IX on platelet.
Activation/degranulation: α granules and δ (dense) granules, the latter carrying ADP > ATP, calcium, histamine, serotonin. Aggregation: Gp IIb-IIIa with fibrinogen binding to platelets.

UNITS.title: Clotting Cascade (Intrinsic, Extrinsic, Common), Fibrinolysis Checkpoints, Antifibrinolytics & aPTT/PT Tests
UNITS.sec: Clotting Cascade (Intrinsic, Extrinsic, Common), Fibrinolysis Checkpoints, Antifibrinolytics & aPTT/PT Tests
UNITS.guide:
Clotting cascade (p172): intrinsic (in vitro) with back amplification of thrombin — XII → XIIa (high molecular weight kininogen, kallikrein), XI → XIa, IX → IXa (vIII, Ca²⁺, phospholipid), then X → Xa (vII, Ca²⁺); extrinsic (in vivo) — endothelial injury → thromboplastin/tissue factor (factor III) with calcium and phospholipid → factor VIIa, converging on factor X.
Common cascade: X → Xa → prothrombin → thrombin (factor II) with calcium phospholipase va → fibrinogen → fibrin → clot stabilisation by XIII. Fibrinolysis: tPA converts plasminogen to plasmin, generating FDPs; check points are protein C and S (V, VIII), t-PA and TFPI; t-PA inhibitors that promote thrombosis are α-2 antiplasmin, TAFI, PAI and lipoprotein A.
Tests: aPTT assesses intrinsic and common cascade with poor sensitivity; PT assesses extrinsic and common cascade.

UNITS.title: Evaluation Protocol I: Platelet vs Coagulation Bleed Table, Lineage Chart, Count-Based Bleeding Risk & Drug-Induced Thrombocytopenia
UNITS.sec: Evaluation Protocol I: Platelet vs Coagulation Bleed Table, Lineage Chart, Count-Based Bleeding Risk & Drug-Induced Thrombocytopenia
UNITS.guide:
Protocol step 1 (p173): platelet bleed starts immediately after trauma whereas coagulation bleed is late; platelet type is mucosal (gum, epistaxis, menorrhagia, intra-operative) with petechiae <3 mm and purpura 3–10 mm; coagulation type is joint (haemarthrosis), muscle (m/c ilio psoas), hematoma and large solitary ecchymotic patch >10 mm; sex male = female vs male > female.
Step 2 lineage: single lineage → 1° platelet bleeding; trilineage (leukemia, aplastic anemia, MDS) → platelet related bleeding. Platelet-count risk: >20,000/µL no bleeding, <20,000/µL bleeding +ve, <10,000/µL severe (GI, cerebral); red purpura in pharynx and retinal bleed indicate risk.
Step 3 drug-induced thrombocytopenia: chemotherapy/alkylating agents dose related; procainamide and gold produce autoantibody; heparin → immune complex with PF4.

UNITS.title: Evaluation Protocol II: Anticonvulsant/Gp IIb-IIIa/NSAID/Quinine/Penicillin Table, Hypersplenism, Smear & ITP Summary Flowchart
UNITS.sec: Evaluation Protocol II: Anticonvulsant/Gp IIb-IIIa/NSAID/Quinine/Penicillin Table, Hypersplenism, Smear & ITP Summary Flowchart
UNITS.guide:
Step 3 table continues (p174): anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin, valproate) and NSAIDs have no mechanism listed ('–'); Gp IIb/IIIa inhibitors act by drug-specific antibody (abciximab within 24 hours, plus eptifibatide and tirofiban); quinine induces antibody; penicillin acts as a hapten-dependent antibody.
Step 4 hypersplenism: sequestration of platelets, seen in liver disease; of the three arms of ↓ platelet count, destruction of platelet is m/c; the marrow arm produces no platelets, RBC or WBC.
Step 5 smear: schistocytes → rule out HUS/TTP; normal smear with a few giant platelets (rare) goes with ITP. The summary flowchart ends: platelet-type bleeding → single-lineage with normal RBC/WBC → not drug induced → no hypersplenism → normal smear → ITP.

UNITS.title: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura I: Causes, Gp IIb/IIIa & Ib/IX Antibody Pathogenesis, Clinical Signs & Investigations
UNITS.sec: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura I: Causes, Gp IIb/IIIa & Ib/IX Antibody Pathogenesis, Clinical Signs & Investigations
UNITS.guide:
ITP basics (p175): AKA Werlhof's disease, not seen in elderly; primary or secondary (SLE, RA, H. pylori, HIV, HCV); IgG antibody-mediated destruction with antibodies against Gp IIb/IIIa and Ib/IX plus inhibition of platelet release from megakaryocytes.
Clinical: mucocutaneous bleeding when the count is <20,000/µL (example gum bleed); petechiae and purpura are non-palpable and non-blanching, unlike palpable branching vascular purpura; photographs show petechiae/purpura, oral petechiae and ecchymosis.
Investigations: normal smear with a few giant platelets; Coombs test only for Evans syndrome or CVID with AIHA plus thrombocytopenia; marrow shows increased megakaryocytes and precursors, done for atypical findings (splenomegaly), first episode >60 years, or failure to respond to steroids.

UNITS.title: ITP II: Features Inconsistent with ITP, Duration-Based Classification & First-Line Treatment (Steroids, IVIg/Anti-D)
UNITS.sec: ITP II: Features Inconsistent with ITP, Duration-Based Classification & First-Line Treatment (Steroids, IVIg/Anti-D)
UNITS.guide:
Features inconsistent with ITP (p176): fever, pallor, jaundice, subconjunctival haemorrhage, bleeding into joints, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, predominant giant platelets, red-cell morphological abnormality, WBC abnormality. Duration: <3 months newly diagnosed, 3–12 months persistent, >1 year chronic.
Treatment aim: raise platelets to 30,000/µL; >30,000 wait and watch, <30,000 ± bleeding treat; children have a self-limiting course.
Adults first line: oral prednisolone full dose × 2 weeks then taper, ± IVIg/anti-D (indications: surgery, life-threatening bleeding, platelets <10,000/µL, relapse). Anti-D binds Rh antigen and is taken up preferentially by the spleen sparing platelets; prerequisites are a spleen and Hb >10 mg/dL.

UNITS.title: ITP III: Second-Line Therapy, Follow-Up & Qualitative Platelet Disorders (Causes, Defect Types, PFA-100 & Aggregation Test)
UNITS.sec: ITP III: Second-Line Therapy, Follow-Up & Qualitative Platelet Disorders (Causes, Defect Types, PFA-100 & Aggregation Test)
UNITS.guide:
Second line in relapse (p177): rituximab + dexamethasone; thrombopoietin analogues eltrombopag (oral) and romiplostim (s/c); splenectomy; azathioprine. Follow-up: counts rise in 2–4 days.
Qualitative platelet disorder = bleeding with a normal platelet count; acquired causes are uremic bleeding (m/c) and drugs, besides inherited causes. Defect types: adhesion (Gp Ib-IX → Bernard-Soulier, and vWD), granulation (α granule → grey platelet, δ granule → Hermansky-Pudlak), activation/aggregation (Gp IIb-IIIa → Glanzmann, and afibrinogenemia).
Investigations: PFA-100 is a screening test with prolonged aperture closure time >80 sec; the aggregation test is the gold standard, weak agents (ADP, epinephrine) giving two waves and all other agents one wave; primary aggregation releases no granules, secondary aggregation releases thromboxane A2 or granular ADP.

UNITS.title: Aggregation Curves (Biphasic vs Monophasic), Ristocetin Agglutination Test + aPTT Logic, Bleeding Time & vWF Functions
UNITS.sec: Aggregation Curves (Biphasic vs Monophasic), Ristocetin Agglutination Test + aPTT Logic, Bleeding Time & vWF Functions
UNITS.guide:
Normal aggregation curves (p178): biphasic with ADP and epinephrine (primary then secondary wave), monophasic with collagen, arachidonic acid and ristocetin.
RAT checks adhesion: negative in Bernard-Soulier syndrome and vWD, positive means normal adhesion. A negative RAT is followed by aPTT (common and intrinsic defect): prolonged aPTT → vWD with low factor VIII, normal aPTT → BSS. Bleeding time is elevated and obsolete.
vWF functions: platelet adhesion and transport of factor VIII. Aggregation interpretation strip: ADP primary wave, collagen deficient, ristocetin normal → granule defect (storage pool defect loses the second ADP/epinephrine wave).

UNITS.title: Optical Density Traces: Aggregation Defect vs BSS/vWD vs Storage Pool (Granule) Defect Interpretation
UNITS.sec: Optical Density Traces: Aggregation Defect vs BSS/vWD vs Storage Pool (Granule) Defect Interpretation
UNITS.guide:
Glanzmann curves on p179 show absent aggregation with all agonists except ristocetin and are labelled 'Aggregation defect'; 'Aggregation defect : No waves seen' while 'granule defect : Primary wave seen in ADP & epinephrine'.
Optical density test: normal agglutination/adhesion lowers optical density (↓ optical density).
Three interpretation panels: aggregation defect (A: RAT +ve, B: aggregation –ve), BSS or vWD (A: RAT –ve, B: agglutination wave +ve), and storage pool/granule defect (A: agglutination wave +ve in ADP).

UNITS.title: Glanzmann Thrombasthenia, Afibrinogenemia, Bernard-Soulier Syndrome, Megathrombocytosis & Drug-Induced Qualitative Bleeding
UNITS.sec: Glanzmann Thrombasthenia, Afibrinogenemia, Bernard-Soulier Syndrome, Megathrombocytosis & Drug-Induced Qualitative Bleeding
UNITS.guide:
Platelet disorders (p180), set against 'Fibrinogen —thrombin time→ Fibrin': Glanzmann thrombasthenia is autosomal recessive with normal thrombin time, GpIIb-IIIa defect (fibrinogen receptor lost), RAT +ve, normal platelet count, prolonged BT and recurrent bleeding or heavy menstrual bleeding.
Afibrinogenemia has a prolonged thrombin time. Bernard-Soulier syndrome is autosomal recessive with Gp Ib-IX deficiency, RAT negative (adhesion defect) and a smear showing megathrombocytosis with mild thrombocytopenia.
Drug-induced qualitative bleeding: aspirin, beta lactams, dipyridamole/theophylline, ticlopidine/clopidogrel and dextran.

UNITS.title: Von Willebrand Disease I: vWF Gene/Structure Domains, ADAMTS13 Processing, Functions & Types
UNITS.sec: Von Willebrand Disease I: vWF Gene/Structure Domains, ADAMTS13 Processing, Functions & Types
UNITS.guide:
vWD is the m/c congenital bleeding disorder, gene on chromosome 12p (p181). Structure domains: A → adhesion (binds GpIb-IX), D3 → carries factor VIII, C → aggregation.
Physiology: megakaryocyte-derived vWF monomers → dimers → HMW multimers which circulate and are degraded by ADAMTS 13; endothelial vWF is stored coiled in Weibel-Palade bodies and released uncoiled after endothelial injury. Functions: platelet adhesion and carriage of factor VIII (T½ 2 → 12 hours).
Types: Type 1 (m/c), Type 2 (2A, 2B, 2M, 2N) and Type 3 (rare).

UNITS.title: Von Willebrand Disease II: Type 1 vs Type 3 Table, Type 2 Subtypes (2A/2B/2M/2N), Acquired vWF & Management
UNITS.sec: Von Willebrand Disease II: Type 1 vs Type 3 Table, Type 2 Subtypes (2A/2B/2M/2N), Acquired vWF & Management
UNITS.guide:
Type 1 vs Type 3 (p182): Type 1 = 85% incidence, autosomal dominant, partial semiquantitative defect, platelet bleed without coagulation bleed (factor VIII unaffected) and ↑aPTT, 2nd decade; Type 3 incidence is not printed ('–'), autosomal recessive, complete quantitative, severe platelet and coagulation bleed, <5 years.
Type 2: 2A AD with absent HMW multimers (platelet bleed); 2B AD gain of function at the A-site with platelet trapping (thrombocytopenia); 2M AD loss of function at the A-site (adhesion, platelet bleed); 2N AR loss of function at the D3 site (factor VIII carriage, pseudohemophilia, presentation in females). Pseudo-vWD = loss of function of GpIb-IX.
Acquired vWF: aortic stenosis (shear stress, ↑ cleavage), myeloproliferative/PCRV (adherence, ↑ cleavage), IgG/IgM paraprotein (immune mediated), hypothyroidism (↓ synthesis). Management: vWF concentrate or desmopressin (best, v2 stimulation, contraindicated in 2B, IV or intranasal, tachyphylaxis and SIADH), used only on bleeding, with anti-fibrinolytic add-on.

UNITS.title: DIC I: Clinical Approach by aPTT/PT/Platelet Combinations (Factor XII/XI/Hemophilia A & B/vWD/LAC/Liver/Warfarin) & Etiology
UNITS.sec: DIC I: Clinical Approach by aPTT/PT/Platelet Combinations (Factor XII/XI/Hemophilia A & B/vWD/LAC/Liver/Warfarin) & Etiology
UNITS.guide:
Clinical approach table (p183): prolonged aPTT with normal PT and platelets — no bleeding implies factor XII, HMW kininogen or prekallikrein deficiency, mild bleeding implies factor XI (hemophilia C), severe bleeding implies hemophilia A/B (clotting factor bleed, chronic proliferative synovitis, muscle symptoms) or vWD (platelet-type bleed, RAT negative); prolonged aPTT with reduced platelets implies antiphospholipid syndrome from lupus anticoagulant.
Prolonged aPTT and PT with reduced platelets implies liver disease (all clotting factors except VIII, dysfibrinogenemia) or DIC; normal aPTT with prolonged INR implies warfarin (vitamin K epoxide reductase inhibition, gamma carboxylation of glutamic acid residues of II, VII with shortest t½ 6 hr, IX, X), factor III or factor VII deficiency.
Etiology: sepsis (m/c), APML, placenta and amniotic fluid, adenocarcinoma (lung, colon, prostate), trauma, pancreatitis, burns, massive transfusion, Kasabach-Merritt syndrome.

UNITS.title: DIC II: Pathogenesis Chain, ICU Monitoring, Purpura Fulminans, Investigations (FDP vs D-Dimer) & Management
UNITS.sec: DIC II: Pathogenesis Chain, ICU Monitoring, Purpura Fulminans, Investigations (FDP vs D-Dimer) & Management
UNITS.guide:
Pathogenesis (p184): stimulus → endothelial activation → tissue factor release → continuous and excessive thrombin formation → consumption of platelets and clotting factors → bleeding plus secondary hyperfibrinolysis with fibrinogen trapping.
ICU monitoring: ARDS (saturation, chest examination, X-ray), DIC with haemorrhagic spots, myocarditis (tachycardia, hypotension unresponsive to fluids, ↑ troponin I). Clinically bleeding exceeds thrombosis with reduced anticoagulant factors; oozing at venipuncture sites, petechiae, ecchymosis; fibrinolysis exceeds antifibrinolysis; purpura fulminans is severe DIC with microvascular thrombosis and skin necrosis.
Investigations: ↓ platelets, ↑ aPTT, ↑ PT, ↑ FDP (most sensitive), ↑ D-dimer (most specific), fragmented RBCs, ↑ TT, ↓ fibrinogen. Management: treat the cause, cryoprecipitate (VIII, vWF, fibrinogen, XIII)/FFP/platelets, EACA; drotrecogin alfa and heparin are obsolete; liver disease is the differential diagnosis.

UNITS.title: Gross Anatomy: Lobes, Oblique/Horizontal Fissures, Lower-Lobe Auscultation, Azygos Fissure 'Tadpole' & Phantom Tumor
UNITS.sec: Gross Anatomy: Lobes, Oblique/Horizontal Fissures, Lower-Lobe Auscultation, Azygos Fissure 'Tadpole' & Phantom Tumor
UNITS.guide:
Lobes (p185): right has 3 (RUL, RML, RLL), left has 2 (LUL, LLL); the oblique/major fissure is bilateral and the horizontal/minor fissure is right-sided. The lower lobe is not seen on a normal film because of its posterior position, needs a lateral film or CT, and is auscultated at the infrascapular and infraaxillary areas.
Fissures are depressions on the lung surface reaching the hila; type 3 is the azygos fissure, giving a tadpole appearance whose head is the azygos vein, present in 1–2% of people.
Phantom tumor/pseudotumor: fluid in the horizontal fissure, from heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, resolving with diuretics.

UNITS.title: Phantom Tumor Resolution Films, Hilar Structures & Relations, Causes of Hilar Enlargement & Weibel's 23 Generations
UNITS.sec: Phantom Tumor Resolution Films, Hilar Structures & Relations, Causes of Hilar Enlargement & Weibel's 23 Generations
UNITS.guide:
Radiograph series (p186): 'Phantom tumor' → 'After 2 weeks of therapy' → 'After 4 weeks of therapy'. Hilar structures: pulmonary artery (PA), pulmonary vein (PV), bronchus, lymphatics; the PA lies anterior to the bronchus on the right and above the bronchus on the left.
Hilar enlargement: hilar lymphadenopathy (TB, sarcoidosis) and PA dilatation are bracketed 'more common'; a mediastinal mass and a mass in the bronchus complete the list.
Weibel generations total 23: conducting zone 0–16 (trachea 0 to terminal bronchioles 16) equals the anatomical dead space, 'air in the conducting zone (150 ml)'; transitional and respiratory zones 17–23 run from respiratory bronchioles through alveolar ducts (20–22) to alveolar sacs (23), bracketed as the site of gas exchange (acinus).

UNITS.title: Bronchi Types, Right vs Left Bronchus Dimensions, Foreign-Body Predilection, Calibre/Area Change, Secondary Pulmonary Lobule & BPS Definition
UNITS.sec: Bronchi Types, Right vs Left Bronchus Dimensions, Foreign-Body Predilection, Calibre/Area Change, Secondary Pulmonary Lobule & BPS Definition
UNITS.guide:
Bronchi (p187) are primary/principal/main, secondary/lobar and tertiary/segmental. Right bronchus: wider (1.5 cm), shorter, steeper, 2 cm, 45° to the carina (carina at T4/5); left: narrower (1.3 cm), longer, more horizontal, 5 cm. Inhaled foreign bodies lodge R > L.
From trachea to alveoli the diameter falls from 25 mm to 0.25–0.3 mm while the cross-sectional area rises from 5 cm² to 7,00,000 cm².
The secondary pulmonary lobule is the functional unit — 3–5 terminal bronchioles within connective tissue septa — with airflow through respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts to alveoli; the bronchopulmonary segment is the anatomical unit supplied by a tertiary/segmental bronchus and contains the intra-segmental pulmonary artery.

UNITS.title: Bronchopulmonary Segments of Right and Left Lung (10 Each) & Position-Dependent Aspiration Segments
UNITS.sec: Bronchopulmonary Segments of Right and Left Lung (10 Each) & Position-Dependent Aspiration Segments
UNITS.guide:
Segment maps (p188): both lungs have 10 segments. Right upper lobe = apical (1), posterior (2), anterior (3); middle lobe = lateral (4), medial (5); left upper lobe = apicoposterior (1, 2) and anterior (3), with the lingula as superior (4) and inferior (5) lingular. Right lower lobe = superior (6), posterior basal (7), medial basal (8), lateral basal (9), anterior basal (10).
Aspiration depends on posture: supine the posterior segment of the right upper lobe exceeds the superior segment of the right lower lobe; standing, the basal segment of the left lower lobe is involved, with R > L.

UNITS.title: Acinus Parts, Centriacinar (Smokers) vs Panacinar (α1-Antitrypsin) Emphysema & Basal/Goblet Cells of Conducting Airways
UNITS.sec: Acinus Parts, Centriacinar (Smokers) vs Panacinar (α1-Antitrypsin) Emphysema & Basal/Goblet Cells of Conducting Airways
UNITS.guide:
Acinus parts (p188): respiratory bronchiole, alveolar duct and alveolus. Clinical significance: normal acinus, centriacinar emphysema (smokers) and panacinar emphysema (α-1 antitrypsin deficiency).
Cells in conducting airways begin with basal cells (stem/progenitor cells during lung injury) and goblet cells (secrete mucus).

UNITS.title: Club (Clara) Cells, CGRP, Kulchitzky Cells, Cartilage/Smooth Muscle/Goblet Table, Epithelial Zonation & Airway Mediators
UNITS.sec: Club (Clara) Cells, CGRP, Kulchitzky Cells, Cartilage/Smooth Muscle/Goblet Table, Epithelial Zonation & Airway Mediators
UNITS.guide:
Club/Clara cells (p189) are non-ciliated cuboidal epithelial cells of terminal bronchioles that detoxify xenobiotics and act as progenitors for bronchiolar cells. CGRP = calcitonin gene-related peptide, a major neurotransmitter in migraine. Kulchitzky cells hold dense-core vesicles with serotonin, calcitonin and CGRP.
Structural table: cartilage + / + / –; smooth muscle – / + / + (maximal in terminal bronchiole); goblet cells – / + / – across trachea, bronchi and bronchioles. Trachea has hyaline cartilage and a glandular plus pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelial layer; bronchus epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar above, ciliated simple cuboidal in the middle and simple cuboidal below; bronchiole is simple cuboidal with no mucus glands, occasional goblet cells, neuroendocrine cells clustered as neuroepithelial bodies, and Clara cells.
Mediators: leukotriene is the most potent constrictor; VIP the most potent dilator, a NANC peptide; cholinergics constrict with the methacholine challenge used to assess hyperresponsiveness; anticholinergics (ipratropium, tiotropium) dilate and are used in asthma.

UNITS.title: Role of Cilia, Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia/Kartagener Triad, Nasal Nitric Oxide Gold Standard & Cystic Fibrosis (F508, Ivacaftor)
UNITS.sec: Role of Cilia, Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia/Kartagener Triad, Nasal Nitric Oxide Gold Standard & Cystic Fibrosis (F508, Ivacaftor)
UNITS.guide:
Cilia (p190) are present up to the terminal bronchiole and absent in the respiratory zone; the mucociliary escalator beats towards the nasopharynx. Immotile cilia syndrome/primary ciliary dyskinesia is autosomal recessive with a defective dynein arm, median presentation at 5 years, recurrent sinusitis and otitis media, and neonatal respiratory distress.
Kartagener's syndrome is the triad plus male infertility; cilia are needed for rotation of body organs, so their failure produces situs inversus — the triad triangle of situs inversus, sinusitis and bronchiectasis. Gold-standard investigation is nasal nitric oxide, which is always low.
Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive with CFTR (F508) mutation on chromosome 7q and a chloride defect: thick secretions with normal cilia affecting bronchi, biliary tract, intestine and reproductive system; ivacaftor is a chloride channel opener.

UNITS.title: Airway Resistance: Poiseuille/Ohm Laws, Generation 5–7 Resistance Peak, Reynolds Number Flow Table
UNITS.sec: Airway Resistance: Poiseuille/Ohm Laws, Generation 5–7 Resistance Peak, Reynolds Number Flow Table
UNITS.guide:
From trachea to alveoli (p191) diameter, velocity and turbulence fall while total cross-sectional area rises. Ohm's law Q = ΔP/R and Poiseuille's law R = 8ηL/πr⁴, so flow ∝ 1/R and R ∝ 1/r⁴; maximal radius gives least resistance and maximal flow — hence turbulence in the trachea and laminar flow in alveoli.
Maximum resistance is at generations 5, 6 and 7 (bronchi > terminal bronchioles) because the parallel arrangement of small airways gives a maximal cross-sectional area and low resistance.
Reynolds number is proportional to velocity; >4000 is turbulent flow (trachea, bronchi), 4000–2000 transitional (respiratory bronchioles) and <2000 laminar (alveolar duct, alveoli).

UNITS.title: Alveolar Type I vs Type II Cells, Bleomycin Effect, Surfactant Function/Components/Synthesis & GM-CSF
UNITS.sec: Alveolar Type I vs Type II Cells, Bleomycin Effect, Surfactant Function/Components/Synthesis & GM-CSF
UNITS.guide:
Alveolar cells (p192) are the pulmonary alveolar macrophage and the type I/II pneumocytes. Type I is 95%, a non-dividing flat squamous cell, prone to oxidative damage and injured by bleomycin, marked by aquaporin-5, caveolin-1 and carboxypeptidase m. Type II is 5%, cuboidal, repairs after injury and makes surfactant, becomes hyperplastic with bleomycin, and is marked by surfactant proteins A–D.
Notes: substance P is a bronchoconstrictor; DPPC = dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine; bronchoconstriction peaks at 6 am and bronchodilatation at 6 pm; beractant is used in hyaline membrane disease/fetal respiratory distress syndrome.
Surfactant lowers surface tension, preventing fluid accumulation (pulmonary edema) and raising compliance. Lamellar bodies in type 2 pneumocytes store and produce it; steroids (used for HMD) and thyroid hormone raise production while insulin lowers it. Lipoprotein is the major component with lecithin (DPPC) > sphingomyelin, plus proteins A–D (A and D in innate immunity); GM-CSF clears excess surfactant and its antibodies cause pulmonary alveolar proteinosis.

UNITS.title: Tidal Volume, Boyle's Law, Three Pressures, Intrapleural Negativity & Intra-Alveolar Pressure Changes
UNITS.sec: Tidal Volume, Boyle's Law, Three Pressures, Intrapleural Negativity & Intra-Alveolar Pressure Changes
UNITS.guide:
Pressures in respiratory physiology (p193): tidal volume is the air moving in and out of the lungs, normal 500 mL; Boyle's law gives tidal volume α 1/TPP. Three pressures are intrapleural, intra-alveolar (IAP) and transpulmonary (TPP = intra-alveolar/intrapulmonary − intrapleural).
Intrapleural pressure is the pressure in the pleura, which has lymphatics and a vacuum (lung collapses, chest expands); it is negative except in forceful expiration, where it becomes positive. Inspiration is active — respiratory muscles and diaphragm contract, the chest wall expands and pleural pressure falls; expiration is passive.
Intra-alveolar pressure is zero at rest, −1 mmHg in inspiration and +1 mmHg in expiration; the printed intrapleural trace runs from −2 to −3 mmHg at the start of inspiration to −7 to −8 mmHg at the end.

UNITS.title: Transpulmonary Pressure Equations, TPP Trace Values, Intrapleural Fluid Cohesiveness, Pneumothorax Note & Static Compliance
UNITS.sec: Transpulmonary Pressure Equations, TPP Trace Values, Intrapleural Fluid Cohesiveness, Pneumothorax Note & Static Compliance
UNITS.guide:
Transpulmonary pressure (p194): total TPP = TPP of lung + TPP of chest wall; TPP of chest wall = intrapleural − atmospheric pressure; total TPP = IAP − atmospheric pressure. The trace is drawn around an atmospheric pressure of 760 mmHg, with intra-alveolar +1 mmHg in expiration and a TPP of 7–8 mmHg at end-inspiration.
Lungs are held to the thorax by intrapleural fluid cohesiveness (water molecules attracting one another and resisting being pulled apart) and by negative intrapleural pressure. In pneumothorax, intrapleural equals intrapulmonary pressure, TPP is 0 and the lung is not inflated.
Static compliance is 200 mL/cm H2O, maximal at mid-range pressure, and equals ΔV/ΔP with ΔP = TPP; at tidal volume it is the inflation of lung per unit change in pressure.

UNITS.title: Hysteresis Loop, Surface Tension vs Elastic Recoil, Elastin/Collagen & Obstructive vs Restrictive Compliance Curves
UNITS.sec: Hysteresis Loop, Surface Tension vs Elastic Recoil, Elastin/Collagen & Obstructive vs Restrictive Compliance Curves
UNITS.guide:
Hysteresis (p195): the ΔV/ΔP curve differs between inspiration and expiration because inspiration occurs against resistance while expiration is passive and needs no extra force. The resistances are surface tension (more important, overcome by surfactant) and elastic recoil pressure of the lung, which arises from elastin (elastic force) and collagen (tensile strength).
Obstructive disease (COPD, emphysema): ↑ static compliance, curve shifted up and left, loss of elastin → ↓ ERP → easier to inflate. Restrictive disease (ILD): ↓ static compliance, curve shifted down and right, fibrosis → ↑ collagen → ↑ ERP → difficult to inflate.
The plotted curves are labelled high compliance (emphysema), normal, and low compliance (pulmonary fibrosis).

UNITS.title: Dynamic Compliance (Only-Dynamic vs Static-and-Dynamic Falls) & Elastic Recoil Pressure of the Respiratory System at RV/FRC/TLC
UNITS.sec: Dynamic Compliance (Only-Dynamic vs Static-and-Dynamic Falls) & Elastic Recoil Pressure of the Respiratory System at RV/FRC/TLC
UNITS.guide:
Dynamic compliance (p196) equals static compliance plus resistance, and static and dynamic compliance move together. Foreign body, kink in the ET tube and intrathoracic obstruction lower only dynamic compliance, whereas pulmonary edema, consolidation, atelectasis and pneumothorax lower both.
ERP of the respiratory system: total ERP = ERP of lung + ERP of chest wall. At residual volume the chest wall alone contributes a negative, outward ERP and inflation is easy; at FRC (equilibrium/relaxation volume, RV + ERV) chest wall and lung together give zero ERP and inflation is easy; at TLC both forces act downwards giving a positive ERP and inflation is difficult. Residual volume is the air left after forceful expiration, normally 1.2 L.

UNITS.title: Lung Volumes and Capacities Tables (TV/IRV/ERV/RV with Male-Female Split; IC/FVC/FRC/TLC Formulas) & Volume-Time Graph
UNITS.sec: Lung Volumes and Capacities Tables (TV/IRV/ERV/RV with Male-Female Split; IC/FVC/FRC/TLC Formulas) & Volume-Time Graph
UNITS.guide:
Lung volumes (p197): tidal volume 500 ml (5–7 mL/kg) is the air moving in and out during quiet breathing; IRV is M 3.3 L / F 1.8 L (maximum inspired after tidal inspiration); ERV is M 1.3 L / F 0.8 L (maximum expired after tidal expiration); RV is 1.2 L (remaining after forceful maximum expiration).
Lung capacities: IC 3.5 L = TV + IRV (0.5 + 3 L); FVC 4.5 L = TV + IRV + ERV (0.5 + 3 + 1 L), the air expired with maximum force after forceful maximal inspiration; FRC 2.2 L = ERV + RV (1 + 1.2 L) = 1/2 FVC, the air remaining after a normal expiration; TLC 5.7 L = FVC + RV (4.5 + 1.2 L).
Closing note: elastic recoil pressure of the system is zero, and the lung's elastic recoil is counter-balanced by expansion of the chest wall. The volume–time spirogram on the same page labels TV, IRV, ERV, RV, IC, FRC, VC and TLC.

UNITS.title: Residual Volume Measurement (Plethysmography vs Obsolete Gas Methods), Spirometry Procedure/Disadvantage, FEV1/FVC & Obstructive-Restrictive-Vascular Disease Tree
UNITS.sec: Residual Volume Measurement (Plethysmography vs Obsolete Gas Methods), Spirometry Procedure/Disadvantage, FEV1/FVC & Obstructive-Restrictive-Vascular Disease Tree
UNITS.guide:
RV (p198) cannot be measured with a spirometer, and therefore neither can FRC or TLC. It is measured by total body plethysmography (photographed), closed-circuit helium dilution or open-circuit nitrogen washout — the last two are bracketed 'Obsolete (doesn't include trapped gas in closed airways/pneumothorax)'.
Spirometry measures volume and flow to plot volume–time and flow–volume graphs; it is physically demanding, so it is avoided after MI, stroke, strenuous activity or smoking. The procedure is maximal inspiration → blast of expiration (continuous exhalation for 15 s or minimum 6 s) → maximum inhalation. FVC is 4.5 L normally expired in 5–6 s and FEV1/FVC is ≥80% (4 L).
The disease tree splits into obstructive (COPD with chronic bronchitis, emphysema and small airway disease; asthma; cystic fibrosis; bronchiolitis; bronchiectasis), restrictive (intraparenchymal ILD; extraparenchymal neuromuscular — myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barré — and chest wall — kyphoscoliosis, obesity, ankylosing spondylitis) and vascular (pulmonary HTN, pulmonary thromboembolism).

UNITS.title: Obstructive Disease (Emphysema): Hyperinflation Phase I vs Air Trapping Phase II Table & Bronchodilator Reversibility Testing
UNITS.sec: Obstructive Disease (Emphysema): Hyperinflation Phase I vs Air Trapping Phase II Table & Bronchodilator Reversibility Testing
UNITS.guide:
Normal forceful expiration (p199) depends on a driving pressure (elastic recoil plus intrapleural pressure) exceeding airway pressure. In COPD the elastic recoil is low, so the lung inflates easily and becomes hyperinflated (Phase 1); driving pressure then falls below airway pressure, bronchioles collapse because they lack cartilage, airways are dynamically compressed and air is trapped (Phase 2).
Phase I: FVC normal, FEV1 ↓↓, FEV1/FVC ↓↓, RV ↑↑, TLC ↑↑, reversibility (−). Phase II: FVC ↓↓, FEV1 ↓↓↓, FEV1/FVC ↓↓, RV ↑↑, TLC normal, reversibility (−).
If FEV1/FVC < 0.7, bronchodilator reversibility is tested with salbutamol 100 mg × 4 puffs or ipratropium 40 mg × 4 puffs (as printed), repeating after 30 minutes; a rise of 200 mL plus >12% ((post FEV1 − pre FEV1)/pre FEV1) indicates reversibility and bronchial asthma, whereas FEV1/FVC < 0.7 indicates COPD.

UNITS.title: Restrictive Lung Disease: Diffusion vs Ventilation Indices, Intraparenchymal vs Extraparenchymal Types & Vascular Lung Disease
UNITS.sec: Restrictive Lung Disease: Diffusion vs Ventilation Indices, Intraparenchymal vs Extraparenchymal Types & Vascular Lung Disease
UNITS.guide:
Restrictive/ILD physiology (p200): fibrosis deranges diffusion and ventilation; initially diffusion from alveolus to capillary fails, giving ↓DLCO with a normal FVC, and as disease progresses diffusion and ventilation both fall — FVC ↓↓↓, FEV1 ↓, FEV1/FVC normal or ↑, RV ↓↓, TLC ↓↓, DLCO ↓↓.
Intraparenchymal disease is a diffusion disorder (eg ILD) with ↓↓↓ DLCO; extraparenchymal disease is a ventilation disorder (↓↓↓ FVC) with normal diffusion, normal DLCO and normal RV. Pure inspiratory (neuromuscular) disorders such as myasthenia gravis give ↑↑ RV/TLC with ↓TLC; combined inspiratory and expiratory disorders such as kyphoscoliosis give a normal RV/TLC.
Vascular lung disease has normal FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC with an abnormal DLCO.

UNITS.title: Small Airway Disease (mmEFR, Closing Volume/Fowler) & Flow-Volume Curve Patterns (Normal, Mild, Severe Obstruction, Restriction)
UNITS.sec: Small Airway Disease (mmEFR, Closing Volume/Fowler) & Flow-Volume Curve Patterns (Normal, Mild, Severe Obstruction, Restriction)
UNITS.guide:
Small airway disease (p201) has normal FEV1/FVC and normal FVC, so it cannot be diagnosed with a spirometer; the diagnostic abnormalities are ↓↓ maximal mid-expiratory flow rate (mmEFR, also FEF 25–75, the flow in the mid half of the manoeuvre) and ↑↑ closing volume, measured by the single-breath nitrogen/Fowler technique (obsolete) with nitrogen read in phase 4 and normally 10% of VC.
On the flow–volume curve the early portion is effort dependent (trachea, large airways) and the rest effort independent; FVC is the area under the curve.
Patterns: normal — PEFR with no coving; mild obstruction — late plateau, FVC preserved, PEFR mildly reduced, coving/scooping/dog-tail; severe obstruction — no plateau, FVC reduced, PEFR severely reduced, coving; restriction — normal plateau, FVC reduced, PEFR normal or mildly reduced, no coving.

UNITS.title: Upper Airway Obstruction Patterns (Extrathoracic/Intrathoracic/Fixed), Neuromuscular & Parenchymal Loops, and GOLD Staging
UNITS.sec: Upper Airway Obstruction Patterns (Extrathoracic/Intrathoracic/Fixed), Neuromuscular & Parenchymal Loops, and GOLD Staging
UNITS.guide:
Upper airway obstruction (p202): variable extrathoracic obstruction flattens inspiration (vocal cord palsy, laryngeal tumour, goitre, obstructive sleep apnoea); variable intrathoracic obstruction flattens expiration (foreign body, tracheomalacia); fixed obstruction flattens both, expiration from high pleural pressure and inspiration from negative intrathoracic pressure (tracheal stenosis). Small loops are also drawn for neuromuscular weakness and restrictive parenchymal lung disease.
GOLD staging uses post-bronchodilator FEV1: stage I ≥80%, II <80% to 50%, III <50% to 30%, IV <30%.

UNITS.title: DLCO: Definition, Normal Values, Alveolo-Capillary Membrane Layers, Advantages of CO, Procedure & Blood Volume Determinant
UNITS.sec: DLCO: Definition, Normal Values, Alveolo-Capillary Membrane Layers, Advantages of CO, Procedure & Blood Volume Determinant
UNITS.guide:
DLCO or transfer factor (p203) is the diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide — a measure of the lung's ability to transfer gas across the respiratory membrane. Normal is 20–30 mL/min/mmHg; 70–140% of predicted is normal physiology and severe disease is <40%.
The respiratory (alveolo-capillary) membrane has a surface area of 70 m² and thickness 0.2–0.5 µm, with six layers: I fluid and surfactants, II alveolar epithelium, III epithelial basement layer, IV interstitial space, V capillary basement membrane, VI capillary endothelium.
CO is advantageous because its affinity for Hb is 210 times that of oxygen, blood levels are negligible and it is diffusion- rather than perfusion-limited. The manoeuvre is a 4-second deep inspiration of 0.3% CO, a 10-second breath hold, then maximal forced expiration. Blood volume is the most important determinant: ↑ blood volume → ↑ Hb → ↑ CO binding → ↑ DLCO.

UNITS.title: Conditions Raising/Lowering DLCO, False-Low DLCO Causes, Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage & DLCO Across Respiratory Disorders
UNITS.sec: Conditions Raising/Lowering DLCO, False-Low DLCO Causes, Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage & DLCO Across Respiratory Disorders
UNITS.guide:
Raised DLCO (p204): diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, polycythaemia, supine posture (↑ venous return), exercise, left-to-right shunting, obesity, pregnancy (↑ blood volume) and mild congestive heart failure. Lowered DLCO: anaemia (↓ blood volume) and pulmonary oedema (thick interstitium).
False-low DLCO is produced by high-flow oxygen (high oxyhaemoglobin) and by smoking (high carboxyhaemoglobin reducing Hb binding of CO). Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage from bleeding within the lungs, as in Goodpasture syndrome, raises DLCO; DLCO is used to diagnose bleomycin toxicity, pulmonary vasculitis and early ILD.
DLCO by disorder: asthma ↑↑ (pulmonary hyperaemia with preferential perfusion), emphysema ↓ (printed as ↑ volume/surface area ratio in alveoli), chronic bronchitis normal, intraparenchymal restrictive disease ↓↓↓ (thickened respiratory membrane), extraparenchymal restrictive disease normal, vascular disease ↓ (↓ blood reaching lungs with normal FEV1 and FVC).

UNITS.title: Coefficient of Diffusion (Kco) & the Stepwise Approach to Evaluation of Lung Diseases Flowchart
UNITS.sec: Coefficient of Diffusion (Kco) & the Stepwise Approach to Evaluation of Lung Diseases Flowchart
UNITS.guide:
Kco (p205) = DLCO / lung volume. In restrictive disease the intraparenchymal pattern is ↓DLCO with ↓ lung volume giving a normal Kco, whereas the extraparenchymal pattern is normal DLCO with ↓ lung volume giving ↑Kco.
Approach flowchart: FEV1/FVC = 0.7 with normal FVC → obstructive disease → post-bronchodilator FEV1 (asthma vs COPD); FEV1/FVC normal or ↑ with ↓FVC → restrictive disease → DLCO, where ↓DLCO means intraparenchymal disease (ILD, normal Kco) and normal DLCO means extraparenchymal disease (↑Kco) → RV/TLC, raised indicating neuromuscular and normal indicating chest-wall disorders; normal FEV1/FVC, normal FVC and ↓DLCO indicate vascular lung disease or early ILD, with FEF 25–75 and closing volume boxed for small airway disease.

UNITS.title: VTE Definition, Mortality, Thrombo-Embolic Pathogenesis, Origin of Thrombi, Acute Cor Pulmonale, Calf DVT & Massive VTE Pathogenesis Chain
UNITS.sec: VTE Definition, Mortality, Thrombo-Embolic Pathogenesis, Origin of Thrombi, Acute Cor Pulmonale, Calf DVT & Massive VTE Pathogenesis Chain
UNITS.guide:
Venous thromboembolism (p206) is AKA pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE), with 60–80% mortality when massive. Pathogenesis is migration of thrombi/microthrombi from the systemic circulation to the pulmonary vasculature, and the origin is deep veins of the lower limb > upper limb, maximal risk from supra-popliteal veins draining to femoral veins and from pelvic veins in pregnancy.
Note: acute cor pulmonale is RV dilatation/hypertrophy ± heart failure and its most common cause is VTE; calf DVT is the most common site but does not embolize.
Massive VTE is any PE with hypotension. Its chain: >50–70% occlusion → hypoxaemia → RV & RA dilatation → septum pushed left → ↓LV volume → ↓cardiac output → SBP < 90 mmHg lasting ≥ 15 mins or requiring ionotropic support.

UNITS.title: Presentation, D/d of Dyspnea with Clear Lung Fields, Golden 4 Assessment (Clinical, ECHO/McConnel Sign, Biomarkers, CTPA) & Submassive/Non-Massive VTE
UNITS.sec: Presentation, D/d of Dyspnea with Clear Lung Fields, Golden 4 Assessment (Clinical, ECHO/McConnel Sign, Biomarkers, CTPA) & Submassive/Non-Massive VTE
UNITS.guide:
Presentation (p207): unexplained dyspnea with clear lung fields is most common, chest pain is the second most common symptom, and sudden cardiac death and syncope complete the list; the only printed D/d for dyspnea with clear lung fields is VTE and metabolic acidosis.
Golden 4: clinical hypotension; ECHO with McConnel's sign (hypocontractile RV free wall plus hypercontractile apex), septal push, LV contraction and exclusion of tamponade; biomarkers NT pro BNP for RV dilatation and troponin I for RV ischaemia; imaging with CTPA as IOC showing dilated PA, clot in PA and large RV.
Submassive VTE has no hypotension — RV dilatation/ischaemia alone is low risk, escalating to high risk when the biomarkers rise. Non-massive VTE is 10–20% of cases from peripheral lodging, with recurrent/non-resolving pneumonia, cough, pleuritic pain and haemoptysis.

UNITS.title: Non-Massive VTE Investigations & Complications, Genetic and Acquired Risk-Factor Lists, Malignancy/Nephrotic/Surgery Risks & Ventilation-Perfusion Physiology
UNITS.sec: Non-Massive VTE Investigations & Complications, Genetic and Acquired Risk-Factor Lists, Malignancy/Nephrotic/Surgery Risks & Ventilation-Perfusion Physiology
UNITS.guide:
Non-massive VTE (p208) has a normal ECHO, BP and biomarkers, and its complication is pulmonary infarction. Genetic risks are factor-V Leiden (most common), antithrombin III, protein C and protein S deficiency; acquired risks are antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, polycythaemia rubra vera, primary myelofibrosis, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.
Further risks: adenocarcinoma; COPD; heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; membranous nephropathy losing antithrombin III in urine; OCPs; HRT; pregnancy and post-partum; surgery with immobilisation > 4 days, orthopaedic surgery being higher risk.
Physiology: ventilation and perfusion both maximal at the base, while the V/P ratio is maximal at the apex because perfusion falls more than ventilation.

UNITS.title: Dead-Space vs Shunt Physiology in PE, Symptoms/Signs, Vagal Bradycardia, Acute Cor Pulmonale Complications & Type I Respiratory Failure with A-a Gradient
UNITS.sec: Dead-Space vs Shunt Physiology in PE, Symptoms/Signs, Vagal Bradycardia, Acute Cor Pulmonale Complications & Type I Respiratory Failure with A-a Gradient
UNITS.guide:
Dead-space physiology (p209) as in PE is V normal, P 0, V/P ∞; shunt physiology is V 0, P normal, V/P 0.
Symptoms depend on embolus size and location: dyspnea within seconds > pleuritic chest pain in small peripheral emboli, with cough and haemoptysis in 10–20%. Signs run tachypnea > tachycardia > rales/↓breath sounds (10–20%), and hypoxia-induced intrapulmonary vagal stimulation causes bradycardia.
Complications: acute cor pulmonale with shock in massive VTE, S3 plus hypotension in acute RV failure, and raised JVP; type I respiratory failure from V/Q mismatch with a normal PaCO2 (no parenchymal involvement), producing respiratory alkalosis and a widened alveolar-arterial O2 gradient. Type 2 failure is hypoxia plus hypercarbia in parenchymal disease.

UNITS.title: CXR Signs (Atelectatic Bands, Hampton's Hump, Pallas, Westermark, Fleischner), PAH Films & ECG Significance and Patterns (S1Q3T3)
UNITS.sec: CXR Signs (Atelectatic Bands, Hampton's Hump, Pallas, Westermark, Fleischner), PAH Films & ECG Significance and Patterns (S1Q3T3)
UNITS.guide:
CXR (p210): long linear bands of atelectasis are the commonest sign; Hampton's hump is a pleural-based wedge-shaped opacity; Pallas sign is an enlarged right descending artery; Westermark's sign is oligaemia of the right upper lung; Fleischner sign is an enlarged central pulmonary artery. The PAH film shows large central pulmonary arteries, RV hypertrophy, rapid attenuation of vessels and clear lung fields.
ECG is done to rule out MI and to identify RV strain/hypertrophy. A normal ECG is the commonest pattern and sinus tachycardia the commonest abnormality, with deep S in lead I exceeding T inversion in V1–V4; the S1Q3T3 pattern is non-specific.

UNITS.title: Pulmonary Angiography Gold Standard, V/Q Scan Indications, D-Dimer, ECHO, the Wells Score Table and CTPA Signs (Saddle Embolus, Polo Mint Sign)
UNITS.sec: Pulmonary Angiography Gold Standard, V/Q Scan Indications, D-Dimer, ECHO, the Wells Score Table and CTPA Signs (Saddle Embolus, Polo Mint Sign)
UNITS.guide:
Pulmonary angiography (p211) is the gold standard and is invasive, cannulating a vein to reach the pulmonary artery. V/Q scan is indicated in pregnancy and contrast allergy; D-dimer is for low-risk cases; ECHO excludes alternate diagnoses such as pericardial effusion. Any unexplained dyspnea with a normal CXR/ECG/examination is VTE unless proven otherwise.
Wells score: clinical signs of DVT 3, alternative diagnosis less likely 3, HR > 100/min 1.5, recent surgery 1.5, previous DVT/PE 1.5, haemoptysis 1, malignancy 1. Low risk goes to D-dimer and, if positive, CTPA; moderate and high risk go straight to helical CTPA.
CT signs: saddle pulmonary embolism and the polo-mint sign, described as a thin rim of contrast persisting around a central filling defect.

UNITS.title: Management: Heparin/LMWH Dosing, Severity Determination, Thrombolysis vs Catheter Therapy, Heparin Target Ranges, 3-Month Switch and IVC Filter
UNITS.sec: Management: Heparin/LMWH Dosing, Severity Determination, Thrombolysis vs Catheter Therapy, Heparin Target Ranges, 3-Month Switch and IVC Filter
UNITS.guide:
Management (p212) starts anticoagulation at the earliest with unfractionated heparin or LMWH: first dose 80 units/kg heparin IV or 1 mg/kg s/c LMWH. Severity is then determined as massive VTE (hypotension +), submassive VTE (RV dilatation +) or extensive clot burden.
When severity is present: if fit for thrombolysis give alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hrs within 14 days, then restart heparin and replace with warfarin; if unfit, catheter-based thrombolysis/embolectomy (preferred). When absent: continue heparin at 18 units/kg/hr targeting aPTT 1.5–2 times the upper limit and INR 2–3.
At the end of 3 months switch to oral anticoagulants (new oral anticoagulants preferred over warfarin/vitamin K), lifelong if a genetic mutation is positive; if contraindicated, insert an inferior vena cava filter.

UNITS.title: Ohm's Law Applied to the Pulmonary Circulation (PAP − LAP = CO × PVR), the Five WHO Classes, Class 1 PAH Features and the Class-to-Affected-Vessel Figure
UNITS.sec: Ohm's Law Applied to the Pulmonary Circulation (PAP − LAP = CO × PVR), the Five WHO Classes, Class 1 PAH Features and the Class-to-Affected-Vessel Figure
UNITS.guide:
Page 213 applies Ohm's law: V is the PAP−LAP gradient, I is cardiac output and R is pulmonary vascular resistance, so PAP − LAP = CO × PVR and PAP = (CO × PVR) + LAP. A raised PAP therefore comes from a raised PVR (classes 1, 3 and 4) or a raised LAP (class 2, commonest cardiac cause mitral stenosis).
Class 1 PAH is mostly idiopathic (hence idiopathic pulmonary HTN), has a very poor prognosis with median survival < 9 months and affects young females. Class 2 is left heart disease with ↑LAP; class 3 follows chronic lung disease via hypoxia-related pulmonary vasoconstriction, with chronic bronchitis as the example and a very poor prognosis; class 4 is chronic thrombo-embolic disease responsive to surgery; class 5 is miscellaneous and multifactorial.
The figure labels the affected structure: class 1 arterioles, class 2 pulmonary vein, class 3 capillary, class 4 pulmonary artery and class 5 multifactorial. A boxed note adds that hypoxia causes vasodilatation everywhere except in pulmonary vessels.

UNITS.title: PAH vs Systemic HTN Mortality Logic, Definition (Mean PAP > 20 mmHg), Cor Pulmonale, Wood-Unit PVR Split, Plexiform Arteriolopathy & Secondary Causes (BMPR2 to Appetite Suppressants)
UNITS.sec: PAH vs Systemic HTN Mortality Logic, Definition (Mean PAP > 20 mmHg), Cor Pulmonale, Wood-Unit PVR Split, Plexiform Arteriolopathy & Secondary Causes (BMPR2 to Appetite Suppressants)
UNITS.guide:
Pulmonary hypertension (p214) kills more than systemic hypertension: PAP <<< SAP and PVR <<< SAR because the lungs are a low-resistance, high-compliance system, so systemic HTN causes LV hypertrophy whereas pulmonary HTN causes RV dilatation, RV failure and ↑mortality.
The definition is a mean PAP > 20 mmHg at rest on right heart catheterisation. Cor pulmonale is RV hypertrophy/dilatation ± RV failure from COPD, pulmonary HTN or thromboembolism (the last being acute cor pulmonale). PVR > 3 wood units places disease in class I/III/IV, while PVR < 3 wood units with PCWP (LAP) > 15 mmHg places it in class II. The PAH lesion is plexiform arteriolopathy affecting the arterioles.
Secondary causes: hereditary BMPR2 mutation; acquired limited systemic sclerosis; HIV; schistosomiasis; portal HTN via splanchnic vasodilatation → hyperdynamic circulation → ↑CO; and drugs — the serotonin appetite suppressants fenfluramine, dexfenfluramine, benfluorex and aminorex, plus toxic rapeseed oil.

UNITS.title: Pathology Triad, Endothelin/NO/Prostacyclin Pathway Treatment Table, Clinical Presentation and the RV Dilatation and RV Failure Sign Chains
UNITS.sec: Pathology Triad, Endothelin/NO/Prostacyclin Pathway Treatment Table, Clinical Presentation and the RV Dilatation and RV Failure Sign Chains
UNITS.guide:
Pathology (p215) is vasoconstriction, remodeling and thrombosis. The pathway table reads: endothelin pathway promoted → endothelin receptor antagonists; nitric oxide pathway (NO → ↑cGMP) inhibited → phosphodiesterase inhibitors; prostacyclin pathway (prostacyclin → ↑cAMP) inhibited → prostacyclin analogues.
Presentation is breathlessness and fatigue without overt signs of heart and lung disease. RV dilatation → septal push → ↑LV volume → ↓CO gives breathlessness, fatigue and syncope; ↓RV filling plus ↑RV afterload → RV ischaemia → chest pain; RV failure gives ascites, edema, hepatomegaly and an apex that shifts outwards.
Signs: loud P2; in RV failure wide splitting of P2 and S3 (from RA-RV dilatation raising diastolic filling pressure); palpable P2, parasternal heave and palpable epigastric impulse; JVP shows 'a' waves. The figure adds a prominent V wave if tricuspid regurgitation is present, clear lungs, fixed splitting of S2, left parasternal lift, large pulsatile liver, cold extremities, rare clubbing and peripheral edema.

UNITS.title: PA Catheterisation Gold Standard, the Three PAH Murmurs (Carvallo, Ejection Systolic, Graham Steell), CXR Findings, PA Aneurysm Causes and ECG RVH Criteria
UNITS.sec: PA Catheterisation Gold Standard, the Three PAH Murmurs (Carvallo, Ejection Systolic, Graham Steell), CXR Findings, PA Aneurysm Causes and ECG RVH Criteria
UNITS.guide:
PA catheterisation (p216) is the gold standard for diagnosis. Three murmurs occur in PAH: a pan systolic murmur that ↑ on inspiration (Carvallo's sign), lower left sternal border, high pitched and blowing; an ejection systolic murmur from pulmonary stenosis; and an early diastolic murmur — Graham Steell's — from PA dilatation in severe PAH, heard sitting up leaning forward in fixed expiration and indicating pulmonary regurgitation.
CXR: large central pulmonary arteries, right ventricular hypertrophy, rapid attenuation of pulmonary vessels and clear lung fields; the PA aneurysm caption names Behçet's and Takayasu. ECG: r/s ratio > 1 in V1 indicates RVH, whereas a normal ECG has a large S wave in V1 and a large r wave in V6.

UNITS.title: Investigations to Exclude Other Causes (PFT, ECHO, V/Q, Sleep Study, HRCT, 6MWT), the Vaso-Reactivity Test, General Treatment and the NYHA-Stratified Drug and Surgical Table
UNITS.sec: Investigations to Exclude Other Causes (PFT, ECHO, V/Q, Sleep Study, HRCT, 6MWT), the Vaso-Reactivity Test, General Treatment and the NYHA-Stratified Drug and Surgical Table
UNITS.guide:
PFT (p217) shows normal FEV1/FVC and FVC with ↓DLCO. ECHO assesses RV function and TR; V/Q scan excludes chronic thromboembolic PAH; sleep study excludes obstructive sleep apnea; HRCT excludes interstitial lung disease; the 6-minute walk test determines prognosis.
Vaso-reactivity testing gives nitric oxide and measures PAP: a positive test (10% of cases) lowers PAP by 10 mmHg or to < 40 mmHg with BP and CO unchanged, implying response to high dose calcium channel blockers — nifedipine 240 mg.
General treatment: oral anticoagulants, long term O2, diuretics for right heart failure and contraindication of pregnancy. Specific treatment by finding: vaso-reactivity + → nifedipine 240 mg; NYHA I–3 → tadalafil + ambrisentan; NYHA class-4 (symptoms at rest) → prostanoids — epoprostenol (m/c) by permanent tunnel catheter in the IJV, treprostinil by microinfusion pump, and selexipag, a chemically stable oral prostacyclin derivative not yet available. Surgical options if not responding to drugs are atrial septostomy and lung transplant.

UNITS.title: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
UNITS.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
UNITS.guide:
Bronchiectasis (p218) is abnormal and irreversible dilatation of bronchi — initially medium sized, later the entire bronchial tree — plus obliterative fibrosis of bronchioles, producing obstructive lung disease that can have a restrictive component. Pseudobronchiectasis is the reversible dilatation that follows influenza or COVID.
It is listed among the obstructive diseases with COPD (emphysema, bronchitis, small airway disease), bronchial asthma, bronchiolitis and cystic fibrosis.
Pathogenesis: infection (mostly TB)/idiopathic → inflammation → loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue in bronchi (bronchi and bronchioles both have smooth muscle) → abnormal and irreversible dilatation; the mucus limb runs goblet cell hyperplasia → mucus hypersecretion → airway obstruction, while loss of cilia removes the mucociliary escalator and pools secretions, feeding microbial colonisation and further inflammation. The diagram contrasts a normal bronchus (outer wall, cilia, mucus, mucous gland) with loss of cilia, increased mucus and destruction of the wall.

UNITS.title: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
UNITS.sec: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
UNITS.guide:
Types of dilatation (p219) are cylindrical/tubular, varicose and cystic, drawn against a normal bronchus (N) as grades C, V and S, with a CT showing cystic changes at the upper lobe. Traction bronchiectasis follows fibrosis and is a restrictive type classified under ILD.
Distribution: usually unilateral though it can become bilateral, most common lobe the left lower lobe, F > M, age 50–70 years.
Histology: fibrosis and cartilage destruction; mucosal and mucous gland hyperplasia; excessive mucus and exudate; inflammatory cell infiltrate.

UNITS.title: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
UNITS.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
UNITS.guide:
Paediatric aetiology (p220): post-infective pertussis and measles; syndromes usually cystic in the upper to mid fields — Mounier-Kuhn (tracheobronchomegaly), William Campbell (absence of cartilage), Kartagener's (primary ciliary dyskinesia with bronchiectasis, sinusitis and situs inversus), Young's (azoospermia causing infertility); cystic fibrosis; yellow nail syndrome; α1-antitrypsin deficiency.
Impaired mucociliary clearance is bracketed for Kartagener's, cystic fibrosis and Young's syndrome. Obliterative bronchiectasis after childhood infection is McLeod's syndrome, and isolated IgA deficiency is the commonest primary immunodeficiency.
Adult causes: idiopathic 30%, post-infection mostly TB 40%, mechanical obstruction such as Brock's syndrome (secondary lymphadenopathy causing right middle lobe bronchiectasis), immunodeficiency (IgA deficiency commonest) and autoimmune disease such as Sjögren syndrome.

UNITS.title: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
UNITS.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
UNITS.guide:
Clinical features (p221): chronic cough with postural variation; copious foul-smelling sputum in three layers — mucus, mucopurulent, pus — with early morning exacerbation; haemoptysis from rupture of a thin-walled vein on the bronchial wall; exacerbations from infection, and bronchiectasis must always be excluded in recurrent pneumonia.
Findings: clubbing in children, seen in the cystic type; early and mid inspiratory coarse crackles with diffuse rhonchi. Note sicca bronchiectasis with haemoptysis and cough points to TB, and ABPA gives central, proximal, upper lobe bronchiectasis, usually bilateral, which can accompany ILD.
X-ray has low sensitivity but shows the tram track sign (dilated airways with lack of tapering), bunch of grape appearance and finger-in-glove appearance from mucus inside. Volumetric multidetector helical CT is the IOC: airway dilatation 1–1.5 times the adjacent vessels, lack of bronchial tapering, and tree-in-bud opacity (non-specific) from endobronchial obstruction giving nodules plus signet ring.

UNITS.title: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
UNITS.sec: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
UNITS.guide:
Complications (p222): cor pulmonale; massive haemoptysis, especially in dry bronchiectasis; empyema with bronchopleural fistula; secondary amyloidosis (AA); lung abscess. Cor pulmonale is RV dilatation/hypertrophy ± failure, acute from thromboembolism and chronic from parenchymal disease such as ILD, chronic bronchitis and bronchiectasis.
Treatment: mainstay is airway clearance with nebulised 7% hypertonic saline, steam inhalation, flutter valves and postural drainage; CF-associated disease gets recombinant human DNase and nebulised gentamycin as prophylaxis; surgery is localized resection for localized disease.
Antibiotics: macrolides and penicillin (beta-lactams) reach effective concentration within lung and bronchial mucosa, and macrolides have an immunomodulatory action recommended for 6–9 months. The organism hierarchy that infects and weakens the bronchial wall is Pseudomonas >> H. influenzae > S. pneumoniae.

UNITS.title: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
UNITS.sec: Disease Types, Pneumoconiosis Definition, the Dust-Particle Size/Site Table, the Four Pneumoconioses and Byssinosis (Organic Dust, Monday Fever)
UNITS.guide:
Occupational lung diseases (p223) divide into pneumoconiosis, occupational asthma and hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Pneumoconiosis is accumulation of dust in lung with tissue reactions to its presence.
Dust size decides the site: >3 µm lodges in secondary bronchi, 0.5–3 µm in the bronchiole and <0.5 µm in the alveoli, which is why the finest dusts cause parenchymal disease.
The four pneumoconioses are silicosis (most common), asbestosis, coal worker pneumoconiosis and berylliosis. Byssinosis is different — hypersensitivity to organic dust with recurrent Monday fever.

UNITS.title: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
UNITS.sec: Silicosis: Industries, Crystalline vs Amorphous Silica, Parenchymal-Only Involvement, Malignancy/COPD Risk and the Acute-vs-Chronic Table (Exposure, Pathogenesis, Clinical Triangle, BAL, PFT, Prognosis)
UNITS.guide:
Silicosis risk factors (p224) are mining, quarries, blast furnaces, slate industry, sand stone industry, ceramics and rock cutting. Crystalline silica (quartz) is most common, composed of SiO2 (free silica) and carries the higher occupational hazard; amorphous silica is the second type.
Features are lung parenchymal involvement with NO pleural involvement, plus a risk of malignancy and COPD.
Acute silicosis follows a large quantity over 2 years, has a dash for pathogenesis, presents acutely with severe dyspnea, hypoxia and weight loss, gives PAS-positive milky white BAL and has a very poor prognosis. Chronic silicosis follows 10–30 years, acts through injury to pulmonary alveolar macrophages with silicotuberculosis (reactivation of latent TB) and autoimmune illness (SLE, RA), gives chronic dry cough with dyspnea on exertion and chest signs in 25%, and shows a mixed PFT pattern.

UNITS.title: Radiology of Silicosis: Acute Crazy-Pavement CT Pattern and the Chronic Nodule-to-PMF Sequence with Egg-Shell Calcification and Upper Lobe ILD
UNITS.sec: Radiology of Silicosis: Acute Crazy-Pavement CT Pattern and the Chronic Nodule-to-PMF Sequence with Egg-Shell Calcification and Upper Lobe ILD
UNITS.guide:
Acute silicosis CT (p225) shows the crazy pavement appearance: ground glass opacifications with intact lung structure, thickened septa and multiple centrilobular small nodules in the parenchyma.
Chronic silicosis progresses from small bilateral symmetric centrilobular parenchymal nodules to large conglomerate nodules with an angel wing appearance, ± cavitations, with hilar lymphadenopathy showing egg-shell calcification, then to progressive massive fibrosis, and finally upper lobe interstitial lung disease.

UNITS.title: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
UNITS.sec: Crazy-Pavement Differential (DAH, AEP, PAP with Anti-GM-CSF), Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis, the CWP-vs-Silicosis Table and Caplan Syndrome
UNITS.guide:
The crazy pavement pattern (p226) also occurs in diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, acute eosinophilic pneumonia and pulmonary alveolar proteinosis — in PAP there are antibodies against GM-CSF causing abnormal clearance of surfactant, with PAS-positive milky white BAL.
CWP (black lung) shares with silicosis upper lobe involvement, injury to PAMs causing TB or autoimmune disease, ↑COPD, and parenchymal nodules >1 cm ± cavitations progressing to PMF; the pigment is carbon.
CWP versus silicosis: malignancy association present in silicosis and absent in CWP; hilar lymphadenopathy absent in silicosis and present in CWP; Caplan syndrome absent in silicosis and present in CWP. Caplan syndrome is CWP (necrobiotic nodule) plus rheumatoid arthritis with IgA rheumatoid factor positive plus active synovitis.

UNITS.title: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
UNITS.sec: Chronic Asbestosis: Fibre Types, Industries, Pleural Plaques (Candle Dripping, Holly Leaf), BAPE Fluid Criteria, Crow Feet Sign, Shaggy Heart Sign and Parenchymal Fibrosis
UNITS.guide:
Asbestos fibres (p227) are 90% serpentine/chrysotile with curly strands and less toxicity, and 10% amphibole with brittle long straight rods — crocidolite and amosite, amosite being more dangerous. Risk industries are textile, cement, ship building and automobile, and smoking adds parenchymal and malignant risk.
Pleura: parietal pleural calcification with pleural plaques (X-ray candle dripping, holly leaf sign) and subpleural linear densities parallel to the plaque; BAPE, the earliest finding, is unilateral, hemorrhagic and exudative with eosin <25% and mesothelial cells <50%; visceral pleural calcification gives the crow feet sign. Pleural disease is printed with 'no clinical signs'.
Parenchyma: bilateral lower lobe infiltrates with pleural plaques (shaggy heart sign) and diffuse massive fibrosis of the lower lobe, with chest pain, dyspnea, bibasal fine inspiratory crackles, clubbing and a restrictive PFT pattern.

UNITS.title: Asbestos Malignancy: Lung Cancer vs Mesothelioma Table, Ferruginous Body, Berylliosis as Delayed Hypersensitivity with Non-Caseating Granulomas and the Granuloma Differential
UNITS.sec: Asbestos Malignancy: Lung Cancer vs Mesothelioma Table, Ferruginous Body, Berylliosis as Delayed Hypersensitivity with Non-Caseating Granulomas and the Granuloma Differential
UNITS.guide:
Asbestos malignancy (p228): lung cancer is adenocarcinoma > squamous cell carcinoma > small cell carcinoma with a 10–30 year latency, a present smoking association and cough with haemoptysis; mesothelioma is epitheloid > sarcomatoid with a > 30 year latency, no smoking association, chest pain with mass, and pathology markers pancytokeratin/calretinin with electron microscopy showing microvilli, desmosomes and tonofilaments. The lung cancer pathology cell is printed as a dash.
A ferruginous body is an asbestos body with a transparent core surrounded by iron and protein. Berylliosis is a delayed hypersensitivity with non-caseating granulomas, clinically similar to sarcoidosis; the non-caseating granuloma list is sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, lymphoma, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, cat scratch disease, berylliosis and Crohn's disease.

UNITS.title: Berylliosis: Sarcoidosis Features That Are Absent, Industries, Upper Lobe ILD to PMF, Lymphocyte Proliferation Test, X-ray in 50% and the HRCT Triad
UNITS.sec: Berylliosis: Sarcoidosis Features That Are Absent, Industries, Upper Lobe ILD to PMF, Lymphocyte Proliferation Test, X-ray in 50% and the HRCT Triad
UNITS.guide:
Sarcoidosis findings absent in berylliosis (p229) are CNS symptoms, ocular symptoms, parotid findings and erythemoid lesions. Risk factors are ceramic industry, battery manufacturing and alloy industry.
Features are dyspnea with upper lobe ILD progressing to PMF. Investigations: lymphocyte proliferation test positive; chest X-ray normal in 50% of patients, with hilar adenopathy and ↑ interstitial markings in the remainder; HRCT shows the classical ground glass appearance with parenchymal nodules and septal lines.

UNITS.title: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
UNITS.sec: Definition of Respiratory Failure, Hypoxemic/Hypercapnic Thresholds, the Partial-Pressure Abbreviation Box and the Type I Table (Diffusion Failure, CO Diffusion Potential, Etiology List Including the Asthma Exception)
UNITS.guide:
Respiratory failure (p230) is the pulmonary system's inability to meet the body's demands: hypoxemic when PaO2 < 60 mmHg on room air with SpO2 < 90%, hypercapnic when PaCO2 > 50 mmHg on room air. The box defines PAO2 as alveolar oxygen, PaO2 as arterial oxygen (normal ~97 mmHg), PaCO2 as arterial carbon dioxide (normal ~40 mmHg) and PAO2 − PaO2 as the alveolocapillary oxygen gradient.
Type I is impaired diffusion causing oxygenation failure, with the high (150 times) diffusion potential of CO and no hypercapnia; pressures are ↓PaO2, normal PaCO2 and ↑PAO2 − PaO2. Causes are interstitial fibrosis/ILD, fluid in the interstitium with pulmonary edema or ARDS, exudate/consolidation in pneumonia, the reduced surface area/volume of emphysema, vascular disease such as thromboembolism and pulmonary HTN, pneumothorax, granulomatous lung disease, cystic congenital heart disease and bronchiectasis.
Bronchial asthma is entered separately: airway disease with normal parenchyma means absent CO2 retention, so ↓PaO2 with (N)PaCO2 but ↑DLCO, reflecting normal diffusion.

UNITS.title: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
UNITS.sec: Type III (Parenchymal Damage) and Type IV (Shock) Rows, the Anaesthesiology 'Type-3' FRC Note, the V/Q Ratio Zones and the Dead-Space-vs-Shunt Table
UNITS.guide:
Type III (p231) runs oxygenation failure → parenchymal damage → ventilatory failure with ↓PaO2, ↑PaCO2 and ↑PAO2 − PaO2; ILD acts by ↓diffusion and ARDS by ↓lung compliance, with the brace showing type 1 becoming type 3 as disease progresses. Type IV is hypotension → ↓perfusion of respiratory muscles with a dash for partial pressures, caused by cardiogenic, hypovolemic or septic shock.
The anaesthesiology 'Type-3' note describes ↓functional residual capacity (residual volume + expiratory reserve volume) causing collapse and post-op atelectasis, with causes of supine position/obesity/ascites, residual anaesthesia, upper abdominal incision and airway secretions.
The hypoxemic approach uses V/Q matching: normal 0.8, upper zone > 1 (non-dependent, ↓↓V and ↓↓Q) and lower zone < 1 (dependent). Dead space physiology has ventilation present, perfusion absent and V/Q ∞ (pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vascular disease); shunt physiology has ventilation absent, perfusion present and V/Q zero (intracardiac/vascular shunts).

UNITS.title: The Two Flowcharts: Hypoxemic Failure Branches (V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, Dead Space, Type II vs Type III, Oxygen-Responsiveness, High Altitude) and Hypercapnic Failure Branches
UNITS.sec: The Two Flowcharts: Hypoxemic Failure Branches (V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, Dead Space, Type II vs Type III, Oxygen-Responsiveness, High Altitude) and Hypercapnic Failure Branches
UNITS.guide:
The hypoxemic flowchart (p232) starts from ↓PaO2 and branches to V/Q mismatch (Type I, diffusion abnormality), V/Q = 0 shunt and V/Q = ∞ dead space.
It then splits on PaCO2: a raised CO2 with a normal gradient ends in hypoventilation (Type II), and with a raised gradient in hypoventilation plus another mechanism (Type III). Without CO2 retention, a raised gradient with oxygen-correctable hypoxaemia means V/Q mismatch and uncorrectable hypoxaemia means shunt, while a normal gradient leads to high altitude.
The hypercapnic flowchart starts from ↑PaCO2 and splits on the A-a gradient: normal → hypoventilation → generator, pumps, effector organ; increased → V/Q mismatch, eg ARDS and ILD.

UNITS.title: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
UNITS.sec: ARDS Synonyms, the 1992 AECC Criteria, Limitations and Mortality, the Berlin 2012 Definition with PEEP and Severity Table and the Factors Preventing Pulmonary Edema
UNITS.guide:
ARDS (p233) is AKA shock lung, acute lung injury, DAD, blast lung and acute alveolar injury. The 1992 AECC criteria are non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema with PCWP < 18 mmHg (the wedge measures left atrial pressure and suggests no cardiac abnormality), bilateral alveolar and interstitial infiltrates on X-ray, and PaO2/FiO2 < 200; only 20% of patients meet them, mortality is 70–75% and post-ARDS residual disability is present.
The Berlin 2012 definition requires acute onset within 1 week of the insult, bilateral infiltrates not explained by effusion/collapse/nodules, a non-cardiogenic cause with normal ECHO, and oxygenation measured when PEEP ≥ 5 cm of H2O — mild 200–300, moderate 100–200, severe < 100.
Pulmonary edema is prevented by retained intravascular protein, interstitial lymphatics draining fluid, and tight junctions between epithelial cells.

UNITS.title: ARDS Etiology (Primary and Secondary), the Toxin-to-Hyaline-Membrane Pathogenesis Chain, Alveolar Consequences and the Three Pathological Phases
UNITS.sec: ARDS Etiology (Primary and Secondary), the Toxin-to-Hyaline-Membrane Pathogenesis Chain, Alveolar Consequences and the Three Pathological Phases
UNITS.guide:
Primary ARDS (p234) follows pulmonary sepsis, massive blood transfusion, acute pancreatitis, TRALI, smoke inhalation, drowning or post surgery; secondary ARDS follows non-pulmonary sepsis (UTI, surgical site infection) or major trauma/burns.
Pathogenesis: toxin/sepsis → alveolar epithelial injury → inflammatory mediators (IL-1, IL-6, TNF α) and cytokines → neutrophil recruitment, with capillary endothelial injury causing exudation of fluid and protein; the alveolar space fills with proteinaceous fluid and debris, causing loss of surfactant → collapse, ↓compliance and impaired gas exchange. Type 1 (most common) or type 3 respiratory failure is seen.
Phases: acute exudative phase (7 days) with diffuse alveolar damage, interstitial and alveolar edema and eosinophilic hyaline membrane deposition as the hallmark (AKA hyaline membrane disease); fibroproliferative phase (7–14 days); fibrotic vasoconstriction (14–21 days).

UNITS.title: ARDS Clinical Features, Mechanical Ventilation Strategies, the VILI Table (Volume, Baro and Atelecto Trauma) and the Differential of Acute Breathlessness
UNITS.sec: ARDS Clinical Features, Mechanical Ventilation Strategies, the VILI Table (Volume, Baro and Atelecto Trauma) and the Differential of Acute Breathlessness
UNITS.guide:
Clinical features (p235): rapid onset dyspnea, hypoxemia, bilateral crackles with diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, tachypnea, tachycardia, diaphoresis, and pulmonary hypertension from hypoxemic vasoconstriction.
Management is mechanical ventilation as the mainstay, with inverse ratio ventilation with inspiration, prone ventilation and permissive hypercapnia.
VILI: volume trauma (↑lung volume → alveolar injury) is treated with low tidal volume ventilation (high frequency ventilation); baro trauma (↑transpulmonary pressure) with low plateau pressure (low driving pressure); atelecto trauma (collapse and decollapse during tidal breathing) with high PEEP.
The differential of acute breathlessness is pulmonary edema (unless proven otherwise), pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, acute exacerbation of asthma, aortic dissection and myocardial infarction.

UNITS.title: Interstitium and Its Types, Lung Parenchyma, TGF-β/PDGF Fibrosis, ILD Classification and the Seven Idiopathic Interstitial Pneumonias
UNITS.sec: Interstitium and Its Types, Lung Parenchyma, TGF-β/PDGF Fibrosis, ILD Classification and the Seven Idiopathic Interstitial Pneumonias
UNITS.guide:
The interstitium (p236) is connective tissue holding the lungs together: alveolar (subpleural and lobar), vascular (surrounds vessels) and axial (connects lung to chest wall); lung parenchyma is alveoli plus alveolar and vascular interstitium.
ILD is 'diffuse parenchymal lung fibrosis', TGF-β > PDGF mediated, with TGF-β boxed as the most potent pathogenic fibrogenic cytokine, and classifies into idiopathic interstitial pneumonia (most common), autoimmune ILD, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, sarcoidosis and miscellaneous.
The seven idiopathic interstitial pneumonias run IPF/UIP (most common), NSIP (2nd), COP (3rd), RB-ILD and DIP bracketed as smoking-associated, acute interstitial pneumonia (ARDS with diffuse alveolar damage after COVID/viral infection, very poor prognosis), and LIP.

UNITS.title: Autoimmune and Miscellaneous ILD (Occupational Lobes, Vasculitis, Inherited, Drug-Induced, LCH, LAM) with the UIP/NSIP/COP/LIP Important Points
UNITS.sec: Autoimmune and Miscellaneous ILD (Occupational Lobes, Vasculitis, Inherited, Drug-Induced, LCH, LAM) with the UIP/NSIP/COP/LIP Important Points
UNITS.guide:
Autoimmune ILD (p237) complicates rheumatoid arthritis, diffuse systemic sclerosis, polymyositis/dermatomyositis, MCTD, Sjogren's syndrome and ankylosing spondylitis.
Miscellaneous ILD covers occupational disease (asbestosis lower lobe; silicosis, berylliosis and coal-worker's pneumoconiosis upper lobe), EGPA/Churg-Strauss vasculitis, inherited neurofibromatosis and tuberous sclerosis, bleomycin, smoking-associated LCH (printed 'Langerhan's') and LAM.
Important points: idiopathic UIP/IPF is most common and RA-ILD affects smoking males of 50–70 years; NSIP affects young females as a subacute restrictive process linked to drugs and connective tissue disease; COP is most common in inflammatory muscle disease; LIP links to Sjogren syndrome and HIV; and the commonest pattern is UIP in RA but NSIP in other conditions.

UNITS.title: Clinical Features of ILD: Cardinal Symptoms, the Crackles-and-Clubbing Table versus Bronchiectasis, Skin Signs, Pulmonary HTN Prognosis and CXR
UNITS.sec: Clinical Features of ILD: Cardinal Symptoms, the Crackles-and-Clubbing Table versus Bronchiectasis, Skin Signs, Pulmonary HTN Prognosis and CXR
UNITS.guide:
ILD (p238) presents with two cardinal symptoms, dry non-productive cough and dyspnea on exertion, often misdiagnosed as bronchitis; fever with arthralgia suggests sarcoidosis, wheeze is specific to bronchiectasis/ABPA/hypersensitivity pneumonitis, pleuritic pain to asbestosis, and hemoptysis is rare.
