Crackles in ILD are bilateral bibasal, fine 'velcro', end to early expiratory as printed, without cough/posture variation, against unilateral coarse early-to-mid inspiratory crackles in bronchiectasis; clubbing is present in ILD and absent in bronchiectasis except childhood cystic bronchiectasis, with cafe-au-lait spots, erythema nodosum and Raynaud's pointing to neurofibromatosis, sarcoidosis and scleroderma.
Hypoxia drives pulmonary vasoconstriction to pulmonary HTN, the most significant prognostic factor; OSAS (ruled out by sleep study) and ILD (by CT scan) present directly with pulmonary HTN, and the CXR shows bilateral bibasal subpleural reticular/reticulo-nodular infiltrates.

UNITS.title: PFT in Initial versus Advanced ILD, HRCT as Investigation of Choice and the UIP Pattern with Its Image Captions and New Antifibrotic Drugs
UNITS.sec: PFT in Initial versus Advanced ILD, HRCT as Investigation of Choice and the UIP Pattern with Its Image Captions and New Antifibrotic Drugs
UNITS.guide:
Initially (p239) ILD is a type 1 respiratory failure with only diffusion impaired — impaired DLCO with normal FEV1 and FVC — advancing to type 3 failure with ventilation impaired, FVC falling sharply and FEV1/FVC normal or raised.
HRCT is the investigation of choice to determine pattern and prognosis: in UIP, linear shadows (intralobular septal thickening) and reticular shadows (net of linear opacities) are suggestive, while subpleural basal-predominant honeycombing (small polyhedral cystic spaces), loss of lung architecture and traction bronchiectasis complete the set bracketed specific for UIP, and nodules with ground glass opacification are absent.
The six scans are captioned honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, reticular shadows and linear shadows, and the new UIP-ILD drugs are pirfenidone (anti-TGF) and nintedanib (anti-FDGF as printed, anti-VEGF, anti-PDGFR).

UNITS.title: NSIP Pattern and Its Treatment, Drugs Causing ILD, COP/BOOP with Halo Signs, and Cysts on HRCT (LAM, LCH, LIP)
UNITS.sec: NSIP Pattern and Its Treatment, Drugs Causing ILD, COP/BOOP with Halo Signs, and Cysts on HRCT (LAM, LCH, LIP)
UNITS.guide:
NSIP (p240) shows bilateral postero-basal ground glass without parenchymal destruction, honeycombing or cystic spaces and a prognosis better than UIP; MMF is printed best, ahead of steroids and azathioprine.
Ten drugs cause NSIP-pattern ILD — amiodarone, bleomycin, busulfan, bromocriptine, nitrofurantoin, cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, anti-TNF, carmustine and mitomycin — with cyclophosphamide and methotrexate braced to hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
COP/BOOP affects elderly males (>60–70 years as printed) with Masson's buds, a pneumonia-like presentation and polymyositis/dermatomyositis associations; its restrictive type responds to steroids while the constrictive obstructive type does not, the reverse-halo sign (GGO inside consolidation) contrasts with the halo sign of invasive aspergillosis, and HRCT cysts split into LAM (young females, tuberous sclerosis/angiomyolipoma, pneumothorax and chylous effusion, everolimus), LCH (young male, upper lobe fibrosis, CD1a and Birbeck granules positive, smoking, lytic lesions, diabetes insipidus) and LIP (Sjogren's, HIV).

UNITS.title: HRCT Finding–Disease Table, Nodular Shadows and Tree-in-Bud Notes with the Mosaic Attenuation and Lower-Lobe Infiltrate Captions
UNITS.sec: HRCT Finding–Disease Table, Nodular Shadows and Tree-in-Bud Notes with the Mosaic Attenuation and Lower-Lobe Infiltrate Captions
UNITS.guide:
The HRCT table (p241) maps reticular/linear shadows, traction bronchiectasis and honeycombing to UIP; nodular shadows to LCH/LAM; ground glass to NSIP; consolidations to COP; mosaic attenuation/air trapping to HP; and cysts to LCH/LAM/LIP.
Nodular shadows are a non-specific feature caused by LAM, LCH, LIP and RB-ILD, and tree-in-bud reflects endobronchial obstruction associated with infections.
The page's scans are captioned 'HRCT findings in ILD: Nodular shadows', 'mosaic attenuation in ILD (Hypersensitivity pneumonitis)' and 'Ill-defined infiltrates in lower lobe'.

UNITS.title: Conditions with Upper-Lobe ILD, the LL Reticular Caption in IPF, and Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis (PAP)
UNITS.sec: Conditions with Upper-Lobe ILD, the LL Reticular Caption in IPF, and Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis (PAP)
UNITS.guide:
Upper-lobe ILD (p242) groups the occupational trio silicosis, berylliosis and coal-worker's pneumoconiosis, the CTD pair sarcoidosis and ankylosing spondylitis as printed, and ABPA, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, TB with upper-lobe fibrosis and LCH; the illustrating film is nonetheless captioned 'LL reticular shadows in IPF'.
PAP affects 30–50-year males as printed without a unit: congenital disease from SP-B mutation, and acquired most-common disease from anti-GM-CSF antibodies reducing surfactant clearance.
Its clinical feature is chunky gelatinous PAS-positive sputum, the X-ray shows a batwing appearance with silicosis as differential, and treatment is whole lung lavage.

UNITS.title: General Features of Asthma, the Bronchodilator Reversibility Box, GINA Features and Respiratory Symptoms with Triggers
UNITS.sec: General Features of Asthma, the Bronchodilator Reversibility Box, GINA Features and Respiratory Symptoms with Triggers
UNITS.guide:
Asthma (p243) is a pure airway disease without parenchymal involvement — hence no hypercapnia, pulmonary HTN or cor-pulmonale — chronic, eosinophilic-inflammatory and reversibly bronchoconstricting.
Reversibility is tested with 4 puffs of SABA read at 30 minutes: an FEV1 rise of 12% plus 200 ml in absolute value is reversible (Asthma), its absence irreversible (COPD).
GINA features stack chronic airway inflammation with reversible bronchoconstriction, variable expiratory airflow obstruction and the symptoms shortness of breath, chronic cough, wheeze and chest tightness, which vary in time and intensity, worsen at night and with viral infections (RSV most common), and are triggered by exercise, laughter, allergens and cold air.

UNITS.title: Etiopathogenesis: Triggers, Hygiene Hypothesis and TH2 Cytokines, Early versus Late Phases, and Eosinophil Mediators and Granules
UNITS.sec: Etiopathogenesis: Triggers, Hygiene Hypothesis and TH2 Cytokines, Early versus Late Phases, and Eosinophil Mediators and Granules
UNITS.guide:
Etiology is unknown (p244); triggers are URI, aspirin, beta blockers, sulfur dioxide, paint fumes, obesity, diet, 5q polymorphism and hyperventilation.
The hygiene hypothesis holds that increased childhood antigen exposure converts TH2 to TH1 cells for better immunity; TH2 products are IL-4 (raises IgE), IL-5 (recruits eosinophils via eotaxin) and IL-13, the early phase runs on histamine, tryptase and PGD2, and the late phase after 4–6 hours lists the basophil.
Eosinophils release newly synthesised membrane mediators (leukotriene B4, platelet activating factor, 15 HETE, prostaglandin E1/E2, thromboxane B2) and granule basic proteins MBP, ECP, EDN and EPO, with primary granules forming Charcot Leyden crystals and secondary granules holding MBP, ECP and EDN.

UNITS.title: Histopathology of Asthma with Curschmann Spirals, the Extrinsic versus Intrinsic Table and Samter's Triad
UNITS.sec: Histopathology of Asthma with Curschmann Spirals, the Extrinsic versus Intrinsic Table and Samter's Triad
UNITS.guide:
Histopathology (p245) numbers chronic airway inflammation (eosinophils, mucus plugs, mast cells, Curschmann spirals — the captioned micrograph — and Charcot Leyden crystals), bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy, submucosal glandular goblet-cell hyperplasia and patchy epithelial necrosis.
Extrinsic/atopic Asthma is allergy-associated with positive skin tests, raised IgE, family history, house dust mite (Dermatophagoids) etiology, childhood onset peaking at 3 years, equal sex ratio and a good prognosis as children grow out of it, against intrinsic Asthma with staphylococcal enterotoxins, adult onset, male predominance, severe persistent disease triggered by respiratory infections and a poor prognosis.
The closing Samters triad, as printed, triangles adult onset Asthma, aspirin sensitivity and nasal polyps.

UNITS.title: Mild versus Moderate versus Severe Asthma Table and Acute Severe Exacerbation versus Impending Respiratory Failure
UNITS.sec: Mild versus Moderate versus Severe Asthma Table and Acute Severe Exacerbation versus Impending Respiratory Failure
UNITS.guide:
Intermittent Asthma stands apart while persistent Asthma grades mild, moderate and severe (p246): day symptoms 2–6 days/week → daily → continuous, nocturnal awakenings >2 monthly → >1/week → significantly reduced activity as printed, PEFR variability <30% → >30% → >30%, and FEV1 >80% → 60–80% → <60% predicted, under headers that carry over 'Extrinsic/atopic' and 'Intrinsic' from page 245.
An acute exacerbation speaks in words, is agitated and upright with ++ accessory use, loud wheeze, tachycardia, ++ pulsus paradoxus and PEFR 25–40 as printed, whereas impending respiratory failure is speechless, confused, unable to recline, with paradoxical breathing, silent chest, relative bradycardia, absent pulsus paradoxus and PEFR below 25.
Breathlessness at rest, tachypnoea, PaO2 below 60 mmHg (saturation below 90%) and PaCO2 below 40 mmHg are merged across both columns.

UNITS.title: Management: Inhaled Corticosteroids as Mainstay, the ICS–Formoterol Step Protocol with Biologics, and Investigations
UNITS.sec: Management: Inhaled Corticosteroids as Mainstay, the ICS–Formoterol Step Protocol with Biologics, and Investigations
UNITS.guide:
ICS are the mainstay (p247), cutting hospitalisations, exacerbations and symptoms while improving lung function — early use improving future function — with beclomethasone, budesonide and fluticasone as examples, and SABA has no role in persistent Asthma.
The protocol steps from as-needed ICS–formoterol to daily low-dose ICS plus formoterol (preferred over ICS alone), then medium- and high-dose ICS plus formoterol for non-responders, then tiotropium (LAMA) with or without biologics omalizumab (anti-IgE), mepolizumab (printed anti-IL-5 receptor antagonist) and dupilumab (printed 'Dupilumab', anti-IL-4 receptor antagonist).
Methacholine challenge (airway hyperresponsiveness) and RAST (IgE levels) are braced obsolete, leaving fractional exhaled NO as the non-invasive measure of airway inflammation.

UNITS.title: Management of Asthma Exacerbation in the ER and Brittle Asthma Types One and Two
UNITS.sec: Management of Asthma Exacerbation in the ER and Brittle Asthma Types One and Two
UNITS.guide:
The ER chart (p248) confirms the diagnosis and determines status: impending respiratory failure goes straight to intubation and ventilation, while acute severe Asthma receives nasal oxygen to SpO2 above 95%, albuterol 2.5–5 mg nebulised or 4–8 MDI puffs every 20 minutes, ipratropium 500 mg as printed and hydrocortisone 100 mg.
Reassessment at one hour by PEFR and oxygen saturation escalates the non-improver through IV MgSO4 2 g over 20 minutes and non-invasive ventilation to intubation.
Brittle Asthma is childhood Asthma: Type 1 shows wide peak-flow variation despite intense medication (multi-wave trace, oral corticosteroids) and Type 2 sudden severe exacerbations in otherwise well-controlled Asthma (single peak, subcutaneous adrenaline).

UNITS.title: Eosinophilic Lung Disease Defined, Its Three Defining Features, Known versus Unknown Causes and Diseases Not Classified under ELD
UNITS.sec: Eosinophilic Lung Disease Defined, Its Three Defining Features, Known versus Unknown Causes and Diseases Not Classified under ELD
UNITS.guide:
Pulmonary eosinophilia (p249), AKA eosinophilic lung disease, increases eosinophils in airway over parenchyma with an unclear pathogenic role and peripheral counts not elevated in every type; it is defined by raised BAL eosinophils, lung tissue eosinophilia, or peripheral eosinophilia with a lung infiltrate on imaging.
Known causes (four heads) are parasite-related disease (hypersensitivity in Loeffler syndrome, lung invasion by lung fluke), drugs and toxins, tropical pulmonary eosinophilia and ABPA; unknown causes (four) are AEP, CEP, EGPA/Churg-Strauss under its three printed names, and idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome.
Bronchial Asthma, 'cytogenic organising pneumonia' as printed and Langerhans cell histiocytosis (the last two arrowed to ILD), IgG4 related connective tissue disorder and hypersensitivity pneumonitis all sit outside ELD, and BAL of at least 40% marks 'TEP' as printed and CEP.

UNITS.title: Parasite-Related ELD (Loeffler Syndrome versus Lung Fluke Invasion), Drugs and Toxins, and Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia Pathogenesis
UNITS.sec: Parasite-Related ELD (Loeffler Syndrome versus Lung Fluke Invasion), Drugs and Toxins, and Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia Pathogenesis
UNITS.guide:
Loeffler syndrome (p250) is type 1 hypersensitivity to larvae of Ascaris (most common) ahead of Ancylostoma, Necator and Strongyloides, mimicking Asthma with low grade fever, peripheral eosinophilia, raised IgE and migratory infiltrates, and resolving untreated in 1–2 weeks.
True lung invasion by Paragonimus westermani maturing from metacercaria gives eosinophilic pleural effusion, cavitating nodules, ground glass and chocolate colored sputum, is diagnosed by eggs in sputum or ELISA, and takes praziquantel as DOC; drug and toxin causes are led by NSAIDs (most common) with L-tryptophan, rapeseed oil, nitrofurantoin, minocycline and ampicillin.
TPE affects males more than females through hypersensitivity to microfilarial larvae of Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia malayi, an association suggested by microfilariae in lung, liver and lymph nodes, antifilarial titres falling after cure, and dramatic anti-filarial response.

UNITS.title: Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia: Acute-on-Chronic Symptoms, Laboratory and Radiological Findings, DEC Treatment, and the Unknown-Cause Table Histories and Presentations
UNITS.sec: Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia: Acute-on-Chronic Symptoms, Laboratory and Radiological Findings, DEC Treatment, and the Unknown-Cause Table Histories and Presentations
UNITS.guide:
TPE (p251) is acute on chronic: malaise, anorexia and weight loss with or without hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy, under paroxysmal nocturnal dry cough and wheeze that stimulate — as printed — status asthmaticus.
Investigations show eosinophils above 3000 cells/mm³, BAL eosinophilic alveolitis at or above 40%, IgE above 1000 u/ml as printed, and bilateral indefinite middle-and-lower mottling with raised bronchovascular markings, cavitation and effusion; DOC DEC 2 mg/kg thrice daily for 14–21 days / 4 weeks kills adults and microfilariae, improves symptoms in 7 days, and relapses in up to 20%.
Of the unknown causes, AEP follows restarted smoking into an ARDS-like illness over 2–3 days lasting 3–4 weeks, CEP is the subacute disease of atopic women aged 30–40, and the hypereosinophilic syndrome is a JAK2/PDGFRα myeloproliferative disorder damaging lung (40%), CNS (60%), heart and nerves.

UNITS.title: Unknown Causes of ELD: Investigations in AEP, CEP and Idiopathic Hypereosinophilic Syndrome with Their Steroid Responses
UNITS.sec: Unknown Causes of ELD: Investigations in AEP, CEP and Idiopathic Hypereosinophilic Syndrome with Their Steroid Responses
UNITS.guide:
AEP (p252) shows peripheral leukocytosis with BAL eosinophilia and raised IgE, diffuse bilateral ARDS-like infiltrates captioned 'X ray in AEP', and diffuse ground glass with consolidation captioned 'CT in AEP'.
CEP shows BAL at or above 40% eosinophils and the reverse bat wing — photographic negative of pulmonary edema — with perihilar sparing and peripheral, predominantly right, infiltrates and opacities on film and CT.
Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome requires eosinophils above 1500/µL for over 6 months with transient focal or diffuse infiltrates, and alone among the three is unresponsive to the steroid printed across AEP and CEP.

UNITS.title: Aspergillus Microbiology and Its Four Lung Manifestations, with the ABPA Colonisation-to-Bronchiectasis Pathogenesis Flowchart
UNITS.sec: Aspergillus Microbiology and Its Four Lung Manifestations, with the ABPA Colonisation-to-Bronchiectasis Pathogenesis Flowchart
UNITS.guide:
Aspergillus fumigatus, a saprophyte ahead of niger, flavus and terreus (p253), is identified by conidiophore and septate hyphae, illustrated by GMS-stained fungal balls and hyphae and a conidial head.
Its lung manifestations are ABPA, aspergilloma in a cavity mostly due to TB, chronic necrotising/cavitating disease with bronchial wall invasion and thick walled cavities typically in COPD, and angio invasive disease of neutropenic and long-term-steroid hosts with bloodstream and transplant infections.
In long-standing Asthma or CF, airway colonisation triggers a Type I > Type III complex hypersensitivity producing eosinophilia with raised IgE, eosinophilic inflammation with migratory infiltrates and wall-weakening bronchiectasis, and septate-hypha mucus plugs expectorated with eosinophils or causing atelectasis.

UNITS.title: Th2 Eosinophilic Inflammation, Central Proximal Bronchiectasis on Imaging, ABPA Clinical Features and the Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes (Rheumatology)
UNITS.sec: Th2 Eosinophilic Inflammation, Central Proximal Bronchiectasis on Imaging, ABPA Clinical Features and the Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes (Rheumatology)
UNITS.guide:
The eosinophilic inflammation is Th2 mediated via IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 (p254), and ABPA bronchiectasis differs from standard disease by being bilateral, upper lobe, central and proximal.
Images show cystic central bronchiectasis with mucoid impaction, tree-in-bud central bronchiectasis, bronchi distended with mucus, and hyperattenuated mucus plugs on CT.
Clinically, recurrent exacerbations strike chronic, steroid-dependent, refractory or acute Asthma or CF with fever and brownish thick mucosal plugs, crackles and clubbing in only 15–20%, and rarely upper lobe fibrosis — whose rheumatological causes are ankylosing spondylitis and sarcoidosis.

UNITS.title: Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes completed, ABPA Diagnostic Criteria with IgE, PFT Pattern and the Five Imaging Captions
UNITS.sec: Upper-Lobe Fibrosis Causes Completed, ABPA Diagnostic Criteria with IgE, PFT Pattern and the Five Imaging Captions
UNITS.guide:
Upper lobe fibrosis (p255) is completed by occupational silicosis, coal-worker's pneumoconiosis and berylliosis, and by the lung conditions ABPA, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and TB.
Diagnosis needs predisposing Asthma or CF, both obligatory criteria (IgE above 1000 IU/ml and a positive immediate skin test or raised Aspergillus-specific IgE), and any two supportive criteria (eosinophilia above 500/µL, precipitins or raised IgG to Aspergillus, consistent radiographic opacities), with IgE the most useful test for diagnosis and follow-up and PFT obstructive until Stage 5 fibrotic restriction.
Imaging captions define fleeting irregular transient infiltrates, tram track parallel hilar shadows, finger-in-glove mucoid impaction, trees-in-bud proximal upper-lobe bronchiectasis with wall thickening, and saccular dilatation.

UNITS.title: X-Ray Findings Unlikely or Against ABPA, the Steroid–Itraconazole–Omalizumab Treatment Flowchart and IgE Monitoring
UNITS.sec: X-Ray Findings Unlikely or Against ABPA, the Steroid–Itraconazole–Omalizumab Treatment Flowchart and IgE Monitoring
UNITS.guide:
On page 256, bronchial wall thickening and small nodules (only in tree in bud) are merely unlikely in ABPA.
Pleural involvement, lymphadenopathy, consolidation, air fluid level and perihilar involvement are fully against the diagnosis.
Treatment is 12 weeks of steroid (DOC) with airway clearance or hypertonic saline, escalating on steroid dependence or relapse to 16 weeks of itraconazole and on non-resolution to omalizumab, with IgE levels monitored periodically.

UNITS.title: Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis: Type IV over III Pathogenesis, Absent Type I Features, and the Twelve-Disease Etiology Table
UNITS.sec: Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis: Type IV over III Pathogenesis, Absent Type I Features, and the Twelve-Disease Etiology Table
UNITS.guide:
HP (p257), AKA extrinsic allergic alveolitis and usually a disease of non-smokers, follows repeated organic dust inhalation through Type IV > III hypersensitivity into lymphocytic inflammation of terminal airways, alveoli and interstitium.
Without type 1 hypersensitivity there is no eosinophilia, no raised IgE and no migratory infiltrates; infiltrates run diffuse then reticulo-nodular, with non caseating granulomas.
The etiology table ranks farmer's lung (most common, moldy hay), bagassosis (second, moldy sugarcane) and mushroom worker's lung under Thermoactinomyces vulgaris (most common antigen); compost, tobacco worker's, malt worker's and cheese washer's lung under Aspergillus clavatus; hot tub/humidifier lung under Cladosporium and MAC; bird fancier's lung under avian droppings; wood trimmer's under Rhizopus; familial HP under Bacillus subtilis from wood pulp; and chemical worker's lung to polyurethane isocyanate, with the table's blank source and antigen cells preserved.

UNITS.title: Acute, Subacute and Chronic Presentations, Complications, Non-Caseating Granuloma and Emphysema Notes, Precipitins and BAL CD8/CD4
UNITS.sec: Acute, Subacute and Chronic Presentations, Complications, Non-Caseating Granuloma and Emphysema Notes, Precipitins and BAL CD8/CD4
UNITS.guide:
Acute HP (p258) is self-resolving fever, chills and cough with raised ESR settling in 2–4 days; subacute HP is the most common tempo, with gradually progressive dyspnea, cough and fatiguability, no systemic features and upper lobe involvement; chronic HP can fibrose into ILD.
Bird fancier's lung rarely fibroses while farmer's lung turns emphysematous, and the notes list non-caseating granulomas in HP, 30% of TB as printed, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, cat scratch disease, Crohn's disease and berylliosis, and non-COPD emphysema in farmer's lung, COP and rarely coal worker's pneumoconiosis.
Serum precipitins may be positive non-specifically through the type III component, and BAL shows lymphocytosis with CD8/CD4 above 2.

UNITS.title: PFT, CXR and CT in HP with the Head Cheese Pattern, Steroid Response versus Irreversible Fibrosis, and the HP versus ABPA Difference Table
UNITS.sec: PFT, CXR and CT in HP with the Head Cheese Pattern, Steroid Response versus Irreversible Fibrosis, and the HP versus ABPA Difference Table
UNITS.guide:
Chronic HP restricts on PFT (p259), the CXR evolves from diffuse opacities to reticulonodular shadows ('CXR infiltrates in acute HP'), and CT shows centrilobular nodules, bilateral GGO and mosaic or head-cheese attenuation of varying densities, captioned as bilateral GGO with nodular opacity and mosaic tiles in HP.
Sarcoidosis mirrors the lavage with CD4/CD8 above 2, subacute HP responds to steroids, and established fibrosis is irreversible.
Against ABPA, HP shows granulomatous lymphocytic (IV > III) pathology, reticulonodular radiology, clavatus skin positivity, no eosinophilia and normal IgE, sharing only the type III IgG precipitins — ABPA instead colonises airways eosinophilically (I + III) with migratory bronchiectatic infiltrates, fumigatus positivity, eosinophilia and markedly raised IgE.

UNITS.title: Pleural Anatomy and Fluid Composition, Detection Thresholds, and Light's Criteria with the Diuretic Disadvantage
UNITS.sec: Pleural Anatomy and Fluid Composition, Detection Thresholds, and Light's Criteria with the Diuretic Disadvantage
UNITS.guide:
The mesothelial-lined pleural cavity (p260) holds 10–20 ml of fluid at negative pressure from its lymphatics and vacuum, coupling lung to chest wall; parietal pleura from somatopleuric mesoderm is pain sensitive and visceral pleura from splanchnopleural mesoderm is pain insensitive ('Developes' as printed).
Effusions need 50 mL for USG or a lateral film, 200 mL for a PA film and 300 mL clinically; normal fluid is 70% macrophages, 25% lymphocytes and 1–5% mesothelial cells, with blood-level glucose, protein 1–1.5 g/dL and LDH under half of plasma.
Light's criteria separate exudate from transudate — protein ratio at least 0.5, LDH ratio at least 0.6, or pleural LDH above two-thirds of the serum upper limit, any one making an exudate — but misclassify a third of diuresed CCF effusions, where a higher serum–pleural albumin gradient instead indicates a transudate.

UNITS.title: Transudative and Exudative Causes, Drugs Causing Effusion, TB Effusion Presentation and General Examination Signs
UNITS.sec: Transudative and Exudative Causes, Drugs Causing Effusion, TB Effusion Presentation and General Examination Signs
UNITS.guide:
Transudates (p261) number CCF with NT pro BNP in fluid, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypothyroidism, hypoalbuminemia, Budd-Chiari syndrome, chronic constrictive pericarditis, SVC obstruction as printed, peritoneal dialysis and urinothorax with low pH, high creatinine and ammoniacal odor; exudates number TB, pneumonia, malignancy, RA/SLE connective tissue disease and the left-sided pair acute pancreatitis and esophageal rupture, with pulmonary infarction and embolism causing both types and nitrofurantoin, dantrolene, methysergide and bromocriptine as drug causes.
TB effusion strikes women of 20–30 years at first exposure, its pleuritic pain easing as fluid collects, and 25–30% develop pulmonary TB over 5–10 years.
Examination shows contralateral tracheal deviation (the film: left effusion deviating the trachea right), confirmed on palpation with reduced fremitus and movement, stony dull percussion, and reduced breath sounds and vocal resonance.

UNITS.title: Parapneumonic Effusion and Empyema, Low-pH Causes, and Chylothorax versus Pseudochylothorax
UNITS.sec: Parapneumonic Effusion and Empyema, Low-pH Causes, and Chylothorax versus Pseudochylothorax
UNITS.guide:
Uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion (p262) is a sterile inflammatory leak with normal glucose, pH 7.3–7.4 and high protein/LDH, while bacterial invasion with fibrin and septation makes it complicated — glucose below 60 (printed g/L), pH below 7.2, very high LDH above 1000 and protein, Gram stain positive.
Empyema adds macroscopic pus, protein above 8 g/dL, LDH above 1000 IU/L and the CT split pleura sign against a pulmonary abscess; low fluid pH also marks rheumatoid arthritis and malignancy, the latter with poor prognosis.
Milky fluid splits into chylothorax of lymphatic rupture from trauma or lymphoma, rich in triglyceride, and pseudochylothorax of pleural thickening in TB or RA, an exudate enriched with cholesterol crystals above 250 mg/dL.

UNITS.title: Pleural Fluid Glucose, ICD Indications, Eosinophils in Pleural Fluid, and Tuberculous and Neoplastic Effusion Diagnosis
UNITS.sec: Pleural Fluid Glucose, ICD Indications, Eosinophils in Pleural Fluid, and Tuberculous and Neoplastic Effusion Diagnosis
UNITS.guide:
Fluid glucose (p263) falls below 60 mg/dL in RA, empyema, malignancy and SLE (under 20% as printed) and below 30 mg/dL in RA, while NT pro BNP in fluid means a cardiac cause.
An intercostal drain is indicated for 'calculated effusion' as printed, pH below 7.2, glucose below 60 mg/dL or pus; fluid eosinophils suggest lung fluke, asbestosis, histoplasmosis, lung infarction, effusion-causing drugs or hemo/pneumothorax, and the loculated right effusion film keeps its trachea central.
Tuberculous effusion is best proven by biopsy plus culture at 90% sensitivity over fluid CBNAAT 45–50%, culture 25–50% and stain 10–20%; neoplastic effusion is headed by mesothelioma as printed and breast metastasis, needs VAT (as printed) or CT-guided biopsy beyond 50%-sensitive cytology, and carries a poor prognosis except in lymphoma.

UNITS.title: Obstructive Breathing Events in REM, the >10-second Apnea and Hypopnea Thresholds, the Apnea Hypopnea Index Bands and the Eight Risk Factors
UNITS.sec: Obstructive Breathing Events in REM, the >10-second Apnea and Hypopnea Thresholds, the Apnea Hypopnea Index Bands and the Eight Risk Factors
UNITS.guide:
OSAS (p264) = obstructive breathing events manifesting as snoring plus excessive day time sleepiness/fatigue; the events occur in the REM phase, apnea is cessation >10 s and hypopnea is reduced breathing >10 s with amplitude falling >50% or O₂ desaturation ≥4%.
Signs of disturbed sleep are snoring, grunting and choking, and obesity hypoventilation instead gives obesity → hypoventilation → ↑PaCO₂ with day-time sleepiness usually absent.
AHI = total number of apnea and hypopnea / total sleep time: <5 normal, 5–15 mild, 15–30 moderate (the two bracketed as needing only lifestyle modification) and >30 severe needing CPAP; risk factors are obesity, central fat, male 3:1, age 50–60, postmenopausal state, alcohol, sedatives and smoking.

UNITS.title: Snoring and the Day-time Symptom List, the Suspect-OSAS Note, the Vagal Sudden-Death Chain, Complications, the Obsolete Epworth Scale and the Two Polysomnography Traces
UNITS.sec: Snoring and the Day-time Symptom List, the Suspect-OSAS Note, the Vagal Sudden-Death Chain, Complications, the Obsolete Epworth Scale and the Two Polysomnography Traces
UNITS.guide:
Snoring (p265) is the cardinal symptom, intermittent/waxing & waning with long periods of silence and worse supine; nocturia and sudden waking at night share the night list with morning headache/confusion (non-restorative sleep), dry throat, sleepiness, cognitive and mood change, sexual dysfunction and GERD.
Always suspect OSAS in unexplained pulmonary hypertension and unexplained polycythemia; sudden cardiac death runs vagal stimulation → bradycardia + hypoxia → rhythm abnormality (premature beat, asystole, VT, arrest), while stroke and CCF are bracketed 'due to HTN' beside metabolic syndrome.
The Epworth questionnaire is obsolete and polysomnography supplies the two captions — central apnea without respiratory effort against obstructive apnea with persistent respiratory effort.

UNITS.title: Severe OSAS Treated with CPAP and the Nasal and Full-face Mask Captions
UNITS.sec: Severe OSAS Treated with CPAP and the Nasal and Full-face Mask Captions
UNITS.guide:
Page 266 has a single treatment line, 'Severe OSAS : CPAP', matching the >30 AHI rule on page 264.
The only illustrations are the two delivery masks, captioned 'Nasal mask' and 'Full face mask'.
Mild and moderate disease had already been bracketed as needing only lifestyle modification, so CPAP is not a mild-disease option.

UNITS.title: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features
UNITS.sec: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features
UNITS.guide:
COPD (p267) is defined by GOLD 2023 as chronic persistent respiratory symptoms from airway/alveolar abnormalities giving progressive airflow limitation, with diagnosis by symptoms plus spirometry and a clinical/pathological split into chronic bronchitis and emphysema against large airway, small airway (<2 mm), alveoli and vasculature.
Risk factors are tobacco, cooking-fuel smoke, occupational dust, vapours, fumes, other chemicals and low birth weight in preterms.
Clinical features are persistent progressive dyspnea worse on exertion, intermittent chronic cough ± sputum, recurrent LRTI and wheeze.

UNITS.title: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease
UNITS.sec: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease
UNITS.guide:
Chronic bronchitis (p268) is the clinical disease of cough with sputum ≥3 months/year for ≥2 years, aged 40–45, with copious sputum, hypoxia → cyanosis and RV failure → edema (blue bloater), type II failure, cor pulmonale, prominent vessels and a large heart, and normal TLC and DLCO.
Emphysema is the pathological disease of dilatation distal to the terminal bronchiole with wall destruction, aged 50–75, with severe dyspnea, ↓PCO₂, cachexia, Hoover sign, hyper resonance, pursed lips (pink puffer), type I failure, hyperinflation with a small heart, and raised TLC/RV with reduced DLCO.
The functional unit is the secondary pulmonary lobule and the respiratory unit is everything distal to the terminal bronchiole; centriacinar disease is the most common, in smokers, upper lobe.

UNITS.title: Panacinar, Paraseptal and Blank Irregular Emphysema, the Protease-Antiprotease Theory, the SERPINA-1 Alleles with PiMM and PiZZ, and the Spontaneous Pneumothorax Note
UNITS.sec: Panacinar, Paraseptal and Blank Irregular Emphysema, the Protease-Antiprotease Theory, the SERPINA-1 Alleles with PiMM and PiZZ, and the Spontaneous Pneumothorax Note
UNITS.guide:
Panacinar emphysema (p269) affects the entire acinus below 45 years in non-smokers, in the basilar lower lobe, with vasculitis, liver disease and bronchiectasis from α-1 antitrypsin deficiency; paraseptal disease affects the young male smoker and gives spontaneous pneumothorax; irregular disease is printed with a blank characteristics cell.
The protease-antiprotease flow has α-1 antitrypsin (SERPINA-1 gene) inhibiting neutrophil elastase, so deficiency raises elastase activity and destroys extracellular matrix; the alleles are m, Z and Null, with PiMM normal and PiZZ the commonest disease form.
The pneumothorax note lists paraseptal change, Langerhans cell histiocytosis and 'lymphangioma hematosis'.

UNITS.title: Large Airway Disease of Chronic Bronchitis against Asthma, Small Airway Disease of Emphysema, and the Driving-Pressure Physiology of Forced Exhalation
UNITS.sec: Large Airway Disease of Chronic Bronchitis against Asthma, Small Airway Disease of Emphysema, and the Driving-Pressure Physiology of Forced Exhalation
UNITS.guide:
Chronic bronchitis (p270) is large airway disease with neutrophils in sputum, squamous metaplasia, no basement membrane thickening, ↑macrophages and CD8 cells, goblet hyperplasia and mucous hypersecretion, with only a little smooth muscle increase and so no hyperresponsive symptoms.
Against asthma the note table gives mild vs severe bronchospasm, increased mucus in both, epithelial necrosis absent vs present and squamous metaplasia present vs absent.
Emphysema is small airway disease with exudate, a thickened inflammatory wall, peribronchial fibrosis, lymphoid follicles and disrupted alveolar attachments → ↓ERP → easily inflatable alveoli → ↑TLC and ↑RV; DP = IPP + ERP, and forceful exhalation raises IPP with falling ERP so DP < AP, collapsing airways and trapping air.

UNITS.title: The Alveolar DLCO Split, the Hypoxia to Cor Pulmonale Chain, Emphysematous PFT with Reversibility Testing, the GOLD Grades and the ABE Tool
UNITS.sec: The Alveolar DLCO Split, the Hypoxia to Cor Pulmonale Chain, Emphysematous PFT with Reversibility Testing, the GOLD Grades and the ABE Tool
UNITS.guide:
DLCO is normal with parenchymal chronic bronchitis and reduced with the emphysematous alveolo-capillary unit (p271), and parenchymal damage drives chronic hypoxia (↓PaO₂, ↑PaCO₂) → pulmonary vasoconstriction → pulmonary hypertension → cor pulmonale → edema or death.
Emphysema gives FEV₁ reduced with normal FVC and a reduced ratio; a ratio <0.7 sends the patient to reversibility testing, where FEV₁ rising 200 mL or 12% means asthma and no response means COPD, and post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.7 confirms the diagnosis.
GOLD 1 is ≥80%, GOLD 2 <80%, GOLD 3 <50% and GOLD 4 <30%; ≥2 exacerbations or 1 hospitalization a year defines group E; oral glucocorticoids raise side effects and lower benefits.

UNITS.title: Inhaled Corticosteroid Indications and Contraindications, Group E against Groups A and B, LABA and LAMA Examples, and the Follow-up Treatment Flowchart
UNITS.sec: Inhaled Corticosteroid Indications and Contraindications, Group E against Groups A and B, LABA and LAMA Examples, and the Follow-up Treatment Flowchart
UNITS.guide:
Inhaled corticosteroids (p272) are indicated for blood eosinophils ≥300 cells/μL, ≥2 moderate exacerbations a year, concomitant asthma or asthma hospitalisation, and contraindicated by repeated pneumonia, eosinophils <100 cells/μL or a history of tuberculosis, with 2019 guidance to reduce steroid use; in asthma the pair is ICS + formoterol.
Initial treatment gives group E LABA + LAMA ± ICS when eosinophils are ≥300, group A LABA/LAMA and group B LABA + LAMA, with LABA as formoterol or indacaterol and LAMA as tiotropium.
Follow-up moves dyspnea from LABA/LAMA to LABA + LAMA, and exacerbations through eosinophils <300 to LAMA + LABA or >300 to LAMA + LABA + ICS, then roflumilast for chronic bronchitis with FEV₁ <50% or azithromycin for smoking/emphysema.

UNITS.title: Long Term Oxygen Therapy, LVRS and the BODE Index, the Exacerbation Definition, its Three Causes and the Printed Treatment Bundle
UNITS.sec: Long Term Oxygen Therapy, LVRS and the BODE Index, the Exacerbation Definition, its Three Causes and the Printed Treatment Bundle
UNITS.guide:
Long term oxygen therapy (p273) runs 15–16 hours a day for PaO₂ <55 mm Hg, or 55–60 mm Hg with polycythemia or right heart failure, and LVRS is contraindicated below FEV₁ 20%.
The BODE index is BMI, obstructive ventilatory defect, dyspnea and exercise capacity; an exacerbation is dyspnea and/or cough with sputum for <14 days with systemic inflammation, caused by pneumonia, pulmonary embolism or heart failure.
Treatment is nebulization, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg, salbutamol plus ipratropium, MgSO₄, non-invasive then invasive ventilation, antibiotics for 5 days, oral steroids for 7 days and ICS for recurrent exacerbations, with no role for methylxanthines.

UNITS.title: The Necrosis-Free Definition of Pneumonia, Its Five Parenchymal Sites, the Necrotising Note, the Six-Step Pathogenesis and the Three Protective Mechanisms
UNITS.sec: The Necrosis-Free Definition of Pneumonia, Its Five Parenchymal Sites, the Necrotising Note, the Six-Step Pathogenesis and the Three Protective Mechanisms
UNITS.guide:
Pneumonia (p274) is acute infection of lung parenchyma without necrosis, seated in alveoli, alveolar and vascular interstitium, respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts; necrosis or destruction of parenchyma turns it into necrotising pneumonia or lung abscess.
Pathogenesis runs defective cell-mediated immunity with viral infection → disrupted lung microbiota → alveolar epithelial barrier disruption → bacterial microaspiration → alveoli → IL-1/IL-6/TNFα for fever and IL-8 for neutrophil recruitment → capillary leak → alveolo-capillary exudate → impaired diffusion → hypoxia → dyspnea.
Protective mechanisms are the alveolar macrophage, gag reflex and mucociliary clearance, and the commonest access is the oropharynx via aspiration.

UNITS.title: HAP, VAP and CAP by Source with Their 48-hour Rules, the Lobar and Interstitial Anatomy, the Typical and Atypical Split, and the Four-Part CAP Criteria with Auscultation
UNITS.sec: HAP, VAP and CAP by Source with Their 48-hour Rules, the Lobar and Interstitial Anatomy, the Typical and Atypical Split, and the Four-Part CAP Criteria with Auscultation
UNITS.guide:
HAP occurs >48 hrs after admission and is not present at admission, VAP >48 hrs after endotracheal intubation, and CAP has no timing rule; anatomy splits into lobar and interstitial and organisms into typical and atypical (p275).
CAP requires an acute infection <1 week with cardinal features — fever, dyspnea/tachypnea/tachycardia, cough ± sputum, pleuritic chest pain and hemoptysis — plus infiltrates on CXR or CT and no other explanation.
Auscultation gives bronchial breath sounds and crackles, which the page labels subjective.

UNITS.title: The Lobular and Interstitial Organism Columns, the MRSA-in-India Note and the Seven-Row Typical against Atypical Table
UNITS.sec: The Lobular and Interstitial Organism Columns, the MRSA-in-India Note and the Seven-Row Typical against Atypical Table
UNITS.guide:
Lobar pneumonia (p276) is restricted to one lobe with Strep pneumoniae most common, Staph aureus including MRSA, Klebsiella, H. influenzae and Moraxella; the interstitial column opens with virus as most common, then mycoplasma, chlamydia and Legionella with features of both, then Aspergillus, PCP in HIV and Nocardia in the immunocompromised.
The note states MRSA is not common in India.
Typical against atypical runs extracellular vs intracellular, abrupt vs insidious, alveolar capillary exudates vs interstitial infiltrates, neutrophilic vs lymphocytic, detectable vs undetectable on culture, raised CRP/procalcitonin/leucocytosis vs none, and large lobar consolidation vs bilateral patchy interstitial change.

UNITS.title: Community Acquired MRSA, the Outpatient to ICU Organism Shift, MRSA and MDR Risk within Three Months, and Pneumococcal Morphology, Culture and Haemolysis Chart
UNITS.sec: Community Acquired MRSA, the Outpatient to ICU Organism Shift, MRSA and MDR Risk within Three Months, and Pneumococcal Morphology, Culture and Haemolysis Chart
UNITS.guide:
Community acquired MRSA (p277) is suggested by concurrent influenza or by cavity with hemoptysis and pneumatocele.
Outpatients carry strep pneumoniae, virus, mycoplasma, chlamydia and H. influenzae; non-ICU inpatients strep pneumoniae from low CMI, respiratory viruses and Legionella; ICU patients strep pneumoniae, MRSA and MDR gram-negative with high mortality — MRSA and MDR risk being CCF, hemodialysis, antibiotics and hospitalization within the last 3 months, and structural lung disease.
Pneumococci are gram-positive diplococci in chains, flame-shaped or lanceolate, alpha hemolytic with partial hemolysis on 5% blood agar, green colour and a draughtsman/carrom coin colony; complete hemolysis means streptococcus, partial means pneumoniae or viridans, and none means enterococci.

UNITS.title: Pneumococcus against Viridans, the Four Toxins, the Quellung Reaction, Type 3 Invasiveness and the CAP Risk and Poor-Prognosis Notes
UNITS.sec: Pneumococcus against Viridans, the Four Toxins, the Quellung Reaction, Type 3 Invasiveness and the CAP Risk and Poor-Prognosis Notes
UNITS.guide:
Strep pneumoniae is bile soluble, optochin susceptible and inulin fermenting while viridans is negative in all three (p278).
The toxins are capsular polysaccharide, pneumolysin (cytolytic, punching pores in the membrane), IgA1 and pneumococcal somatic C antigen, which precipitates C reactive protein; the Quellung reaction shows swelling of the capsule, and S. pneumoniae is non-invasive except type 3.
CAP risk comes from deficient CMI — diabetes, chronic kidney disease, hemodialysis, COPD, bronchiectasis, cardiac failure and age >65 — or from immunocompromise by steroids/monoclonals, transplant and neutropenia, and poor prognosis is marked by hypothermia and leukopenia with atypical organisms.

UNITS.title: Type 2 Alveolar Binding, the Lobar Pneumonia Cardinal and Abdominal Symptoms, the Older-Patient Caveat, Resolution Timing and the Four-Column Chest Film Table
UNITS.sec: Type 2 Alveolar Binding, the Lobar Pneumonia Cardinal and Abdominal Symptoms, the Older-Patient Caveat, Resolution Timing and the Four-Column Chest Film Table
UNITS.guide:
Bacteria bind type 2 alveolar epithelial cells (p279); lobar pneumonia has cardinal high spiking fever, pleuritic chest pain, cough, hemoptysis and dyspnea, with abdominal pain and hiccups or confusion added, and in the elderly confusion may be the only symptom while classical signs are absent.
Fever and leukocytosis resolve 4–5 days after antibiotics; blood shows leucocytosis, raised CRP and procalcitonin in lobar disease against normal values in interstitial bronchopneumonia.
Films separate into lobar (homogeneous consolidation, silhouette sign, air bronchogram, sharply marginated fissure, usually pneumococcus), bronchopneumonia (poorly defined heterogeneous patchy infiltrates with air bronchogram, staph giving multilobar disease with cavitation, pneumatoceles and abscess), interstitial (bilateral diffuse fine reticular opacity, PCP) and aspiration (airspace opacification, gravity dependent, after stroke or seizure).

UNITS.title: Sputum and Blood Culture Yields, BAL, and the Fourteen-Row Etiology Table from Bacteraemia to Atherosclerosis
UNITS.sec: Sputum and Blood Culture Yields, BAL, and the Fourteen-Row Etiology Table from Bacteraemia to Atherosclerosis
UNITS.guide:
Sputum microscopy and culture are done in atypical pneumonia, blood culture has poor yield and BAL is listed last (p280).
The etiology table pairs bacteremia/diabetes with S. pneumoniae; alcoholism, upper lobe involvement, bulging fissure, cavitation and golden S with Klebsiella; COPD/smoking/bronchiectasis with Pseudomonas; cystic fibrosis with Burkholderia cepacia; lung abscess with MRSA and anaerobes; cavity with MRSA; pneumatocele with Klebsiella; dementia or low consciousness with anaerobes.
Exposures pair sheep, cats and goats with Coxiella, rabbits with Francisella, bats with Histoplasma, cruise ships with Legionella, the Ohio and St. Lawrence valleys with Histoplasma capsulatum and atherosclerosis with Chlamydia pneumoniae.

UNITS.title: Extrapulmonary Mycoplasma, and the Air Bronchogram, Silhouette, Golden S and Mediastinal Shift Captions
UNITS.sec: Extrapulmonary Mycoplasma, and the Air Bronchogram, Silhouette, Golden S and Mediastinal Shift Captions
UNITS.guide:
Mycoplasma adds cold antibody autoimmune hemolysis, Steven Johnson's syndrome and Guillain Barre syndrome (p281).
An air bronchogram is air-filled space within consolidation, not specific and also seen in cardiogenic pulmonary edema; left lower lobe consolidation loses the left heart silhouette with an intact diaphragm, while right upper lobe disease loses the ascending aorta silhouette.
Golden S/reverse S and the bulging fissure sign are bracketed to Klebsiella, and collapse shifts the mediastinum to the same side.

UNITS.title: Mycoplasma against Legionella Films, the Fibrocalcific Scar, Necrotising Klebsiella and the Pneumatocele Cascade with Its 4 mm Rule
UNITS.sec: Mycoplasma against Legionella Films, the Fibrocalcific Scar, Necrotising Klebsiella and the Pneumatocele Cascade with Its 4 mm Rule
UNITS.guide:
Captions on p282 read mycoplasma/chlamydia minimal interstitial infiltrates misdiagnosed as a normal study, Legionella bilateral dense consolidation, bronchopneumonia air space opacification, and a fibrocalcific scar post TB with fibrosis; necrotising Klebsiella shows upper lobe involvement and a bulging fissure.
The pneumatocele cascade runs dense white opacity → focal suppurative abscess → necrosis and destruction → rupture into bronchus → air entry → gas within consolidation inside a wall of minimum 4 mm → air-fluid levels → cavity.
Pneumatoceles occur in IV drug abusers and after viral infection, progress to cavity, associate with MRSA and measure <4 mm, while a bulla is a cavity >4 mm.

UNITS.title: The CURB-65 Score with Its BUN and Blood Urea Equivalents, the BTS Outpatient Algorithm and the Non-Severe against Severe Inpatient Antibiotic Table
UNITS.sec: The CURB-65 Score with Its BUN and Blood Urea Equivalents, the BTS Outpatient Algorithm and the Non-Severe against Severe Inpatient Antibiotic Table
UNITS.guide:
CURB-65 (p283) is confusion, urea >7 mmol/L (BUN ≈21 mg/dL, blood urea ≈42 mg/dL), respiratory rate >30/min, blood pressure <90 systolic or <60 diastolic and age ≥65, scoring 0 for outpatient, 1–2 for inpatient and ≥3 for ICU care.
The BTS outpatient arm without resistance risk gives amoxicillin 1 g TDS plus azithromycin 500 mg day 1 then 250 mg days 2–5 or clarithromycin 500 mg BD, or amoxicillin plus doxycycline; with resistance risk it gives amoxyclav 625 mg TDS plus azithromycin or doxycycline, cephalosporins being an alternative.
Inpatients take a β-lactam (ampicillin + sulbactam 1.5 g QID IV or piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g QID IV) plus a macrolide 500 mg BD, second line levofloxacin 750 mg/day, and severe ICU disease a β-lactam plus levofloxacin without fluoroquinolone monotherapy.

UNITS.title: MRSA Cover and the 48–72-hour Response Rule, Empyema, Lung Abscess and ARDS, the Empyema against Abscess Table and the Definition of a Lung Cavity
UNITS.sec: MRSA Cover and the 48–72-hour Response Rule, Empyema, Lung Abscess and ARDS, the Empyema against Abscess Table and the Definition of a Lung Cavity
UNITS.guide:
MRSA cover follows isolation, recent hospitalization or prior MRSA, and response is judged at 48–72 hours, with no response meaning a complication and CT (p284).
Empyema is macroscopic pus with a complicated parapneumonic effusion, diagnosed by the CT split pleura sign with thickened pleura and ↑protein, ↑LDH, ↓glucose and treated by intercostal drainage; lung abscess is destruction with cavity and takes vancomycin + meropenem + clindamycin for 6–8 weeks; ARDS with MDR and metastatic infection complete the list.
Empyema against abscess is smooth vs irregular wall, obtuse vs acute angle, lentiform vs rounded on X-ray and positive vs negative split pleura sign, a simple synpneumonic effusion being sterile; a cavity is a gas-filled space within consolidation, mass or nodule from expectorated necrotic debris, seen in staphylococcus and klebsiella.

UNITS.title: The Bulla, Cyst and Thin-Walled Cavity Captions, the Four Thick-Walled Causes and the Seven-Letter CAVITY Mnemonic
UNITS.sec: The Bulla, Cyst and Thin-Walled Cavity Captions, the Four Thick-Walled Causes and the Seven-Letter CAVITY Mnemonic
UNITS.guide:
The caption strip on p285 shows a bulla, a cyst and a thin walled cavity, then thick walled cavities.
Thick walled cavities are abscess, necrotising SCC, Wegener's granulomatosis and blastomycosis.
The CAVITY mnemonic gives C cancer with SCC most common, A aspergillosis/autoimmune (Wegener's)/abscess, V vascular emboli, I infection with Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella, T TB, Y young patients with congenital abnormality, and fungus as Cryptococcus, Aspergillus and Coccidioidomycosis.

UNITS.title: Mycoplasma as the Smallest Free-Living Organism, Its Wall-Free Sterol Membrane, the Ten Percent Pneumonia Picture, Seven Extrapulmonary Manifestations, Radiology, PPLO Culture and Azithromycin
UNITS.sec: Mycoplasma as the Smallest Free-Living Organism, Its Wall-Free Sterol Membrane, the Ten Percent Pneumonia Picture, Seven Extrapulmonary Manifestations, Radiology, PPLO Culture and Azithromycin
UNITS.guide:
Mycoplasma (p286) is the smallest free-living replicating organism, with no cell wall so β-lactams fail, sterols present and no flagella; it causes tracheobronchitis/pharyngitis and pneumonia in 10%, spread by droplets, with low grade fever, cough, scanty sputum and few signs.
Extrapulmonary disease covers cold antibody autoimmune hemolysis (IgM), SJS/erythema multiforme, GBS, encephalitis, bullous myringitis, myocarditis/pericarditis and arthralgia with adenopathy; imaging gives reticulonodular or patchy consolidation from the hilum, interstitial and ground glass change and tree-in-bud.
PCR of respiratory secretions and serology are rapid and most sensitive, culture is on PPLO agar by Diene's method with fried egg colonies, and azithromycin is DOC with doxycycline and respiratory quinolones as alternatives; hydrogen peroxide and superoxide injure the epithelium but prognosis is good.

UNITS.title: Chlamydia as an Obligate Intracellular Peptidoglycan-Free Bacterium with Its Elementary Body, Walking Pneumonia, HEp-2 Isolation and Micro-Immunofluorescence, plus the Legionella Phenotype
UNITS.sec: Chlamydia as an Obligate Intracellular Peptidoglycan-Free Bacterium with Its Elementary Body, Walking Pneumonia, HEp-2 Isolation and Micro-Immunofluorescence, plus the Legionella Phenotype
UNITS.guide:
Chlamydia (p287) is an obligate intracellular bacterium without peptidoglycan, transmitted human to human, its elementary body being extracellular, metabolically inactive and infective.
It gives a prolonged asymptomatic upper respiratory illness, atypical pneumonia in 10% and walking pneumonia indistinguishable from mycoplasma, with low grade fever, minimal sputum and dry cough, atherosclerosis being the extrapulmonary link; isolation is by HEp-2 cells and micro-immunofluorescence serology is the gold standard, with no lobar consolidation, resistance to sulfonamide and treatment by azithromycin or doxycycline.
Legionella is gram negative and predominantly intracellular, a strict aerobe, motile, partially acid fast, living in aquatic bodies and biofilms, with type 1 serovar most pathogenic and a type 4 secretion system.

UNITS.title: Legionella Microaspiration, BCYE Medium, the Sterile Gram Stain, Its Four Risk Factors, Typical against Atypical Disease, Pontiac against Legionnaires and DFAT Diagnosis
UNITS.sec: Legionella Microaspiration, BCYE Medium, the Sterile Gram Stain, Its Four Risk Factors, Typical against Atypical Disease, Pontiac against Legionnaires and DFAT Diagnosis
UNITS.guide:
Legionella spreads by microaspiration more than aerosolization and grows on BCYE (buffered charcoal yeast extract) medium; Gram stain shows pus cells and neutrophils but no organisms (p288).
Risk factors are poor CMI, smoking, immunosuppression and hairy cell leukemia; typical disease is rapidly progressive with high grade fever, bilateral dense consolidation and leucocytosis, while atypical disease gives non-productive cough, diarrhea, hyponatremia, elevated LFT, thrombocytopenia and hematuria; mild disease is Pontiac fever and severe is Legionnaires disease.
DFAT and urinary antigen both have high specificity, sputum/aspiration testing is not done, and treatment is azithromycin (DOC) with rifampicin or a quinolone.

UNITS.title: Necrotising Pneumonia and Aspiration as the Two Causes of Lung Abscess, the Five-Step Pathogenesis, the Posterior Right Upper Lobe Site and the Clinical Picture
UNITS.sec: Necrotising Pneumonia and Aspiration as the Two Causes of Lung Abscess, the Five-Step Pathogenesis, the Posterior Right Upper Lobe Site and the Clinical Picture
UNITS.guide:
Lung abscess (p289) has two causes: necrotising pneumonia complicating pneumonia from staphylococcus or klebsiella, and aspiration pneumonia with chronic symptoms, anaerobes and a posterior upper lobe predilection over the superior lower lobe segment.
Pathogenesis runs consolidation + suppuration + necrosis → rupture → drainage into the bronchus → purulent expectoration → abscess with an air fluid level, the commonest site being the posterior segment of the right upper lobe.
Clinically fever and chills ease when the abscess drains, with cough and purulent sputum, tachypnea, impaired percussion, cavity-related bronchial breathing and clubbing in chronic disease; diagnosis is poor response over 2–3 days with purulent sputum and toxicity plus an air fluid level on film or CT.

UNITS.title: The Chest Film and CT Captions, Metastatic Infection to AA Amyloidosis, the Tuberculosis and Malignancy Differentials and the Vancomycin-Piperacillin-Tazobactam-Clindamycin Regimen
UNITS.sec: The Chest Film and CT Captions, Metastatic Infection to AA Amyloidosis, the Tuberculosis and Malignancy Differentials and the Vancomycin-Piperacillin-Tazobactam-Clindamycin Regimen
UNITS.guide:
Captions on p290 run ground glass opacity, pleural effusion, thick walled cavity, consolidation and air fluid levels.
Complications are metastatic infection, pyopneumothorax, bronchopleural fistula and AA (secondary) amyloidosis, the last seen in TB, bronchiectasis and lung abscess; the differential is TB, malignancy, Nocardia and Actinomycetes with no bracketed clue.
Treatment is antibiotics with postural drainage — vancomycin, piperacillin–tazobactam and clindamycin for anaerobes — for 6–8 weeks, fever resolving in 7–10 days and surgery reserved for unresponsive MDR disease.

UNITS.title: The Three Severely Immunocompromised States, the Seven Organisms, and the Renal and Bone Marrow Transplant Infection Timelines with Onset-Based Infection
UNITS.sec: The Three Severely Immunocompromised States, the Seven Organisms, and the Renal and Bone Marrow Transplant Infection Timelines with Onset-Based Infection
UNITS.guide:
The severely immunocompromised (p291) are neutropenic from any cause, transplant recipients of bone marrow or kidney, and those on >30 mg steroid for 3–4 weeks; organisms are mainly MDR gram-negative with Aspergillus, Nocardia and PCP predominant in the lung, plus toxoplasma, CMV and candida.
Post renal transplant: <1 month wound, catheter, drain site, UTI and herpes; 1–6 months (m/c) CMV, PCP, Legionella, Listeria and hepatitis B/C; >6 months drug-induced neutropenia from mycophenolate or calcineurin inhibitors giving BK polyoma, Nocardia and Aspergillus.
Post bone marrow transplant: <1 month gram-negative bacteria and Aspergillus, then 1–4 months CMV, PCP and Aspergillus; acute onset at 24–48 hours means bacteria, subacute means virus, TB or fungi, with CMV ocular/organomegaly, Nocardia neurological/nodules and Pseudomonas ecthyma gangrenosum.

UNITS.title: Invasive Aspergillosis from Conidia to Hyphae, Neutropenia as the Chief Risk, the Halo and Air Crescent Signs, the Reverse Halo and Monad Notes and the Fever-Hemoptysis-Pleuritic Triad
UNITS.sec: Invasive Aspergillosis from Conidia to Hyphae, Neutropenia as the Chief Risk, the Halo and Air Crescent Signs, the Reverse Halo and Monad Notes and the Fever-Hemoptysis-Pleuritic Triad
UNITS.guide:
Invasive aspergillosis (p292) starts with conidia aerosolised from the mold, reaching tissue and forming invasive hyphae, with neutropenia the most important risk.
The CT halo sign is consolidation surrounded by ground glass and suggests invasion, while the air crescent sign means recovery; the reverse halo is ground glass surrounded by consolidation in cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, and the monad sign is an air crescent around a fungal ball that moves with posture in an old TB aspergilloma.
The classical triad is fever, hemoptysis and pleuritic pain, with sinus infection, CNS infection carrying 100% mortality and angioinvasion causing hemorrhagic infarction.

UNITS.title: Aspergillus Diagnosis by BAL, VATS and Galactomannan, Beta-D-Glucan Cross-Reactivity, Voriconazole against Liposomal Amphotericin, the Mucormycosis Contrast and the Opening of Pneumocystis
UNITS.sec: Aspergillus Diagnosis by BAL, VATS and Galactomannan, Beta-D-Glucan Cross-Reactivity, Voriconazole against Liposomal Amphotericin, the Mucormycosis Contrast and the Opening of Pneumocystis
UNITS.guide:
Diagnosis of aspergillosis (p293) rests on BAL showing dichotomous branching septate hyphae, VATS biopsy of a nodule, the specific galactomannan test and β-D-glucan, which is positive in mucor, cryptococcus, candida, aspergillosis and pneumocystis.
Voriconazole is DOC with liposomal amphotericin B as the alternative, and mucormycosis is separated by aseptate right-angle hyphae, negative galactomannan, no voriconazole response and treatment with liposomal amphotericin B plus posaconazole and surgical debridement.
Pneumocystis is a fungal infection of HIV with CD4 <200/μL and the immunocompromised, giving dyspnea and hypoxia then fever and cough after 2–3 days.

UNITS.title: Pneumocystis Diagnosis by GMS Cyst Stain, Fluorescein Antibody and PCR, Its Four HIV Records, the Cotrimoxazole Ladder, Steroids for Hypoxia and Three Prophylactic Drugs
UNITS.sec: Pneumocystis Diagnosis by GMS Cyst Stain, Fluorescein Antibody and PCR, Its Four HIV Records, the Cotrimoxazole Ladder, Steroids for Hypoxia and Three Prophylactic Drugs
UNITS.guide:
Pneumocystis diagnosis (p294) uses a positive but non-specific 1,3 β-D-glucan, raised LDH, BAL microscopy as the best mode with GMS cyst staining, fluorescein conjugated monoclonal antibody, PCR as gold standard and perihilar infiltrates that may cavitate, pneumothorax or pneumatocele.
It is the most common fungal pneumonia, opportunistic infection, cause of pneumonia and cause of pleural effusion in HIV; treatment is oral cotrimoxazole for mild-moderate disease, IV cotrimoxazole for severe, and second line clindamycin + primaquine or IV pentamidine.
Steroids are added for PaO₂ <70 mm Hg or a raised arterio-alveolar gradient, and prophylaxis is cotrimoxazole, dapsone or atovaquone.

UNITS.title: Nocardia asteroides as an Aerobic Acid-Fast Filamentous Organism, Its Mandatory Host Defect, Brain and Lung Disease, the Crooked Beaded Filaments and the Sulfonamide Regimen
UNITS.sec: Nocardia asteroides as an Aerobic Acid-Fast Filamentous Organism, Its Mandatory Host Defect, Brain and Lung Disease, the Crooked Beaded Filaments and the Sulfonamide Regimen
UNITS.guide:
Nocardia asteroides (p295) is a gram positive filamentous 'fungus' that is aerobic, acid fast and filamented, unlike non-acid-fast non-aerobic actinomycetes and acid-fast non-filamentous rhodococci.
A host defence defect is mandatory, entry is by inhalation or a skin defect, and disease is a subacute brain abscess or cavitating lung nodules with nocardial mycetoma.
Sputum or pus shows acid-fast crooked branching beaded filaments and culture is avoided because of slow growth; treatment is sulfonamide as DOC with minocycline and parenteral amikacin.

UNITS.title: Heart Sounds as Discrete Vibrations, Intensity in Decibels against Frequency in Hertz with Their Inverse Relation, the Six-Row High against Low Frequency Table and the Mixed ESM of Aortic Stenosis
UNITS.sec: Heart Sounds as Discrete Vibrations, Intensity in Decibels against Frequency in Hertz with Their Inverse Relation, the Six-Row High against Low Frequency Table and the Mixed ESM of Aortic Stenosis
UNITS.guide:
Heart sounds (p296) are brief, discrete auditory vibrations; intensity is measured in decibels and frequency in hertz, with frequency ∝ 1/amplitude.
High frequency sounds are soft, musical or blowing, with a wide chamber pressure difference, a wider area, no thrill and the diaphragm; low frequency sounds are rough, rumbling or thud-like, with a low pressure difference, a localised area, a thrill and the bell, whose exceptions are S3, S4, tumour plop, MS, TS and Austin Flint.
The mixed frequency sound is the ejection systolic murmur of AS — harsh at the 2nd right ICS, with low pitch radiating to the carotid and high pitch to the apex (Gallavardin).

UNITS.title: The 0.8-Second Cycle, the 0.3-Second Systolic and 0.5-Second Diastolic Phase Lists, the 70 to 30 Per Cent Filling Split, and the S1 Valve Apparatus with Annular Contraction and Coaptation
UNITS.sec: The 0.8-Second Cycle, the 0.3-Second Systolic and 0.5-Second Diastolic Phase Lists, the 70 to 30 Per Cent Filling Split, and the S1 Valve Apparatus with Annular Contraction and Coaptation
UNITS.guide:
The cardiac cycle (p297) lasts 0.8 s, atrial systole 0.1 s against atrial diastole 0.7 s; systole 0.3 s holds isovolumetric contraction, rapid ejection and reduced ejection, and diastole 0.5 s holds protodiastole, isovolumetric relaxation, rapid filling, reduced filling and atrial systole.
During reduced filling the AV valves are open and 70% of filling is passive, atrial systole adds 30%, then ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, the AV valves close and S1 is born into isovolumetric contraction.
The valve apparatus is leaflet, fibrous annulus and commissures; annular contraction → coaptation → sudden tensing gives S1, whose M1 and T1 lie <30 ms apart and are not appreciated separately.

UNITS.title: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
UNITS.sec: The Six Determinants of S1 Intensity from Leaflet Integrity and Diastolic Position through Contraction Velocity, Closure Timing and dP/dt to Chest Wall Transmission
UNITS.guide:
Six factors alter S1 intensity (p298): leaflet integrity (incompetent MR, perforated endocarditis and calcific MS all soften it); diastolic leaflet position (stenosis keeps the valve wide apart so it closes from a distance and is loud, as in MS); contraction velocity (bradycardia with a long PR softens, tachycardia with a short PR loudens).
Closure timing decides too — delayed closure is loud in MS while premature closure is soft in AR — and dP/dt behaves the same way, a leaky valve losing dP/dt and softening as in MR or myocarditis while exercise and high output louden.
Chest-wall transmission closes the list: obesity, emphysema and pericardial effusion soften all auscultatory events, whereas a thin chest wall loudens them.

UNITS.title: S1 in Aortic Stenosis, Regurgitation, Mitral Stenosis and Mitral Regurgitation, Loud T1 Causes, the Aortic Ejection Click, and Varying, Intermittent and Wide Split S1
UNITS.sec: S1 in Aortic Stenosis, Regurgitation, Mitral Stenosis and Mitral Regurgitation, Loud T1 Causes, the Aortic Ejection Click, and Varying, Intermittent and Wide Split S1
UNITS.guide:
S1 is normal in AS, soft in AR from premature closure, loud and unrelated to severity in MS from wide-apart position, increased velocity and delayed closure, and soft and unrelated to severity in MR from loss of integrity and loss of dP/dt (p299).
Loud T1 comes from TS, ASD and total anomalous pulmonary venous connection through increased tricuspid flow; the loud sound of AS is an aortic ejection click from a bicuspid valve that can be mistaken for S1; rheumatic MR with a preserved leaflet gives a soft S1 from myocarditis, MS with MR depends on the predominant lesion, and TR after pulmonary hypertension in moderate MS softens S1.
Variable S1 varies in atrial fibrillation and flutter but is intermittent as cannon S1 in complete heart block and VT with AV dissociation; wide split S1 separates early M1 (LV ectopic or pacing, Ebstein with a sail sound) from late T1 (RBBB, TS, RA myxoma).

UNITS.title: Reverse Split S1, the S1 to S2 Sequence through Crossover Pressure, and the Hangout Interval with Its 30 and 80 Millisecond Aortic and Pulmonary Values
UNITS.sec: Reverse Split S1, the S1 to S2 Sequence through Crossover Pressure, and the Hangout Interval with Its 30 and 80 Millisecond Aortic and Pulmonary Values
UNITS.guide:
Reverse split of S1 puts T1 before M1, from early T1 in right sided pacing or ectopic and from delayed M1 in LBBB or, mechanically, MS and LA myxoma (p300).
After S1 the aortic and pulmonary valves open with ejection clicks, then rapid and reduced ejection raise aortic and pulmonary pressures to the crossover point, where aortic pressure exceeds CVP and pulmonary pressure exceeds RVP.
The hangout interval runs from crossover pressure to valve closure and depends on pressure beyond the valve and vessel distensibility, printing 30 ms for the aorta and 80 ms for the pulmonary artery; the A2–P2 gap is 50 ms and appreciable, exceeding 50 ms in inspiration from increased venous return.

UNITS.title: S2 as Aortic and Pulmonary Closure at 120–150 Hz, the Four Determinants of A2 and P2, Their Behaviour in Valve Disease, the Four-Column Table and the Six Causes of a Single S2
UNITS.sec: S2 as Aortic and Pulmonary Closure at 120–150 Hz, the Four Determinants of A2 and P2, Their Behaviour in Valve Disease, the Four-Column Table and the Six Causes of a Single S2
UNITS.guide:
S2 is aortic and pulmonary closure at a high frequency of 120–150 Hz, with A2 louder because aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary pressure (p301).
A2 and P2 are governed by pressure beyond the valve (systemic HTN loudens A2, pulmonary HTN loudens P2), flow across the valve (hyperkinetic states louden both), valve mobility and vessel dilatation beyond the valve.
AS from a bicuspid valve is loud but degenerative AS is soft, AR is soft from valve pathology and loud (tambour S2) from root disease such as syphilis, moderate MS loudens P2 and with RVF widens the split, and MR loudens P2 only with pulmonary hypertension; single S2 arises in severe PAH (single loud P2), aging, semilunar atresia, severe AS or PS and truncus arteriosus.

UNITS.title: Wide Split S2 above 50 ms with Its Variable and Fixed Arms, and the Paradoxical Split with Early P2 and Delayed A2 Causes
UNITS.sec: Wide Split S2 above 50 ms with Its Variable and Fixed Arms, and the Paradoxical Split with Early P2 and Delayed A2 Causes
UNITS.guide:
A wide split of S2 exceeds 50 ms and is heard even in expiration (p302).
Its variable causes are early A2 (LV pacing or ectopic electrically, MR mechanically) and late P2 (RBBB, pulmonary hypertension with RVF as in MS, PS, VSD with a left-to-right shunt, cardiac tamponade).
Fixed splitting is any wide variable split with significant RV failure, or ASD where RV and LV filling change equally with respiration; the reverse or paradoxical split is heard in expiration with P2 before A2, from early P2 (right sided pacing/ectopic, WPW type B, TR) or delayed A2 (LBBB, AS, AR, HCM).

UNITS.title: The Diastolic Continuation from Protodiastole to Atrial Systole, the O-P-Time-S3-S4 Sequence, Early, Mid and Late Diastolic Position, and S3 with Its Three Mechanisms and Four Valve Lesions
UNITS.sec: The Diastolic Continuation from Protodiastole to Atrial Systole, the O-P-Time-S3-S4 Sequence, Early, Mid and Late Diastolic Position, and S3 with Its Three Mechanisms and Four Valve Lesions
UNITS.guide:
The cycle continues (p303) from protodiastole through closed semilunar valves, isovolumetric relaxation, opening AV valves, rapid and reduced filling (70% passive) to atrial systole (30% active).
Diastolic sounds run opening snap, pericardial knock and tumour plop as early diastolic, S3 mid diastolic and S4 late diastolic, with S3, S4 and tumour plop the low pitched ones.
S3 is the ventricular or protodiastolic gallop of rapid filling, requiring a non-stenosed AV valve and so absent in MS and TS; its mechanisms are physiological hypercompliant filling in the young, increased end systolic volume in LV/RV failure, and reduced filling of a hypertrophic non-compliant ventricle in LVH, RVH and RCMP, with pathological S3 earlier than physiological; it is heard in MR and severe AS but not MS or AR.

UNITS.title: S3 Features with Left Lateral Position, Leg Raising and the Heart-Failure Caveat, the Pericardial Knock of Constrictive Pericarditis, and S4 with Its Four Prerequisites and Its Valve-Disease Table
UNITS.sec: S3 Features with Left Lateral Position, Leg Raising and the Heart-Failure Caveat, the Pericardial Knock of Constrictive Pericarditis, and S4 with Its Four Prerequisites and Its Valve-Disease Table
UNITS.guide:
S3 is heard in the left lateral position at the apex, does not vary with respiration, disappears upright when physiological, and appears with passive leg raising; heart failure without S3 means MS, TS or pericardial tamponade (p304).
The pericardial knock of chronic constrictive pericarditis is high pitched, louder with inspiration and early diastolic, increasing with cardiac output and disappearing after pericardiectomy.
S4 is the atrial or presystolic gallop of atrial systole correlating with the JVP A-wave, needing healthy atria in sinus rhythm contracting vigorously across a non-stenosed AV valve into a non-dilated ± hypertrophic non-compliant ventricle; its mechanism is a rise in LV end-diastolic fibre length, and it is not seen in MS, MR or AR but is heard in AS, and in acute MR and AR; the table gives AS +/+, AR in failure/–, MS –/– and MR +/–.

UNITS.title: The Three S4 Settings, the Opening Snap in Mitral Stenosis with Its S2-OS Interval Ladder and Auscultation Rules, and the Low Pitched Tumour Plop of Atrial Myxoma
UNITS.sec: The Three S4 Settings, the Opening Snap in Mitral Stenosis with Its S2-OS Interval Ladder and Auscultation Rules, and the Low Pitched Tumour Plop of Atrial Myxoma
UNITS.guide:
S4 also appears with concentric LVH from systemic HTN or HCM, concentric RVH from PS, PAH or RCM, and RV ischaemia from coronary disease (p305).
The opening snap is AV valve opening representing isovolumetric relaxation, heard with the bell at the apex in expiration, requiring mobile leaflets, good LV function and organic MS as the predominant lesion; raised LAP with thickened leaflets causes sudden doming, so OS α LAP and S2–OS α 1/LAP, printing S2–OS >120 mmHg with LAP <5 mmHg in mild disease and 40–60 mmHg with LAP >15 mmHg in severe disease.
It is heard standing midway between apex and lower left sternal border and does not vary with respiration; tumour plop is low pitched, from atrial myxoma, and early diastolic.

UNITS.title: Systolic Added Sounds as Clicks, the Valvular and Vascular Ejection Clicks with Their S2 and S1 Rules, and the Non-Ejection Click of Mitral Valve Prolapse with Dynamic Auscultation
UNITS.sec: Systolic Added Sounds as Clicks, the Valvular and Vascular Ejection Clicks with Their S2 and S1 Rules, and the Non-Ejection Click of Mitral Valve Prolapse with Dynamic Auscultation
UNITS.guide:
Systolic added sounds are clicks, split into ejection clicks (valvular and vascular) and non-ejection clicks (p306).
Ejection clicks come from semilunar valve opening: valvular clicks from a doming valve halted abruptly in AS, PS and bicuspid aortic valve, and vascular clicks from sudden distension beyond the valve in aneurysm; root pathology loudens S2 while valvular pathology softens it, fever with tachycardia loudens S1.
Ejection clicks disappear in severe calcific stenosis, are best heard in the aortic area, are often confused with a loud S1, do not vary with respiration, and a pulmonary click is better heard in expiration; non-ejection clicks belong to mitral valve prolapse, where standing or Valsalva lowers preload, shrinks the cavity, reduces chordal stretch, increases prolapse and moves the click toward S1.

UNITS.title: Aortic Valve Anatomy, Cusp Number and Function, the Surface Area and Normal Systolic Physiology
UNITS.sec: Aortic Valve Anatomy, Cusp Number and Function, the Surface Area and Normal Systolic Physiology
UNITS.guide:
The aortic valve has three equal cusps and three commissures around one fibrous annulus; its surface area is 3–4 cm² (p307).
Cusps are crescent shaped, open fully for unimpeded flow and close tightly against regurgitation; congenital counts are four (quadricuspid), two (BAV) or one (unicuspid), and fewer cusps favour stenosis over regurgitation, with BAV stenosis 75% against regurgitation 20–25%.
Normal systole runs IVC → aortic and pulmonary valves open → rapid then reduced ejection; LVP and aortic pressure are each 120 mmHg, so a completely opening valve produces no gradient.

UNITS.title: The Aortic-Sclerosis-to-Stenosis Pathogenesis Chain, Rheumatic Valve Combinations, Demographic Notes, Specimen Captions and Etiology
UNITS.sec: The Aortic-Sclerosis-to-Stenosis Pathogenesis Chain, Rheumatic Valve Combinations, Demographic Notes, Specimen Captions and Etiology
UNITS.guide:
A bicuspid or tricuspid valve plus a pathological process gives aortic sclerosis; inflammation and lipoprotein deposition lead into the atherosclerotic process of RAAS activation, myofibroblast-to-osteoblast change and calcium hydroxyapatite deposition (p308).
Adding a transvalvular gradient turns sclerosis into aortic stenosis and symptoms; rheumatic combinations are MS + MR (m/c), MS + AR (2nd m/c) and AR + AS, while 30% of elderly have non-severe sclerosis, 80% of patients are male and valve replacement requires coronary angiography.
The four captions cover BAV calcific stenosis, L/R cusp fusion with a calcified noncoronary cusp, TAV stenosis with fused commissures and the 1 cm scale; degenerative calcification is the worldwide AS cause, BAV in the young, aortic sclerosis the commonest valvular pathology and MR the commonest valvular heart disease, with rheumatic AS less common.

UNITS.title: Bicuspid Aortic Valve Genetics and Aortopathy, Location-Based Types, Severity-Based Types and the 40/4/1 Rule
UNITS.sec: Bicuspid Aortic Valve Genetics and Aortopathy, Location-Based Types, Severity-Based Types and the 40/4/1 Rule
UNITS.guide:
BAV is the commonest congenital valve defect, linked to NOTCH-1 and eNOS defects, M > F, autosomal dominant inheritance and aortopathies (aneurysm and dissection) requiring CT aortogram before valve replacement (p309).
Location types are valvular AS, subvalvular AS with HCM and supravalvular AS with Williams syndrome (increased calcium, growth failure and mental retardation); mild/moderate disease stays asymptomatic through concentric LVH that preserves cardiac output at the expense of cavity size.
Severe AS has symptoms, a 1% sudden-death risk and needs valve replacement, with the 40/4/1 rule of mean gradient >40 mmHg, peak velocity >4 m/s and area <1 cm²; very severe AS gives LV failure and a bad prognosis, and the gradient exists because the stenotic valve does not open completely.

UNITS.title: The ASD 5/3/1 Symptom Clock, Angina, Syncope and Dyspnea Mechanisms, Association Notes, Pulse, Blood Pressure, JVP and Apex
UNITS.sec: The ASD 5/3/1 Symptom Clock, Angina, Syncope and Dyspnea Mechanisms, Association Notes, Pulse, Blood Pressure, JVP and Apex
UNITS.guide:
The ASD symptom clock prints angina 5 years, syncope 3 years and dyspnea 1 year for valve replacement (p310). Angina comes from increased LV mass/oxygen demand, reduced coronary flow with atherosclerosis and reduced capillary density relative to wall thickness; syncope is a fixed cardiac output that fails to rise with activity.
Dyspnea follows concentric LVH → smaller cavity → raised LVEDP/LAP/PCWP → pulmonary exudation. AF is called fatal because the atria contribute 40% of CO when LVEDP is high; systemic HTN masks severity and needs tight control; LV failure marks very severe AS and complete gradient loss is low-flow low-gradient AS; Heyde syndrome and acquired von Willebrand disease are added.
Severe AS has pulsus tardus (slow rise but reaches amplitude) and very severe AS pulsus parvus et tardus (does not reach amplitude); LVF narrows pulse pressure, JVP remains normal and the LVH apex is displaced outward and heaving.

UNITS.title: Heart Sounds and the Mixed-Frequency Murmur with Its Carotid and Apical Components, ECG, X-Ray and ECHO
UNITS.sec: Heart Sounds and the Mixed-Frequency Murmur with Its Carotid and Apical Components, ECG, X-Ray and ECHO
UNITS.guide:
Heart sounds on p311 include an ejection click in BAV, soft S2 in degenerative disease, loud S2 in BAV and reverse-split S2 (late A2) in severe AS, with S3 from LVH/LVF and S4 present.
The murmur is a harsh mixed-frequency ejection systolic murmur with late systolic accentuation that separates it from an innocent ESM; its low-pitch component radiates to the carotid and its high-pitch component to the apex (Gallavardin phenomenon), and it is best heard in the aortic area.
Investigations show an LV strain pattern with Sokolov–Lyon >35 mm, not much ST depression and asymmetric T inversion on ECG, a dilated aortic arch on X-ray, and ECHO as the definitive test that also grades severity.

UNITS.title: Aortic Valve Replacement and Its Indications, Dobutamine Stress Testing, Disadvantages, TAVR and the Two Transcatheter Valves
UNITS.sec: Aortic Valve Replacement and Its Indications, Dobutamine Stress Testing, Disadvantages, TAVR and the Two Transcatheter Valves
UNITS.guide:
AVR commonly uses a bioprosthetic valve because it causes fewer complications and avoids continued anticoagulation (p312). Indications are severe symptomatic AS; severe asymptomatic AS with EF <50%, gradient >60 mmHg or peak flow ≥5 m/s; rapid progression on yearly echo; another planned procedure; or symptoms on a dobutamine stress test that separates very severe AS from LVF with incidental AS.
